exp.8:28:
This verse tells us that while Jesus was praying on the mountain, the appearance of his face changed and his clothing became white and dazzling. "Appearance" is the way something looks, and "dazzling" means it gave off light.

Luke is the one telling the story. Eight days earlier, Jesus had spoken about the kingdom of God, and now he takes Peter, John and James up to pray. They see a glimpse of Jesus' glory. Soon Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him about his departure, that is, his death in Jerusalem. Many believe this scene confirms who Jesus is, although it is explained in several ways.

For today: prayer draws us close to Jesus and helps us see him as he truly is. Take a few minutes to pray in silence, without hurry, and ask him to show you his greatness and his love.
exp.23:6:
This verse recalls what Jesus had said before he died. The phrase "must be" means "it was necessary" or "it had to happen." The words "delivered into the hands of sinful men" mean that he would be betrayed and handed over to the power of wicked people. After that he would be nailed to a cross, and on the third day he would rise to life again.

The speakers are two angels, who appear in the form of men wearing shining clothes. They speak to the women who went to the tomb and found it empty. The women were afraid and did not understand. The angels ask them to remember the words Jesus had spoken to them in Galilee. What happened was not an accident, for he had already announced it.

For today: when life seems meaningless or hurts deeply, remember that God may be at work even in what looks like defeat. Keep his promises in your heart and trust them, as these women did.
exp.20:25:
Luke 21:26 says that men's hearts will fail them from fear and from anticipation of what is coming upon the world. The phrase "the powers of heaven" refers to the forces or powers of the heavens, which will be shaken. Some understand this as the heavenly bodies; others understand it as spiritual powers.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He announces the fall of Jerusalem and signs that will come before his return. The verses that follow show that his coming is not only a cause for dread: for his people, it is a hope of redemption.

For today: when news or crises fill you with fear, do not let fear drain the courage out of you. Pray, trust that Christ is in control, and live with your head held high, waiting for his promise.
exp.19:25:
They could find nothing in his answer that they could use to accuse him before the people. Instead, they were amazed by his reply and kept quiet.

Luke tells us that spies sent by the religious leaders wanted to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar. If he said yes, the people would be angry; if he said no, they could accuse him before Rome. Jesus left them with no way out through his wise answer.

For today: when someone asks us questions with bad intentions, we do not have to answer in anger. We can ask God for wisdom, speak with truth and calm, and remember that what matters most is giving God first place in our lives.
exp.9:7:
Jesus tells his followers that when they enter a town and the people welcome them, they should eat whatever is set before them.

Jesus is speaking to the seventy whom he sends out two by two as messengers of the kingdom of God. They go with little in the way of supplies and depend on the hospitality of others. Many scholars think that eating whatever they were served kept them from worrying about food customs or preferences, although the text does not fully explain this. The focus is on the mission: to heal and to announce that the kingdom of God is near.

Today we can learn to serve with humility and gratitude. When someone welcomes us, we should not place conditions or demands on them. Receiving gladly what is offered to us helps build trust and opens doors for sharing the message of Jesus.
exp.0:17:
Zechariah asks the angel how he can be sure of what he has heard. He gives as his reason that he is an old man and that his wife is also well along in years. The phrase "advanced in days" means that she is already of advanced age. The words "How shall I know this?" mean "How can I be sure this is true?" or "What sign will you give me?"

Zechariah was a priest, and he was in the temple offering incense when the angel announced that he would have a son, John. His question sounds different from Mary's, and the angel takes it as a lack of faith, so he takes away his ability to speak until the child is born. It is notable that Zechariah knew the story of Abraham and Sarah, yet he still doubted.

When a promise from God seems impossible because of our circumstances, let us not put our limitations first. Let us ask God to strengthen our trust in Him.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that listening to Jesus' messengers is listening to Jesus himself, and rejecting them is rejecting him. And rejecting Jesus is rejecting God the Father, who sent him.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples whom he sent out two by two to proclaim the kingdom of God. He has just warned the towns that did not believe, such as Capernaum. He gives his messengers his backing: they do not go with their own authority, but with his. Afterward, they return joyful from their mission.

Today, this verse invites us to listen with humility to the faithful teaching of God's Word, whether it comes from a pastor, a teacher, or a brother. It also reminds us that when we speak about Jesus, we must do so with care and love, because we represent his message.
exp.1:30:
It says that God's salvation is not something hidden, but something He has prepared in advance, in plain view of all the peoples. The word translated as "prepared" here means to arrange or get ready beforehand. The salvation Simeon sees is Jesus, and God prepared it so that all nations could know it.

Simeon speaks; he is a righteous and devout man of Jerusalem. The Holy Spirit had shown him that he would not die without seeing the Christ. When Joseph and Mary bring the child Jesus to the temple, Simeon takes him in his arms and praises God, glad that he can now depart in peace.

For today: the good news of Jesus is for everyone, without exception. We can ask ourselves who near us believes that God does not include them, and kindly share this hope with them, just as God has prepared it for all.
exp.4:37:
This verse says that new wine must be put into new wineskins, and that way both are cared for: the wine and the skin.

Jesus is speaking with Pharisees and teachers of the law, who asked him why his disciples ate and drank instead of fasting like others. He answers with this parable. Many understand that his teaching brings something new that does not fit into a rigid and familiar religiosity. The following verse shows that many find it hard to let go of what is familiar.

For today: ask God for a flexible and willing heart. Do not cling to customs just because they are comfortable; let Jesus renew your way of thinking and living.
exp.10:40:
Jesus says to give alms, that is, to help those in need, from what is within them or from what they have left over. In this way everything will be clean. In both cases, it speaks of a generosity that comes from within.

Jesus speaks to some Pharisees during a meal in the home of one of them. They had been shocked because He did not wash before eating. Jesus answers them that they cared about appearances, but their hearts were full of greed and wickedness.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith is only outward appearance. A practical way to begin changing on the inside is to help someone in need joyfully, without seeking applause.
exp.19:27:
The Sadducees tell Jesus that Moses left a law: if a married man died without children, his brother was to marry the widow and raise up seed for the dead man, that is, give his dead brother descendants, so that his name and his inheritance would not disappear. Seed means children or descendants. This custom appears in Deuteronomy 25:5-6.

The speakers are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. After several debates, they try to set a trap for Jesus with an exaggerated case of seven brothers. They were not interested in learning; they wanted to mock the idea of life after death and make Jesus look bad before the people.

For today: we can bring our questions to God with sincerity, but let us guard our hearts. Seeking the truth is one thing; using the Bible to win an argument is another. Let us come to the Word with humility.
exp.0:78:
God says he comes to give light to those who live in darkness and under the threat of death. The verse also says he wants to guide our steps onto a path of peace. The word "shadow of death" describes a deep darkness, of danger and hopelessness.

The one speaking is Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he sings this song when his son is born. He praises God for his mercy and announces that John will prepare the way. The "dayspring from on high" is an image of light rising from above; many Christians understand it as a reference to Jesus.

For today: if you feel lost or afraid, ask God to guide you step by step. Today, take one concrete step of peace: forgive, ask for forgiveness, or pray before you decide.
exp.1:27:
This verse tells how Simeon took the child Jesus in his arms and praised God. The word "blessed" here means that he gave thanks and praised God.

Simeon was a man who was waiting for the consolation of Israel. The Holy Spirit had promised him that he would not die before he saw the Christ, that is, the Messiah. Guided by the Spirit, he arrived at the temple just when Joseph and Mary were bringing Jesus to do what the law required. What he says next is his prayer of joy, because he saw the promise fulfilled.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a long time. Just as Simeon waited in faith and stayed attentive to the Spirit's guidance, we can wait with patience and, when God answers, give him thanks with our whole heart.
exp.21:68:
It says that from now on Jesus, the "Son of man," will be seated "at the right hand" of "the power of God." "Power" is one way of naming God himself and his might. To sit at the right hand was the place of honor and authority.

Jesus speaks before the council of the Jewish leaders, on the night of his arrest. They ask him to say whether he is the Christ, and he knows they will not believe him. With these words he recalls images from Daniel 7 and Psalm 110. They understand that he is claiming to be divine, and that is why they ask whether he is the Son of God. Some scholars debate exactly how to understand the "from now on," but the general meaning is clear.

For today: even when everything seems unjust or out of control, Jesus reigns. You can trust him and rest in his authority.
exp.17:20:
Here a wealthy and important man comes to Jesus to ask how to inherit eternal life. Jesus reminds him of several commandments, and he answers that he has kept all of them since he was young. "Kept" means obeyed or fulfilled, and "youth" refers to his childhood and adolescence.

The one speaking is this rich ruler. His answer sounds sincere, and Mark 10:21 says that Jesus looked at him and loved him. Even so, he was focused on what he did on the outside. Jesus does not argue with his obedience; he takes it deeper and touches what truly ruled his heart: his wealth. Some interpret that Jesus was showing that no one is saved by keeping rules.

For today: do not measure yourself against a list of good works. Ask God to show you what thing is occupying the place that belongs only to Him, and surrender it to Him with confidence.
exp.12:10:
This verse presents a woman who had carried her condition for eighteen years, described as a "spirit of infirmity." That is, her ailment had to do with something more than the physical. She was bent over, and she could not straighten herself up at all.

Luke tells us that Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath. This woman appears there, and in the verses that follow, Jesus calls her over and heals her. Luke is the one narrating. The scene sets up the discussion about whether it is right to do good on the Sabbath. Scholars understand the expression "spirit of infirmity" in different ways, but the text shows that Jesus set her free.

For today: Jesus notices those who bear suffering for years and go unnoticed. If you carry a long burden, bring it to God in prayer. And if you see someone weighed down, do not ignore them; go to them with compassion and concrete help.
exp.15:28:
Abraham answers that the rich man's brothers already have Moses and the prophets, that is, the Scriptures of the Old Testament. He tells the rich man to let them hear them. The phrase "let them hear them" means to listen to them and take their words to heart. The word "let" here is an older English usage meaning "allow" or "permit," so the sentence can be read as "let them hear them" in the sense of "allow them to listen to them."

Jesus tells this story about a rich man and Lazarus, the poor man. The rich man, already in the place of torment, asks that someone warn his five brothers so that they do not end up the same way. Abraham replies that the warning they need is already available in the Word of God. Jesus teaches that listening to God matters more than seeing a miracle.

For today: do not wait for an extraordinary sign in order to believe or change. God has already spoken in his Word. Set aside time regularly to read the Bible, and ask God to help you obey what he already shows you.
exp.15:27:
Here the rich man, who is suffering in the place of torment, asks Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house. He wants Lazarus to warn his five brothers, so that they do not also come to that place. The word "testify" in this verse means giving a serious warning, like a witness who speaks up.

The rich man speaks in the parable Jesus tells about himself and Lazarus. Before, he had been careless about everything, but now he is worried about his brothers. Abraham answers that they already have Moses and the prophets, that is, the Scriptures. Some think Jesus was also speaking to the Pharisees, who loved money.

For today: do not wait for an extraordinary sign in order to believe or to change. Read the Bible carefully and obey it now, and pray for your family members so that they also will listen to it.
exp.18:36:
He says that Jesus was already near the descent of the Mount of Olives, on his way to Jerusalem. Then the whole multitude of his disciples, full of joy, began to praise God for all the mighty works they had seen. The disciples rejoiced and praised God with a loud voice, which is the same as saying they praised him at the top of their voices.

Luke is the one who tells this. Jesus rides on a young donkey, and the people spread their cloaks on the road, as was done to honor a king. The disciples praise him for the mighty works they witnessed, and in the verses that follow they call him king. Some of the Pharisees are upset and ask that the disciples be silenced. Scholars agree that this is a scene of celebration, although Jesus knows the cross awaits him.

For today: our praise arises as we remember what God has done. Today you could write down three things God has done for you and give thanks to him out loud, without fear of what others think.
exp.23:34:
This verse says that the two disciples, as soon as they arrived in Jerusalem, told what had happened to them on the road to Emmaus. They also explained how they recognized Jesus when he broke the bread. The phrase "how he was known of them" simply means that they recognized him.

Luke is the narrator. The two disciples returned in a hurry, at night, to share the news with the eleven apostles and the others. There it was already being said that the Lord had risen and had appeared to Simon. Their testimony adds to the others. Soon after, Jesus himself appeared among them.

For today: when Jesus becomes real in your life, in the Word, in prayer, or at the table with other believers, do not keep it to yourself. Tell simply what you have lived. Your testimony may encourage someone who still doubts or is afraid.
exp.3:3:
Jesus answers the devil with a line of Scripture: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." The phrase "by every word of God" refers to everything God says.

Jesus speaks after fasting forty days in the wilderness. He was hungry, and the devil proposes that he use his power to turn a stone into bread. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, where Moses reminded Israel that God sustained them in the wilderness. In this way, Jesus chooses to trust the Father and not act on his own.

For today: bread, money and daily needs are important, but they are not the only thing that sustains us. When you feel pressure or need, before deciding anything, seek God's voice in his Word and trust that he cares for you.
exp.15:15:
The Law and the Prophets, that is, the Old Testament, were the great guide until John the Baptist appeared. Since then the good news of the kingdom of God has been announced, and people press forward to enter it.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, who loved money, mocked him, and boasted of being righteous. He reminds them that God sees the heart.

Commentators explain the phrase "press forward to enter" in different ways: it may be a sincere effort by the people, or an eager pressing forward in the face of the kingdom's urgency. What is certain is that the kingdom was already being proclaimed with force and called for a response.

Today, do not put off your response to God. Seek to enter his kingdom with a sincere heart, not merely with religious appearances.
exp.3:18:
It says Jesus came to announce "the acceptable year of the Lord," that is, a time when God shows his favor and grace. "To preach" here means to proclaim or announce publicly. The phrase recalls Israel's year of jubilee (Leviticus 25), when debts were forgiven and freedom was restored, though some scholars understand it in a more spiritual than literal way.

Jesus is in the synagogue at Nazareth, his hometown, and reads the passage from Isaiah 61. He stops before finishing the prophetic sentence, and then says, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." With that he affirms that he is the Anointed One that Isaiah announced, and that this time of grace begins with his ministry.

Today we can remember that God's grace is not only a matter of the past: it is open now. If you carry guilt, sadness, or chains, you can come to Jesus with confidence. And you can also be a bearer of good news to those who are near you.
exp.11:10:
Jesus says that when his followers are brought before the synagogues, the rulers and the authorities, they should not live worried about how to defend themselves or what they will say. "Worried" here means being anxious or troubled about it. The "authorities" are the officials who hold power.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and there was a large crowd around them. He warns them that they will be persecuted for following him. Shortly before, he asked them to confess him without fear before others. The next verse promises that the Holy Spirit will teach them what they need in that hour.

Today, when you face pressure or mockery for your faith, do not freeze up from fear of getting it wrong. Prepare yourself by praying and getting to know the Word, and trust that God will give you wisdom to speak with truth and gentleness.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that Joseph and Mary brought the offering that the Lord's law required: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. The word "offering" here refers to the sacrifice that was taken to the temple after the birth of a child.

Here Luke speaks as the narrator. He tells how Mary and Joseph fulfilled the law of Moses about purification after childbirth (Leviticus 12). That law allowed birds to be offered when a family could not afford a lamb. Many understand this as showing the modest means of Jesus' family, though the text does not state this directly.

For today: God values sincere obedience more than the amount we can give. We can offer him what we have, with humility and faithfulness, without being ashamed of our poverty or comparing ourselves with others.
exp.19:46:
Jesus says that some scribes "devour widows' houses," that is, they take advantage of widows and take their property. To cover this up, they make long prayers and appear very pious. Because of this, he says, they will receive "greater damnation," that is, a more severe judgment.

Jesus speaks to his disciples while all the people listen. The scribes were teachers of the Law and enjoyed respect. Jesus warns them to be careful not to imitate those who seek honor and pretend to be religious. We do not know exactly how they took advantage of widows; several explanations have been proposed, but the text does not give the details.

Today, this invites us to examine whether our faith is sincere. Prayer and service must not be used to gain esteem or benefit. God cares for the vulnerable, and we too must do so with honesty.
exp.19:17:
It says that whoever stumbles over the stone and falls on it will be broken, injured, and shattered. But if the stone falls on someone, it will grind him to powder, that is, reduce him to dust. The phrase "whosoever shall fall" in the verse means the same as "whoever falls," and "grind him to powder" means to reduce him to very small pieces.

Jesus speaks in the temple, after telling the parable of the wicked tenants who rejected the son of the owner of the vineyard. He quotes Psalm 118:22: the stone that was rejected becomes the chief stone. He is referring to himself. The religious leaders understood that he was speaking about them, and they wanted to arrest him, though they feared the people.

For today: it is better to surrender to Christ with humility, even though it hurts, than to resist him with pride. Being broken before him leads us to healing; hardening ourselves can lead us to lose much more.
exp.15:9:
Jesus says that the way we act in small things shows how we will act in great things. Whoever is faithful in the very least, that is, in things that are minimal or of little value, will also be faithful in much, that is, in what is important. And whoever is unjust, that is, dishonest, in the little, will be so in the great as well.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable of the shrewd manager, who used his master's money to secure his own future. Jesus does not applaud his deception, but his foresight. Now he teaches that the money of this world is a small thing, and that the way we handle it reveals the heart and prepares us to receive greater responsibilities.

Today we can practice faithfulness in everyday details: keeping our word, being punctual, paying what is fair, caring for what has been lent to us, and not lying even in matters that seem small. God notices that daily constancy.
exp.11:14:
Jesus tells the people to take care and guard themselves against all greed, which is the desire to have more and more. The word "goods" refers to possessions and money. According to him, a person's life is not measured by how much they have stored up.

Jesus is teaching a crowd. A man asks him to make his brother divide the inheritance with him. Jesus does not agree to be a judge in that dispute, but he uses the moment to get to the heart of the matter: the heart. Right away he tells the parable of the rich man who thought only about storing up his harvests.

Today we can honestly ask ourselves: what takes away our peace, what we lack, or what we want to have in excess? A good practice is to give something, help someone, or thank God for what we already have, so that things do not rule over our hearts.
exp.23:52:
This verse says that the disciples spent a great deal of time in the temple, praising and blessing God. The word "á" is simply an older spelling of "a," so that comment does not apply to the verse you see. "Blessing" here means giving thanks to God and speaking well of him. "Continually" is understood as with constancy, not as meaning they never left the temple.

The one telling the story is Luke, and he closes his Gospel this way. Jesus had just gone up into heaven after blessing his disciples. They returned to Jerusalem full of joy, not in sadness at his departure. Luke shows that the resurrection and Jesus' promise filled them with joy and worship. Then, in Acts, the story continues.

For today: when God has been faithful to you, let your joy become a habit. Set aside time each day, alone or with other believers, to thank him and praise him, even when circumstances are not easy.
exp.16:33:
It says that, on the day when Jesus is revealed, two people will be sleeping in the same bed, and one will be taken away while the other is left behind. "Will be taken" means that they are carried off; "left" means that they are left behind. The verse does not say where they go or explain the detail.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about the day of the Son of Man. He compares that time with the days of Noah and Lot, when people lived at ease until judgment came suddenly. Christians understand this in different ways: some see a rescue of the faithful, others see a judgment in which the wicked are taken away. What is clear is the warning to be ready.

For today: do not live distracted by everyday things. Examine your heart, trust in Jesus, and place your life in his hands each day, without waiting for "tomorrow."
exp.12:34:
Jesus says that their "house" is left empty and abandoned, with no one living in it. He also says that they will not see him again until the time comes when they say, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

Jesus speaks on the way to Jerusalem, grieved over a city that rejects the prophets. He has just said how much he wanted to protect it, like a hen gathering her chicks under her wings, but they did not want that. The "house" may refer to the temple, to the city, or to the people; it is interpreted in several ways. The final phrase recalls Psalm 118:26, and many see it as a promise that one day they will recognize him.

God invites us with tenderness, but he respects our decision. Today we can respond to his call with humility, without hardening our hearts.
exp.19:8:
Jesus tells the people a parable. A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenant farmers (that is, rented it to them so they would work it), and went away on a long journey. The words "leased" and "went away" are older forms of "rented it out" and "went away," so they are not separate things here. Replace them with the verse's own wording: "let it forth" and "went into a far country."

Jesus is speaking in the temple, after the religious leaders asked him by what authority he acted. He did not answer them, since they also refused to answer his question about John the Baptist. Now he addresses the people, although the leaders are listening. Many readers understand the vineyard to represent Israel and the owner to represent God, and the context that follows points in that direction.

For today: God has entrusted us with valuable things, such as life, time, and gifts. May his patience never make us forget that we are stewards, not owners. Today you can ask yourself: what fruit am I giving him?
exp.1:32:
This verse says that Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, were amazed and astonished at what Simeon was saying about the child. The word "marvelled" means that they were filled with wonder and kept thinking about it.

We are in the temple in Jerusalem, when Jesus is presented as a baby. Simeon, a righteous and devout man, took the child in his arms and praised God, saying that Jesus would be a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. Although his parents already knew that Jesus was special, hearing these words left them astonished. Soon, Simeon would also speak to them about sorrow.

For today: even when we have known Jesus for a long time, God can show us something new about Him. We can keep an open and wondering heart, and listen to His Word with attention.
exp.7:6:
It says that another part of the seed fell among thorns. The thorns grew up at the same time as the plant and did not let it develop; they choked it, meaning they smothered it until it could not bear fruit.

Jesus is speaking to a large crowd and uses this parable of the sower. Later in the same chapter, he explains to his disciples that the thorns stand for the worries, riches, and pleasures of life (Luke 8:14). He teaches them how the human heart responds to the word of God.

For today: check what things are growing alongside your faith. Worries and the desire to have more are not always wrong in themselves, but they can choke what God has planted in you. Ask him to help you remove what is excess and to give his word first place.
exp.23:31:
What it says: The two disciples tell each other that their hearts "burned" while Jesus talked with them along the road. The phrase "opened to us the Scriptures" means that he explained to them the meaning of the Bible, which they had not understood before. Speaking of a heart that burns expresses deep emotion, encouragement, and conviction.

Context: The two disciples speaking were on their way to Emmaus, sad over the death of Jesus. The risen Jesus walked with them, but they did not recognize him until he broke the bread. When he vanished, they understood why they had felt such a great emotion. Afterward they hurried back to Jerusalem to tell what had happened.

For today: When you read the Bible, ask Jesus to open it to you and speak to you. Do not look only for information; seek to encounter him. If your heart is encouraged and stirred up, do not keep that joy to yourself: share it with someone.
exp.18:15:
This verse tells of the first servant coming before his lord to give an account. It says the mina he received produced ten more minas. A mina was a considerable sum of money, roughly the pay for about three months of work. The phrase "thy pound hath gained" means that it brought in a profit.

Jesus is telling a parable on the way to Jerusalem. A nobleman travels to receive a kingdom, and his citizens reject him. When he returns as king, he calls his servants to account for the money he had entrusted to them. Jesus tells it because some people thought the kingdom of God would appear right away. The first servant shows faithfulness with what was entrusted to him.

For today: God has entrusted us with time, gifts, and resources. They are not ours to hoard, but to use faithfully and with a view to honoring him. Today you might ask yourself: what has God given me, and how can I use it to serve others?
exp.0:0:
This verse says that many people had already tried to write in order the account of the events that God carried out among the believers. The word "tried" in the sense of "attempted" is what the verse conveys, and the phrase "most surely believed" means "held with great certainty" or "fully confirmed."

The speaker is Luke, the author of the Gospel, although his name does not appear in this passage; Christian tradition attributes the book to him. He writes a formal introduction addressed to Theophilus. Later he explains that he investigated carefully, relying on eyewitnesses. We do not know with certainty which earlier writings existed before his.

For today: our faith rests on real events, not on mere ideas. We can read the Bible calmly and seek to understand it well, without fear of questions, and share it with others in a clear and orderly way.
exp.0:23:
After those days had passed, the days of Zechariah's service in the temple, his wife Elisabeth became pregnant, just as the angel had told him she would. She "hid herself" for five months, meaning she kept to herself and did not show herself in public. The word "reproach" in the next verse means shame or disgrace.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke, and then Elisabeth herself in her own words. She and Zechariah were elderly and had no children, something that in their culture was lived with great shame. Why she withdrew is not stated clearly; some think it was to give thanks to God in private, others that she wanted to wait until the pregnancy was obvious.

For today: when God keeps a promise in your life, take time to thank him quietly and to recognize that it was he who acted, before telling everyone else about it.
exp.10:1:
Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray. He tells them to begin by addressing God as "Our Father," who is in heaven. Then they ask for three things: that his name be hallowed, that is, treated as holy and honored; that his kingdom come, or in other words, his rule; and that his will be done on earth as it already is in heaven.

Jesus had been praying alone, and when he finished, one of his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, just as John the Baptist taught his own followers. Jesus answers with this model prayer. Luke presents it in a shorter form than the one found in Matthew 6.

For today: before asking for your own needs, begin your prayer by remembering who God is and desiring that his will be done. This helps you pray with confidence, like a child before his Father, and with a heart ready to trust in him.
exp.0:67:
It says God deserves to be praised because he came near to his people and rescued them. "Blessed" means worthy of praise. "Has visited" means that God intervened and made himself present to act. "Redeemed" means that he paid a ransom, that is, he set his people free.

Zechariah speaks, the father of John the Baptist. He had just recovered his voice, after months of being unable to speak, and he was filled with the Holy Spirit. His song gives thanks because God is beginning to fulfill his promises. Although he speaks in the past tense, he looks toward the salvation that would come through Jesus, and John would prepare the way. Some understand that redemption as spiritual liberation, others also as hope for Israel.

For today: when it seems to you that God is taking his time, remember that he keeps what he promises. Today, before asking for something, take a moment to thank him for what he has already done for you.
exp.3:38:
This verse tells how Jesus stood over Simon's mother-in-law, who was very sick, and rebuked the fever, that is, he sharply commanded it to leave her. The fever left her at once. She got up immediately and began to serve them.

Luke is the one telling the story. Jesus had just left the synagogue, where he had taught and cast out a demon. When he arrived at Simon's house, some people asked him to help the sick woman. His authority was not only for crowds; it also reached one family in a home. As evening came, many more were healed.

For today: bring your needs to Jesus, even those that seem small or familiar, and pray for others too. When he helps you, respond with gratitude by serving others with what you have.
exp.19:6:
They replied to Jesus, "We do not know where John's baptism came from." It is an evasive answer. The explanation of the wording needs no separate comment here, since the verse above is clear.

The chief priests, the scribes and the elders had asked Jesus by what authority he acted in the temple. He answered them with another question about John's baptism. They reasoned among themselves: if they said "from heaven," he would accuse them of not believing; if they said "from men," the people would stone them. Out of fear and self-interest, they preferred to pretend ignorance. That is why Jesus did not answer their question.

For today: let us be honest with God and with others. It is tempting to keep silent about the truth for fear of looking bad or losing acceptance. Let us ask for courage to say what we really believe.
exp.17:19:
Jesus reminds this man of five commandments from God's law: do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness against others, and honor your father and your mother. The words "do not steal" mean not taking what belongs to someone else, and "bear false witness" means lying about someone, especially before a judge.

He speaks to a man of high standing, perhaps a leader, who asked him how to inherit eternal life. Jesus first points out that only God is good, and then he cites commandments that deal with how we treat our neighbor. After that, he invites him to something deeper: to give up his wealth and follow him. Some understand that Jesus wanted to show him what truly held his heart.

For today: it is not enough to keep the rules on the outside. Ask God whether there is something, like money or pride, that is hard for you to let go of in order to follow Jesus wholeheartedly.
exp.10:44:
One of the experts in the law of Moses interrupts Jesus and says that, by speaking this way about the Pharisees, he is insulting them too. The word "insult" in the verse above means to insult or humiliate someone in public. The teachers who specialized in the Scriptures are the ones this man belongs to.

Jesus is eating at the house of a Pharisee and has just criticized their hypocrisy: they cared about appearances, but not about their hearts. The lawyer realizes that these words apply to him as well. Jesus does not back down but keeps speaking clearly.

For today: when a teaching from the Bible makes us uncomfortable, we should not immediately defend ourselves. Let us humbly ask whether God is showing us something we need to correct.
exp.17:27:
Peter tells Jesus that he and the other disciples left their belongings, that is, their possessions, their work, and their former life, to follow him. In the verse, the phrase "Lo, we have left all" is the wording that draws Peter's attention, so Peter wants Jesus to notice what they have given up.

Jesus had just spoken with a rich man who would not give up his wealth to follow him. Then he said it is very hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God, and the people asked who could be saved. Peter speaks here, perhaps with some doubt, and Jesus answers with a promise: whoever leaves something for the sake of the kingdom of God will receive much more, both now and in eternal life.

Today, we can follow Jesus with confidence, without boasting about what we give. If God asks us to let go of something, we can do so knowing that he cares for us and is never left in debt to us.
exp.15:16:
It is easier, says the verse, for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tittle of the law to fail or be made void. A tittle was a tiny stroke of a Hebrew letter. "To fail" means to come to nothing, to fall or to be set aside.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, whom Luke describes as lovers of money. They justified themselves before people, but God knew their hearts. Jesus makes clear that although the kingdom of God is now being announced, this does not cancel the law. Then he gives the example of marriage, and scholars explain in several ways how these ideas are connected.

For today: let us take God's Word seriously, not only to appear good before others, but to obey it with a sincere heart, trusting that what God says remains firm.
exp.8:9:
The explanation says that the apostles came back from the mission to which Jesus had sent them and reported everything they had done. Then Jesús took them with him and withdrew with them to a lonely place near a city called Bethsaida. The word "the apostles" in the verse refers to the same group, and "a lonely place" here means an uninhabited place, not necessarily a sandy one.

The one who narrates is Luke. The twelve had been sent to preach and heal (Luke 9:1-6). Herod, meanwhile, was wondering who Jesus was. After so much activity, Jesus seeks a moment of rest with his disciples. Some scholars note that the ancient texts vary a little in the name of the place, but the central idea is the same.

For today: after serving, it is good to stop, speak with Jesus, and tell him everything, both the joys and the weariness. Resting alone with him is not wasted time, but part of the service that renews one's strength.
exp.12:32:
He says that Jesus must keep on his way today, tomorrow, and the day after. Where the source uses an old word meaning "it is necessary," rewrite it as "must," and where the source uses an old word for "but," rewrite it as "but." It explains that it cannot be that a prophet should die outside Jerusalem, meaning that his death would take place there.

He speaks in response to some Pharisees who warn him that Herod wants to kill him. Jesus is not frightened; he calls Herod a fox and goes on healing and casting out demons. The "three days" probably indicate a short, fixed period of time, not necessarily an exact count. Jesus knows that his path leads him to Jerusalem, and that there his mission must be fulfilled.

For today: threats and fear should not turn us away from what God asks of us. We can ask him for courage to keep doing good faithfully, trusting that our days are in his hands.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that Jesus taught in the synagogues of the Jews in Galilee, and that everyone praised him. "Being glorified" means honored and spoken well of. "Of them" refers to the synagogues of the people in that region.

Luke, the narrator, is summarizing here the early period of Jesus' ministry. He had just overcome temptation in the wilderness and returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit. His reputation was spreading, and people received him warmly. This summary prepares the scene that follows in Nazareth, where things would change, since not everyone there welcomed him with the same applause.

For today: Jesus taught faithfully, without depending on applause. We can ask the Spirit to help us serve and share his word with faithfulness, whether or not others praise us.
exp.2:2:
Luke tells us that John went out to travel through the whole region near the Jordan River. His message was a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Forgiveness means that God wipes away the debt of sin. To repent is to change direction, to turn back to God with the heart, and the baptism was a public sign of that change.

Luke, the narrator, has just placed John at a very specific political time and place. After a long silence, God speaks again to a prophet in the wilderness. John preached to prepare the people for the coming of the Lord, as Isaiah had foretold. Scholars debate exactly how this baptism related to other Jewish practices of purification, but its purpose here is clear: to prepare hearts.

Today, if your heart has strayed, do not wait any longer. Honestly acknowledge what you have done wrong, ask God for forgiveness, and take a concrete step to change. He receives with grace whoever turns back to Him.
exp.17:0:
He tells them a parable with a clear teaching: it is necessary to pray always and not to faint, that is, not to give up or lose heart. The verse tells us ahead of time what the story is for.

The one speaking is Jesus, and he is addressing his disciples. Shortly before, he had spoken to them about his coming and about difficult times (Luke 17). So he tells them the story of a widow who keeps pressing an unjust judge. The point is not that God is like that judge, but that if a widow gained her request through persistence, how much more can we trust God, who is good.

For today: choose a need you have stopped praying about out of weariness, and bring it before God again each day this week, with confidence and without losing heart.
exp.10:53:
The explanation says that the scribes and Pharisees were lying in wait for Jesus. "Laying wait" means watching him closely, waiting for a slip. "Catch" means to seize, as one seizes an animal. They wanted Jesus to say something wrong so they would have grounds to accuse him.

Jesus had just spoken firmly to the teachers of the law. He told them they were hiding the true knowledge of God: they did not enter in themselves, and they hindered others. Instead of reflecting, they became angry and pressed him with questions. They were not seeking to learn, but to find a reason to accuse him. Luke presents this as the beginning of an opposition that grew stronger.

For today: when God's Word corrects us, we can either defend ourselves or listen. Let us ask for a humble heart, one that asks in order to learn and not in order to win an argument.
exp.0:71:
This verse says that God acts to show mercy, that is, compassion and kindness, toward the ancestors of Israel. He does so because he remembers his holy covenant, the solemn promise he made with them. Here, "remember" does not mean that God had forgotten, but that he is going to fulfill what he promised.

The speaker is Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he praises God because the salvation announced by the prophets is about to arrive. The verses that follow connect this with the oath made to Abraham.

For today: when waiting drags on, remember that God is faithful to his promises, even when they take longer than we expect. You can pray with confidence, relying on his character and not on how you feel at the moment.
exp.22:32:
The soldiers led Jesus to the place called "the Skull," and there they crucified him. The two criminals were crucified with him, one on each side, and Jesus was in the middle. "Malefactors" are people who did wrong, that is, criminals. In Aramaic that place was called Golgotha, and some versions translate it as "Calvary."

Luke, the narrator, tells the events simply, without embellishment. Jesus had already been condemned, and here what he himself had foretold comes to pass. Luke shows that Jesus died among criminals, as one of them. Many Christians connect this with Isaiah 53:12, which speaks of someone counted among the transgressors.

For today: Jesus did not turn away from those who had failed, but was at their side in the hardest moment. If you feel unworthy or alone, remember that Christ knows suffering and draws near to you. You can pray with confidence, without pretending to be perfect.
exp.9:20:
Jesus is filled with joy through the Spirit and praises the Father, whom he calls Lord of heaven and earth. He gives thanks because certain truths have been hidden from the wise and prudent, meaning those who trust in their own understanding, and have been revealed to babes, that is, simple and humble people. He says that this is what pleased the Father.

Jesus has just received back the seventy disciples he sent out, who were very happy about what they had accomplished. He had asked them to rejoice even more because their names are written in heaven. Now he celebrates that the Father reveals his work to ordinary people, not to the proud.

For today: draw near to God with humility, like a child who listens. To understand Jesus you do not need to be brilliant, but to open your heart and ask him to show you himself.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that Jesus was about thirty years old when he began his ministry. The phrase "about thirty" shows that his age was approximate. It also says that people believed Jesus was the son of Joseph, although in reality his origin was divine. Then a list of ancestors begins, and the first name is Heli.

Luke, who writes the account, pauses the story after Jesus' baptism and the voice from heaven. He wants to show who Jesus is and where he comes from, so he presents his genealogy, which goes back to Adam. There are different explanations for why this list differs from the one in Matthew; some think it follows the line of Mary, others the line of Joseph, and there is no certainty.

Today we can remember that God is not in a hurry. Jesus waited for the right time before serving publicly. If you are waiting for a new season, trust that God is also preparing you.
exp.7:4:
Jesus begins to tell a story about a sower who went out to scatter his seed. Some of the seed fell along the path, where people walked. There it was trodden down, and the birds ate it before it could grow.

Jesus speaks to a large crowd that had come from many towns. He uses a parable, that is, a simple story with a deeper message. Later in this same chapter, he explains that the seed is the word of God and that the different kinds of ground represent the ways people receive it.

For today: when you hear the word of God, do not let it fall on hard, hurried ground. Take a quiet moment to think about what you heard, to pray, and to keep it in your heart, so that nothing takes it away.
exp.20:21:
Jesus says that the days he announces for Jerusalem will be days of "vengeance," that is, of God's punishment or justice. This happens so that everything that the Scriptures had already warned about may be fulfilled.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple, shortly before his crucifixion. He warns them that Jerusalem will be surrounded by armies and destroyed. Many understand this to refer to the fall of the city in the year 70 AD. The ancient prophets, such as Jeremiah and Daniel, had already spoken of similar judgments. Jesus gives them instructions to flee and save themselves.

For today: God keeps his word, both his warnings and his promises. If he shows us something that we need to correct, let us listen in time and respond with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.21:31:
Jesus tells Simon Peter that he has prayed for him, so that his faith will not run out. He also gives him a task: when he gets up again after his fall, he must strengthen his brothers. "But" means "but," and the word the source used for it has been replaced here. "Once you have returned" speaks of turning back to God, repentant.

Jesus is speaking at the Last Supper with his disciples. He has just warned that Satan asked permission to sift them, the way wheat is shaken. Jesus knows Peter will deny him, but he does not abandon him: he prays for him and announces that he will get up and serve others.

For today: if you have failed, do not think everything is over. Jesus intercedes for his own, and he can restore you. When you get up, use your experience to encourage others who are struggling in their faith, with humility.
exp.5:13:
This verse begins the list of the twelve apostles whom Jesus chose. It names Simon, whom Jesús also named Peter, and his brother Andrew. Then it names James (who is Santiago), John, Philip, and Bartholomew.

Luke is the one telling the story. Before choosing the twelve, Jesus went up the mountain and spent the whole night praying to God. Then, at daybreak, he chose these men from among his disciples. They were ordinary people, and the list continues in the next verse, including Judas Iscariot.

For today: Jesus prayed before making an important decision. We can follow his example, seeking God in prayer before choosing a job, a friendship, or a path. Also, God calls ordinary people, so you too can serve him just as you are.
exp.19:0:
This verse tells us that one day, while Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, the chief religious leaders came up to him. The chief priests were the leaders of the priests; the scribes were the teachers of the Law; the elders were respected leaders of the people. The good news is what the word gospel means.

The account takes place in Jerusalem, in the last days before the cross. Luke is the one who tells the story. These groups, who were part of the religious council, approach Jesus, and the next verse shows that they want to challenge his authority. They felt threatened because the people were listening to him closely.

For today: while Jesus taught with simplicity, some were only looking to challenge him. We can examine our hearts and ask whether we come to the Word to listen and obey, or only to argue. Let us approach Jesus with humility.
exp.13:21:
Here the servant reports to his master that he has carried out the order: he has brought in the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind from the city. "It is done as you commanded" means "what you ordered has already been done." And he adds that "there is still room," that is, there are still empty places at the table.

Jesus tells this parable while eating in the house of a Pharisee. The first guests turned down the dinner with excuses. The servant now speaks with his master, and his report shows that the invitation is still open. Many understand it to illustrate God's grace toward the despised, although there is debate about exactly who the guests who are missing would be.

God still has room for more people. We can simply invite someone who feels left out, a neighbor or coworker, to come to know his love, without judging whether they deserve it.
exp.7:42:
This verse introduces a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. "Substance" means all her belongings and her money. She had spent it all on doctors, yet none of them could heal her.

The one telling the story is Luke, the writer of the Gospel. Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairus, whose daughter is dying, and a crowd is pressing around him. In the middle of that crush, this woman appears. Under the law of Moses, a condition like hers left her ceremonially unclean, so she probably lived set apart and in shame. Luke also points out that her twelve years of illness match the age of the girl.

For today: when you have tried many solutions and still feel worn out, do not stay silent. Bring your need to Jesus with honesty and faith, even if you feel small or without strength.
exp.7:21:
Luke tells us that one day Jesus got into a boat with his disciples and suggested they cross to the other side of the lake. So they set out. The lake is the Sea of Galilee, and the boat here is a small fishing boat.

Jesus is the one speaking, and he does so as a teacher who guides his followers. Shortly before this, he had said that his true family is made up of those who hear the word of God and put it into practice. Now the disciples follow that invitation and go with him. What comes next is a storm, so the voyage began at Jesus' suggestion, not through any carelessness on their part.

For today: sometimes following Jesus does not spare us from storms, but it leads us to face them with him in the boat. When you face difficulties, remember that you are not alone, and trust his word even when the way becomes hard.
exp.17:42:
It says that the blind man received his sight immediately. After being healed, he followed Jesus and gave glory to God. The people who saw the miracle also praised God.

This happens near Jericho. A blind man was crying out for help, and Jesus called him. When the man asked to see, Jesus told him that his faith had made him well. Luke, the narrator, shows that the healing was real and that it moved this man to follow Jesus. It also stirred praise among the witnesses. The word "saved" can include healing and also a deeper rescue.

When God helps us, we can respond as this man did: giving thanks, following Jesus, and speaking about what God has done. Our gratitude can encourage others to praise God as well.
exp.11:24:
Jesus asks whether anyone, by worrying, could add even one cubit to their height, which is about half a meter. The answer is no one. Some translations render it as "add one hour to his life," because the Greek word can mean either height or length of life.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and also to the crowd, shortly after the parable of the rich fool. He teaches them that life is worth more than food or clothing. He uses the ravens and the lilies to show that the Father cares for what he has created, and that they matter to him far more.

Today, when a worry you cannot control steals your sleep, write it down and bring it to God in prayer. Then do what is yours to do today, and leave the rest in his hands. Trusting God does not mean doing nothing, but working without being enslaved by fear.
exp.8:43:
Jesus asks his disciples to listen carefully and not to forget what he is about to tell them. The phrase "Let these sayings sink down into your ears" means "let these words sink deep into your minds." He announces that the Son of man, that is, himself, will be delivered into the hands of men, meaning he will be betrayed and will fall into the power of people who will harm him.

Jesus speaks to his disciples right after healing the boy, when everyone was amazed at his miracles. In the middle of the praise, he reminds them that his path includes suffering. The text says they did not understand, and that the meaning was hidden from them, an idea some understand as part of God's plan and others as a lack of openness on their part. Then they began to argue about who would be the greatest.

For today: when everything is going well, do not lose sight of what is essential. Ask God for a humble heart that listens to his Word, even when it is not easy to understand or to accept.
exp.7:33:
The explanation says that the men who were tending the pigs, seeing that the pigs had drowned and that the man who had been possessed had changed, ran away. They went to tell the news in the town and out in the countryside. "Fields" are land or property out in the country, and "to give notice" means to report or inform.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened in the region of the Gadarenes, after Jesus drove a crowd of demons out of a man. The herdsmen were direct witnesses and, frightened, carried the news. Their reaction is not explained in detail: it may have been fear, worry over the loss of the animals, or both. The Bible does not make it clear.

For today: when God works in powerful ways, we may react with fear or with wonder. Let us ask God for an open heart to recognize his work, and let us share simply what we have seen of him, without keeping it silent.
exp.1:35:
This verse introduces Anna, a woman whom the text calls a prophetess. She was the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser, and she was already of great age. When she was young she was married and lived seven years with her husband. The phrase "from her virginity" means from the time she married, while she was still a maiden.

Here Luke speaks, recounting what happened when Joseph and Mary brought the child Jesus to the temple. After the words of Simeon, Anna appears as another witness. Luke names her tribe and her family to show that she was a real and known person. What follows says that she was widowed and served God in the temple with fasting and prayers. She also spoke about the child to those who were waiting for the redemption.

For today: God values those who are faithful to him day after day, regardless of their age. We can pray with perseverance and share with others what God shows us about Jesus.
exp.4:21:
Jesus perceived what the scribes and Pharisees were thinking, though they had not said it aloud. So he asks them what they are thinking in their hearts. The word "perceived" means that he knew, and "reason" refers to the thoughts they were reasoning through.

A group of friends had lowered a paralyzed man through the roof so that Jesus would heal him. Jesus told him that his sins were forgiven, and the teachers of the law thought this was blasphemy. Jesus responds by showing that he knows their doubts, and then he heals the man, to prove that he has authority to forgive sins.

God knows what we think and feel inside, even what we keep silent. We can bring our doubts and questions honestly before him, instead of hiding them, and let him speak to us.
exp.3:4:
The explanation says that the devil took Jesus up to a high mountain and, in a moment, showed him all the kingdoms of the world. The phrase "á" is the old form of "a," and "in a moment of time" means in the blink of an eye, very quickly.

This takes place during the temptation in the wilderness. Luke tells us that, after the test of the bread, the devil now offers him power and glory if he worships him. It is not known whether it was a vision or a physical place; interpreters understand it in different ways. Jesus had already answered with Scripture, and he will continue to do so.

For today: the enemy often offers attractive shortcuts, such as success, power or recognition, in exchange for putting God second. Before deciding, ask yourself what price comes with what is being offered to you. And like Jesus, keep the Word of God in your heart so that you can answer with truth.
exp.1:37:
What it says: Anna arrived at the very moment when Simeon had finished speaking with Mary and Joseph. She gave thanks to God and spoke about the child Jesus to all who were waiting for the deliverance of Jerusalem. The word "coming in" means that she arrived suddenly, and "gave thanks" here means praising or thanking God. "Deliverance" means liberation or rescue.

Context: Luke is the narrator. Jesus is presented in the temple as a baby. Anna, an elderly widow and prophetess, spent her days there praying and fasting. Many understand that she recognized Jesus as the promised Savior. The text does not say exactly what she said, nor how many people heard her.

For today: Anna did not keep the good news to herself. Although she was old and perhaps had little influence, she shared with others what God had shown her. Today too we can give thanks to God and speak of Jesus simply, with those who have hope or need encouragement.
exp.2:25:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Jesus, going back from generation to generation, descended from people such as Naggai, Maat, Mattathias, Semei, Joseph and Judah. "Which was" is the older form of "was," and here it means "son of" or "descendant of."

Luke, the author, writes this genealogy after Jesus's baptism. No one speaks here; it is a historical record. Luke wants to show that Jesus is truly human and that his story is connected to all of humanity. Almost all of these names appear only here in the Bible, and we do not know much about them. Some scholars think this line follows Mary and others follow Joseph; it is a matter that is interpreted in several ways.

God works through ordinary and unknown people. Even though no one remembers your name, your faithfulness in everyday life can be part of what God is doing in your family and in the generations to come.
exp.8:44:
This verse says that the disciples did not understand what Jesus had just told them about being handed over to men. The disciples did not grasp the meaning, because it was hidden from them. Moreover, they were afraid to ask him about it, meaning they felt fear or dread at the thought of asking him for an explanation.

Luke recounts this right after the crowds were amazed at the miracles of Jesus. In the middle of that admiration, Jesus announces his suffering. The disciples expected something else, and that is why they did not understand. The phrase "that they perceived it not" is hard: some see it as a veil that God allowed to remain until the right time, while others emphasize that their own ideas kept them from understanding. Shortly afterward they begin arguing about who would be the greatest.

Today, when something about God does not sit well with us or fills us with fear, we should not keep silent. We can bring our questions to him honestly, trusting that he teaches with patience.
exp.10:37:
It says that a Pharisee, when he saw that Jesus sat down to eat without washing first, was surprised. The phrase "marvelled" means that he was amazed or puzzled. The washing was not for hygiene but a religious custom.

Luke tells that a Pharisee invited Jesus to eat, and Jesus accepted. The Pharisees followed with great care the traditions of purification that the teachers had added to the Law. Jesus did not wash in that way, and the host was puzzled. Luke does not say that Jesus did it out of carelessness. Many understand it as an opportunity Jesus uses to teach about the purity of the heart, which continues in the following verses.

We can care for our religious customs, but without forgetting what matters most: a sincere heart before God. Before judging others by what is seen on the outside, let us ask God to examine our inner life.
exp.21:19:
Jesus takes the cup after supper and says that this cup is the new covenant in his blood, which would be poured out for you. The word "cup" here means the drinking vessel, and a covenant is a solemn agreement or promise between God and his people.

Jesus speaks with his disciples during the last supper, the night before his death. When he speaks of a new covenant, he recalls the promise in Jeremiah 31:31-34 of forgiveness and of a close relationship with God. He says this knowing that one of them would betray him and that his death was already near. The blood that is poured out points to a sacrifice given for the benefit of others.

When you take part in the Lord's Supper, or when you pray, remember that your forgiveness and your closeness to God do not depend on your merits but on the love of Christ. Thank him with a humble heart and live today with gratitude.
exp.23:30:
This verse tells us that the eyes of the two disciples were opened, and they recognized Jesus. At that same moment, he stopped being visible to them. The phrase about him vanishing from their sight means that he was no longer seen; the text does not explain how it happened.

This is the account of the road to Emmaus, on the day of the resurrection. Luke, who tells the story, says that Jesus walked with two sad disciples, but they did not recognize him. They invited him to stay, and when he broke the bread, they recognized him. Some believe God kept them from recognizing him until that moment; the text suggests this, but does not spell it out.

For today: Jesus often makes himself known in simple things, such as his Word and prayer. Invite him to stay with you through your day, and pay attention to what he shows you, even when you do not see him.
exp.5:19:
Jesus looks at his disciples and tells them they are blessed, that is, happy and favored by God, even though they are poor. The reason is that the kingdom of God belongs to them.

Jesus has just healed many people who were trying to touch him and receive his power. After that, he teaches his followers. In Luke, this blessing is linked with other blessings about hunger, weeping, and rejection. Some understand that he is speaking of material poverty, others of humility before God; many believe it includes both.

Today we can remember that our worth does not depend on what we have. If you feel lacking or in need today, come near to God with confidence: he cares for you and invites you into his kingdom.
exp.7:48:
As Jesus was still speaking with the woman he had healed, a messenger came from the house of Jairus, the leader of the synagogue. He told Jairus that his daughter had already died and that there was no need to bother the Teacher any further. "Ruler of the synagogue" was the person in charge of leading the meetings held there. The phrase "trouble not the Master" means "do not bother him."

Context: Jairus had asked Jesus to heal his daughter, who was very sick. Jesus had stopped for the woman who touched him, and for Jairus that delay must have been agonizing. The messenger spoke from a human point of view: if she has already died, there is nothing more to be done. Jesus answers at once with different words: "Do not be afraid; only believe."

For today: When a situation seems hopeless and the people around you say there is no remedy left, remember that Jesus is still speaking. Bring him your fear, trust him, and wait for his answer, even when you do not understand his timing.
exp.8:21:
Jesus says that the Son of man, a title he uses for himself, must suffer many things. The elders, the chief priests, and the teachers of the law would reject him. He would be killed, and on the third day he would rise again.

Jesus speaks to his disciples just after Peter recognizes him as the Christ of God. He asks them to keep quiet, probably because the people were expecting a different kind of Messiah, one of political power. Jesus makes clear that his path goes first through suffering and death, and then through resurrection.

Today, following Jesus is not always comfortable or immediately successful. We can trust him even when the path includes difficulty, rejection, or sacrifice, remembering that his suffering was not the end, but the road to life.
exp.15:4:
This verse tells how the manager, who looked after the property of a rich man, called in the people who owed money to his master, one by one. He asks the first one how much he owes. Here "lord" means the master or owner, and "manager" is the role of the one who runs the affairs.

Jesus is telling this parable to his disciples. The manager had been accused of wasting his master's goods, and he knew he was about to lose his job. So he thinks quickly and makes friends for the future. Scholars debate whether he changed the debts by trickery or only gave up his own commission. Jesus does not praise his dishonesty, but his shrewdness and foresight.

Today we can learn to plan ahead with eternity in mind. If people use so much cleverness for their material future, we too can use money and time wisely, helping others and serving God.
exp.23:11:
Peter is said to have got up and run to the tomb. He looked in and saw only the linen cloths that had wrapped Jesus's body, lying there. Then he went back home, amazed at what had happened. The "linen cloths" are those strips of linen; "departed, wondering in himself" means he left in wonder, without fully understanding.

Luke tells this right after the women reported that Jesus had risen, and the apostles thought their words were nonsense. Peter, though still doubtful, wanted to check for himself. He saw the empty tomb, but this verse does not say he already believed fully. Some understand that he was confused; others, that he was beginning to believe. The text does not make it clear.

For today: when something about God is hard for us to believe, we should not dismiss it right away. We can come to it honestly, look into it, pray, and ask him for light, even when we do not yet understand everything.
exp.14:0:
It says that all the tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him. The phrase "drew near" means that they were coming closer, and "to hear him" means listening to him. Tax collectors were men who collected taxes for Rome, and many people despised them for their reputation of overcharging and cooperating with the foreign power. "Sinners" was a common way of naming those who were considered far from religious life.

Luke is not recounting a speech of Jesus here, but rather setting the scene. These people came eager to listen to him, and the verses that follow show that the Pharisees and scribes were upset by this. That complaint is what leads Jesus to tell the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son.

For today: come to Jesus just as you are, without waiting to get yourself cleaned up first. And when someone arrives with a difficult past, receive them with the same openness that Jesus showed.
exp.5:39:
The explanation says that a student is not above his teacher. But whoever lets himself be well trained will come to be like his teacher. The word "perfect" here means complete, well prepared, or mature, not someone without any mistakes.

Jesus speaks in the Sermon on the Plain, before his disciples and a crowd. He has just spoken about loving enemies and not judging. With the parable of the blind leading the blind, he warns that a guide with poor spiritual sight makes those who follow him fall. Then he speaks about the beam and the speck.

For today: choose carefully whom you follow, and learn from Jesus. If you teach others, begin by examining your own life, because people end up imitating what they see in you.
exp.17:35:
This verse says that the blind man, hearing the noise of the crowd passing near him, asked what was happening. "He" refers to the blind man. The crowd passing by is the throng that was going along the road. He could not see, so he depended on what he heard.

Luke records this as Jesus approaches Jericho. Shortly before, Jesus had announced his death and resurrection, but the disciples did not understand. Now, a blind beggar sitting by the road notices something out of the ordinary and wants to know what is going on. His question leads him to learn that Jesus was passing by, and then he calls out for mercy.

For today: when you sense that God is drawing near, even through small signs, do not stay silent or indifferent. Ask, seek, and come to Jesus with your need.
exp.2:28:
He says Jesus descends from a long line of people: Joshua, son of Eliezer, son of Jorim, son of Matthat. It is part of a list that goes backward, from son to father. The phrase "which was the son of" is the same as "which was the son of," and the spelling used for this kind of phrase is an old one. These names hardly appear anywhere else in the Bible.

The author, Luke, presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. He wants to show that Jesus is truly human and belongs to all of humanity, since the list reaches back to Adam. Many think this line follows Mary, or Joseph by legal descent, but scholars interpret it in several ways and there is no complete agreement.

God works in history through ordinary people, even those whom almost no one remembers. Your life and your daily faithfulness also matter to Him, even when others do not see them.
exp.19:31:
It says that after the seven brothers died without leaving children, the woman also died in the end.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They present Jesus with this invented case, based on the law that a brother should marry the widow of the deceased to raise up offspring for him. Their goal was not to learn, but to mock the idea of the resurrection. Jesus answers them right away, showing that they understand neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

For today: sometimes we ask questions to argue, not to learn. Before asking God something, let us examine our hearts. If we come with humility, He teaches us; if we come with pride, we can miss what is essential.
exp.0:64:
It says that a fear came over all the neighbors of Zacharias and Elizabeth. Here "fear" is not dread of some danger, but a reverent awe before something that only God could do. Also, these reports were spread throughout the hill country of Judea.

Luke, the narrator, recounts what happened when John was born, after Zacharias, unable to speak because he did not believe the angel, wrote the name God had given and regained his speech. The neighbors saw that God was working in an unusual way. In this way Luke prepares the path for the birth of Jesus.

For today: when God works in your life, do not keep it to yourself. Share it with humility and gratitude, so that others also think of God and are amazed at his faithfulness.
exp.5:34:
Jesus says that we should love our enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything back. Some older words need care: the word "reward" is what is meant by the old word for a payment owed for faithful service, and the word for "kind" is what is meant by the old word for being good-natured. God will reward this way of living, and those who practice it resemble their Father, the Most High, who is kind even to the ungrateful and the evil.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to a crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Earlier he said that loving only those who love us is nothing special, since even sinners do that. He presents a different kind of love, one that imitates the mercy of God, as the following verse says.

Today we can choose someone who annoys us or has hurt us. Let us pray for that person and do something good for them, without expecting them to thank us. In this way we practice the kindness that God has already shown us.
exp.0:7:
What it says: Zechariah was a priest, and it was his turn to serve in the temple. The phrase about his turn in service is rendered in the verse above as "in the order of his course," so the reader can take it as meaning that he served according to the rotation assigned to his group of priests. Everything happens in God's presence, that is, with God as witness.

Context: Luke, the writer, explains how the story of Jesus began. He has just said that Zechariah and Elisabeth were faithful but had no children. This verse sets the scene where an angel will bring them an unexpected message. God acts while Zechariah is carrying out his ordinary duty.

For today: Sometimes we think God only acts in extraordinary moments, but He is also present in everyday life. Do your work and your responsibilities faithfully, as before God. Even in the middle of routine, He may surprise you with something new.
exp.20:12:
Jesus says that the persecutions his followers will suffer will end up serving "as a testimony." That is, they will be an opportunity to make their faith known before others. The word "you" refers to the disciples.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in the temple, in Jerusalem, about things that would happen before the end. He warns them that they will be arrested and brought before kings and governors because of his name. Instead of seeing that only as a misfortune, he shows them that God can use it so that others hear the message. Then he promises to give them words and wisdom.

Today, when you go through a difficulty or mockery because of your faith, do not think only about defending yourself. Ask God to help you respond with calm, truth and love, so that your way of acting speaks well of Christ.
exp.14:31:
Here the father says it was right to hold a feast and to rejoice. The word "necessary" in the old wording means something needful or right, and the phrase about rejoicing together means being glad with one another. He explains that his younger son was as if dead, but has come back to life; he was lost, but has now been found.

The father in this passage is speaking in the parable of the prodigal son. He is answering the older son, who became angry and refused to go into the celebration because he felt his brother did not deserve such treatment. Jesus tells this story before Pharisees and scribes who were criticizing him for welcoming sinners. The father does not deny his love for the older son, but he shows him that the brother's return is a reason for joy.

Today, God invites us to celebrate when someone returns to Him, instead of judging them or comparing ourselves to them. We can ask ourselves whether we are glad at the restoration of others, even of those who have failed us. Let us ask God for a heart like the Father's.
exp.19:20:
The spies say to Jesus: "Master, we know that you speak and teach rightly. You show no partiality, but you teach the way of God truly." The phrase about not accepting the person of anyone means that he is not swayed by anyone's rank or power.

The ones speaking are spies sent by the chief priests and the scribes. They pretended to be honest people, but their goal was to trap Jesus in some word so they could hand him over to the Roman governor. Their praise was true, but they spoke it with bad intent. Jesus noticed their cunning right away.

Today: do not let yourself be fooled by pleasant words. A compliment does not prove that the intention is good. Ask God for discernment, and make sure your own words are sincere, never using the truth as a trap to harm others.
exp.18:7:
Zacchaeus stands up and speaks firmly to Jesus. He promises to give half of everything he owns to the poor. He also says that if he has cheated or wronged anyone, he will pay back four times what he took.

Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector and was wealthy. Many people looked down on him because of his job, and that is why they complained when Jesus went into his house.
