Zacchaeus speaks after welcoming Jesus with joy. His promise does not buy forgiveness; Jesus declares salvation afterward, and his change of life shows that his heart had been touched.

When Jesus truly comes into our lives, he also changes what we do. Think about whether there is someone you should ask forgiveness from or make right a wrong, and take one concrete step toward doing it today.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that everyone in the synagogue spoke well of Jesus and was amazed at his gracious words, that is, kind, good words full of God's favor. "Bare him witness" means they praised him or spoke well of him. But then they asked, "Is not this Joseph's son?"

Jesus is in Nazareth, the town where he grew up. He has just read the passage from Isaiah and said that it was being fulfilled that day. The people are amazed, but they also doubt, because they know him as the carpenter's son. Some understand that question as wonder, others as contempt; the text leaves it open, and from what follows, Jesus perceives unbelief.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus or speak well of him. We must receive him with faith, even when his message makes us uncomfortable or seems too close and too simple.
exp.7:17:
Jesus says that we must be careful about how we listen to his word. Whoever receives and practices what they hear will receive more understanding. But whoever does not value it will lose even the little they thought they had.

Jesus speaks to the crowd, just after the parable of the sower. He explains that the light of his teaching is not meant to be hidden, but to be seen. What is hidden will come to light. That is why the attitude of the heart when hearing matters so much. Shortly after, Jesus will say that his true family is those who hear the word of God and do it.

For today: before reading the Bible or listening to a sermon, ask God for an attentive heart, and decide on one concrete action you will put into practice that same day.
exp.8:30:
This verse says that Moses and Elijah appeared surrounded by glory and spoke with Jesus about his departure. The word "departure" comes from the Greek word for exodus, and it refers to his death, his resurrection, and his return to the Father. "Jerusalem" is the city of Jerusalem, and the phrase about what he was to accomplish means that Jesus would carry out that plan.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened on the mountain of the transfiguration while Jesus was praying. Moses represents the Law and Elijah represents the prophets, and both speak of the cross. This shows that the death of Jesus was not an accident but part of God's plan. Peter, half asleep, did not fully understand what was happening.

For today: when you go through difficult moments, remember that God can have a purpose even in suffering. Jesus walked toward the cross with obedience. Pray, trust, and keep going, knowing that God fulfills his plans.
exp.20:6:
The disciples ask Jesus two questions: when will what he said about the temple happen, and what will be the sign that it is about to begin? "Master" is the respectful way of addressing him.

The people asking are followers of his, probably the disciples and others who were in the temple. They had just admired its beautiful stones, and Jesus told them it would be completely destroyed. They were amazed and wanted to know more. Jesus does not give them a date. Instead, he first warns them not to be deceived by those who say, "The end has already come."

Today it is also natural to want answers about the future. But Jesus invites us to something wiser: not to live in fear or chase every voice that promises dates, but to stand firm in his word and trust that he is in control.
exp.3:19:
This verse tells that Jesus closed the scroll of Isaiah, gave it back to the attendant of the synagogue (the one in charge of looking after the scrolls), and sat down. Everyone was looking at him closely. The explanation of the older wording is not needed here, so the word-level notes are omitted.

Jesus was in Nazareth, his hometown, on a Sabbath in the synagogue. He had just read the prophecy of Isaiah about the anointed one who would bring good news to the poor and freedom to the captives. Sitting down was the usual posture of a teacher who was about to teach. Everyone waited for his words, and soon he said that this Scripture was being fulfilled in him.

For today: Jesus did not only read the Word, he also presented it as a living promise. When you read the Bible, pause, stay in silence, and ask God what he wants to say to you today. Listening with attention prepares us to receive his grace.
exp.12:18:
Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a mustard seed, which is very small. A man sows it in his garden, and it grows until it becomes a large tree. Even the birds of the air make their nests in its branches.

Jesus is speaking in a synagogue, after healing a woman who was bent over on the Sabbath. His opponents were put to shame, and the people were rejoicing. Then he explains what the kingdom of God is like: it begins in a humble way, almost unnoticed, but it truly grows. Some see in the birds an image of peoples who find shelter in him; scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: do not despise small beginnings. A kind word, a prayer, or a simple act of faith can bear fruit much greater than you imagine. God knows how to make grow what seems little.
exp.18:32:
This verse tells us that the two disciples were untying the colt, that is, the young donkey, when its owners came up and asked them why they were doing it. Untying means setting loose what was tied, and the phrase refers to the young donkey.

Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem and had sent two disciples to a nearby village. He told them they would find a colt tied up there and that, if anyone asked, they should answer: "The Lord has need of him." The owners ask the natural question, and everything happens just as Jesus had said. Some understand this as a sign of his prior knowledge; others think there may have been an arrangement made beforehand. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when God asks us for something we have, whether time, money, or a talent, we can hand it over with confidence. What we place in his hands, he uses for something greater than we imagine.
exp.7:32:
It says that when the demons came out of the man, they entered the pigs. Then the whole herd rushed down a steep bank into the lake and was drowned. The words "herd" and "swine" refer to a group of pigs, and the steep bank is a cliff or slope.

This account follows the freeing of the demon-possessed man in the region of the Gadarenes. Luke is the one who tells it. The demons begged Jesus not to send them into the deep, and He allowed them to enter the pigs. It shows Jesus' authority over evil. Why the pigs ran into the lake can be understood in several ways, but the text only says that it happened.

For today: Jesus has the power to free a person from what oppresses them, and a restored life is worth more than any material loss. We can trust Him and put people above possessions.
exp.1:9:
What it says: The angel calms the frightened shepherds. He tells them not to be afraid, because he brings good news that brings great joy. This joy is not only for a few, but for all the people. The word "but" here is the same as "but," and "behold" is like saying "look" or "listen."

Context: An angel of the Lord speaks to shepherds who were watching their flocks at night. The glory of God surrounded them with light, and they were filled with fear. The angel first reassures them and then announces the birth of the Savior in Bethlehem. God chooses to give the news to simple people who worked through the night.

For today: When God draws near, we sometimes feel fear or doubt. This verse reminds us that his central message is good news and not condemnation. Today you can pause, read this passage calmly, thank God for Jesus, and then share that joy with someone who needs it.
exp.19:34:
This verse says that those who are considered worthy to share in the coming age and in the resurrection of the dead will no longer marry. "Age" means era or period, and "considered worthy" means that God regards them as fit for that new world. "Given in marriage" referred to parents handing over their daughters to be wed.

Jesus is speaking with the Sadducees, a group that denied the resurrection. They put forward an exaggerated case: a woman who married seven brothers, one after another. Jesus answers that life after the resurrection is not a simple continuation of this life. Marriage belongs to this world, where death exists; in the resurrection, according to the text, there will be no more death.

For today: value your present relationships, but do not place your ultimate hope in them. Put your trust in God and in the life He promises.
exp.21:36:
Jesus says that what the prophet Isaiah wrote must be fulfilled in him: he was counted among the transgressors, that is, treated like a criminal. "I say to you" means "I tell you." The word "was" is the simple past of the same verb, and "has its fulfillment" means that what was written about him is reaching its completion.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He warns them that difficult times of rejection are coming. When they mention two swords, he answers "Enough," and many understand that he was closing the subject, since he was not speaking of a physical war. Some interpret it in other ways.

For today: Jesus accepted being treated unjustly out of love for us. When you face injustice or rejection because of your faith, remember that he went through this before, and ask him for strength to respond with peace and not with violence.
exp.12:21:
This verse says that Jesus went from town to town, through large cities and small villages, teaching the people. All the while he was moving steadily toward Jerusalem. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and the phrase "teaching as he journeyed toward Jerusalem" means that he was teaching while he traveled on the way there.

Luke is the one telling the story. Jesus had already told parables about the kingdom of God, such as the one about yeast that spreads slowly through the dough. Here Luke reminds us that Jesus had a clear direction: Jerusalem, where he would later be crucified. His teaching did not stop, not even on the road. Soon someone asks him how many will be saved, and Jesus answers with firmness.

For today: Jesus taught as he walked, never losing sight of his purpose. We can do the same: let his word guide us in our daily lives, and live with a clear direction, attentive to his call each day.
exp.0:3:
Luke tells Theophilus that he is writing his account so that he may know with certainty the truth of what he had already been taught. The word "truth" here suggests firmness, something secure and reliable. The aim is not to teach him something entirely new, but to affirm what he had already received.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of the Gospel, and he addresses Theophilus, whose name means "friend of God." We do not know with certainty who he was; some think he was a real person of some standing, others that the name stands for any reader. Luke investigated carefully and wrote in order, relying on eyewitnesses.

Today, faith does not have to rest on vague ideas. We can read the Bible calmly, ask sincere questions, and affirm our confidence in what we have learned. Set aside a few minutes this week to read a passage from Luke and note what gives you assurance.
exp.21:26:
Jesus asks a question that everyone would answer the same way: the one who sits at the table is greater than the one who serves the meal. That is how the world thinks. But Jesus says that He, though He is the Master, is among them as one who serves.

Jesus is speaking with His disciples during the Last Supper, the night before His death. They had just been arguing about which of them would be the greatest. Jesus teaches them that in His kingdom greatness is not measured by power but by service, and He points to His own example.

For today: instead of looking for others to wait on you or recognize you, find one concrete way to serve today, at home, at work, or at church, without expecting applause.
exp.18:20:
Here the servant explains why he kept the mina (a sum of money) without using it. He says he was afraid of his master, whom he calls a hard, demanding man. He accuses him of taking what he did not put down and reaping what he did not sow, that is, of wanting profit without having worked for it.

Jesus tells this parable near Jerusalem. A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and leaves a mina to each servant to put to work. On his return he asks for an account. This servant did nothing and blames the master's character. The master does not accept the excuse: if he truly believed that about him, he should at least have deposited the money in the bank to earn interest. Some see here a picture of how the servant misunderstood God.

For today: do not let fear or a mistaken idea of God paralyze you. Use with faith what he has given you, even if it is little, and serve him with confidence.
exp.0:40:
When Elisabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby she was carrying moved with force, and she was filled with the Holy Ghost. "Greeting" is the word here for the salutation, "baby" is the child not yet born, "womb" is the inside of the mother, and "was" is the word that appears in the verse above.

Luke tells us that Mary, already pregnant with Jesus through the angel's announcement, went quickly to visit her relative Elisabeth, who was expecting John, the future Baptist. The one speaking here is the narrator. Then Elisabeth, filled with the Spirit, recognizes Mary as the mother of her Lord. Some think the baby's leap was a sign of joy at the presence of Jesus; the text does not explain more.

For today: when someone visits you or greets you in faith, let the Spirit move you to bless and encourage them. A sincere word can fill another person with joy.
exp.6:7:
Here the centurion explains why he believes Jesus does not need to come to his house. He says he is a man set under authority, meaning he lives under authority and also exercises it. His soldiers obey his orders: to one he says "Go" and he goes, to another "Come" and he comes, and to his servant "Do this" and he does it. The word "authority" here means power or the right to command.

The speaker is a Roman centurion, a military officer, who sent friends to Jesus because his servant was sick. He felt unworthy to receive Jesus in his home. His reasoning is this: if his word carries weight because of the authority he holds, then Jesus' word has even greater power to heal. Jesus marveled at that faith.

For today: we can trust that the word of Jesus is enough, even when we do not see how or when he will act. Today you can bring a need to him in prayer and rest in the knowledge that his word has authority.
exp.12:6:
Jesus tells of a man who owns a vineyard and says to the gardener that for three years he has come looking for fruit on his fig tree and has found none. So he orders the tree cut down. He asks: why should it use up the ground? In other words, why let that tree take up space in the soil for nothing?

The phrase "three years ago" in this account means "three years back," that is, three years have passed since the owner first began looking.

Jesus speaks to a crowd, just after warning that whoever does not repent will perish. The parable shows God's patience and also the seriousness of bearing fruit. Many understand the fig tree to represent Israel, though it also applies to anyone.

For today: do not take God's patience lightly. If you have put off changing something, use this time to repent and to live in ways that show faith, such as love, truth, and service.
exp.19:38:
This verse says that some of the scribes, that is, teachers who were experts in the Law of Moses, answered Jesus: "Master, you have spoken well." Here the phrase about answering him means that they took up the word to speak to him. It was a compliment: they recognized that his answer had been good and right.

Jesus had just replied to the Sadducees, who said there is no resurrection, and who had put a difficult question to him to trap him. Jesus used Moses' words at the burning bush to show that God is the God of the living. The scribes, most of whom believed in the resurrection, agreed. Some of them, however, were also opponents of Jesus, so their praise does not necessarily mean faith in him.

For today: we can recognize the truth when it is spoken well, even when it comes from someone with whom we sometimes disagree. But it is not enough to praise Jesus with words; God invites us to follow him and trust him, knowing that those who belong to him live for him.
exp.2:13:
The soldiers ask John what they should do to live in line with the repentance he preaches. He answers them with three instructions: do not extort, that is, do not take money from anyone by threats or by force; do not accuse falsely, that is, do not bring false charges against others; and be content with your wages, that is, be satisfied with your pay.

John the Baptist was preaching, calling the people to repent and be baptized. Earlier, ordinary people and tax collectors (tax gatherers) had also asked him what they should do. It is not known for certain whether these soldiers were Jews or not, and scholars interpret this in different ways. What is clear is that John does not ask them to leave their job, but to live justly in it.

For today: true faith shows in daily work. Whatever your job, treat everyone with honesty, do not abuse your power or position, and practice gratitude for what God gives you.
exp.4:16:
This verse tells us that one day, as Jesus was teaching, there were Pharisees and teachers of the law sitting nearby, who had come from every town of Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. The teachers of the law were experts in the Scriptures. The power of the Lord means the power of God, which was present to heal the people.

Luke is the one telling the story. Before this, Jesus' fame was growing and crowds were seeking him out, but he would withdraw to lonely places to pray. Now we see religious leaders coming to watch him, and it is not said that they came in faith. Soon, some men will bring a paralyzed man to him, showing a very different kind of faith.

For today: even if we have a great deal of religious knowledge, we need an open heart. Come to Jesus with humility and trust, not only to listen, but to receive what he wants to do in you.
exp.19:35:
This verse says that those who rise will no longer be able to die. They will be "equal unto the angels", meaning they will be like them in not dying. They are "children of God" because they share in the resurrection.

Jesus is speaking with the Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection. They brought him a difficult case about a woman who had been married to seven brothers. Jesus answers that the life to come is not simply a continuation of this one, and then he quotes Moses to show that God is the God of the living.

For today: we can live with hope, knowing that death does not have the last word for those who belong to God. That hope helps us hold less tightly to what passes away and to comfort others in their grief.
exp.20:31:
Jesus confidently states that "this generation" will not pass away before "all be fulfilled," that is, accomplished. "Verily I say unto you" is a solemn way of saying: "I assure you, truly."

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He explains signs about the destruction of the temple and the difficult times that will come. He has just used the image of the fig tree: just as its branches announce summer, these signs announce that the kingdom of God is near. Then he adds that his words will never pass away.

For today: do not live distracted or frightened by the future. Trust that the word of Jesus is firm, and set aside a moment each day to read it and pray, keeping your heart attentive and at peace.
exp.12:24:
What it says: Jesus tells how the master of the house gets up and shuts the door. Those who were left outside knock and ask, "Lord, open to us." He answers, "I do not know where you are from." The words "strive" and "master of the house" mean "make every effort" and "owner of the house."

Context: Jesus is speaking on the way to Jerusalem. Someone had asked him whether few are saved. He gives no number but warns with urgency: the chance to respond will not last forever, and being near Jesus or knowing his teachings is not enough.

For today: Do not put off your decision to follow Jesus. Look beyond religion or family tradition, and seek a sincere relationship with him, trusting in his grace and obeying him today.
exp.4:2:
He got into one of the boats, the one belonging to Simon (Peter), and asked him to push it out a little from the shore. Then he sat down and taught the people from the boat.

Luke tells us that the crowd was pressing around Jesus to hear the word of God, beside the lake of Gennesaret (the Sea of Galilee). Jesus used the boat as a simple place where everyone could see and hear him better. The fishermen had already gotten out to wash their nets, worn out after a night without catching anything.

Jesus can make use of whatever we offer him, even if it is little or if we are already tired. Your work, your home, or your time can serve so that others may hear God. Place what you have at his disposal.
exp.5:16:
He came down with them and stood on a level place. There his disciples were waiting for him, and a great crowd from all over Judea, from Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon. They came to hear him and to be healed. "Stood" means he stopped where he was; "to hear" means to listen to him; "crowd" here means ordinary people.

Luke tells this right after Jesus spent the night in prayer and chose the twelve. It is the start of what many call the Sermon on the Plain. Some think it is a version similar to Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and others think they are separate teachings; the Bible does not make this clear. Jesus draws even people from lands outside Judea.

For today: the people came with two needs, to listen and to be healed. We can come to Jesus in the same way, honestly, bringing him our doubts and wounds, and ready to hear what he says.
exp.3:1:
Luke tells us that Jesus spent forty days in the wilderness, and that the devil tempted him the whole time. He ate nothing in those days, and when they were over, he became hungry. "Tempted" means put to the test in order to make him fall. The fact that he became hungry shows that Jesus was truly human.

Luke, the narrator, has just told how Jesus was baptized and how the Spirit led him into the wilderness. This was no accident: the Spirit guided him there. Then comes the first temptation, and Jesus answers with Scripture. Some see here a parallel with Israel's forty years in the wilderness, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: trials do not always mean that God has moved away. Jesus faced temptation full of the Spirit and grounded in the Word. When you are weak or tired, seek God and remember what He has said.
exp.9:8:
Jesus tells his disciples that, in the town where they are welcomed, they should heal the sick and say to them: "The kingdom of God has come near to you." The words "heal," "say to them" and "has come near to you" are the older wording of "heal," "say to them" and "has come near to you."

Jesus speaks to the seventy-two whom he sends out two by two to the places where he himself plans to go afterward. He gives them simple instructions: rely on the hospitality of others, do not keep moving from house to house, and carry a double task, caring for people's bodies and announcing God. Healing was a sign that the kingdom, that is, God's loving rule, was near through Jesus.

Today we can draw near to those who suffer with concrete help, such as a visit, a meal or a prayer, and then humbly share the hope we have in God.
exp.0:36:
This verse says that nothing is beyond the power of God. What seems impossible to us is not impossible for Him. The word "thing" here means any matter or situation, and "impossible" means that it cannot be done.

The angel Gabriel speaks to Mary. She is frightened and surprised because he announces that she will have a son while still a virgin. To encourage her, the angel tells her that her relative Elizabeth, already old and called barren, is also expecting a child. That sign shows that God works beyond what is natural. Mary answers with trust and surrender: "Let it be to me according to your word."

For today: when you face a situation that seems to have no way out, do not just stare at the problem. Bring it to God in prayer and trust that He can act, even if you do not know how or when. Trusting is not understanding everything, but responding as Mary did.
exp.15:12:
Jesus says that no one can serve two masters at the same time. Sooner or later a person will love one of them more and will look down on the other. He then applies this: you cannot serve God and money. The word "cling" in the old wording means to stay attached to someone or be loyal to them, and "despise" means to treat with contempt. Here, "money" means wealth and possessions, seen as a master.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, just after the parable of the unfaithful manager. He teaches them to use money faithfully, since it is a small thing compared with what is eternal. The Pharisees, who loved money, were listening and mocked him. Jesus answers them that God knows their hearts.

For today: ask yourself whom your heart truly obeys when you decide how to use your money. You can start by giving generously and paying your debts honestly, so that money becomes your tool and not your master.
exp.14:15:
This verse says that the young man was so hungry that he wanted to fill his stomach with the carob pods, which were the food of the pigs. The word "fill" is what the verse means by "filled." Carob pods were hard pods used as fodder for animals. But no one gave him anything, not even that.

Jesus tells this parable of the prodigal son. The young man had asked for his inheritance and spent all of it. A great famine came, and he ended up tending pigs, a very humiliating job for a Jew, since the pig was considered an unclean animal. This is the lowest point of his fall, and right after it he comes to his senses and decides to return.

For today: when our choices leave us empty, we do not have to stay in that place. Recognizing our situation honestly can be the first step back to God, who receives us like a father.
exp.13:10:
Jesus says that whoever exalts himself above others will end up being brought low, and whoever humbles himself will end up being honored. "Exalteth himself" means that he lifts himself up, and "shall be abased" means that he will be put in a low place.

Jesus is invited to eat in the house of a leader of the Pharisees. There he noticed how the guests chose the best seats. So he told a parable about a wedding, to teach that God honors the humble and not those who seek applause.

Today we can practice this without showing off: at work, in church, or in the family, serve without seeking recognition, and rejoice when others receive honor. Let God be the one who lifts you up in his time.
exp.20:35:
Jesus says that we should stay alert and pray always. "Watch" means to stay awake and on guard. "Accounted worthy" means being considered capable, by grace, of escaping what is coming and of standing with confidence before the Son of man, who is Jesus himself.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple in Jerusalem, when he announces difficult things that will come: the destruction of the city and signs before his return. He has just warned them not to let their hearts grow dull through excess or through worries. Interpreters differ on how much this passage refers to the fall of Jerusalem and how much to the end of the age.

For today: set aside a fixed moment each day to pray and ask God to keep you alert. That way your worries will not distract you from what matters most: living ready to meet Christ.
exp.10:9:
This verse says that whoever asks with faith receives, whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks on the door it is opened. These are three ways of saying the same thing: drawing near to God with persistence.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after teaching them the Lord's Prayer. He tells the story of a man who asks a friend for bread at midnight, and this friend ends up getting up because of his persistence. Then Jesus makes the comparison: if a friend gives in, how much more the good Father, who gives the best to his children, as the bread, the fish and the egg that follow show.

For today: pray with confidence and without growing weary, speaking with God as a child speaks with his father. He listens and answers with kindness, though in his own time and his own way, which is not always the way we expect.
exp.22:14:
Pilate reminds the leaders and the people that Herod also found no fault in Jesus. The phrase "I sent you to him" means "I sent him to him." "Worthy of death" means that he has done nothing that deserves the death penalty.

Pilate speaks before the chief priests, the rulers, and the people. He had already questioned Jesus and found no crime. He had sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, and Herod sent him back without condemning him. Pilate uses that fact as a second witness in Jesus' favor. Even so, he later gives in to the pressure of the crowd.

For today: the truth can be plain and still be ignored out of fear of people. Let us ask God for the courage to do what is right, even when it is unpopular, and not to stay silent in the face of injustice.
exp.0:76:
This verse says that John the Baptist would give his people knowledge of how to be saved. "Salvation" here means being saved, not physical good health. That salvation would come through the forgiveness of sins.

The one speaking is Zechariah, John's father, filled with the Holy Spirit. He is prophesying after his son's birth. First he praises God for sending the Savior, and then he speaks to the child about his mission: to prepare the way of the Lord. Zechariah understands that salvation would not come through human effort, but through the mercy of God.

Today, this verse reminds us that what we need most is God's forgiveness. We can come to Him with sincerity, acknowledge our failures, and receive His forgiveness with gratitude. Then we can share that hope with someone else.
exp.19:22:
Jesus perceives that his questioners are not sincere. "Craftiness" means deceit or wickedness disguised as cleverness. "Tempt" means to test me with bad intent, hoping I will make a mistake. So Jesus asks them why they are trying to trap him.

The people asking are spies sent by the scribes and the chief priests. First they flatter him, but their plan is to make him fall. If Jesus said that taxes should not be paid, they would accuse him before Rome; if he said that they should, the people might reject him. Jesus sees their hearts and does not fall into the trap.

God knows our intentions, even when our words sound pleasant. Before asking God something or looking for answers in his Word, let us examine our hearts: are we truly seeking to obey and learn, or do we only want to justify ourselves? Let us approach him with sincerity.
exp.12:22:
Someone in the crowd asks Jesus whether only a few people are saved. Luke notes that Jesus is about to begin his answer. "Saved" here means being rescued from God's judgment and brought into his kingdom.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, teaching in towns and villages. He has just spoken about the kingdom of God through the parables of the mustard seed and the yeast, which show small but real growth. A man asks him a curious question, almost like a debate. Jesus does not give him a number, but turns the attention to each listener's personal response.

For today: instead of speculating about how many will be saved, we can ask ourselves honestly whether we are trusting in Christ and following him. Today is a good day to answer him, without putting it off.
exp.9:17:
Jesus says that he saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, meaning quickly and visibly.

Jesus speaks with the seventy disciples who return joyful because the demons obeyed them. He answers that the power of the enemy is already being defeated. Interpreters explain this saying in several ways: the original fall of Satan, his defeat through the work of Christ, or both. The Bible gives no further detail here.

For today: you can face fear and evil with confidence, because Christ has the victory. But do not place your joy in what you accomplish, but in belonging to God, for your name is written in heaven.
exp.3:5:
Here the devil tells Jesus that he will give him "all this power", that is, all the power and authority over the kingdoms of the world, and "the glory of them", that is, their wealth and splendor. He claims that all of it has been handed over to him and that he gives it to whomever he wishes.

The devil speaks during Jesus' temptation in the wilderness. He has just shown him the kingdoms of the earth, and now he offers a shortcut to them, but in exchange for worship. Jesus does not argue over whether the devil has any influence in the world; interpreters understand this in different ways. What he does is answer with Scripture and reject the offer.

For today: when something promises us success or quick power at the cost of giving up what is right, let us remember that God alone is worthy of our loyalty. Shortcuts that lead us away from Him are never worth what they cost.
exp.8:6:
This verse tells that Herod, who was called tetrarch because he ruled over a fourth part of the region, heard about everything Jesus was doing. He was perplexed, that is, confused and not knowing what to think, because people gave different explanations. Some were saying that John the Baptist had risen from the dead.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking. The disciples had just gone out to preach and to heal in the villages, and because of this the name of Jesus became known everywhere. Herod had ordered John's execution, so the news troubled him. The verses that follow show that he wanted to see Jesus, although it is not said that he sought him in faith.

For today: it is not enough to hear things about Jesus or to be curious. Ask yourself honestly who he is for you, and seek him in the Gospels with a heart willing to believe.
exp.10:4:
Jesus begins a parable with a question: which of you has a friend whom you would go to at midnight to ask for three loaves of bread?

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, just after teaching them the Lord's Prayer. They had asked him to teach them to pray. With this story, Jesus illustrates how to pray with confidence and persistence. The verses that follow explain that the friend asks because a visitor has arrived and he has nothing to offer him. Many understand that the central point is the character of God, who is far better than the troublesome friend in the story.

For today: bring God your real needs, including the urgent ones or those that weigh on your heart, and keep praying with confidence, knowing that he hears you as a good Father.
exp.22:27:
Jesus turns to the women who are following him, weeping, and speaks to them tenderly: "Daughters of Jerusalem." He asks them not to weep for him, but to weep for themselves and for their children. "Turning unto them" means that he turned around to look at them.

Jesus is on his way to the cross, so weak that Simon of Cyrene carries his cross. Many follow him, and some women weep for him. His words that follow speak of days of great distress. Many think he is referring to the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem, though some also see a broader warning. He does not reject their compassion, but he looks beyond his own suffering.

We may feel sorrow for Jesus, but we also need to examine our hearts. Today, rather than staying only with emotion, it is good to repent, trust in him, and pray for our families.
exp.5:15:
This verse completes the list of the twelve apostles whom Jesus chose. It names Judas, the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot. The phrase "brother of James" can also be understood as "son of James"; the Greek text allows both ideas. In other passages this Judas is called Thaddaeus.

Luke is the one who tells this. Before this, Jesus had spent the night praying on the mountain, and in the morning he chose twelve of his disciples. Luke names Judas Iscariot as the one who betrayed him because he wants his readers to know from the beginning what happened afterward. Then Jesus comes down with them to a level place, where the crowd comes to hear him and to be healed.

For today: Jesus called ordinary people, with their strengths and weaknesses, and even one who would fail him. This reminds us that being close to Jesus requires a sincere heart, not merely a title or a position. Today we can ask him to examine our hearts and keep us faithful.
exp.7:37:
This verse tells us that the man who had been freed from the demons begged Jesus to let him go with him. But Jesus did not allow it; he sent him away, that is, he told him to go back home. The sentence is left open, because what Jesus said to him comes in the next verse.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke. The man had been possessed by demons in the region of the Gadarenes, and now he was well. The people of the place, frightened, had asked Jesus to leave, and Jesus was already getting into the boat. It is natural that the man wanted to stay with the one who had rescued him. Jesus gave him another task: to tell what God had done for him.

For today: following Jesus does not always mean going far away or doing something extraordinary. Sometimes it means staying at home, with our family and neighbors, and telling them simply what God has done in our life.
exp.9:14:
Jesus says to Capernaum that it thought of itself as "lifted up to heaven," that is, exalted and privileged. But he announces that it will be "brought down" to the "depths." Here the original word refers to Hades, the place of the dead, and expresses a total fall, not necessarily a detailed description of the final punishment.

Jesus speaks to the seventy whom he sent out two by two to announce the kingdom. He warns that those who reject the message face serious consequences. Capernaum was the center of his ministry in Galilee, where he saw many miracles and heard many teachings. Its unbelief was more serious because it had received more light. This statement recalls the language of Isaiah 14:13-15 against the pride of Babylon.

Receiving much from God brings responsibility. If we have heard the Bible many times, it is not enough merely to know it or admire it. Today we can ask ourselves, with humility, whether we are responding with a repentant and obedient heart to what God has already shown us.
exp.23:42:
It says that the risen Jesus received the fish and the honeycomb, and ate them while his disciples watched him. "Took" means that he received what they gave him. "Before them" means that he did it in full view of everyone.

Luke tells us that the disciples were full of joy, but also of amazement and doubt. Jesus asks them whether they have anything to eat, to show them that he was not a ghost or merely a vision. It was him, alive, with a real body. Afterward he explains to them that everything that happened fulfilled the Scriptures. Some scholars see here clear evidence of the bodily resurrection.

For today: our faith does not rest on a vague idea, but on a living Christ who draws near to people with doubts. If you have questions, bring them to him with sincerity; he is patient and knows how to meet you in everyday life.
exp.8:32:
Peter sees Jesus in his glory with Moses and Elijah, and as they are about to leave, he proposes to stay there. He offers to make three shelters, simple huts or booths, one for each of them. The text notes that Peter did not know what he was saying.

Peter speaks in the middle of an astonishing scene: Jesus is transfigured on the mountain, and Moses and Elijah talk with him about his departure, that is, his death and leaving in Jerusalem. Peter, having just woken up and frightened, wants to prolong the moment. Then the voice of the Father speaks, saying to listen to him, which shows that Jesus is the one who must be heard above all others.

We can love special moments with God, but they are not a place to stay. God shows us his glory to encourage us to listen to Jesus and to follow him also in ordinary life and in what is hard.
exp.11:12:
A man from the crowd that was listening to Jesus asks him to step into a family problem: to tell his brother to share the inheritance with him. "Teacher" was a title of respect, and "divide" here means to split or share out.

The one speaking is someone from the crowd that was listening to Jesus. Up to that moment, Jesus had been talking about confessing him without fear and trusting the Holy Spirit. Suddenly, this man breaks in with a matter of money. The law of Moses governed inheritances, and teachers often settled these disputes. Jesus refused to be a judge and went to the heart of the matter: greed.

For today: before we fight over what is rightfully ours, let us ask what is in our hearts. We can seek peace in the family and remember that life is worth more than possessions.
exp.11:11:
The explanation says that the Holy Ghost will help the disciples at the very moment they need it, showing them what to say. "Will teach you" means that he will guide or instruct them. "In the same hour" means at that very instant. "Anxious" (in the previous verse) means worried or deeply concerned.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and there is a large crowd around them. He warns them that they will be brought before religious and civil authorities for following him. He wants them not to live in fear or be troubled about preparing a perfect defense. He promises them God's help in that difficult hour.

Today, when you find yourself having to speak about your faith or defend what is right, do not freeze in fear. Prepare yourself through prayer and the Word, and trust that God will give you calm and the right words at the right moment.
exp.12:33:
Jesus speaks to Jerusalem with sorrow. He tells the city that it has killed the prophets and stoned those whom God sent to it. He wanted many times to gather its people, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they would not. The explanation of the word "would" is that it means willing, and "ye would not" shows that they refused.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, and he has just answered a threat from Herod, whom he calls a fox. He knows that he will suffer death there, as other prophets did. His words do not sound like hatred but like deep grief. The verses that follow say that the house would be left "desolate," and many understand this as a reference to the temple or to the city.

For today: God invites us with tenderness, but he does not force us. If you feel that he is calling you, do not harden your heart. Come under his care today.
exp.22:40:
Here the criminal who does not mock speaks with sincerity. He says that he and his companion receive a just punishment, because they are paying for what they did. The phrase rendered in the source as an emphatic "truly" is simply rendered here as "indeed," and the word "suffer" carries its ordinary meaning of enduring a penalty. By contrast, he affirms that Jesus "hath done nothing amiss," that is, that he is innocent.

The one speaking is one of the two criminals crucified alongside Jesus. The other was mocking him and demanding a miracle. This one, however, rebukes his companion, acknowledges his own guilt, and defends Jesus. Shortly afterward he asks, "Lord, remember me," and Jesus promises him paradise.

For today: honesty before God opens the door to his forgiveness. Instead of making excuses or blaming others, we can acknowledge our faults with simplicity and trust in the mercy of Jesus, who receives those who come to him in faith.
exp.8:24:
Jesus asks what good it does a person to gain the whole world if in the end they lose themselves or are cast away. "Gain" here means to get or acquire something, and the verse's own word "advantaged" means "helped" or "benefited." Nothing that a person might acquire is worth what their own life and soul are worth.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, shortly after Peter recognized him as the Christ and after Jesus announced his coming suffering. He teaches them that following him means denying oneself and taking up the cross every day. This question explains why it is worth it: to save one's life at any cost is to lose it.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are pursuing most strongly: money, success, or approval. Before we sacrifice faith, honesty, or family for those goals, let us remember that following Jesus is what truly gives life.
exp.2:37:
This verse ends the list of Jesus' ancestors, going backward. It says that Cainan was the son of Enos, Enos was the son of Seth, Seth was the son of Adam, and Adam was the son of God. The names "Seth" and "Adam" are the figures Seth and Adam.

Luke, the author of the gospel, presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. Unlike Matthew, which goes back to Abraham, Luke goes back to Adam. In this way he shows that Jesus belongs to all of humanity, not only to Israel. Some names in the list vary among the ancient manuscripts, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: your worth does not depend on your family or your past. We all come from God and have a place before Him. Today, treat every person with the respect due to someone created by God.
exp.16:7:
Jesus asks a question that expects the answer "yes." When the servant comes in from the field, the master does not tell him to sit down and eat. He asks him to prepare supper, to tie up his clothing so he can work freely, and to serve him until he has finished. Afterward, the servant may eat and drink.

Jesus speaks to his disciples just after teaching them about faith like a grain of mustard seed. He uses the custom of his time, in which a servant carried out his duty without expecting praise. The following verse clarifies the teaching: even after obeying, we are servants who have only done what we were obligated to do. Some see here a warning against religious pride.

Serve God and others with humility, without thinking that He owes you anything or seeking applause. Serving is already a privilege.
exp.11:54:
Jesus says that when people feel the south wind blow, which is the wind from the south, they already know it is going to be hot, and so it happens.

Jesus speaks to the crowd after warning his disciples about the divisions that following him would bring. He uses the weather as a comparison: if people know how to read the sky, they should be able to recognize that a decisive time had arrived with Jesus. That is why, in the verse that follows, he calls them hypocrites, because they did not want to see what was obvious.

For today: we give great attention to practical things, such as the weather forecast, money, or work. Ask yourself whether you give the same attention to what God shows you in his Word and in your conscience, and respond with humility and obedience.
exp.12:1:
Jesus answers with a question to those who told him that Pilate had killed some Galileans while they were offering sacrifices. He asks whether they think these men suffered this way because they were worse sinners than all the other Galileans. The word "suffered" means endured, and "suppose ye" means "do you think."

Some people brought this news to Jesus, perhaps assuming the tragedy was a special punishment from God. In that time many believed that suffering showed a great sin. Jesus corrects that idea, and in the verses that follow he calls everyone to repentance. The Bible says nothing more about this historical event, so we do not know other details.

When we see someone suffer, let us avoid judging them or thinking that they deserved it. Instead, let us use such news to examine our own hearts, draw near to God with humility, and show compassion to those who are suffering.
exp.18:24:
Those standing nearby point out to the nobleman that the faithful servant already has ten minas. A mina was a considerable sum of money, equal to several months of wages. It is a brief objection, as if they were saying, "Why give more to someone who already has so much?"

Jesus tells this parable near Jerusalem, at a time when many believed the kingdom of God would appear right away. A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and leaves a mina with each servant to put to work. When he returns, he rewards the faithful servant and rebukes the one who kept his mina out of fear. Those present are surprised, but the nobleman answers in the verse that follows.

God entrusts us with gifts, time, and opportunities, not so that we hold on to them out of fear, but so that we use them faithfully. Today you might ask yourself: what do I have that God has given me, and how can I use it to serve others?
exp.10:42:
Jesus says "Woe to you" to the Pharisees. "Woe" is an expression of grief and serious warning. He points out that they love to take the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and to receive greetings in the markets, where everyone could see them.

Jesus is speaking in the house of a Pharisee, where he has just eaten. Earlier he told them that they were careful about small details, such as tithing mint and herbs, but neglected justice and the love of God. Now he shows another problem: they were seeking the applause of people more than seeking to please God.

For today: examine your heart when you serve in the church or help others. Ask yourself whether you do it out of love for God or so that others will see you. Ask him to give you humility, and serve also in what is hidden.
exp.23:24:
The risen Jesus speaks with two disciples who are walking toward Emmaus, without them recognizing him. He calls them "fools", that is, people lacking understanding, and "slow of heart", meaning slow to believe. The problem was not a lack of information, but that they did not believe everything the prophets had already announced.

The two travelers were sad because Jesus had been crucified. They had heard the women's account of the angels and the empty tomb, but they did not fully believe it. Jesus corrects them firmly, yet with care, and immediately explains the Scriptures, beginning with Moses and the prophets.

Today we too can fall into believing only part of what God says. When you doubt or feel discouraged, return to the Bible and read it in full, asking God to open your heart to understand it and to trust it.
exp.23:16:
The risen Jesus comes near to two disciples who are walking and asks them what they are talking about. The English verse uses "communications" for what they are discussing, which means the conversation between them. The verse also says they are "sad," so he notices the sorrow on their faces.

The one speaking is Jesus, but they do not recognize him, because their eyes were kept from seeing who he was. They are on the road to Emmaus, discouraged by the crucifixion. Jesus already knows the answer, but he asks so that they can express their pain and so that he can later teach them from the Scriptures.

For today: Jesus invites us to tell him what saddens us, even though he already knows it. We can speak to him honestly about our doubts and disappointments, trusting that he walks beside us, even when we do not perceive him.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that Jesus, on hearing the centurion's words, was amazed at him. He turned around and told the people who were following him that he had not found such great faith, not even in Israel. The sentence explaining the old wording is removed, since the verse above does not use those words and the reader needs only the meaning, which is that Jesus was astonished with admiration and turned to face the crowd.

The one speaking is Luke, narrating what Jesus said. The centurion was a Roman officer, not a Jew. He had sent word that he did not feel worthy to have Jesus come into his house, and he trusted that Jesus' word alone was enough to heal his servant, just as he himself gave orders and his soldiers obeyed. Jesus praises that humble trust.

For today: true faith trusts that Jesus can act by his word alone, even when we cannot see how. We can come to Him with humility, without claiming merit, and trust in His power and His goodness.
exp.0:51:
He has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the humble. "Brought down" means to pull down or remove; "rulers" are those who hold authority; "lifted up" is the word used for raising someone; "humble" are the lowly, those of little standing. It is a contrast: those who think themselves great fall, and the little ones are honored.

Mary speaks these words in the song known as the Magnificat. She has just learned that she will be the mother of Jesus, and she praises God for the way he acts. She speaks in the past tense, as something God is accustomed to doing, and also as a promise that is already beginning to be fulfilled. Scholars debate how much of this is a spiritual image and how much speaks of real social change.

For today: do not trust in your position, your achievements, or your strength. Live with humility, treat everyone with respect, and if you feel small or forgotten, remember that God sees you.
exp.8:58:
Jesus invites a man with a simple command: "Follow me." The man agrees, but first asks for permission to go and bury his father. Two ways of understanding his request are possible: that his father had already died, or that the man wanted to stay at home until his father passed away someday. The text does not make this clear.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, and he has just spoken with someone who promised to follow him without thinking about the cost. Now he calls this other man, and Jesus's reply in the next verse shows that the kingdom of God must come first, even before duties that seem very respectable.

Today, this invites us to examine what we put ahead of obeying Jesus. Even good things can become an excuse for delay. Ask yourself: which step of obedience am I leaving for "later"?
exp.0:73:
He says that God promised Abraham that he would deliver us from our enemies so that we could serve him without fear. "Without fear" means without anxiety or threat. "Delivered" means rescued or set free. The deliverance is not an end in itself: its purpose is to serve God.

Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, speaks, filled with the Holy Spirit, in his song of praise. He has just regained his speech and celebrates that God is keeping his covenant with Abraham. His words look forward to the coming of the Savior, and then he announces that his son will prepare the way of the Lord. Some understand the "enemies" as oppressive nations, others also as sin and death; the text allows both readings.

For today: God does not free you only so that you may be at ease, but so that you may serve him in freedom. Today, hand over to God one specific fear, and take a step of service without letting that fear hold you back.
exp.23:26:
This verse tells how the risen Jesus began with the books of Moses and continued through all the prophets. In all the Scriptures, he explained to them what those writings said about himself.

Two disciples were walking toward Emmaus, sad over the death of Jesus, and they did not recognize him. Luke is the one who tells the story. Jesus had just gently corrected their difficulty in believing what the prophets had said. Then he showed them that the suffering of the Christ and his glory had already been announced. The text does not say which exact passages he used.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to help you see Jesus in it. Read calmly, without hurry, and let Christ be the center that unites everything you read.
exp.12:13:
He says the leader of the synagogue was angry because Jesus healed a woman on the Sabbath. He did not speak directly to Jesus but to the crowd: there are six days for work, so come to be healed on those days, not on the Sabbath. "Ruler of the synagogue" means the person in charge or leader of the local worship. "Crowd" is what is meant by the people gathered there.

The one speaking is this religious leader. The woman had been bent over for eighteen years, and Jesus had just set her free while he was teaching. He thought that healing was forbidden "work" on the Sabbath. Jesus would answer him by calling him a hypocrite and reminding him that everyone looks after their animals on the Sabbath.

For today: let us not allow rules or customs to make us hard toward the pain of others. Before judging someone, let us ask whether we are seeing that person with God's compassion.
exp.6:28:
All the people who heard Jesus, including the tax collectors (who were looked down on by many), "justified God." This means they acknowledged that God is righteous and that his way was right. They showed this by being baptized with the baptism of John.

Jesus is speaking about John the Baptist, the messenger who prepared the way. Many who heard him repented. Some understand these words to be Jesus' own, while others think Luke added them as a comment. Either way, the contrast is clear: ordinary people accepted God's plan, but the Pharisees and the teachers of the law rejected it, as the following verse shows.

For today: humility opens the heart to God. Let us ask him to help us recognize our faults and receive his word without pride or excuses.
exp.6:49:
Jesus tells the woman that her faith has saved her and that she can go in peace. The word "saved" here speaks of being rescued from the guilt of sin. "Go in peace" was a common farewell, but here it also means she can now live at rest, reconciled with God.

Jesus is having dinner at the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known as a sinner came in, wept at the feet of Jesus, dried them with her hair, and anointed them with perfume. The guests were scandalized when Jesus forgave her sins. He responds by looking not at what she had done, but at her faith, which showed itself in her love and humility.

For today: you do not need to make yourself presentable before you come near to Jesus. Come with sincerity and trust, and receive his forgiveness. Then live in peace, without carrying guilt that he has already taken away.
exp.21:10:
Jesus sends two disciples (Peter and John, according to verse 8) to prepare the Passover meal. He tells them to speak to the owner of a house and ask him where the guest room is, the room where Jesus will eat with them. "The master of the house" means the owner or head of the household. Jesus says he wants to eat the Passover with his disciples.

Jesus speaks these words shortly before he is arrested. His crucifixion was near, and this meal would be his last supper with his disciples. He gives very precise instructions, and the disciples find everything just as he said. Some see here his knowledge of what was to come; others think there may have been an arrangement made beforehand. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when God asks you for something you do not fully understand, obey step by step. The disciples simply followed the instructions, and they discovered that Jesus had already prepared the way.
exp.10:25:
It says that the unclean spirit returns to the house he came out of, but this time he brings seven other spirits even worse than himself. All of them enter and live there, and that person's final condition is worse than the first. The word for "last" in the original is rendered here simply as "last," and "that man" refers to this person.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd, after some had accused him of casting out demons by the power of Satan. He answers them with this warning. The house was swept clean and put in order, but it stood empty. Being cleaned was not enough; someone had to occupy it. That is why Jesus goes on to say that blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.

For today: it is not enough to leave something bad behind; we must fill our lives with God. Read his Word, obey it, and seek his company every day, so that your heart does not remain empty.
exp.1:42:
When the days of the feast were over and they set out for home, Joseph and Mary began the journey back. Jesus, who was twelve years old, stayed behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not realize it. The phrase "when they had fulfilled the days" means that the festival had already come to an end. Jerusalem is the city where the family had been.

Here Luke speaks as the narrator, telling the story. He tells us that the family went up to the feast every year, as was the custom. Most likely they traveled in a group with relatives and acquaintances, and that is why they assumed Jesus was with them. Luke does not say this was a serious oversight, only that they did not know.

For today: we sometimes take for granted that Jesus is with us, without stopping to check. It is worth examining from time to time whether we truly keep him in mind on our daily path, through prayer and through reading his Word.
exp.21:38:
Luke tells us that Jesus left the city and went out to the Mount of Olives, as he was accustomed to do. His disciples followed him. The word "was wont" means "was accustomed to," and "went" appears in the verse with its usual spelling, so nothing needs to be explained about it.

It is the night after the Last Supper. Luke, the narrator, tells us that Jesus had already spoken about his coming suffering. Going to this place was not something done on the spur of the moment: it was a known spot where he often withdrew. There he goes to pray before he is arrested. The disciples go with him, though they do not fully understand what is coming.

For today: Jesus had the habit of seeking God in a place and time of prayer. When trials come, that habit sustains us. We can set aside a regular time, even a brief one, to pray and rest in God.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that Zechariah will feel joy and gladness over the son who is about to be born, and that many other people will also rejoice when he is born. The word "rejoice" means to be glad. "You will have joy" is a promise: the happiness will not be small or short-lived.

The one speaking is the angel, who in verse 19 identifies himself as Gabriel. Zechariah was a priest, and he was frightened by the appearance. The angel calms him and announces that God has heard his prayer: he and Elizabeth would have a son, John. The following verses explain why many would rejoice: John would prepare the people for the Lord.

For today: God can answer our prayers in his own time and in ways that bring blessing to others, not only to us. We can keep praying with patience, trusting that he hears us, and share the joy with others when he answers.
exp.11:16:
This rich man is thinking to himself, alone. His field produced such a large harvest that he no longer has room to store it. He asks himself what he should do. "Fruits" here means his crops, and "bestow" means to store or keep them.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd, and someone had asked him to step into a dispute over an inheritance. For that reason he warns against all greed and tells this parable. Notice that the man speaks only to himself: he does not think of God or of others. His problem is not wealth in itself, but the direction his heart is turned.

Today, when we receive more than we expected, before deciding how to keep it, we can ask ourselves: how can I thank God and bless others with this?
exp.4:0:
This verse tells us that Jesus was standing by the shore of the lake of Gennesaret, and that a large crowd pressed in around him to hear the word of God. The phrase "pressed upon him" means that the people were crowding together, pushing toward him to be close to him. The lake of Gennesaret is another name for the Sea of Galilee.

Here Luke, the narrator, begins a new scene in Jesus' ministry in Galilee. There is no earlier context in this passage, but the verses that follow show that Jesus got into Simon's boat so that he could teach the crowd better. What drew the people was their desire to hear God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we hunger for the Word of God as those people did. Setting aside a time each day to read the Bible, even if it is only a little, and to listen to it with attention, is a good way to draw near to Jesus.
exp.21:21:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, that is, himself, goes to his death as it was determined, that is, established beforehand in God's plan. But he warns with sorrow: "woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed!" The word "betrayed" means handed over to his enemies, given up into their hands.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper with his disciples, just after sharing the cup of the new covenant. He has just said that one of those at the table will betray him. His grief is real. Christians have debated how God's plan and Judas's responsibility fit together, but the text affirms both: Jesus moves toward the cross with purpose, and the betrayer remains guilty for his decision.

For today: God can use even what is unjust to accomplish his purpose, but that does not remove our responsibility for our choices. Let us examine our hearts and be faithful to Jesus, especially when it is hard.
exp.8:13:
This verse says there were about five thousand men there. Jesus asked his disciples to have the people sit down in groups, or "ranchos," of fifty people each.

Jesus is speaking. It is already getting toward evening, and the disciples ask him to send the crowd away so they can find food in the villages, because they are in a deserted place. Jesus answers that they themselves should give the people something to eat, even though they have only five loaves and two fish. By arranging the people in groups, everything is done calmly and in an orderly way. Some think this also made the distribution of the food easier, but the text does not explain it.

For today: when a need seems too great, let us do with faith what Jesus asks of us, step by step, and place in his hands the little that we have.
exp.16:30:
Jesus says that on "that day," the one who is on the rooftop (the flat roof of the house) must not go down to get his belongings, meaning his things or possessions. And the one who is in the field must not turn back either. It is an order to flee without looking back.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples about the coming of the Son of Man. He compares that day to the time of Lot in Sodom, when everything changed suddenly. His point is that there will be little time, and attachment to possessions can cost dearly. Then he adds: "Remember Lot's wife." Interpreters debate exactly which moment he is describing, but the call to be ready is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have a grip on our hearts. Living with open hands, trusting God more than our possessions, prepares us to obey him without hesitation.
exp.20:15:
Jesus says that his followers will be handed over to the authorities even by people very close to them: parents, brothers, relatives and friends. To be "handed over" means to be betrayed or reported. And the phrase "some of you" means that some of them would be put to death for their faith.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple, shortly before his arrest, announcing what would come before and after the fall of Jerusalem. He is preparing them for persecution. He warns them clearly so they will not be caught off guard, and he promises to give them words and wisdom. He then adds that not a hair of their head will be lost, which many understand as God's care and final hope, not as an absence of suffering.

For today: if following Jesus brings you rejection, even within your family, you are not alone. Respond with gentleness, pray for those who reject you, and trust that God sustains you.
exp.5:33:
Jesus says that lending only to those who can repay us has no special merit. "What thank have ye?" means: "what reward or credit will you have?" Even "sinners," that is, those who do not follow God, lend to others expecting to receive back "as much again," that is, the same amount they gave.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, in the passage called the Sermon on the Plain. He teaches that the love of his followers must go beyond an exchange of favors. He asks them to love even their enemies, to give without expecting anything in return, and so to resemble God, who is merciful to all.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I help only those who will return the favor? This week, try to help someone who cannot repay you with time, money, or support, without seeking anything in return, trusting that God sees that gesture.
exp.3:15:
Luke tells us that Jesus came to Nazareth, the town where he had been brought up. As was his custom, on the Sabbath he went into the synagogue, which was the gathering place for prayer and for hearing the Scriptures. There he stood up to read aloud.

Luke is the one narrating. Jesus had just returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, teaching in the synagogues, and people spoke well of him. This moment sets the stage for his first message in Nazareth, where he will read Isaiah's prophecy about good news for the poor and freedom for the captives.

For today: Jesus had the habit of gathering with others to hear the Word of God. We can set aside a fixed time each week to come together and read the Bible, not as an empty routine, but to listen to God.
exp.21:60:
Luke 22:61 describes what happened right after the third denial: the Lord turned and looked at Peter. At that moment Peter remembered what the Lord had told him, that before the rooster crowed he would deny him three times. The phrase "looked at Peter" simply means that Jesus looked at Peter.

Luke is narrating the night of Jesus' arrest. Peter had promised to follow him even to death, but now, out of fear, he said he did not know Jesus. The crowing of the rooster confirmed the warning. The texts do not say what expression was on Jesus' face; they only say that he looked at him. Afterward Peter went out and wept bitterly.

For today: when we fail, we should not hide or make excuses. The look of Jesus can awaken sincere repentance. Remembering his word leads us to return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.23:15:
The explanation says that the two disciples walking toward Emmaus could not recognize Jesus, even though he was at their side. "Their eyes were holden" means they were held back or kept from seeing, as if something covered their sight. The text says "that they should not know him," but it does not explain how this happened or the exact reason.

Luke tells what happened on the same day as the resurrection. The two disciples were sad and talking about the death of Jesus. Then Jesus himself came near and walked with them. Some believe God kept them from recognizing him so that he could first guide them through the Scriptures; others emphasize their grief and their doubts. The text does not make this clear.

Often Jesus is near even when we do not notice him because of sadness or confusion. You can speak to him honestly, open the Bible, and ask him to help you see him with faith.
exp.23:13:
This verse says that two disciples were walking and talking with each other about everything that had taken place in Jerusalem. The word translated "happened" in the verse above is the one the commentary is pointing to, and it refers to the death of Jesus and the news of the empty tomb.

Luke tells us it was the same day as the resurrection. These two followers of Jesus, who were not among the Eleven, were going from Jerusalem to Emmaus, about seven miles (sixty stadia). They were talking in confusion and sadness, trying to make sense of what had happened. They did not yet know that Jesus was alive, and in the next verse He Himself comes near to walk with them.

For today: when we do not understand what God allows, it is good to speak honestly with other believers, without pretending to be strong. We can also remember that Jesus draws near to those who, in the middle of their doubt and pain, still keep searching for answers.
exp.21:32:
Peter answers Jesus with great confidence. Peter says, "Lord, I am ready to go with you, both into prison and to death."

Peter speaks at the Last Supper. Jesus had just told him that Satan had asked to sift them like wheat, and that He had prayed for Peter's faith not to fail. Peter does not see his own weakness, but Jesus does: He tells him that he will deny Him three times that very night. Even so, Jesus promises that He will return and strengthen his brothers.

It is good to want to be faithful, but we should not trust only in our own strength. Recognize your weakness, ask God for help, and remember that if you fall, Christ prays for you and invites you to rise again.
exp.22:21:
Pilate speaks to the crowd for the third time. He asks what evil Jesus has done and states that he has found in him no fault that deserves death. He says he will chastise him, that is, have him flogged, and then let him go, that is, set him free.

Pilate was the Roman governor and had the authority to decide. He wanted to release Jesus, but the crowd, along with the chief priests, kept shouting for him to be crucified. Pilate tried to calm them with a lesser punishment. Even so, his proposal was not just, for he declared Jesus innocent while at the same time wanting to punish him.

Knowing what is right is not enough; courage is needed to act. When we feel pressure from others, let us ask God for firmness to defend the truth and justice, even when it costs us.
exp.5:11:
This verse tells how Jesus went up a mountain to pray in those days and spent the whole night talking with God.

Lucas records this right after Jesus healed a man's hand on the Sabbath, and some religious leaders became furious with Him. Then, at daybreak, Jesus chose twelve disciples, whom He named apostles. So the night of prayer comes before a very important decision. The text does not say what He asked for in His prayer.

For today: before making a big decision, or when you feel pressure, set aside a quiet time to pray. You do not need to pray all night; it is enough to seek God sincerely and wait for His direction.
exp.13:15:
Jesus answers with a parable: a man prepared a great dinner and invited many people. The old wording is simple: "invited" is the sense of the word "bade" in the verse, and "great supper" refers to an important banquet, not an ordinary meal.

Jesus is eating in the house of a prominent Pharisee, on a Sabbath. One of the guests has just said that blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of heaven. Jesus answers him with this story. Many interpret the host as representing God and the supper as speaking of his kingdom, although the text of this verse only begins the account.

God invites with generosity, and the invitation is real. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are letting our occupations keep us from responding to him. A practical good step is to set aside a moment each day to pray and read his Word, before everything else.
exp.17:4:
The judge, though he was not a just man, decided to help the widow only because her persistence was wearing him out. The verse's wording "troubleth me" means that she was bothering him and causing him distress.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples to teach them that they should always pray and not lose heart. The judge does not represent God but serves as a contrast: if even an unjust judge responds to persistence, how much more will God, who is good, attend to his children who cry out to him.

Today, this invites us not to give up on prayer when the answer is slow. We can keep presenting our needs to God with confidence, knowing that he hears us with love, and not out of weariness as the judge did.
exp.19:39:
After that conversation, the explanation says, no one dared to ask Jesus any more questions. Here the reader should simply take the verse's wording: they no longer had the nerve to keep testing him with questions.

Jesus was in the temple in Jerusalem, and several religious groups were asking him hard questions to trap him. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, had just brought him a complicated case. Jesus answered them clearly, and even some scribes said, "Teacher, you have spoken well." After that, no one else felt bold enough to question him. Then Jesus himself asked a question about the Christ.

For today: we can come to Jesus with sincere questions in order to learn, not to win an argument. He welcomes the person who truly seeks him. But we should also ask ourselves whether we are listening to his answer with humility.
exp.15:24:
Abraham answers the rich man by calling him "son" and asks him to remember his life. He says the rich man received his good things, that is, comforts and riches, while Lazarus received evil things, that is, suffering and need. Now the situation is reversed: Lazarus is comforted and the rich man is tormented.

Jesus tells this parable. Abraham speaks with the rich man, who has asked for relief. Before this, the rich man lived without noticing the poor man who lay at his gate. Interpreters debate how much of the scene literally describes the afterlife, but all agree that it teaches about God's justice and the danger of indifference.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we have overlooked at our gate without ever really seeing them. What God has given us is not only for our own comfort, but also to help with generosity and compassion while there is still time.
exp.23:14:
As they walked along, talking and debating with each other about everything that had happened, Jesus himself came up and began to walk with them.

This verse tells of two disciples walking and talking together, discussing what had taken place. While they talked, Jesus himself came near and started walking with them. The phrase "asking one another" means that they put questions to each other and voiced their doubts among themselves.

It is the day of the resurrection. Luke, who is telling the story, says that these two followers of Jesus, who were not among the Twelve, were traveling from Jerusalem to Emmaus, about seven miles away. They were confused and sad over the death of Jesus. According to the next verse, something kept them from recognizing him. The text does not explain how this happened.

Jesus draws near just as they are speaking about their doubts and their grief. You can speak honestly to him about what you do not understand, even when you feel confused. He can be with you on the road even if you do not notice him right away.
exp.13:20:
What it says: The servant returned and told his master everything. The master of the house was angry and ordered him to go out quickly into the squares and streets of the city to bring in the poor, the maimed (people with a damaged hand or arm), the lame, and the blind.

Context: Jesus tells this parable while eating in the house of a Pharisee. The first invited guests made excuses and turned down the invitation to the great banquet. Many understand that the banquet represents the kingdom of God, and that Jesus shows the open invitation extended to those whom society despised. Some see the first invited guests as the religious leaders, although the text does not say this in those words.
