For today: God invites everyone with grace, regardless of their condition. Ask yourself whether some good occupation is keeping you from responding to Him, and to whom you could extend an invitation to the table today.
exp.8:59:
Jesus answers a man who wanted to wait to bury his father before following him. He says that the dead should bury their own dead. It is a figurative phrase: he probably calls "dead" those who have no spiritual life. Then he tells the man to go and proclaim the kingdom of God. To proclaim means to make known the good news.

Jesus speaks while walking with his disciples toward Jerusalem. He has just said that he himself has nowhere to lay his head, so following him involves a cost. It is not clear whether the father had already died or whether the man was asking to wait until he died. Scholars understand it in several ways. What is certain is that Jesus places the call of the kingdom above everything else.

For today: ask yourself what good but postponable thing is standing in the way of your response to God. Take a concrete step of obedience today, such as praying, forgiving, or sharing your faith with someone.
exp.2:29:
This verse is part of a list of Jesus' ancestors. The phrase "which was" is a way of saying "which was the son of." Here appear Levi, Simeon, Judah, Joseph, Jonan, and Eliakim. These are probably not the famous patriarchs of the Old Testament, but other men who bore the same names, which was common among the Jews.

Luke, the author, presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. The list goes backward, passes through David, and reaches as far as Adam. With it he shows that Jesus is truly human and an heir of the promises made to Israel. Scholars do not agree on whether this line follows the family of Joseph or the family of Mary.

For today: of most of these men we know only the name, but God used them in his plan. Your simple life also matters to him. Serve him faithfully, even when no one sees you.
exp.7:28:
This verse explains why the man was crying out to Jesus. Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of him. That spirit had been seizing the man with violence for a long time. They tied him with chains and shackles (iron rings for the feet) and kept watch over him, but he broke the bonds, and the demon drove him out into lonely places.

The one telling the story is Luke, the physician who wrote this Gospel. He pauses the scene to show how serious the case was: no one had been able to control this man. This shows that Jesus' authority is greater than any force that held him. The demons recognize Jesus and fear him.

Today we can remember that no situation is beyond the reach of Christ. If something in your life enslaves you and human strength is not enough, go to Jesus with confidence, and ask for help from brothers and sisters in the faith as well.
exp.1:46:
The explanation says that all who were listening to Jesus in the temple were greatly amazed. "Were astonished" means they were filled with wonder, almost left speechless. They were impressed by his understanding, that is, his grasp of the things of God, and also by his answers, what he replied to the questions of the teachers.

Luke, the writer, tells of when Jesus was twelve years old. Mary and Joseph had lost him on the journey home from the Passover feast, and after three days they found him in the temple, among the teachers of the law. He was listening to them and asking them questions. This is the only account of his childhood after his birth.

For today: learn with humility. Jesus listened and asked questions before he answered. We can come to the Bible eager to learn, asking sincere questions and listening to others who know the Word.
exp.21:53:
They arrested Jesus and took him away, bringing him into the house of the high priest. Peter followed behind, but at a distance, not getting too close.

Luke tells what happened after the arrest in Gethsemane. Jesus had just pointed out that they were treating him like a robber, even though he had taught in the temple every day in full view of everyone. He himself said that this was the hour of darkness. Peter, who had promised to follow him to prison and to death, now follows him in fear. What comes next is his denial.

For today: following Jesus at a distance is easy when pressure comes. Let us ask him for the courage to draw near to him sincerely, even when it frightens us, and trust that he restores us when we fail.
exp.9:25:
Jesus answers with two questions: "What is written in the law?" and "how readest thou?", that is, "how do you understand it?" Instead of giving a direct answer, he invites the man to speak from what he already knows of the Scriptures. "Law" here refers to God's teaching in the Old Testament.

The one speaking is Jesus. A teacher of the law stood up to test him, asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus, who knows his intentions, leads him to the Scriptures, where he himself gives the answer: love God and love your neighbor. This prepares the parable of the good Samaritan.

For today: before looking for complicated answers, return to the Word of God with humility. Read it not only to know more, but to practice it, for both what you read and the way you understand it and live it matter greatly.
exp.21:7:
Jesus sends two of his disciples, Peter and John, with a specific task: to prepare the Passover, which means getting the Passover meal ready. That Jewish meal remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. The phrase "that we may eat" shows that Jesus wanted to share that meal with his disciples.

Jesus speaks. The day of Unleavened Bread arrives, the day when the lamb was sacrificed. While Judas looks for the moment to betray him, Jesus carries on with the plan calmly. The verses that follow show that he already knew how the details would unfold. Some see in this his command of the situation, though the text does not explain everything about how it happened.

For today: serving God often begins with simple, practical tasks. Prepare, help, and obey with confidence, even when you cannot see the whole path.
exp.13:26:
He says that whoever wants to be a disciple of Jesus must bear his cross, that is, carry it, and come after him. If someone does not do this, they cannot be his disciple. The word "whosoever" means "anyone who," and "come after me" means "following me."

Jesus speaks to large crowds that were traveling with him, perhaps out of enthusiasm. He warns them that following him has a cost. Earlier he said that a person must "hate" their family and even their own life, a strong way of speaking that many understand to mean loving Jesus far more than anything else. The cross was a symbol of suffering and complete surrender. He then speaks of counting the cost before building a tower.

Today, following Jesus is not only feeling close to him, but obeying him every day, even when it costs comfort, approval, or personal plans. Ask yourself: what is something I find hard to let go of in order to follow him today?
exp.15:3:
Here the manager, who is about to lose his job, comes up with an idea. Being put out of the position means that he is going to be dismissed. He thinks of a plan so that, when he no longer has a job, other people will take him into their homes.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples. The manager had been accused of wasting his master's goods, and he must give an account. Since he cannot dig and does not want to beg, he quickly thinks about his future. The verses that follow show his plan: reducing the debts to win friends. Jesus does not applaud his dishonesty; he notices his foresight and his quick decision.

For today: if that man thought so promptly about his temporary future, we can think with greater wisdom about the eternal. Let us use well what God entrusts to us, such as money and time, to bless others and not only ourselves.
exp.9:39:
Martha was very busy, almost pulled in two directions inside, with so many household tasks. The phrase about her attention going back and forth is simply a way of saying she was pulled this way and that. Her coming to Jesús suddenly describes how she came up to him all at once. Her question, "Lord, dost thou not care?", amounts to asking: "Don't you mind that I am left to do this alone?" She asks Jesús to tell Mary to come and help her.

The one speaking is Martha, who had welcomed Jesus into her home. While she tended to the guests, Mary was sitting at the feet of Jesus, listening to his teaching. Martha feels alone with the burden and complains. Jesus answers with tenderness, but shows her that her anxiety was robbing her of peace.

Serving is good, but it should not take away our time with Jesus. Today you can set aside a few quiet minutes to listen to his word before you begin your tasks.
exp.15:10:
This verse says that if we have not been honest and responsible with the money of this world, which Jesus calls "unrighteous mammon," no one will entrust us with the true riches, that is, the spiritual and eternal goods.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable of the shrewd manager. He uses that story to teach that money is temporary, and that the way we handle it reveals the faithfulness of our hearts. Some understand "unrighteous mammon" as wealth marked by human greed; others, simply as something temporary.

For today: deal honestly with what you have, whether little or much. Pay what is fair, keep your commitments, and give generously. God sees that daily faithfulness.
exp.19:43:
Jesus points out that David, when he wrote Psalm 110, calls the Messiah "Lord." It was unusual for a father to call his own descendant "Lord." So Jesus asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and his Lord.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, before the people and the teachers of the law who were testing him. Many thought the Messiah would be only a descendant of David, a human king. Jesus does not give the answer here, but he lets it be seen that the Messiah is more than that: he is a descendant of David and also his Lord. Many Christians understand this to point to the divine nature of Christ.

Today, do not reduce Jesus to a comfortable idea, such as that of a good teacher. Acknowledge him as Lord and let him direct your decisions, your time, and your priorities.
exp.5:2:
Jesus answers the Pharisees with a question: "Have ye not read so much as this?" He reminds them of what David did when he was hungry, together with the men who were with him. The men who were with him are his followers. The answer continues in the next verse, where it is told that they ate the holy bread.

The disciples were picking heads of grain on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees accused them of breaking the law. Jesus answers them with a story from the Scriptures (1 Samuel 21), which they knew well. He implies that human need mattered to God, and that they had misunderstood the purpose of the Sabbath. Some scholars see here a comparison between David and Jesus as a leader with authority.

God gave us his commandments for the good of people, not to make us hard toward others. Before judging someone, ask yourself whether you are guarding the letter of the rule or the heart of God, who is merciful.
exp.16:17:
Jesus asks a sad question: of the ten men healed of leprosy, only one came back to give glory to God. "Glory" here means praise and acknowledgment. The one who returned was a foreigner, a Samaritan, someone from a people the Jews were used to looking down on.

Jesus speaks after healing ten lepers as they were on their way to show themselves to the priests. Nine went on their way; the Samaritan turned back, fell down at Jesus' feet, and thanked him. Jesus does not rebuke them harshly, but he points out that the one who was least expected to be grateful was the one who gave thanks. Then he tells him that his faith has made him well, that is, he received something more than healing.

For today: let us not take God's favors for granted. Let us take a moment each day to return to Him with gratitude, thanking Him specifically for something we have received.
exp.18:31:
Luke tells us that the two disciples Jesus sent went off and found everything just as He had told them. There was a colt tied up, exactly as described. "Found even as he had said" means they found it just the way He said. A colt is a young donkey.

Jesus was approaching Jerusalem, and shortly afterward He would enter the city riding on that animal. Luke, the narrator, emphasizes that Jesus' words were fulfilled exactly. Some see here His supernatural knowledge; others think He may have made arrangements beforehand. The text does not settle the question, but it shows that He was in control of what was coming.

When God asks you to take a step, you can obey even when you cannot see the whole path. The disciples simply did what they were told, and they found that their Master was worthy of trust. Obey today what you already understand, and trust Him for the rest.
exp.23:46:
This verse says that, by the authority of Jesus, it must be proclaimed to all peoples that God calls people to turn around and change direction (repentance), and offers the forgiveness of sins (forgiveness means cancelling the debt). It was to begin in Jerusalem and from there reach out to all nations.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after rising from the dead. He has just opened their minds to understand that the Scriptures foretold his suffering and his resurrection. Now he explains that this message would not stay hidden: they would be witnesses and would carry it far, while first waiting for the power of the Holy Spirit.

For today: you do not need to be perfect to share this hope. You can tell someone close to you, with humility and kindness, how Christ has forgiven you and given you a new life. Start with your own "Jerusalem": your family, your neighborhood, your work.
exp.11:18:
Here the rich man speaks to himself. He thinks that, since he has many things stored up for many years, he can now rest and enjoy himself. In this verse, "soul" means himself, his own life. "Take thine ease" means rest, and "be merry" means enjoy yourself, have a good time.

Jesus tells this parable when someone asks him to step into a dispute over an inheritance. Jesus warns against greed and says that life does not depend on possessions. The man plans everything thinking only of himself, without taking God or others into account. Then God calls him a fool, because his security was false.

Today we can ask ourselves: where does my peace rest, in what I have or in God? Planning is good, but it is wise to live with gratitude, to share generously, and not to forget what truly matters.
exp.5:3:
Jesus continues his question to the Pharisees and recalls that David entered the house of God, took the bread set out before God in the sanctuary, ate it, and also gave it to his companions. The law said that only the priests could eat it.

Jesus' disciples had plucked heads of grain on the Sabbath, and some Pharisees criticized them. Jesus answers them with the story of David (1 Samuel 21). He shows them that human need and mercy do not stand against God's will. Then he says that he is Lord of the Sabbath.

God did not give us his commandments to make us hard, but to guide us in love. Before judging someone, let us ask ourselves whether we are caring for people or only defending rules. With Christ, mercy matters greatly.
exp.17:9:
These two men went up to the temple to pray. "Went up" is used because the temple stood in Jerusalem, on high ground. One was a Pharisee, a man respected for his devotion to the law. The other was a tax collector, that is, a man who collected taxes, whom many looked upon with contempt.

Jesus is the one speaking. He tells this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and looked down on everyone else. With two characters so different, he prepares a surprising lesson about what true prayer is like.

For today: before praying, examine your heart. It is easy to compare ourselves with others so that we feel better. Better to draw near to God with sincerity and truth, without looking down on anyone.
exp.1:10:
It says that on that same day, in Bethlehem, the city of King David, a Saviour was born. He is called "Christ," which means "the Anointed One," the promised Messiah, and "the Lord," a title of authority that the Bible also uses for God. The phrase "is born for you" shows that this child is a gift for them. "Good news" means tidings.

The angel of the Lord speaks to some shepherds who were watching over their sheep at night. They were terrified by the brightness of the glory of God. The angel calms them and announces good news for all the people. Then he gives them a simple sign: a baby in a manger.

For today: Jesus did not come only for important people, but for ordinary people, like those shepherds. When you feel afraid or think you are of little worth, remember that God brings you good news. Come to Jesus with confidence and receive him as your Saviour.
exp.19:41:
Jesus recalls words that David wrote in the Psalms (Psalm 110:1). David says that the Lord spoke to my Lord and asked him to sit at his right hand, that is, at his right side, the place of honor and authority.

Jesus is teaching in the temple, in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. The religious leaders had just asked him difficult questions, and now he asks them one. Many believed that the Messiah would be only a descendant of David. Jesus invites them to think: if David calls him "Lord," the Messiah must be more than simply his son. Christians see here a sign of his divinity and his authority.

For today: let us not reduce Jesus to a good teacher or a figure from the past. Acknowledge him as Lord, and place in his hands today a specific decision or concern.
exp.0:30:
It says that Mary will become pregnant, give birth to a son, and name him Jesus. Some older wording needs a note: "you will conceive in your womb" means that she will become pregnant, and "bring forth" means to give birth. The name Jesus comes from the Hebrew Yeshua, which is related to the idea of "the Lord saves."

The angel Gabriel speaks to Mary, a young woman from Nazareth. She was troubled by such a strange greeting, and the angel calms her, telling her not to be afraid because God has shown her favor. Right away he announces who this child will be: the Son of the Most High, who will reign forever.

For today: God often speaks in the middle of our fears and doubts. Mary was troubled, but she listened. When you feel fear about something new, take a moment to pray and listen to what God says, remembering that He sees you with grace.
exp.22:9:
The chief priests and scribes were there, accusing Jesus with great insistence and force. The chief priests were the leading figures of the temple. The scribes were the experts in the Law of Moses. To accuse with insistence means to press charges stubbornly and with great determination.

Luke tells the scene in which Pilate sends Jesus before Herod Antipas. Herod wanted to see a miracle and asked Jesus many questions, but Jesus remained silent. Meanwhile, the religious leaders, who had brought Jesus before the authorities, kept accusing him with great energy. Luke does not detail here what they were saying.

For today: a person can have much zeal and still be wrong. Before speaking firmly against someone, it is wise to examine our hearts and seek the truth with humility, as Jesus did, who answered with calm.
exp.13:8:
Luke 14:9 says that if you sit down in the best place at a wedding feast, the host may come and say to you, "Give this man place." Then you would have to move with shame to the lowest seat, the one left empty at the end.

Jesus speaks in the house of a Pharisee, on a Sabbath, while he eats with other guests. He sees how everyone looks for the first seats, and he tells them a parable. With an example from everyday life, he teaches them about pride and humility.

For today: do not live worried about being noticed or being given the first place. Serve with simplicity, let God and others honor you, and treat everyone with respect, including those whom nobody applauds.
exp.21:64:
This verse says that the men guarding Jesus did not only beat him, but also kept saying many other hurtful things to him. Luke sums up a long and cruel mockery in this way.

This happens on the night of Jesus' arrest, before dawn. The ones speaking are the guards who were watching him. They mocked him for claiming to be a prophet, and that is why they covered his face and struck him. Then, when day came, they would take him before the council. Luke shows that Jesus endured the mistreatment without answering back with revenge.

For today: when someone insults you or treats you with contempt, remember that Jesus understands that pain. Ask him for help not to repay evil with evil, and to respond with self-control and peace.
exp.20:8:
Jesus says that when his disciples hear of wars and uprisings (disorder, unrest, and rebellions), they should not be alarmed. Here, being alarmed means being overcome with terror. He makes clear that these things must happen first, but that the end does not come right away.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. His disciples ask him when what he has announced about the destruction of the temple will happen and what the sign will be. He warns them not to be deceived by false teachers or by those who claim to know the date. Scholars disagree about how much of this passage refers to the year 70 AD and how much to the end of the age.

For today: when the news fills you with fear, do not let panic carry you away or be swayed by those who predict dates. Trust in Christ, who is in control, and keep living with faith and peace.
exp.17:15:
Jesus calls the children to himself and asks that they be allowed to come near him. He says that no one should stop them, because the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like them. "Forbid" means to hinder or prevent. Earlier forms of this verb used a different spelling, which is why the old wording looks unfamiliar. "Of such" means "of those who are like this."

Jesus is the one speaking. Some people were bringing children to him, even infants, so that he would touch them and bless them, but the disciples were scolding them. Just before this, Jesus had praised the humility of the tax collector. The children show that same attitude: they have no merits to present, and they simply receive with trust.

Today we can draw near to God without pretending to be anything, with simplicity and dependence. We can also make room in our church and family so that children may come to know Jesus, without seeing them as a nuisance.
exp.6:31:
Jesus says that the people of that generation are like children sitting in the marketplace, calling out to one another: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang songs of mourning, and you did not weep."

Jesus speaks to the crowd after praising John the Baptist. The Pharisees and the teachers of the law had rejected God's purpose by not being baptized by John. With this picture, Jesus shows that they criticized John for being strict and Jesus for being close to the people. There was no way to please them, because their problem was not the message but a closed heart.

For today: examine whether you make excuses for not obeying God. Ask him for a humble heart, ready to respond when he speaks to you, whatever the style of the messenger.
exp.22:37:
This verse tells that a sign was placed above Jesus' cross. "Titulus" means a sign or inscription. It was written in three languages, Greek, Latin and Hebrew, and it said: "This is the King of the Jews."

Luke records this while the Roman soldiers are mocking Jesus. It was Roman custom to post a sign stating the charge for which a person was condemned. The Romans used it as an insult and as a warning to the people. The three languages allowed many people to read it. Without intending to, the sign spoke a truth: Jesus is indeed King, even though his throne was a cross.

Today we can remember that God can reveal the truth even through those who mock. Honor him as King not only in the good days, but also when his path seems humble or hard.
exp.21:49:
One of the disciples struck a servant of the high priest with a sword and cut off his right ear. Here the word "high priest" is the one used in the verse itself.

Jesus had just been betrayed by Judas with a kiss in the garden. The disciples asked whether they should fight with the sword, but one of them acted without waiting for an answer. Luke does not give his name; the Gospel of John says it was Peter and that the servant's name was Malchus. Immediately Jesus stops the violence and heals the wounded man.

Today, when we feel threatened or treated unfairly, reacting in anger usually makes everything worse. Jesus shows us another way: to halt the urge for revenge and to do good, even to someone who stands on the other side.
exp.22:33:
This verse says that Jesus, while he was being crucified, asked God to forgive those who were mistreating him, because they did not understand the full weight of what they were doing. The sentence about the soldiers dividing his clothing and casting lots for them simply describes that they shared out his clothes, deciding by a drawing of lots, like rolling dice, who would keep each piece.

Jesus speaks while already nailed to the cross, between two criminals. He prays to his Father in the midst of his pain. The soldiers were dividing his clothing while the people watched and the leaders mocked him. Some early manuscripts do not include the first sentence, and scholars debate it, but many accept it as part of the text.

For today: when someone wounds you, ask God to help you not to answer with revenge. You can pray for that person, even though it still hurts, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.22:30:
Jesus says that if they treat him this way, though he is innocent and full of life like a green tree, what will happen to what is dry? A dry tree is something without life, ready for the fire.

Jesus speaks on the way to the cross to the women of Jerusalem who were weeping for him. He warns them of very hard days that are coming. Many think he is referring to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, but others also see a wider judgment. The image of the green tree and the dry one is interpreted in several ways, but the general meaning is a serious warning.

For today: do not stay only with pity for Jesus' suffering. His cross calls us to take our relationship with God seriously, to turn back to him today, and to live with true life in Christ.
exp.11:15:
He tells a parable about a rich man whose fields produced a very abundant harvest. The phrase translated here as "ground" refers to a piece of land that he owned. Up to this point, nothing bad is said about him; only his great abundance is presented.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd. A man had asked him to step into a family matter about an inheritance, and Jesus refused to act as judge in it. Then he warned against greed, which is an excessive desire to have more. This parable illustrates his teaching: life is not measured by what a person possesses.

For today: when things go well for us at work or with money, let us honestly ask ourselves whether we are trusting in what we have more than in God. Let us give thanks to him and think about how to share generously.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that all the people went to be registered in a census. Each person traveled to "su ciudad," that is, to the place where their family originated.

Luke, who tells the story, explains the reason: the emperor Augustus ordered a census. In this way he sets the scene for the journey of Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem. Scholars debate how this census fits with other historical records, but Luke wants to show that Jesus was born at a real time and in a real place, and that God works even through the decisions of rulers.

For today: although we sometimes feel moved by orders from others, paperwork, or circumstances we did not choose, God can carry out his plans in the midst of them. Trust that he continues to guide your path.
exp.23:50:
This verse tells how Jesus, while blessing his disciples, was gradually parted from them and carried up into heaven. The phrase "was parted from them" conveys that he was moving away from them step by step, while they watched him.

Luke is the one who tells the story. Jesus had already risen, and he had just asked them to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father, that is, the power of the Holy Spirit. He led them out to Bethany and lifted up his hands to bless them. His farewell was not one of sadness but of blessing. The disciples responded by worshiping him and returning with great joy.

For today: even though we do not see Jesus, we can trust that he remains present, blessing and caring for us. We can wait in prayer, with joy and confidence, until God gives us strength for what comes next.
exp.1:34:
It says that Mary would feel a very deep pain, as if a sword were piercing her soul. The phrase "pierce through" means to go right through from one side to the other. And that suffering would serve so that the hidden thoughts of many hearts would be revealed, uncovered for all to see.

The one speaking is Simeon, a righteous man who took the child Jesus in his arms in the temple. He has just said that Jesus would be a sign that people argue against: some would accept him and others would reject him. It is commonly understood that the sword refers to Mary's pain as she sees the rejection and death of her son, though some interpret it in other ways.

Following God does not free us from pain, but God does not leave us alone in it. Moreover, the way we respond to Jesus shows what is truly in our hearts. Today we can ask ourselves honestly: how am I responding to Him?
exp.21:8:
Here the disciples ask Jesus where he wants them to prepare the Passover supper. He had already told them to make the preparations, and they want to know the exact place.

It is Peter and John who speak, the two whom Jesus sent. It was the day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, a feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. The disciples do not decide the place on their own; they wait for Jesus' direction. He answers them with very specific instructions, and they come to pass just as he said.

For today: before making plans, even good ones, we can ask the Lord how and where he wants us to serve. Obeying with humility and step by step helps us trust that he guides the details.
exp.23:4:
This verse says that the women who went to the tomb were afraid and bowed their faces to the ground. Then the two men in shining clothing asked them, "Why do you seek the living among the dead?" The phrase "bowed their faces to the ground" means they bent their heads down to the earth.

The women had come early on Sunday to anoint the body of Jesus, but the tomb was empty. The ones speaking are two men in dazzling clothing, who from the context appear to be angels (Luke calls them "men"; later on they are understood as messengers of God). Their question does not scold, but invites them to remember what Jesus had already said.

Today, we sometimes look for hope or comfort in things that cannot give us life. This question invites us to turn to Christ, who lives, and to trust his promises with renewed courage.
exp.10:6:
Here Jesus tells a scene from everyday life. A man arrives at midnight to ask his friend for bread, and the friend answers from inside: "Do not bother me; the door is already shut, my children are with me in bed, and I cannot get up to give them to you." The children are young ones, and being with him in bed suggests that the whole family slept together in one place.

Jesus is teaching his disciples about prayer, right after giving them the Lord's Prayer. He uses this example to make a contrast: if a tired friend ends up giving in because of persistence, how much more will God respond, since he is a good Father. Many understand that the point is not that God is reluctant, but that we can pray with confidence and perseverance.

Today we can keep talking to God about our needs, even the urgent or inconvenient ones, without growing weary or thinking that we are bothering him. He listens to us with love.
exp.7:23:
The explanation says that the disciples, very frightened by the storm, woke Jesus, crying out that they were going down. He got up, spoke with authority to the wind and the waves, and everything became calm. "Rebuked" means he corrected them with firmness. "Calm" is quiet and tranquility. "We perish" means we are about to die.

Luke tells this during a journey across the Sea of Galilee. Jesus himself had said, "Let us go over to the other side," and while they were sailing, he fell asleep. The disciples, some of them fishermen, saw the boat filling with water and asked for help. Afterward Jesus asked them where their faith was, and they were amazed.

For today: when you feel your life is sinking, cry out to Jesus without fear or shame. He listens and has power over what frightens you, even though sometimes his calm does not come the way we expect. Remember that he is in your boat.
exp.21:69:
What it says: All the Jewish leaders ask Jesus whether he is the Son of God. He answers, "Ye say that I am," which we would say today as "You are saying it: I am." It is a way of affirming the truth without denying it, letting them speak the words themselves.

Context: Jesus is before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish religious council, on the night or early morning after his arrest. He has just said that the Son of Man will sit at the right hand of the power of God, and they understand that he is speaking of himself. That is why they ask. Some scholars see in his answer a clear affirmation; others see an indirect reply. They take it as a confession, and that leads them to hand him over to Pilate.

For today: Jesus spoke with truth and calm even when he knew it would cost him dearly. We can ask God to help us be sincere about our faith with calm and respect, without fear, trusting that he sustains those who are faithful to him.
exp.14:25:
This verse says that the older son, hearing the music and dancing, called one of the servants and asked what was going on.

Jesus tells this parable of the father and his two sons. The younger son had already come home, and the father was throwing a feast. The older son was coming in from the field and knew nothing about it. It is noteworthy that he does not go straight into the house but stays outside and asks someone else. Many see in this the beginning of his distance from his father, though the text does not explain it in detail.

For today: when someone receives forgiveness or a blessing we did not expect, we can stay outside asking from a distance, or we can go in and rejoice. Let us ask God for a heart that celebrates grace with others, without comparing ourselves or measuring who deserves it.
exp.10:50:
Jesus says that God will hold this generation accountable for the blood of all the prophets who were killed, from Abel, the first person put to death that the Bible mentions, to Zacharias, who died between the altar and the temple. The word "required" means that a reckoning, an answer, will be demanded for that injustice. "Generation" refers to the people of that time.

Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and teachers of the law, in the house of a Pharisee. He has just rebuked them because they honored the prophets with beautiful tombs, yet they shared the attitude of those who killed them. About which Zacharias is meant, there are several opinions; many think of the one in 2 Chronicles 24, but this is not certain.

Today, this passage invites us to listen with humility when God corrects us, rather than admiring the truth in others while resisting it in ourselves.
exp.12:19:
Jesus asks another question to draw the attention of his listeners: "Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God?" He is not asking because he does not know the answer; it is a way of teaching that prepares the heart to listen. He will go on at once with the parable of the yeast.

Jesus is teaching on the way to Jerusalem, as Luke tells it. He has just healed a woman on the Sabbath, and some people were opposed to it (Luke 13:10-17). With the parable of the mustard seed and now with the yeast, he explains what the kingdom of God is like: it begins small, almost unnoticed, but it truly grows.

For today: do not despise what is small. A prayer, an act of kindness, or a word of faith may seem like little, but God knows how to make them grow. Remain faithful in the simple things, and trust that he is the one doing the work.
exp.9:5:
She says that when the disciples arrive at a house, they offer peace. A "son of peace" is a person who is open and willing to receive that message. If such a person is there, the peace stays with them. If not, the peace returns to the disciples; that is, it is not lost or wasted.

Jesus speaks to seventy disciples whom he sends out two by two to the towns where he himself intended to go. He asks them to go simply, trusting in God, and to offer peace first. Here he does not send them to impose themselves, but to offer and see who responds. Some understand that "peace" as an ordinary greeting, and others as the blessing of the kingdom of God; perhaps it includes both.

For today: offer kindness and the message of Christ with humility, without forcing anyone. If someone rejects it, do not be discouraged or embittered; your peace stays with you, and God continues to work.
exp.23:43:
Jesus reminds his disciples that what had happened was no accident. While he was still with them, he had told them that everything written about him had to be fulfilled. The phrase "I told you" means "I spoke to you," and "had to" means that it had to happen. He mentions the three parts of the Hebrew Scriptures: the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms.

Jesus has already risen, and he appears to the disciples, who are frightened and confused. To show them that he is not a ghost, he eats fish in front of them. Then he explains to them that his death and resurrection were part of God's plan announced in the Scriptures. After that, he opens their minds so they can understand them.

When you read the Bible, ask God to open your understanding, and look for how the whole text points to Jesus. When something in your life seems confusing or painful, remember that God is still carrying out his plan.
exp.3:0:
Luke says that Jesus was full of the Holy Ghost when he came away from the Jordan River, where he had just been baptized. Then the Spirit led him into the wilderness.

The word "led" in the verse above is the same idea as being guided or conducted.

The one speaking here is Luke, the narrator. He tells what happened right after Jesus' baptism, before his public ministry began. The important point is that the Spirit himself guides him toward a place of testing, where he will be tempted by the devil. Luke shows that Jesus faces this test in obedience to God, not by mistake or by chance.

For today: being close to God does not free us from trials. But we can face them by trusting the Spirit and not only our own strength. When you go through a hard time, pray and ask for his guidance.
exp.2:20:
Luke tells us that many people were being baptized, and that Jesus was also baptized. While he was praying, the heaven was opened.

The one speaking is Luke, the narrator. Shortly before, he mentions that John the Baptist was imprisoned by Herod, and here he presents Jesus' baptism as a separate moment. Luke emphasizes that Jesus was praying. Right after this come the Holy Spirit like a dove and the voice of the Father. Scholars explain in various ways why Jesus, who had no sin, was baptized, but the text shows that he identified himself with his people and began his mission.

For today: before starting something important, pause to pray. Jesus, even as the beloved Son, sought the Father in prayer at the beginning of his path. You too can do this.
exp.19:21:
The spies ask Jesus whether it is right, according to God's law, to pay the tax to the Roman emperor. The word "lawful" means permitted or right. The "tribute" was the tax paid to Rome. "Caesar" was the title of the emperor.

The people asking are men sent by the religious leaders, who pretended to be sincere. First they flatter him, but in reality they are looking for a trap. If Jesus said yes, many of the people would reject him; if he said no, they could accuse him before the Roman governor of rebellion. Jesus, however, sees through their cunning.

For today: sometimes people ask us questions not out of sincere interest, but to catch us out. Let us ask God for wisdom to answer with truth and calm, and also examine our own hearts, so that we always seek God with sincerity and not with duplicity.
exp.1:40:
This verse tells us that Joseph and Mary, the parents of Jesus, traveled to Jerusalem every year to celebrate the feast of the Passover.

Here Luke, the narrator of the Gospel, speaks. After telling of the birth and childhood of Jesus, he shows the setting in which he grew up: a family faithful to God's law. The Passover recalled Israel's deliverance from Egypt, and the law encouraged the Israelites to observe it. Nazareth was far from Jerusalem, so the journey required real effort. This detail prepares the story that follows, when Jesus was twelve years old.

For today: faith is strengthened through steady habits. Joseph and Mary did not wait until they felt inspired; year after year they sought God together as a family. We can choose a simple habit, such as praying together or attending church, and keep it faithfully.
exp.9:9:
Luke 10:10 says that if the disciples enter a town and the people do not welcome them, they should go out into its streets and give a public message. The quoted wording about entering and receiving is old phrasing, so I have left it out here. The verse ends with the word "say," and what they are to say continues in the next verse.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples he sends out two by two to the towns he himself planned to visit. He has already explained how to act when they are welcomed well. Now he tells them what to do when they are rejected: to announce clearly that the kingdom of God has come near, even though the town does not accept it. The rejection carries serious consequences, as the mention of Sodom shows.

Today we can share our faith with respect and sincerity, without forcing anyone. If someone rejects it, we should not respond with anger or give up in discouragement. We do our part with love and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.2:14:
The people were in a state of expectation, and everyone wondered in their hearts about John, whether he might be the Christ, that is, the Messiah, the Anointed One whom God had promised to send.

Luke is the one who tells this. John the Baptist had just preached repentance and given specific advice to the crowds and to the soldiers. His message was so firm and sincere that many thought he could be the Messiah. For this reason, John quickly answers and points toward Jesus, someone greater than himself.

For today: when someone helps us in our spiritual lives, let us be thankful, but let us not place in that person the hope that belongs only to Christ. May everything lead us to Jesus.
exp.5:31:
Jesus says that loving only those who love us is nothing special. The phrase "what thank have ye?" means: what credit or reward will you have? Even "sinners," meaning those who live without seeking God, love those who love them back.

Jesus teaches his disciples and a crowd during what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Shortly before, he commanded them to love their enemies, to give to whoever asks, and to treat others the way they would want to be treated. Here he shows that his followers' love must go beyond the ordinary and resemble the generous love of God.

Today we can think of someone who annoys us or has let us down. This week we can do one concrete good for that person: pray for them, greet them respectfully, or help them, without expecting anything in return.
exp.20:20:
Jesus says that when that time comes, those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains. Those who are inside Jerusalem must leave the city. Those who are out in the countryside must not go into it seeking shelter.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He warns them that the city will be surrounded by armies and destroyed. Many understand that this was fulfilled in the year 70 A.D., when the Romans took Jerusalem. Some think it also points to future events. Jesus gives them this instruction so that lives will not be lost through trusting in false security.

When God warns us of danger, the best response is to obey quickly and humbly, without clinging to what seems safe. Ask him for wisdom to recognize his warnings and for courage to act.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that all the people who heard the shepherds were amazed at what they were telling them. "Wondered at" means they were greatly surprised, hardly able to believe it. The shepherds were talking about the child they had just found.

Luke recounts here what happened after angels announced to the shepherds the birth of the Savior. They went quickly to Bethlehem, found the child in the manger, and shared the message they had received. The text does not say exactly who the people who heard were; they were probably people who were nearby. Luke shows their reaction of amazement, and then contrasts it with Mary, who kept all these things quietly in her heart.

When God speaks to us or acts in our lives, we can tell others about it simply, as the shepherds did. It is not necessary to be experts; it is enough to share what we have seen and heard, and to let God touch the hearts of those who listen.
exp.2:12:
John the Baptist tells the tax collectors not to collect more than the law required them to collect. "Exact" means to demand something firmly, as if it were a right. The tax collectors were the men who collected taxes for the Roman government.

John is preaching repentance beside the Jordan. Some tax collectors come to be baptized and ask him what they must do. He does not ask them to leave their work, but to do it with honesty. It was known that many collectors used to keep something extra for themselves, and for that reason people looked on them with distrust. Their repentance had to show in their everyday conduct.

For today: if your job gives you authority or access to other people's money, be fair. Do not collect too much or take advantage of your position. God wants to see a faith that shows in everyday honesty.
exp.8:15:
Luke tells us that Jesus takes the five loaves and the two fish, looks up to heaven, and gives thanks to God for them. "Blessed" here means that he gave thanks and asked for God's blessing on the food. Then he breaks them and gives them to the disciples to distribute to the people. "Set before" means that they served them.

Jesus is in a remote place with a crowd of about five thousand men, besides other people. Earlier, the disciples asked him to send the people away, but he told them to give them something to eat themselves. Jesus performs the miracle, but he involves the disciples in the serving.

For today: the little we have, placed in Jesus' hands with gratitude, can be enough to bless others. Give thanks for what you have and share it with confidence, even when it seems insufficient.
exp.6:10:
This verse tells that, shortly after healing the centurion's servant, Jesus went to a town called Nain. Many of his disciples went with him, and also a large crowd. The words "came to pass" and "much people" in the verse above are the ones explained here. The "city" was a small town in Galilee.

The narrator is Luke, who is putting the events of Jesus' ministry in order. He comes from a moment where Jesus praised the faith of a foreign centurion. Now the account shifts scene: Jesus walks with many people around him, not knowing that the crowd would soon meet another group, one in mourning. Luke thus prepares the encounter with a widow.

For today: Jesus was not walking aimlessly; his path led him right to where there was a sorrow. We can trust that God knows our paths and can come to meet us in unexpected moments. We can also ask him to make us attentive to those who suffer near us.
exp.1:41:
This verse tells us that when Jesus was twelve years old, his family went up to Jerusalem for the feast, as was the custom. The old spelling "Jerusalem" is simply Jerusalem. The reason for the word "went up" is that the city stood on high ground, so whoever traveled toward it always went up.

Luke, the narrator, has just said that Joseph and Mary went to the Passover feast every year. That feast remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. This is the only account of Jesus' childhood after his birth, and it sets the scene for his staying behind in the temple. Luke shows a family faithful to the customs of their faith.

For today: faith grows through simple, steady habits. Just as this family went every year, we can set aside fixed times to pray, read the Bible, and meet with other believers, and teach that by example to the younger ones.
exp.8:7:
This verse shows what people were saying about Jesus. Some thought Elijah had come back, and others believed that one of the prophets of ancient times had risen from the dead.

Herod the tetrarch, a local ruler, heard about the miracles and the preaching of Jesus and his disciples. He was puzzled because people gave several different explanations. Some mentioned John the Baptist, whom Herod had ordered put to death. Elijah was a prophet who was greatly remembered, and the Jews were expecting his return. The people could see that Jesus was extraordinary, but they still did not understand who he really was.

Today there are also many opinions about Jesus. It is not enough to repeat what others say about him. Read the Gospels calmly and ask God to help you come to know him personally.
exp.12:26:
Jesus says that the owner of the house will answer those who knock on the door: "I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you who do evil." The phrase "workers of iniquity" means people who practice injustice. "I tell you" is the same as "I say to you," and "ye" means "you."

Jesus speaks while he is on the way to Jerusalem, teaching the people. Someone asked him whether only a few are saved, and he answers with this parable about the narrow door. His warning is for those who heard him and felt secure because they knew him from a distance, or because they belonged to God's people, without really living in obedience.

For today: it is not enough to be near the things of God, such as going to church or knowing the Bible. Today you can ask yourself whether you truly trust in Jesus and whether your life reflects that relationship with him. Ask him to give you a sincere heart willing to obey him.
exp.15:2:
The steward, learning that he is about to lose his position, thinks quietly to himself about what he will do. The word that was rendered as "stewardship" refers to the job of managing another person's possessions. He admits his limits: he has no strength for the hard labor of the field, and he is ashamed to ask others for charity.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and tells a parable. A rich man accuses his manager of wasting his goods and demands an account of his management. This moment is the turning point: the steward realizes his situation is urgent and begins to think about his future. In the verses that follow he acts with shrewdness. Interpreters debate the exact meaning of the parable, but here we see the importance of responding in time.

For today: do not wait until a crisis arrives to think about what truly matters. Use wisely what God has entrusted to you, and prepare yourself with responsibility.
exp.0:47:
He looked with favor on Mary, a humble servant woman, of no importance in the eyes of the world. So she declares that from now on all generations will call her "blessed," that is, happy and fortunate because of the favor she has received. The word for her humble condition speaks of lowliness, and the word for her role means servant.

Mary is the one speaking, in the song commonly called the Magnificat. She has just visited her relative Elizabeth, and she already knows she will be the mother of the Messiah. Her joy is not centered on herself: she keeps praising God, who is the one who did the work. The verses that follow confirm this, as she speaks of the mighty things the Mighty One has done.

For today: God does not first look at prestige or achievements, but at humble and willing hearts. If you feel small or of little worth, remember that God sees you. And when you receive something good, respond as Mary did: give the glory to Him.
exp.18:1:
This verse introduces a man named Zacchaeus. He was the chief among the tax collectors, and he was rich. The phrase that introduces him draws attention to someone new in the story.

Luke tells us that Jesus was passing through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem. Tax collectors worked for the Roman government and were looked down on by many Jews, since they collected taxes and sometimes grew wealthy beyond what was fair. The text does not say how Zacchaeus gained his wealth, but his reputation placed him far from being respected by others. Luke wants to show us whom Jesus is seeking.

For today: no one is too far from God. If you feel curiosity or a hunger for God, even if you have doubts or a complicated past, take a step toward Jesus. He also comes out to meet you.
exp.21:9:
Jesus answers Peter and John with very specific instructions. When they enter Jerusalem, they will meet a man carrying a water jar. They are to follow him to the house he enters.

Jesus speaks with his two disciples before the Passover supper, the feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. They had asked where to prepare the meal. It was unusual for a man to carry water, since women normally did this, so he would be easy to recognize. Some see here Jesus' foreknowledge; others think there may have been an arrangement made beforehand. The text does not make this clear.

For today: God cares for the details of our path. We can take simple steps of obedience even when we do not see the whole plan, trusting that He goes before us.
exp.8:49:
Jesus answers John and tells him not to stop the man from casting out demons. He explains that whoever is not against them is for them.

Jesus is speaking with John and the other disciples. Shortly before this, they had been arguing about who was the greatest, and Jesus had taught them humility by using a child as an example. Then John reports that they saw someone using the name of Jesus to free people, and they stopped him because he was not part of their group. Jesus corrects this attitude of rivalry.

Today we can rejoice when other people or churches do good in the name of Christ, even if they are not part of our group. Instead of competing or being suspicious, we can pray for them and celebrate the good that God does through them, without neglecting to guard the truth of the gospel.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous before God. That is, God saw them as upright people. Their way of living each day is shown in the words "walking in," and "blameless" means that no one could rightly accuse them of anything wrong. "Commandments and ordinances" are the laws and rules that God gave to his people.

Here Luke, the writer of the gospel, tells the story in an orderly way. He introduces this couple of priests before the birth of John the Baptist. Their faithful life sets the scene, even though they suffered because they had no children. Being righteous does not mean they were perfect, since only Jesus was, but that they lived with sincerity before God.

For today: even if you go through a trial or a long wait, keep obeying God with sincerity. His care does not depend on your life turning out as you expected.
exp.20:30:
Jesus says that just as you recognize that summer is coming when the trees put out their buds, his followers should recognize that the kingdom of God is near when they see these things happening. The explanation's remark about an old form of a word and the meaning of another word belongs to the older wording, so it is left out here.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, in his teaching about the future, where he mentions the fall of Jerusalem, signs, and his return. Interpreters disagree about exactly which events he has in mind and what "this generation" means. What is clear is that Jesus wants them to be alert and confident.

For today: live awake and full of hope, without fear or excessive curiosity about dates. Ask God today to help you live faithfully, forgiving, serving, and praying, because his words will not pass away.
exp.8:50:
This verse says that the time was drawing near when Jesus would be taken up, that is, carried up to heaven (his ascension). Then it says he "set his face" steadfastly, a phrase meaning that he made a firm decision and did not turn back. His destination was Jerusalem. The word "when" here means "as the time came."

Luke is the narrator. With this verse a new stage begins: the journey toward Jerusalem, where Jesus would suffer, die, and rise again. Many scholars see here the beginning of the great travel section of the Gospel. Jesus walks with determination, even knowing there will be rejection, as with the Samaritans mentioned right after.

For today: when we know that God calls us to do something difficult but good, we can look at the example of Jesus, who moved forward with firmness and trust in the Father. Let us ask him for courage to keep going without letting fear or rejection stop us.
exp.7:47:
Jesus speaks to the woman with tenderness and calls her "daughter." He tells her that her faith has made her whole, that is, it has healed her and fully restored her. Then he sends her away with "go in peace," which means to be calm and well. The word "whole" here can include the healing of the body and also the well-being of her whole life.

Jesus speaks. A woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years touched him in the crowd, and she was healed. She came trembling, because she did not want to be discovered. Jesus does not scold her. He has her speak in front of everyone so that her healing is known and she is received with dignity. Soon news arrives about Jairus's daughter.

When you feel fear or shame, come to Jesus with confidence. He does not reject a small and sincere faith. You can bring your need to him today and rest in his peace.
exp.0:48:
It says that God, whom Mary calls "the Mighty One," has done great things in her life. She does not speak of her own merits, but of what God did for her. She ends by saying that God's name is holy, that is, that he is pure, set apart from all evil, and worthy of the highest respect. The word "servant girl" in the previous verse means handmaid or servant.

The one speaking is Mary, the mother of Jesus. She has just visited her cousin Elizabeth, who confirmed to her that she was carrying the Lord in her womb. Mary responds with a song of praise, called the Magnificat. She rejoices because God, being mighty, looked upon a humble and simple young woman.

For today: before thinking about what you lack, calmly remember the good things God has done in your life, even if they seem small. Thank him out loud, as Mary did, and acknowledge that everything comes from his hand.
exp.6:15:
All the people were seized with awe and praised God after seeing that Jesus had restored life to the young man. "Fear came on all" here means a deep reverence, not terror. "Glorified God" means they acknowledged and honored God for what had happened. "God has visited his people" means that God had come near to help and rescue his people.

The one speaking is Luke, the narrator, who recounts the reaction of the crowd in the town of Nain. Jesus had just been moved with compassion for a widow burying her only son, and he raised him. The people called him "a great prophet," perhaps recalling Elijah and Elisha, who also raised the dead. Luke shows that Jesus is more than a prophet, but that was their first conclusion.

When God acts in our lives, the right response is wonder and gratitude. Today we can pause to recognize how God has helped us and thank him out loud, without taking his care for granted.
exp.19:45:
Jesus warns his disciples: "Beware of the scribes." These teachers of the Law liked to walk around in long robes to draw attention. They loved being greeted with respect in the markets, and having the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts.

Jesus is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, in his final days before the cross. He has just silenced his critics with the question about David and the Messiah. While all the people listen, he turns to his disciples. The verse that follows shows how serious this is: some used their religious reputation to take advantage of the most vulnerable, such as widows.

For today: examine your motives. Ask yourself whether you serve God to be seen and admired, or out of love for him and for other people. Ask God for a humble heart.
exp.23:25:
Jesus asks whether it was not necessary for the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, to suffer these things before entering into his glory. "Suffered" here means to undergo pain and hardship. The "glory" refers to his honor and power as the risen King, beside the Father. Jesus shows that suffering and glory were joined together in God's plan.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, although two disciples walking to Emmaus do not yet recognize him. They are sad and confused about his death and about the report of the empty tomb. Jesus calls them "foolish and slow of heart" because they had not believed what the prophets had announced. Right away he explains the Scriptures to them, beginning with Moses and going on through all the prophets.

For today: when you go through difficult moments you do not understand, do not conclude that God has absent himself. Return to the Scriptures and ask him to open your understanding, trusting that he can work even in the midst of pain.
exp.23:40:
This verse says that the disciples were so full of joy and amazement that they still could not believe what they were seeing. Then Jesus asked them whether they had anything to eat. The word "wondered" in the verse above means filled with awe.

Here Jesus, risen, has just appeared to his frightened disciples, who thought they were seeing a spirit. He had already shown them his hands and feet. Now he asks for food to give them one more proof: he has a real body, he is not a ghost. Luke tells us that afterward he ate fish in front of them.

For today: when it is hard to believe something good from God, do not be anxious or ashamed. Jesus was patient with his friends' doubts and gave them simple proofs. You can bring your doubts to him honestly, and he knows how to come close to you with tenderness.
exp.0:33:
Luke 1:34 shows Mary asking a question of the angel Gabriel. She wants to know how she can have a child if she has not been with any man. The phrase "seeing I know not a man" is an old way of saying that she has not been intimate with a man.

The angel has just told her that she will have a son who will be great, the Son of the Most High, and a king forever on the throne of David. Mary was pledged to Joseph, but they were not yet living together. Her question does not sound like mockery or refusal, but like sincere wonder at something that seemed impossible. For this reason the angel explains how God will act.

For today: when you do not understand how God will accomplish something, you can ask Him with sincerity and respect. God does not become angry at questions asked with faith. Bring them to Him in prayer, and keep trusting while you wait for His answer.
exp.21:24:
Jesus says that the kings of the pagan nations rule with a heavy hand over their peoples. The phrase "exercise lordship" means to dominate or command as masters do. Those who hold authority over them are called "benefactors," that is, people who do good, although in reality they seek honor for themselves.

Jesus speaks with his disciples during the last supper. Just before, they had been arguing about who was the greatest among them. Jesus uses that argument to show them that his kingdom is not like the governments of the world. Then he tells them, "But ye shall not be so," and presents himself as one who serves.

For today: if you have any authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, ask yourself whether you are seeking to be admired or to truly help. Today you can do a simple service, without expecting recognition.
exp.7:34:
The people of the town went out to see what had happened with the pigs. When they arrived where Jesus was, they found the man who had been possessed sitting at his feet, clothed and in his right mind, that is, thinking clearly. They were filled with fear.

Luke is the one who tells this scene. Jesus had just freed a man tormented by many demons, who had previously lived naked and away from people. The herdsmen had reported in the town, and that is why the people came. Their fear showed that they did not know how to understand such power. Afterward, they asked Jesus to leave.

For today: Jesus can restore peace and dignity to a broken life. Even so, his power can frighten us if we do not want to change. We can come to his feet with confidence and let him heal what we cannot fix ourselves.
exp.20:27:
Jesus says that when these things begin to happen, his followers should look up with attention and lift up their heads, that is, take courage and not live in fear. The reason is that their redemption is near.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, in his teaching about the future. Earlier he described signs that will make people tremble, and then he announced the coming of the Son of Man. Interpreters debate how much of this refers to the destruction of Jerusalem and how much to the return of Christ. "Redemption" here points to the final deliverance that God will bring to his people.

Today, when news or crises fill you with fear, do not shut yourself in anxiety. Pray, remain faithful, and lift up your gaze, trusting that God will keep his promises.
exp.4:4:
Simon answers Jesus that they have toiled all night and caught nothing. Even so, he says he will let down the net because Jesus asks him to. The word "Master" was a title of respect. The phrase "at thy word" means "because you say so." The word "taken" means "caught."

Jesus had just been teaching the crowd from Simon's boat. Then he asked Simon to go out into deeper water and let down the nets. Simon was an experienced fisherman, and night was when fishing was often best. He was tired and discouraged, but he decided to obey. Afterward the net was so full that it nearly broke.

For today: when God asks you to do something that seems pointless, or that you have already tried without result, you can obey with confidence. We will not always see such a quick answer, but sincere obedience is never lost.
exp.17:38:
The explanation says that those who walked at the front of the crowd scolded the blind man so that he would keep quiet. But he, instead of heeding them, cried out all the more, asking Jesus for mercy.

Luke tells the story of a blind man who was begging by the road near Jericho. Hearing that Jesus was passing by, he called out, "Son of David," a title linked to the promised Messiah. The people wanted to silence him, perhaps out of annoyance or because they considered him unimportant. But he did not give up, and Jesus stopped to attend to him.

For today: when you feel that others discourage you or that your need is too small, keep coming to Jesus with sincerity. He listens to you, even when there is noise or criticism around.
exp.10:49:
This verse says that God will hold the generation of that time accountable for the blood of all the prophets who were murdered, from the beginning of the world. The word "required" means that an answer or reckoning will be demanded for that harm.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees and the teachers of the law while he is eating at the home of a Pharisee. He rebukes them because they honor the prophets who have died by building beautiful tombs, yet they reject those whom God sends to them now. Like their ancestors, they resist God's message. Some scholars understand that this generation takes on the responsibility by being just as hard of heart.

For today: it is not enough to admire the heroes of faith from the past. Ask yourself whether you truly listen to the voice of God when he corrects you, even when the correction is uncomfortable or comes through someone you did not expect.
exp.4:30:
Jesus answers with a well-known saying: those who are well do not need a doctor, but the sick do. With this simple image, Jesus compares himself to a doctor who goes to where those who need help are.

Jesus is the speaker. Levi, a tax collector, held a banquet, and the table filled with people who were looked down upon. The scribes and Pharisees, who considered themselves very upright, criticized the disciples for eating with "pecadores." Jesus replies that his mission is to draw near to those who recognize their need. Some think there is a touch of irony toward those who saw themselves as "sanos," though the text does not say this directly.

For today: do not turn away from God because you feel unworthy, and do not look down on someone who is wounded. Come to Jesus with honesty, and come to others with the same compassion.
exp.10:26:
A woman in the crowd raised her voice and declared that happy is the mother who gave birth to Jesus and raised him. The word "blessed" here means happy or greatly favored. The words "womb" and "breasts" are ways of referring to his mother, who carried him and nursed him.

Jesus had just spoken about evil spirits and the danger of leaving a life that is clean but empty. In the middle of that serious teaching, the woman expressed admiration for Jesus by praising his mother. Jesus does not rebuke her, but in the next verse he redirects attention: more blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.

Admiring Jesus or respecting religious things is not enough. True blessing lies in listening to what God says and putting it into practice. Today you might choose a passage of the Bible and ask yourself: what one thing can I obey this week?
exp.1:11:
This verse says that the angel gives the shepherds a sign to recognize the newborn: a baby wrapped in strips of cloth and lying in a manger. "This will be a sign for you" means "this will serve as proof for you." Swaddling clothes were strips of cloth used to wrap newborn babies, and the manger was the trough where the animals ate.

An angel of the Lord speaks to some shepherds who were watching over their sheep at night. He has just announced to them that the Savior has been born, Christ the Lord. He gives them a simple and checkable sign so they can find him. It is striking that the promised King arrives in such a humble place.

For today: God often works in what is simple and hidden. If you feel small or overlooked today, remember that Jesus came without luxuries, and that God draws near to those who know they are in need. Seek Christ with humility.
exp.12:17:
Jesus asks a question to introduce a teaching: "What is the kingdom of God like? And with what shall I compare it?" The words "like" and "compare" mean "similar to" and "to set beside something familiar." It is not that Jesus does not know the answer; he uses the question to awaken the attention of those who hear him.

He is speaking in a synagogue, after healing on the Sabbath a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years. His opponents were put to shame, but the people rejoiced. With this question, Jesus moves from the healing to explaining how the kingdom of God works: small at first, but with real growth.

For today: do not despise the small. If God is at work in your life, in your family or in your church, even if it seems to be little, trust that he can make it grow.
exp.2:16:
It says that Jesus, the one who comes after John, is like a farmer who separates the grain from the husk. The "fan" was a wooden pitchfork used to toss the threshed grain into the air so the wind would carry the chaff away. The "threshing floor" is the place where the grain was threshed, and the "barn" is the storehouse. The wheat is kept; the chaff is burned with a fire that cannot be put out.

John the Baptist speaks to a crowd that was wondering whether he might be the Christ. He makes clear that he is not, and announces someone greater than himself. He uses this image of the field, familiar to everyone, to warn that there will be a judgment and that each person's life will be examined. Some understand the fire as the final judgment; others understand it as purification; the text stresses the seriousness of the decision.

For today: do not live by appearances. Ask God to examine your heart and help you return to Him every day.
exp.8:37:
A man in the crowd cried out to Jesus, "Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, because he is my only child." The explanation of the words "I beseech thee, look upon" means "I beg you, look at him," that is, that Jesus would have compassion and attend to him. "Company" means crowd.

The father speaks as Jesus comes down from the mountain, where he had been with Peter, James, and John. Below, a large crowd was waiting for him. The man is desperate, for his son suffers violent fits that, according to the account, come from a spirit. He had already asked the disciples for help, but they could not heal him. For that reason he goes directly to Jesus.

When pain overwhelms us, we can do what this father did: bring to Jesus what we love most and sincerely ask him to look at our need. He is not annoyed by our desperation; he listens to us with compassion.
exp.8:39:
This verse says that a desperate father had asked Jesus' disciples to drive out the evil spirit that was tormenting his son, but they could not.

The father speaks, coming to Jesus after He came down from the mountain with Peter, John, and James. His son was his only child, and he suffered terrible seizures. In telling of the disciples' failure, the man shows his anguish. Jesus responds with sadness at the lack of faith in that generation, and then He heals the boy and returns him to his father.

For today: when our strength or resources fall short, let us not remain in frustration. Let us bring our need to Jesus, because He is able, and trust in Him with simple faith.
exp.7:41:
This verse explains why Jairo asks for help so urgently: his only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying. The crowd pressing around Jesus as he walked toward Jairo's house shows how hard it was for him to make progress through the throng, since the people surrounded him and pushed on every side.

Luke is the one narrating. Jairo was a ruler of the synagogue, a respected leader who looked after the order of the gatherings. Even so, he fell at Jesus' feet. His grief as a father outweighed his standing. The crowd pressing in also shows that the road was not easy, and soon Jesus would stop for another person in need.

For today: when you face an urgent need, bring it to Jesus with humility and without pride. And if he seems slow or stops for others, keep trusting, because his timing does not forget anyone.
exp.5:0:
Luke tells us that Jesus was walking through fields of wheat or barley on a sabbath day. His disciples picked ears of grain, rubbed them between their hands to loosen the kernels, and ate them.

The phrase "the second sabbath after the first" is unclear. Some scholars think it refers to a sabbath close to the Passover, but no one knows this for certain.

Here the narrator, Luke, presents a simple scene that soon sparks debate. The Pharisees, who were very careful about the rules of rest, thought the disciples were doing work by harvesting. The law allowed people to take grain from a neighbor's field to eat (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the question was whether doing so on the sabbath broke the rest.

For today: God gave his commands for the good of people. Before judging others over details, let us ask what God intends with each command: mercy, care, and love.
exp.8:42:
It says that all the people were amazed at the mighty power of God, after Jesus healed the boy. While everyone was marveling at what Jesus was doing, he turned to his disciples.

Luke tells what happened as they came down from the mountain of the transfiguration. The disciples had not been able to heal the child, but Jesus did it with authority. In the middle of the praise, Jesus gives them a serious message: soon he would be handed over. They did not understand it, and the text says it was hidden from them, without explaining in detail why.

We can admire Jesus for his works and, even so, not listen to what he wants to teach us. Today we can ask him to give us attentive ears and a humble heart, so that we follow him also when his words are hard for us to understand.
exp.5:41:
It is absurd to want to correct a small flaw in another person while ignoring a much bigger flaw in oneself. The first word refers to a tiny splinter or speck; the second refers to a large beam from a building. The word "let me" is what one would say to ask for permission. Jesus calls the person who seems to be helping others, yet does not examine himself, a hypocrite. First the large beam must be removed, and then one will see clearly enough to help one's brother.

Jesus speaks, teaching his disciples and the crowd in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has been speaking about not judging and about mercy. What follows, the tree and its fruit, suggests that what is in the heart shows itself in life.

For today: before pointing out someone else's mistake, ask yourself honestly where you need to change, and ask God to examine you. This does not forbid helping others, but calls us to do it with humility, clarity, and love.
exp.2:26:
This verse is part of the list of Jesus' ancestors. It names Joanna, Rhesa, Zorobabel and Salatiel. The phrase "which was the son of" means "son of" or "descendant of."

Luke, the writer of the Gospel, presents this genealogy after Jesus' baptism. He traces the line backward, from Jesus to Adam. Zorobabel and Salatiel also appear in Matthew's list, but the names around them do not match. Some think Luke follows the line of Mary and others the line of Joseph; there is no certainty. What is clear is that Luke wants to show that Jesus is truly human and comes for all humanity.

For today: God works through little-known people, like these names. Your faithfulness each day, even when no one notices, can be part of what God is building in your family and in others.
exp.22:47:
This verse tells us that a large crowd had gathered to watch the crucifixion as a public sight. After seeing how Jesus died, they went back to their homes beating their breasts. In that culture, this gesture showed deep sorrow, grief, and also repentance. The word "sight" here means something that people watch in public.

The one telling the story is Luke. Just before, Jesus prayed and gave up his spirit to the Father, and the Roman centurion recognized that he was righteous. Now the crowd, who perhaps had come out of curiosity or because of the pressure of the moment, is left deeply moved.
