The Bible does not explain in detail what each person was thinking, but the gesture shows that something touched their hearts.

For today: do not remain only a spectator of the cross. Come to Jesus with sincerity, acknowledge what you need to change, and let his self-giving lead you to a humble and grateful heart.
exp.0:8:
According to the custom of the priests, Zechariah was chosen by lot to offer the incense. The explanation of "by lot" is that his name was drawn in the lottery. In this way he entered the temple, into the holy place, to carry out that task.

Here Luke speaks, the one who recounts the events in an orderly way. Zechariah and Elisabeth were elderly and had no children. The priests served in turns, and those in charge of the incense were chosen by lot. The texts do not say how many times the duty could fall to a given person, so we do not know whether it was unusual for him. What matters is that, in that ordinary moment of service, God was going to act with an unexpected announcement.

For today: God can work in the middle of everyday life. Serve faithfully in what falls to you, even when it seems like routine or when your wait feels long. He remains attentive to your life.
exp.11:48:
Jesus says that he came to bring fire to the earth, and he wonders what more he could want if that fire were already burning. "Cast" here means to throw or hurl. The second sentence is hard and can be understood in more than one way: as an intense desire for the fire to already be burning, or as an expression of urgency.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and earlier he had warned them that whoever receives much will be required to give an account for much. Right after this, he speaks of his "baptism," which many understand as his suffering and death. The fire can represent judgment, purification, or the work of the Spirit; scholars interpret it in different ways. His message divides people.

For today: if we have received the truth of Jesus, let us not treat it with indifference. Let us ask God for a sincere heart, ready to obey him, even when that costs us.
exp.13:2:
Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees a direct question: "Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?" Old-fashioned words: "lawyers" here means the experts in the Scriptures; "lawful" means permitted; and "answering" here shows that Jesus is responding to what they were thinking, though no one had spoken.

Jesus is eating in the house of a leading Pharisee, on a sabbath, and they were watching him closely to see what he would do. In front of him was a man with dropsy, a disease that swells the body through a build-up of fluid. Jesus brings their intention into the open with a question. They say nothing, and he heals the man.

Today, the question invites us to examine whether our religious rules help us love people or leave them suffering. Doing good should never have to wait until it is convenient.
exp.21:27:
Jesus tells his disciples that they have stayed by his side through his trials.

Jesus speaks during the Last Supper. The disciples had just been arguing about who was the greatest among them. Jesus teaches that the true leader serves, and he presents himself as one who serves. Then he recognizes them for their faithfulness, even though failures would soon come, such as Peter's denials and everyone's flight. He promises them a place in his kingdom.

For today: God values simple faithfulness, even when it is imperfect. If you are going through a trial today, stay close to Jesus, and look for ways to serve others rather than seeking to be the most important.
exp.21:61:
Luke 22:62 says that Peter, after denying Jesus for the third time, went out of the place and wept with great pain. The word "bitterly" describes a deep sorrow, a heart broken by realizing what he had done.

The one who tells the story is Luke. Peter had promised to be faithful to Jesus, but that night, out of fear, he said three times that he did not know him. When the rooster crowed, Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered what the Lord had told him. That memory broke his heart. Meanwhile, Jesus was being mistreated and mocked.

For today: when we fail, sincere sorrow over what we have done can be a first step toward returning to God. Do not stay hidden in shame; bring your fall to Jesus, who looks at us with truth, but also with mercy.
exp.12:9:
This verse says that Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the sabbath. A synagogue was the place where Jews gathered each week to pray, read the Scriptures, and listen to teaching. The sabbath was their day of rest and worship.

Luke is the one who tells this. It comes right after the parable of the fig tree without fruit, which speaks of God's patience and the opportunity to repent. Here a new account begins: Jesus teaches, and in the middle of that teaching he will see a bent-over woman and heal her. Thus Jesus' word and his compassion go together.

For today: make gathering for worship and teaching a habit, and go there with an open heart. God may speak to you or touch you exactly where you most need it.
exp.10:36:
It says that, when Jesus had finished speaking, a Pharisee invited him to dine at his home. Jesus accepted, went in, and sat down to eat. A few older words: "as soon as" means "hardly" or "when"; "begged" means "asked him"; "to meat" means "to the table," in the spelling of the time.

Jesus had just been teaching about light and the need to have clean eyes and a clean heart. Luke tells us that a Pharisee invited him, and we do not know for certain his reasons. Jesus accepted, and right away the scene shows the clash between outward cleanliness and inward cleanliness.

For today: Jesus draws near to people who are very different, even to those who question him. We can receive his word with sincerity, letting him examine not only what we show on the outside, but also what is in our heart.
exp.13:3:
What it says: The Pharisees and the experts in the law did not answer Jesus' question. Then Jesus took the sick man, healed him, and let him go. The man had a swollen body from a buildup of fluid, and "let him go" means he sent him home.

Context: Jesus had been invited to eat at the home of an important Pharisee, on the Sabbath, and they were watching him to see what he would do. He himself asked whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath. Their silence shows that they did not want to answer, perhaps because they would not admit that doing good should not wait. Afterward Jesus spoke to them about the ox or donkey that had fallen into a well.

For today: Religious rules and customs should never make us cold toward someone's suffering. When we have the chance to do good, even if others criticize us or stay silent, let us do it with love and without delay.
exp.16:9:
It says that when someone does everything God asks of him, he should not feel that he is doing God a favor. "Unprofitable servants" does not mean that we are worth nothing, but that we have no merit to demand a reward. The explanation's note about an old form of a word is removed here, since that word does not appear in the verse above, and "was our duty to do" is the phrase the verse itself uses, so it is simply rendered as "that which was our duty to do."

Jesus speaks to his disciples and uses the example of a servant who, after working in the field, must still prepare the supper for his master. No one thanks him as if he had done something extraordinary. Shortly before, the disciples asked for more faith (v. 5), and Jesus teaches them to serve with humility, without pride.

For today: serve others and obey God without seeking applause or feeling superior. Do what is right with gratitude, remembering that everything you have comes from His grace.
exp.3:7:
Jesus firmly rejects the devil's offer. "Get thee behind me" is a command to leave his presence. Jesus quotes Scripture: only God is to be worshiped and served. "Worship" means giving honor and total loyalty, and "him only" means no one else.

Jesus is in the desert, being tempted by the devil after fasting forty days. The devil offers him power and glory over the kingdoms of the world, if he will worship him. Jesus answers with words from Deuteronomy 6:13, and so shows that God's Word stands firm against temptation.

Today, many things promise success or security if we give them first place. Ask yourself: whom am I truly serving? When temptation comes, answer with what God says, and put God first again.
exp.21:46:
What it says: While Jesus was still speaking with his disciples, a crowd appeared. Leading them was Judas, one of the Twelve, and he came up to Jesus to kiss him. The word "went before them" in the King James Version shows he was at the front. A kiss was a common greeting between friends, but here it was a sign of betrayal.

Context: Luke tells this in the Garden of Olives, right after Jesus prayed and found his disciples asleep. He had asked them to pray so that they would not fall into temptation. Now the moment of his arrest arrives, and Judas, who knew him closely, hands him over. Jesus responds with a question that shows he knows what is happening.

For today: We can fail even while staying close to Jesus. That is why we need to pray and stay alert, and to examine honestly whether our words of affection match what is in our hearts.
exp.18:28:
This verse tells that Jesus, as he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount called the Mount of Olives, sent two of his disciples ahead.

Luke narrates the final stretch of Jesus' journey toward Jerusalem. Shortly before, he had told the parable of the ten minas, in which a king goes away and then returns. Jesus continues on his way up to Jerusalem, knowing what awaits him. Now he prepares his entrance into the city, and the charge to the two disciples is the first step.

For today: Jesus calls his disciples to take part in what he is doing, even in simple tasks. Perhaps today he is not asking you for something great, but for a small step of obedience. Do it with confidence, for he already knows what is coming.
exp.9:27:
Jesus commends the teacher of the law for his answer. Jesus tells him that if he does what he has just said, that is, love God and love his neighbor, he will live. The word "live" speaks of the true life that God gives, eternal life.

Jesus is speaking with an expert in the law of Moses, who wanted to test him by asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus makes him think, and the man himself quotes the law. But then, wanting to justify himself, he asks who his neighbor is, and Jesus answers with the parable of the good Samaritan.

Today, knowing what is right is not enough; God invites us to live it out. This week, do something concrete for someone who needs help, even if they are not part of your circle.
exp.14:16:
The explanation says that the younger son, after reaching the bottom of his misery, came to his senses and began to think clearly. "Coming to himself" means he regained his good judgment, like someone waking up from a deception. He realized that the hired servants, that is, the workers hired by the day, had bread enough and to spare in his father's house, while he was dying of hunger.

Jesus tells this parable. The young man had asked for his inheritance, wasted it far from home, and ended up tending pigs, a very humiliating job for a Jew. This thought is the beginning of his return: he recognizes his situation and remembers his father's goodness.

For today: when things go wrong because of our own choices, it is good to stop and think honestly, without excuses. That moment of clarity can be the first step toward returning to God, who receives us with grace.
exp.1:51:
This verse says that Jesus, as a child and a young man, grew up in every way. He increased in wisdom, that is, in understanding and good judgment; in stature, meaning in his body and over the years; and in favour, which here means goodwill and esteem, both with God and with people.

The speaker is Luke, the narrator. He has just told how Jesus, at twelve years old, stayed behind in the temple and his parents did not understand his words. Then Jesus returned to Nazareth and lived in obedience to them. Luke sums up the years of his growing up before beginning his account of Jesus's ministry.

For today: growing is a process of a whole lifetime. We can ask God to help us advance spiritually, mentally, physically and in our relationships, with patience and obedience, as Jesus did.
exp.19:10:
The explanation says that the owner of the vineyard sent a second servant to receive the fruit that was due to him. The tenants beat him, treated him shamefully, and sent him away with nothing. "Insulted" means being treated with contempt. Receiving nothing means going away without anything.

Jesus tells this parable to the people in the temple, in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. Many understand that the owner represents God, the vineyard represents Israel, the servants represent the prophets, and the beloved son represents Jesus himself. The religious leaders understood that he was speaking about them (v. 19).

For today: God speaks to us with patience again and again. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his voice or rejecting it out of pride. Let us respond with humility and offer him the fruit of an obedient life.
exp.15:20:
Lazarus, the beggar, was hungry and longed to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. To be fed means to be satisfied after eating. In addition, the dogs came near and licked his sores, that is, the open wounds on his body. He was a poor man, sick and forgotten.

Jesus is telling this parable to his listeners, among them Pharisees who loved money (Luke 16:14). Some think the crumbs may have been the bread people used to wipe their hands at the table, but the text does not make this clear. The contrast with the rich man, who lived in luxury, prepares the reversal that comes after the death of them both.

Today we can ask ourselves who is lying at our gate without our having noticed. God calls us to see the one in need and to help them with what we have, whether food, time, or company.
exp.11:37:
It says that even if the master comes late at night, in the second or the third watch, happy are the servants who find him awake and ready. "Watch" was each of the parts into which the night was divided for taking turns on guard duty. "Blessed" means very happy, favored. "Those" refers to those who are found in that state.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd. He uses the picture of servants waiting for their master who is returning from a wedding feast. He wants to teach them to live prepared for his coming, without knowing the exact moment. The verses that follow reinforce this with the example of the thief.

For today: live each day faithfully, doing what God has entrusted to you, without putting off your obedience or your prayer. Being ready is not living in fear, but living with steadfastness and hope.
exp.21:28:
Jesus says that he gives a kingdom to his disciples, just as his Father gave one to him. The word "appoint" here sounds like "assign" or "grant": it is like leaving something as an inheritance.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. The disciples had just been arguing about who was the greatest. Jesus answers them that he himself is among them as one who serves. Then he acknowledges their faithfulness in the trials and promises them a place in his kingdom. Scholars debate exactly when and how this will be fulfilled, but the promise is clear.

For today: in the kingdom of God, greatness is measured by service, not by rank. If Jesus honors us with a promise so great, we can serve others with humility, without competing to be first.
exp.22:43:
It was about noon, the sixth hour by the Jewish way of counting hours from sunrise (that is, twelve o'clock), when a darkness covered the land until the ninth hour (three in the afternoon).

Luke, the narrator, tells us what happened while Jesus was on the cross, just after he promised paradise to the repentant thief. We do not know for certain what caused the darkness or how far it extended across the land (it may have covered the whole region). Luke presents it as a sign of the weight of that moment, which is followed by the torn veil of the temple and Jesus' last words.

For today: even in the darkest moments, God is not absent. Jesus trusted the Father in the midst of the darkness; we can pray and trust Him when we do not understand what is happening.
exp.13:9:
Jesus says that when someone invites you to a feast, you should not look for the best seat. Go and sit down in the lowest place. Then, when the host arrives, he will say to you, "Friend, go up higher." Then you will be honored in front of all the other guests.

Jesus is eating at the house of a leader of the Pharisees, on a Sabbath, and he observes how the guests choose the first seats. He tells this as a parable, but the following verse shows the underlying teaching: whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Today we can practice humility without seeking applause or recognition. At work, in church, or in the family, serve gladly and let God be the one who honors you in his time.
exp.10:7:
Jesus says that, although this man will not get up out of friendship, he will get up because of the "importunity," that is, the bold and shameless persistence of the one who asks. Then he will give him all that he needs.

Jesus is teaching his disciples how to pray, right after the Lord's Prayer. He tells a parable about a man who asks for bread at midnight so he can take care of a visitor. Many understand the point to be a contrast: if an annoyed neighbor ends up giving in, how much more will God, who is good and loves us, listen to us.

For today: do not grow tired of praying. Bring your needs to God with confidence and persistence, knowing that you are not speaking to someone who is annoyed, but to a Father who listens with affection.
exp.2:34:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It names four people, Saruch, Ragau, Phalec and Heber, going backward in time. The verse's wording "which was the son of" simply means the person named was the son of the next name in the list. The older spellings, such as Phalec, correspond to Peleg in the Old Testament.

Luke, the author of the Gospel, presents Jesus's genealogy right after his baptism. Unlike Matthew, who starts with Abraham, Luke goes backward all the way to Adam. In this way he shows that Jesus is connected to the whole human race and not only to Israel. Some scholars think this list follows the line of Mary, and others the line of Joseph; there is no certain agreement.

For today: God works through generations, even through people who are little known. Your life and your faith count, even though no one may remember your name. Be faithful today.
exp.9:34:
On the next day, the Samaritan took out two silver coins and gave them to the innkeeper. He said, "Take care of him," and promised to pay any extra expense when he came back. A denarius was, as is commonly understood, the pay for one day's work, so it was real help, though we do not know exactly how much it covered.

Jesus is the one speaking, in the parable of the good Samaritan. A lawyer had asked him, "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus answers with this story, in which a man despised by many Jews is the one who shows mercy to the wounded man.

For today: compassion does not end with a good gesture in the moment. Think of someone who needs help and ask yourself how you can support them steadily, by giving time, money, or company, and by keeping the promises you make.
exp.1:13:
This verse is the song of the angels. It says that God deserves honor in the highest heavens, and that on earth there is peace and good will toward people. The old wording used a different form than the one your Bible uses, and the phrase "peace to men of good will," meaning peace for those whom God favors, appears in some older translations. Scholars debate which reading is most likely, but both emphasize God's favor.

A multitude of angels appears suddenly before shepherds on the night Jesus was born. They praise God because the promised Savior has come. The message is not for the powerful but for ordinary people who were tending sheep.

For today: the peace that God offers begins with Jesus. When you feel anxious, go to Him in prayer, and let His favor encourage you to live at peace with others.
exp.0:35:
Here the angel Gabriel tells Mary that her relative Elizabeth, who was already old, is expecting a son. Moreover, she is already in her sixth month of pregnancy, although people said she was barren, that is, that she could not have children. The word for relative simply means a family member, and to have conceived means to have become pregnant.

The angel speaks with Mary after announcing that she will be the mother of Jesus. She had a sincere question: "How shall this be?" Gabriel offers her a concrete sign: what God was already doing with Elizabeth. The Bible does not explain in detail the exact degree of kinship between them; it only says they were relatives.

For today: when something seems impossible to you, remember what God has already done in other people. Those stories can strengthen your trust, and you can answer God with the simplicity of Mary.
exp.13:22:
The explanation says that the master of the house tells his servant to go out again, this time to the roads and the hedges (the fences that border the fields), where homeless people or travelers were to be found. "Compel them" means urging with great earnestness, so that no one is left outside. The goal is that his house may be filled.

Jesus tells this parable during a meal at the home of a Pharisee. The first guests made excuses and turned down the dinner. Then the owner opens the invitation to the poor, the sick, and then to those from far away. Many understand that it shows the breadth of the kingdom of God. Here "compel" is understood as persuading with insistence, not as forcing with violence.

For today: invite others sincerely and persistently to know Christ, especially those who feel far away or unimportant. And examine your own heart, so that you do not make excuses when God calls you.
exp.5:46:
Jesus says that whoever comes to Him, hears His words, and puts them into practice is like someone he is going to show us through an example. The King James wording "shew" is an older form of "show," and "I will shew you" means "I am going to show you."

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and a large crowd, at the end of what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has just said that the heart shows itself in words and deeds. He asks them why they call him "Lord" if they do not do what he says. This verse introduces the parable of the two houses, one built on rock and the other without a foundation.

Today, it is not enough to listen to sermons or read the Bible. Choose one of Jesus' teachings that you already know, such as forgiving or being generous, and practice it this week. Obeying is what gives firmness when trials come.
exp.12:4:
Jesus repeats a serious warning: unless they repent, they will all perish in the same way. "I tell you" is the same as "I say to you." "Repent" means changing one's heart and direction. "Perish" means to be lost or destroyed. "Likewise" means "in the same way."

Jesus speaks to a crowd who told him about some Galileans who died in a tragic way. He also mentions eighteen people crushed by a tower in Siloam. He corrects the idea that those who suffer tragedies are worse sinners. Everyone needs to repent. Right after this, he tells the parable of the fig tree without fruit, which shows God's patience and also the urgency of responding.

For today: do not use other people's misfortunes to make yourself feel better or to judge them. Instead, examine your own heart, ask God for forgiveness, and change today what you know you need to change, without putting it off for later.
exp.5:20:
Jesus says that those who are hungry now are happy, or blessed, because God will fill them. He also says that those who weep now are blessed, because afterward they will laugh. To be "blessed" means to be happy or favored. To be "filled" means to be completely satisfied.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, with a large crowd around him who had come seeking healing. This passage resembles the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew, but here Luke speaks of real hunger and real weeping, not only spiritual ones. Jesus announces that God will change the situation of the poor and of those who suffer. Some understand that this is fully fulfilled when the kingdom of God comes.

For today: if you are going through need or sadness, do not think that God has forgotten you. Bring your pain to him honestly, and help others who suffer, trusting that God sustains those who wait on him.
exp.1:3:
This verse tells that Joseph left Nazareth, a town in Galilee, and traveled to Bethlehem in Judea. There he went to the city of David, the ancient king of Israel. Joseph had to go because he belonged to David's house and lineage, that is, he was a descendant of David.

Here Luke speaks, the writer who narrates the birth of Jesus with historical care. There was a census ordered by the Roman government, and each person had to register in their city of origin. Luke shows that, even with the decisions of an empire, God's plan was being fulfilled: the Messiah, of David's family, would be born in Bethlehem, as had been announced in Micah 5:2.

For today: God can use uncomfortable circumstances, such as bureaucratic requirements or difficult journeys, to accomplish his purposes. Trust that he guides you, even when you do not understand the whole path.
exp.0:46:
Mary speaks of a deep joy, felt in the innermost part of her being, because God is her Saviour. "Hath rejoiced" speaks of a gladness that springs from the heart. "My spirit" refers to the innermost part of a person, and "Saviour" is the one who rescues and gives life.

Mary speaks in the song known as the Magnificat. She has just been greeted by her cousin Elizabeth, who called her blessed for believing what God had told her. Mary responds by praising God. She acknowledges that he looked upon her with kindness, despite being a humble young woman, and that he has done great things for her. Some scholars note that by calling God her Saviour, she recognizes that she also needs his help and his mercy.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to rejoice in what he has already done for you. Give thanks aloud for his care and his salvation.
exp.11:19:
God speaks to a rich man and calls him a fool, that is, someone without wisdom. He tells him that this very night his life will be demanded of him. Then he asks whose the riches will be that you have stored up, meaning the goods he has kept and prepared for the future.

Jesus tells this parable to a crowd, after someone asked him to step in on an inheritance. The man in the story planned to build bigger barns to rest and enjoy himself. Jesus warns against greed and concludes that whoever stores up for himself and is not rich toward God is a fool.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are living only to secure our material future. Planning is not wrong, but it is good to make room for God, for generosity, and for other people. Today you can give or help someone with what God has entrusted to you.
exp.3:11:
Jesus answers the devil with a sentence from Scripture: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." Here "tempt" means to put God to the test, to demand that He prove His care or His power.

Jesus speaks during his trial in the wilderness. The devil had just quoted a psalm about the protection of angels and used it to encourage him to throw himself down from the temple. Jesus replies with Deuteronomy 6:16. He trusts God, but he does not force Him to put on a show. It is hard to know exactly which part of the temple is meant, but the sense of the scene is clear.

For today: trusting God does not mean doing reckless things to see whether He will rescue us. It means obeying Him, using wisdom, and resting in His care.
exp.4:35:
Jesus tells a simple parable: no one tears a piece from a new garment to patch an old one. If someone does, the new cloth shrinks, tears the garment, and the patch does not match the old.

Jesus is speaking with Pharisees and teachers of the law, who were asking why his disciples did not fast as others did. He answers that the bridegroom is with him, and that is a time of joy. With this parable he shows that what he brings is not a simple repair of the old religion, but something new.

For today: do not use Jesus as a patch on a life that stays the same. Let him transform your habits, priorities, and thoughts, instead of adding him only to what you already have.
exp.18:13:
It says that the citizens of the nobleman hated him. That is why they sent a delegation after him, that is, a group of messengers, to say that they did not want him to be their king. "But" is the word the verse uses to introduce this contrast, and "hated" means to despise or reject with strong feeling.

Jesus tells this parable near Jerusalem, and the people thought the kingdom of God was going to appear right away. The nobleman represents Jesus himself, who would go away and return as king. Some interpreters also see here an echo of what happened with Archelaus, son of Herod, although this is debated. The parable shows that there will be those who openly reject his authority.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly let Jesus govern our decisions, or whether in practice we say, "We will not have this man to reign over us." Today you can give him a specific area of your life, such as your work, your money, or your relationships.
exp.4:6:
The explanation says that the fishermen, seeing that the net was full and about to break, signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help. They came, and together they filled both boats with so many fish that the boats almost sank. The word for "filled and sinking" in this verse means that the boats were filling with water and going under. "Partners" were fishing partners.

Luke tells this after Jesus taught from Simon's boat. Then he asked Simon to let down the nets again, even though they had fished all night and caught nothing. Simon obeyed because of Jesus' word, and the result was more than they could handle. This verse shows the abundance that leads up to the moment when Peter recognizes who Jesus is.

For today: when God asks us to obey, even when we are tired or discouraged, we can trust his word. And when he blesses us, let us share the burden and the joy with others, asking for help from those who are near.
exp.18:41:
Jesus says, "If only you too had understood, at least today, the things that bring peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes." The word for "understood" here is a less common wording, so I have simply rendered it in plain English. Jesus speaks as he approaches Jerusalem riding on a donkey, amid shouts of praise from his disciples. Seeing the city, he weeps. He grieves that many do not recognize in him the Messiah who brings true peace with God. The verses that follow announce the siege and destruction of the city, and Jesus explains the cause: they did not recognize the time in which God visited them.

Today, God continues to offer peace through Jesus. Let us not harden our hearts through pride or distraction. Today we can stop, listen to his voice, and respond with humility, before we put it off until later.
exp.18:3:
What it says: Zacchaeus, wanting to see Jesus, ran ahead of the crowd and climbed up into a sycamore, a tree with low branches that are easy to climb. He did it because Jesus was going to pass right along that road.

Context: Luke narrates Jesus passing through Jericho on the way to Jerusalem. Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector, and he was rich. Many looked on tax collectors with distrust. He was short in stature and the crowd kept him from seeing, so he looked for another way to see Jesus.

For today: When we truly want to draw near to God, sometimes we have to set aside shame, pride, or comfort. Zacchaeus did not stay content with the excuse of the crowd or of his height. Let us seek Jesus with simplicity, and we will see that He also seeks us.
exp.18:47:
They could find nothing they might do, because all the people hung on his words, listening to him very closely.

The phrase "hung on his words" here means that the people were attentive, as if they were held by what he said. The phrase about what they might do means what means they could use against him.

Luke, the writer, tells what happened after Jesus cleansed the temple in Jerusalem. Jesus taught there every day. The chief priests, the scribes, and the leaders of the people wanted to kill him, but they feared how the crowd would react, since the crowd followed him with great interest.

For today: Jesus taught the Word of God with firmness, even when some rejected him. We can imitate that attitude by listening with close attention and an open heart, not letting pride or our own interests shut us off from what God wants to tell us.
exp.0:63:
In that very moment, Zechariah regained the ability to speak. Where the verse says his mouth was "opened," the meaning is that he could talk again. The phrase "immediately" describes that it happened right then. The first thing he did was bless God, that is, praise Him and give Him thanks.

The context: Zechariah had been made mute for not believing the angel's announcement about the birth of John (Luke 1:20). Eight days after the birth, the family wanted to name the child after his father, but Zechariah wrote on a tablet that his name was John, obeying what the angel had told him. By obeying, he recovered his voice. Luke recounts this as a sign that God was at work.

For today: after a time of silence or doubt, we can respond with obedience and praise. When God restores us or answers us, may the first thing that comes from our mouth be gratitude to Him.
exp.20:33:
Jesus says we must take care of ourselves so that our hearts do not become heavy. Gluttony is eating to excess, and drunkenness is getting drunk. The cares of this life are the daily worries and anxieties. If the heart is dulled in this way, that day can arrive suddenly, catching us unprepared.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, at the end of his teaching about the destruction of the temple and the last times. He has already warned them that his words will not pass away. Now he asks them to stay alert. What follows confirms this: watching and praying so that they may stand firm before the Son of Man. Scholars understand "that day" in several ways, but all of them see a call to watchfulness.

Today, examine which things dull your heart, whether excess or worry. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and put God first again.
exp.3:16:
It says that the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Jesus. He opened it and found the passage he wanted to read. The verse itself says "delivered," meaning the scroll was given to him, and a "scroll" was a long roll of parchment, not a book like the ones we have today.

Luke tells what happened in Nazareth, the town where Jesus grew up. It was the Sabbath, and Jesus went into the synagogue, as he usually did. He stood up to read, and the scroll was given to him. Some think the passage had already been marked out for that day, but the text does not make this clear. What follows is a prophecy of Isaiah that Jesus will apply to himself.

For today: Jesus knew the Scriptures and read them regularly. We can set aside a consistent time to open the Bible, not only when we have a problem, and let God speak to us through it.
exp.14:14:
He told how the younger son, now out of money and hungry in that region, looked for help from one of the local residents. That man sent him out to his fields to take care of pigs.

The verse says he "joined himself" to a citizen of that country, meaning he came to him and put himself at his service. The word "fields" here refers to the land or property. Caring for animals means feeding and looking after them.

Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees and teachers of the law, who criticized him for welcoming sinners. The young man was a Jew, and pigs were considered unclean animals under the law of Moses. So caring for them shows how far he had fallen. Jesus wants to show the condition of someone who turns away from the father, and God's compassion toward him.

When we turn away from God, what promised freedom can end up enslaving us. If you find yourself in an empty place, do not stay there out of shame. Recognizing your need is the first step to coming home.
exp.1:43:
This verse tells how Joseph and Mary thought Jesus was traveling with the group of pilgrims. So they walked for a whole day without worrying. When they realized they did not see him, they began to look for him among their relatives and acquaintances. The word "company" refers to the caravan or group that was traveling together. The phrase "they sought him" means that they were searching for him.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. He tells what happened when Jesus was twelve years old and the family was returning from the Passover feast in Jerusalem. It was common to travel in large groups of relatives and neighbors, so it was not unusual that they did not see him right away. Luke sets up the scene in which they find him in the temple.

For today: it is easy to assume that Jesus is "with us" while we go about our routine. It is worth stopping often, praying, and checking whether we really have him close, rather than taking it for granted.
exp.16:35:
This verse says that two people will be together in the field, doing the same work, but one will be taken and the other left. Some scholars point out that this verse is missing from many early manuscripts and was probably copied from Matthew 24:40. For that reason, some modern Bibles do not include it.

Jesus speaks with his disciples about his coming and the day of judgment. He compares that day to the times of Noah and Lot, when life went on as usual until judgment came suddenly. Being taken can be understood as being carried away to judgment or being gathered up by God; Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: it is not enough to be close to faith, or to do what other believers do. Each person answers to God personally. Live today with a ready heart, and do not put off your relationship with him.
exp.22:28:
Jesus says that hard times are coming, so severe that people will call blessed the women who never had children. Normally it would be seen as a misfortune not to have children, but then it will be the other way around.

Jesus is walking toward the cross, and a group of women is weeping for him. He speaks to them tenderly, but he is preparing them for suffering that lies ahead. Many believe he is referring to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70 AD, though some also see a broader warning about God's judgment.

For today: Jesus does not ignore the pain of others, but he invites us to think about our own relationship with God. Today you can take a moment to pray sincerely and turn back to him, without waiting for difficult times to arrive.
exp.6:6:
Here the centurion says that he did not consider himself worthy even to go personally to find Jesus. For that reason he asks Jesus to just speak a word, and so his sick servant will be healed. The word "worthy" means deserving, and "servant" is an attendant or slave. Being healed means the servant will be cured.

A Roman officer, a centurion, had a servant who was very sick. First he sent Jewish elders, and now he sends friends with this message. His humility is joined to a great confidence: he believes Jesus has authority like the authority he exercises over his soldiers. Jesus marveled at his faith.

For today: we can come near to God with humility, without boasting of our own merits, and at the same time trust that the word of Jesus has power. To pray this way is to say: "I do not deserve it, but I trust in you."
exp.11:31:
Jesus tells his followers not to be afraid. He calls them "little flock," that is, a small and fragile group, like sheep. The phrase "it is your Father's good pleasure" means that it has pleased the Father, and gives him joy, to give them the kingdom: giving them the kingdom is something God wants to do, not something they must earn.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after teaching them not to live anxious about food or clothing. He reminds them that the Father knows their needs. Then he invites them to put the kingdom first and to be generous with what they have, because their true treasure is in heaven.

For today: when fear of lack or of the future grips you, remember that God is a generous Father. This week, give something with joy to someone in need, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.10:29:
Jesus says that Jonah was a sign to the people of Nineveh, and that he will be a sign to the people of his own time. "Son of man" is a title Jesus uses for himself. The explanation of the old spellings is removed here, since the reader sees the words as they are in the verse. "Generation" refers to the people living at that time.

Jesus speaks to the crowds who were asking him for a miraculous sign so that they could believe. He calls them an evil generation because they already had enough evidence and still doubted. In Matthew 12:40 Jesus connects the sign of Jonah with his death and resurrection; Luke does not explain it here, and some think it also refers to his preaching, which calls people to repentance.

For today: let us not wait for extraordinary proof before obeying God. We already have his Word and the risen Christ. Let us listen with humility, repent, and live what we already know.
exp.8:38:
A spirit seizes the boy and, without warning, makes him cry out. It shakes him violently, makes him foam at the mouth, and when it finally releases him, it leaves him badly hurt and worn out. "Crieth out" here refers to the boy's sudden shout, and "teareth him" means shaking and throwing him about with force. "Bruising him hardly" means leaving him battered and in a bad state.

The one speaking is a desperate father, in the crowd, the day after the transfiguration. He pleads with Jesus to look at his only son. He had already asked the disciples for help, but they could not do it. Luke, who was a physician, describes the boy's suffering in detail. Some think the symptoms resemble epilepsy, but the text attributes them to a spirit; it is not easy to be more precise.

For today: when the pain of someone you love overwhelms you and your strength falls short, do as this father did. Bring the whole situation to Jesus, honestly and without hiding anything.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that Jesus was watching how the guests chose the best places at the table. Then he told them a parable. The words "guests" and "put forward a parable" in the original wording are rewritten here as the verse itself describes: he noticed how they chose the chief rooms, and he spoke to them in a story that taught a lesson.

Jesus is speaking in the house of an important Pharisee, on a Sabbath day, where people were watching him closely. He had just healed a sick man and had answered those who criticized it. Now, seeing how eager the guests were to take places of honor, he uses the moment to teach them about humility.

Today we can ask ourselves when we look for others to notice or praise us. A good practice is to serve without seeking applause and to let God be the one who honors us in his own time.
exp.21:23:
This verse tells us that the disciples began to argue about which of them was considered the most important. "Strife" means a fight or dispute, and "seemed to be the greatest" refers to who had the most standing or worth in the eyes of the others.

Luke tells this during the Last Supper. Jesus had just spoken of his betrayal and his death, and the disciples were asking which of them would betray him. Even so, they ended up arguing about first place. Jesus answers that, unlike the rulers of the world, the greatest among them must act like the one who serves.

For today: before seeking recognition in the church, at work, or in the family, ask yourself whom you can serve today in a concrete way, without expecting applause.
exp.11:23:
Jesus invites us to look carefully at the ravens. They do not sow or reap, and they have no storehouse or barn. Even so, God feeds them. Then he asks: if God cares for the birds, how much more value do you have to him?

Jesus speaks to his disciples after warning about greed with the parable of the rich fool. He tells them not to live anxious about food or clothing, because life is worth more than that. He is not teaching them to be lazy, but to trust the Father.

Today, when worry about money or the future takes away your peace, pause. Name in prayer what troubles you, give it to God, and take the next responsible step that is yours to take, trusting in his care.
exp.0:28:
She was frightened and deeply disturbed when she saw the angel and heard his words. The explanation of the verse's wording is that she was stirred up or startled. She did not understand what kind of greeting this was, and she began to think about what it meant.

Luke tells how the angel Gabriel came to Mary, a young woman engaged to Joseph. The greeting called her highly favored and told her that the Lord was with her. It was not an ordinary greeting. That is why she reflects in silence. Soon the angel calms her and announces that she will have a son named Jesus.

Today, when God surprises us or something is hard for us to understand, we can do as Mary did: not react in haste, but stop, think, and pray. Feeling fear or doubt is not a lack of faith; what matters is bringing those questions to God with humility.
exp.0:77:
This verse says that God visited us through his great compassion. "Tender mercy" is an old way of speaking of a loving kindness that comes from the very depths of the heart. The dayspring is the rising sun, the light of a new morning. "From on high" shows that this light comes down from heaven.

The words belong to Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, who was filled with the Holy Spirit. He is praising God for the birth of his son, who would prepare the way of the Lord. Many understand that the dayspring refers to Jesus, the light God sends. The context suggests this, since it speaks of giving light to those who live in darkness.

For today: God does not save us out of obligation, but out of love. When you find yourself in darkness, remember that his help comes from his compassion, not from your merits. Draw near to him with confidence.
exp.21:50:
Jesus answers the disciples' question and tells them: "Suffer ye thus far." He then touches the wounded ear of the servant and heals him.

It is the night of Jesus' arrest in the garden. The disciples ask whether they should fight, and one of them acts without waiting for an answer and cuts off the ear of a servant of the high priest. Luke is the only Gospel writer who tells that Jesus healed this man. Jesus stops the violence because his path to the cross was voluntary. Some understand "thus far" as a command to the disciples, and others as a request to the captors to let him act. The text allows both readings.

Today: Jesus did good even to the one who came to arrest him. When someone wrongs us or opposes us, let us look for a concrete way to respond with kindness and not with revenge.
exp.4:10:
It says that when the boats had been brought to land, Simon, James, and John left everything and followed Jesus. The word for the boats here means fishing boats, not large ships. "Everything" refers to their boats, their nets, and the very large catch they had just brought in.

Luke, the writer, tells what happened after the miraculous catch of fish on the lake of Gennesaret. The fishermen felt amazement and fear before Jesus. He had said to Simon: "Do not be afraid; from now on you will catch men." Luke does not explain everything they were thinking, but he shows that they responded with a concrete decision: to follow him.

For today: following Jesus may ask us to let go of something that gives us security. It is not always leaving our work, but it does mean putting Jesus first. Today you can ask him in prayer what you find hard to surrender to him, and take a small step of obedience.
exp.7:29:
Jesus asks the man what his name is, and he answers: "Legion." The text explains why: many demons had entered into him. "Legion" was the name of a large unit of the Roman army, made up of thousands of soldiers. Here it suggests a great crowd, although the text does not say exactly how many there were.

The narrator, Luke, tells of Jesus' encounter with a tormented man in the country of the Gadarenes. This man lived outside society, bound with chains and impossible to control. Jesus asks his name, and the spirits answer through the man. In this way we see how great their hold was and how great Jesus' authority over them is.

For today: no burden or bondage is too great for Jesus. We can bring to him honestly what dominates us, without hiding it, trusting that he has the power and the compassion to set us free.
exp.17:11:
Here the Pharisee presents his religious works as proof that he is good. He says he fasts twice a week, and that he gives a tenth of all that he gains or has. Those practices are not wrong in themselves; the problem lies in how he uses them.

Jesus tells this parable to some people who trusted in themselves as righteous and looked down on others. The Law required fasting only one day a year, so the Pharisee was doing more than what was required. But his prayer speaks more about himself than about God, and it ends with him comparing himself to the tax collector.

Today we can ask ourselves: do my good habits bring me closer to God, or do they make me feel superior to others? Practice your faith with humility, and ask God for mercy instead of comparing yourself.
exp.1:15:
They told the shepherds that they went quickly to Bethlehem and found Mary, Joseph, and the newborn baby lying in a manger. A manger was the trough where the animals ate.

An angel had announced to the shepherds the birth of the Savior, and gave them as a sign that they would find the child in a manger. Then a group of angels praised God. Luke tells us that the shepherds decided to go and see for themselves what God had made known to them. When they arrived, they saw that everything was just as they had been told.

When God speaks to us in his Word, it is not enough to be amazed by it; it is right to respond with action. The shepherds believed and went without delay. Today we can do the same: obey promptly what God shows us, even when the path seems simple or humble.
exp.18:35:
This verse says that as Jesus rode forward on the young donkey, the people were spreading their cloaks (their outer garments or robes) on the road. "Spread" here means they laid them out flat, and "as he went" means "while he was going."

Luke recounts here Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. The disciples had brought the young donkey and had covered it with their garments. Now the people spread their cloaks as a gesture of honor, something done before a king. Soon after, the crowd praises him as "the king who comes in the name of the Lord."

For today: honoring Jesus can cost us something. Those people gave what they had at hand, their own cloaks. We might ask ourselves what we can offer him today with simplicity: our time, our abilities, or our sincere praise.
exp.0:42:
What it says: Elizabeth wonders, in amazement and humility, how it is possible that the mother of her Lord should visit her. Her words "whence is this to me" express her surprise. She calls the child María carries in her womb "my Lord," that is, Jesus.

Context: Elizabeth, cousin of Mary, speaks while filled with the Holy Spirit. Her own son, John, leaped in her womb when he heard Mary's greeting. Through the Spirit, Elizabeth recognizes that Mary is expecting the Messiah. Some think "Lord" here is a title of great honor; others see a clear statement that Jesus is divine. The text does not settle the matter further.

For today: Elizabeth does not compare herself to Mary or feel jealous, even though she was older and was expecting John. She rejoices with humility in what God is doing in others. Today we can imitate her: recognize with gratitude the work of God in someone else's life, without competing, and honor Jesus as our Lord.
exp.23:0:
On Sunday, the first day of the week, very early in the morning, some women went to Jesus' tomb. They were carrying the "aromatic spices," which are perfumes and spices for the body. "Prepared" means made ready. Other women went along with them.

Here the narrator, Luke, tells what happened after Jesus' death. The women had followed him from Galilee and had seen where he was buried. Because of the Sabbath they could not act then, so they went as soon as it was dawn. They were going to honor Jesus as one who had died; the text does not say they expected to see him alive.

For today: sometimes we serve God faithfully even when we do not understand what is coming. These women did what they could out of love, and God showed them something far greater than they imagined. Keep loving and obeying; God can surprise you.
exp.1:0:
In those days, the emperor Augustus issued an official order for a census to be taken across the whole earth. To be "registered" means to be recorded on a list of inhabitants. "The whole earth" refers to the known world under Roman rule. "Came to pass" means "happened."

Here Luke, the narrator, speaks. He wants to give an orderly account grounded in real history. He names the emperor to place the birth of Jesus in a specific time. The details of the census, such as its exact date or the governorship of Quirinius, are debated by scholars, and there are several explanations.

For today: God can carry out his plans even in the midst of decisions made by rulers who do not know him. When you feel that others control your situation, trust that God is still at work and guiding your life.
exp.6:11:
As Jesus approached the gate of the city, he saw a dead man being carried out. He was the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A large crowd from the city was with her. The explanation of the word "dead man" and the word "only son" has been left out, since those words do not appear in this verse.

Luke, the writer, describes the scene before the miracle. Jesus had just healed the servant of the centurion, and his disciples and a great many people were following him. Two groups meet: one full of life and hope, the other in mourning. In that time, a widow without children was left very unprotected, and this makes her grief even greater.

For today: Jesus stops before people's pain. We can imitate him by paying attention to those who suffer beside us, and by accompanying them with presence and compassion, even when we have no words.
exp.10:16:
Jesus knows what the people are thinking in their hearts. He explains to them that a kingdom divided against itself is brought to ruin, and that a house divided falls.

Jesus has just driven out a demon. Some accuse him of doing it by the power of the prince of the demons, and others ask for a sign from heaven to test him. Jesus answers with simple logic: if Satan fought against his own demons, his kingdom would come to an end. In this way he shows that the accusation makes no sense.

Today, constant division destroys families, churches, and friendships. Before we argue, we can ask ourselves: am I seeking unity, or do I only want to win? Let us ask God for humility to listen, to forgive, and to care for peace at home.
exp.10:18:
Jesus asks them a simple question: if he casts out demons by the power of Beelzebul, the prince of demons, then by whose power do their own followers cast them out? "Sons" here probably refers to his disciples or to other Jews of his time who also performed exorcisms. "Cast out" means to drive out. So, he says, they themselves will be their judges: their own practice contradicts them.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd. Some were accusing him of using Beelzebul's power to drive out demons. First he showed them that a divided kingdom cannot stand. Now he shows them that their accusation is inconsistent, because they do not accuse in the same way those who do the same thing. Later he will say that he does it by the finger of God.

For today: before criticizing someone, let us check whether we use the same measure for everyone. Let us ask God for humility to judge fairly and to recognize his work, even when it comes from someone we do not expect.
exp.7:46:
The explanation says that the woman understood that Jesus had noticed and that she could no longer stay hidden. So she came forward trembling, fell down before him, and told in front of everyone why she had touched him and how she had been healed at once. The word "saw" is the word in the verse, and the phrase "declared unto him" means she told him, and the word "immediately" means at once.

Luke tells us that Jesus was on his way to the house of Jairus, surrounded by a crowd. This woman, who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, touched the edge of his garment in secret. Jesus asked who had touched him, not because he did not know, but so that she would come out of her hiding place. Her trembling shows fear, perhaps because of her state of ritual impurity under the law, although the text does not explain this.

For today: Jesus does not want our faith to stay hidden. We can come to him with our fears and honestly tell what he has done in us.
exp.0:61:
The verse tells how the neighbors and relatives made signs to Zacharias, the baby's father, to ask him what he wanted the child to be called. The word "by signs" means with hand movements, without words.

Zacharias had not been able to speak since the angel Gabriel announced to him that he would have a son, because he doubted the news. On the baby's eighth day, it was the custom to give him a name. People wanted to call him after his father, but Elizabeth said he would be named John, just as God had instructed. So they sought Zacharias's opinion. Some think they also believed he was deaf, and that is why they used signs.

Today we can learn that obeying God sometimes means going against what everyone expects. If God shows us something clearly in his Word, we can follow it with humility and firmness, even when no one else understands it.
exp.21:13:
It says that when the time came for the Passover supper, Jesus sat down at the table, and the apostles with him. The phrase about the time having come means the appointed moment had arrived. The phrase about sitting down at the table means that he reclined to eat, as was customary then.

Luke is the one who tells this. The disciples had already prepared the upper room and the Passover meal, just as Jesus had instructed them. It is the last supper before his death. Right after this, Jesus tells them that he had longed deeply to eat this Passover with them before he suffered. His closeness with his friends shows through.

For today: Jesus sat at the table with his own, even knowing what was coming. We can do the same: make time to be with God and with other believers, and remember his love, especially in difficult moments.
exp.19:11:
The explanation says that the owner of the vineyard sent a third servant to collect the fruit that was due to him. The tenants also wounded him and threw him out. The word "wounded" here means that they struck him and threw him out beaten.

Jesus is speaking in the temple, before the people and the religious leaders, when he tells this parable. Many understand the owner to represent God, the vineyard to represent Israel, and the servants to represent the prophets who were sent. The tenants would represent the leaders who rejected those messages. The verses that follow carry the story forward to the sending of the beloved son.

For today: God is patient and keeps speaking to us, but we can become used to ignoring his voice. Today, when something in his Word makes you uncomfortable, do not cast it out. Listen with humility and obey.
exp.10:39:
Jesus calls the Pharisees "fools," that is, people who do not think wisely. He asks them whether God, who made what is outside (the body, the objects), did not also make what is inside (the heart). The word "greed" in this passage means theft or an intense desire to take what belongs to others.

Jesus is eating at the house of a Pharisee, who is surprised that He did not wash His hands before eating, according to religious custom. Jesus answers that they take great care with outward cleanliness, but inside there is greed and wickedness. He reminds them that God cares about the whole human being, not only appearance.

For today: it is not enough to seem good before others. Today you can ask God to examine your heart, and to correct a hidden attitude, such as pride, envy or selfishness, as much as you care for your image.
exp.7:12:
They hear the message of God and receive it with joy. But that faith is shallow, like a plant without roots. They believe for a while, and when "temptation" comes, that is, a trial or difficulty that tests their faith, they fall away. The word "rock" here refers to hard, shallow ground.

Jesus himself is speaking. He has just told the parable of the sower to the crowd and now explains it to his disciples. The seed is the word of God, and each kind of ground shows how the human heart responds. This is the second of the four types of ground.

For today: it is not enough to be moved when you hear the Bible. Seek to put down roots, reading the Word steadily, praying, and living alongside other believers, so that when trials come your faith remains firm.
exp.11:46:
This verse says that the servant who knew what his master wanted, but did not get ready or do what was asked of him, will receive a severe punishment. The words "not prepared himself" mean that he did not get ready or was not set to act. "Beaten with many stripes" speaks of a strong punishment.

Jesus speaks to his disciples with a parable about being ready for his return. Before this, he described a servant who takes advantage of his master's delay and mistreats others. Then Jesus explains that responsibility grows according to what a person has understood. Whoever knows more answers for more; whoever knew less receives a lighter sentence.

For today: if you already know what God asks of you, do not leave it for later. Choose one concrete step of obedience today, such as asking forgiveness, helping someone, or setting aside time to pray, and do it with the confidence that God gives you his grace to carry it out.
exp.15:25:
It says that between Abraham and the rich man there is a great gulf, a very large and deep chasm. No one can cross it, neither from one side to the other nor the reverse. The word "fixed" means that it was put in place and remained firm, and the phrase "would pass" means "would want to pass."

Abraham is the one speaking, in the parable Jesus tells about the rich man and Lazarus. The rich man, in torment, asks for relief. Abraham explains that his situation can no longer change. Christians interpret this parable in different ways regarding the details of the afterlife, but all agree on its emphasis: our decisions in this life matter.

Today it invites us not to postpone what is important. We must listen to God now, and share generously what we have with those who suffer near us.
exp.7:20:
Jesus answers that his true family is made up of those who hear the word of God and put it into practice. The word "do" here means "keep" or "practice." Hearing is not enough; one must obey.

Jesus is teaching a very large crowd. His mother and his brothers arrive, but they cannot get close to him because of the people, and someone tells him they are there. He uses the moment to teach something important. He does not reject his family; rather, he widens the idea of family to include everyone who obeys God. Shortly before, he had spoken of the parable of the sower, which deals precisely with how the word is received.

For today: this week, choose a teaching of the Bible that you already know and decide to live it out in one concrete act, such as forgiving someone or helping a person in need.
exp.5:36:
Jesus says three similar things: do not judge, do not condemn, and forgive. With each one he links a promise: you will not be judged, you will not be condemned, and you will be forgiven. "Judge" here means to criticize harshly, and "condemn" means to declare someone guilty without mercy.

Jesus teaches his disciples and a crowd, right after commanding them to love their enemies. He asks them to be merciful as the Father is merciful. Then he speaks of the measure by which we give and receive, and of the blind man who leads another blind man. Many understand that he does not forbid all discernment, but rather an attitude of superiority and lack of compassion.

For today: before you criticize someone in your mind or with your words, stop and pray for that person. If there is an offense you can forgive, do it today.
exp.14:22:
The explanation says the father orders the fattened calf to be brought, killed, and a feast prepared to celebrate. A "fattened calf" is a well-fed young cow kept for a very special occasion. "Let us make merry" means to celebrate with joy. The commands to bring, kill, and eat are phrased as direct orders to the servants.

Jesus tells this parable of the prodigal son. The father speaks to his servants just after his younger son, who had squandered his inheritance, returns repentant. Before the son finishes asking for forgiveness, the father has already embraced him, put a ring and sandals on him, and now orders the feast. Jesus tells it to show how greatly God rejoices when someone returns to Him.

For today: if someone repents and comes back, welcome them with joy and not with reproach. And if you have drifted away from God, remember that He is waiting for you with open arms.
exp.16:2:
Jesus says to his disciples: "Take heed to yourselves." In other words, be careful and watch yourselves. If a brother sins against you, you should speak to him and correct him. If he repents, you should forgive him.

Jesus speaks to his disciples right after warning them about causes of stumbling, that is, things that make others fall away from the faith. He teaches them to care for the life of the community: not to be a cause of falling, and not to hold a grudge when someone fails. The verses that follow say that forgiveness must be given many times, and so the apostles ask: "Increase our faith."

For today: if someone offends you, don't keep silent and don't gossip about it. Speak to them calmly and with a desire to be reconciled, and if they ask forgiveness, forgive them from the heart. Ask God for help to do it.
exp.10:51:
Jesus says "Woe unto you" to the teachers of the law, that is, the experts in the Law of Moses. He accuses them of having "taken away the key of knowledge," meaning the key to knowing God. They did not enter in themselves, and they also hindered those who were trying to enter. "Hindered" means that they put obstacles in the way.

Jesus is eating at the house of a Pharisee and speaks frankly to the religious teachers. He rebukes them for teaching with heavy burdens and not helping people to truly know God. Many understand the "key" to refer to grasping the message of Scripture, which points to God himself. Afterward, they reacted with anger.

If you teach the Bible, take care that your words bring people closer to God and do not push them away. Be humble, live out what you teach, and help others to enter in.
exp.6:9:
The explanation says that the messengers whom the centurion had sent to Jesus returned to the house and found the servant who had been sick now healed. "Found whole" means they saw him already restored to health. "Returning to the house" means they went back home.

Luke, the narrator, closes the story of the Roman centurion. This man asked Jesus for help through Jewish friends and elders, and he trusted that a word from Jesus was enough, without Jesus needing to enter his house. Jesus marveled at that faith. Here the account confirms that Jesus' word took effect, even from a distance.

For today: We can trust that Jesus hears and is able to act, even when we do not see His response right away. Pray with confidence for someone who is sick or in need, and leave the outcome in His hands, knowing that His word has power.
exp.0:20:
This verse tells how the people who were outside were waiting for Zacharias and marvelled that he stayed so long in the temple. "Marvelled" means that they were surprised and wondered what was happening. "Tarried so long" means that he was taking longer than usual.

Zacharias was a priest, and it was his duty to offer the incense, while the people prayed outside. Inside, the angel Gabriel had announced to him that he would have a son, John, but Zacharias doubted and was left unable to speak. So, when he came out, he could not give the blessing or speak to them, and the people understood by his gestures that he had seen a vision. Luke is the one who tells the story.

For today: God sometimes acts in places and at times where no one sees, while others wait. Learn to wait with patience, and when God speaks to you, believe his words with confidence instead of doubting.
exp.21:11:
Jesus says that the owner of the house will show them a large room, furnished and ready, upstairs. The original word for this kind of room is a dining room, and the other terms are rendered in the wording "make ready." The disciples were to make the preparations for the supper there.

Jesus is speaking to Peter and John shortly before his arrest. They are going to prepare the Passover supper, the Jewish feast that remembers Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Jesus already knows what they will find, and the verses that follow say that everything happened just as he had announced. The Bible does not explain how the arrangement with the owner of the house was made, and we know nothing more about that.

We can trust that God knows what is coming and cares about the details. Even so, he asks us to do our part: to obey step by step and to prepare what is within our reach, without waiting to see everything first.
exp.22:55:
The text says that the women, on returning from the tomb, prepared spices and ointments for the body of Jesus. Their preparations were the spices and ointments themselves, which were fragrant. Then they rested on the Sabbath, as the law of Moses commanded.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened after the death of Jesus. The Galilean women, who had followed him, saw where they laid him. Since the Sabbath was already beginning, they could not finish their labor of love. They made everything ready and waited, obeying the command to rest. They did not know that Jesus would rise.

For today: These women served with love and also respected the timing of God. We can do the same: do with care what is in our hands, and trust God when it is time to rest and wait, even when we do not understand what is coming.
exp.7:43:
A sick woman came up behind Jesus and touched the edge of his cloak, and at once her bleeding stopped. The bleeding was a continuous flow of blood. The "edge" probably refers to the tassels or fringes of the cloak, though some understand it simply as the hem of the clothing.

Luke tells this as Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairus, whose twelve-year-old daughter is dying. The crowd presses in on him from every side. The woman had been ill for twelve years and had spent everything on doctors without being cured. Because of her condition, she probably felt ritually unclean under the law, which is why she comes quietly, without drawing attention.

For today: when you feel weak or without a way out, come to Jesus in faith, even with a simple and trembling prayer. He is not lost in the crowd; he knows who is truly seeking him.
exp.12:25:
They will say, "We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets." Here "streets" refers to the public roads and open spaces of the town.

Jesus is speaking on his way to Jerusalem, as he teaches through cities and villages. Someone had asked him whether few people are saved. He answers with a warning: it is not enough to have been near him, to have heard him, or to have shared his table. Those people knew Jesus only superficially, and he tells them that he does not know them, because they kept living in injustice.

For today: let us not confuse religious closeness with a real relationship with Christ. Going to church, knowing the Bible, or having a Christian background does not replace trusting Jesus and obeying him from the heart. Ask yourself today: do I truly know him, or have I only been near him?
exp.15:1:
He says that the rich man calls his manager and asks him what this is that he has heard about him. He demands that the man give an account of his work, because he is about to lose his position. The steward is the one who looks after another person's property, and his responsibility is the stewardship entrusted to him.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and tells this parable. The manager had been accused of wasting what was not his. Now the time has come to give an account. Interpreters debate some details of the story, but here the central point is clear: the responsibility is temporary, and there will be a review.

For today: everything we have, such as time, money, and talents, we receive from God to look after. Ask yourself calmly today: am I managing well what has been entrusted to me? Today you can correct one habit and make better use of what God has given you.
exp.16:28:
It says that on the same day Lot went out of Sodom, God made fire and brimstone fall from heaven, and all who remained were destroyed. "Brimstone" is a mineral that burns and has a strong smell. The phrase "destroyed them all" means that those who stayed in the city did not survive.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples about the coming of the Son of Man. He compares that moment to the days of Noah and Lot: life went on as normal, with eating, business and work, and the judgment came suddenly. He does not condemn those things in themselves, but living without thinking about God.

For today: do not live as if God did not exist. Work, eat and make plans, but check each day whether your heart is close to God and ready to obey him. If there is something you need to put right with him or with someone else, do it today.
exp.13:1:
Suddenly, there was a man in front of Jesus who had dropsy. The phrase "behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "notice." Dropsy was a condition in which the body swelled up from holding too much fluid.

Jesus had gone in to eat at the house of a leader of the Pharisees, on a Sabbath, and those present were watching him to see what he would do. Luke is the one who tells the story. The text does not say how the man got there or whether he was put there on purpose; some think it was a trap, but the text does not make this clear. Jesus then asks whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and afterward he heals the man.

For today: let us not allow rules or appearances to make us indifferent to suffering. Let us ask God for attentive eyes to see the person in need and, if it is within our power, to help them with compassion.
exp.21:52:
Jesus reminds those who have come to arrest him that he was with them every day in the temple, teaching in plain view of everyone, and they never laid a hand on him. "Stretched forth hands" means grabbing or arresting him, and it refers to the act of seizing someone by force. Now they are doing it at night, in secret. He calls this moment "your hour," a time that has been given to them to act, and "the power of darkness," that is, the power of evil.

Jesus speaks in the garden, after Judas has betrayed him. He addresses the chief priests, the temple guards, and the elders. He has just healed the ear of the servant injured by Peter. He shows them that his arrest is unjust and that he does not run away, but accepts God's plan.

For today: when you face injustice or dark moments, remember that God is still in control. You can respond as Jesus did: with truth, calm, and kindness, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.22:36:
The explanation says that the Roman soldiers mocked Jesus on the cross. They said to him: "If thou be the king of the Jews, save thyself." The word "mock" here means to ridicule with contempt. The vinegar was a sour drink, and they offered it to him as part of the mockery.

The ones speaking are the soldiers. Earlier, the leaders of the people had also laughed at Jesus. Everyone thought a true king could not be nailed to a cross. Above his head there was a sign that read "This is the King of the Jews," and the soldiers used it to scorn him. Without knowing it, they were repeating a truth: Jesus is indeed King. He did not come down from the cross, because his mission was to save others, not himself.

Today we can remember that the love of Jesus was stronger than the mockery. If someone mocks your faith, trust in him and respond with patience and kindness.
exp.20:7:
Jesus warns his disciples to be careful not to be deceived. He says that many will come using his name, claiming "I am he" and announcing that "the time is near." His advice is clear: do not follow them. "Going after" means following behind, and "deceived" means led astray by an error.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He has just announced that the temple will be destroyed, and his disciples ask him when this will happen and what the sign will be. Before giving them any signs, Jesus warns them about deception. Some understand these words as referring mainly to the fall of Jerusalem, and others as also referring to the last days.

Today, before following anyone who claims to speak for Christ or predicts dates, compare what they teach with the Scriptures. Keep your eyes fixed on Jesus, not on attention-grabbing voices.
exp.21:33:
Jesus says to Peter, calling him by name, that before the rooster crows that very day, he will deny three times that he knows Him.

Jesus speaks with Peter during the Last Supper. Peter has just declared that he is ready to go with Him to prison and even to death. Jesus does not say this to humiliate him. Earlier He had told Peter that He prayed for him, so that his faith would not fail, and that after he turned back again, he should strengthen his brothers. Jesus knows Peter's weakness and also his restored future.

For today: let us not rely only on our good intentions. Let us ask God for strength instead of boasting in our own. And if we fail, let us remember that Christ still prays for us and calls us to return.
exp.23:17:
This verse tells us that one of the two travelers, named Cleopas, answers Jesus with surprise. He asks whether he is the only visitor in Jerusalem who has not heard what happened in those days. Here "visitor" means a stranger or outsider, someone just passing through.

It is the day of the resurrection, and two disciples are on their way to Emmaus. Jesus has come near them, but they do not recognize him; the text says their eyes were kept from seeing him, that is, prevented. Cleopas speaks because Jesus asked them why they were sad. We do not know for certain who the other disciple was.
