There is an irony here: they explain the story of Jesus to Jesus himself. Sometimes we are so caught up in our sadness that we fail to see that the Lord is walking beside us. Today we can honestly tell him our doubts and pains, trusting that he listens and accompanies us, even when we do not feel it.
exp.0:38:
Luke 1:39 tells us that, a few days after the angel's visit, Mary got up and went quickly into the hill country, to a city of Judah. The word "haste" is an older way of saying "hurry," and "hill country" here refers to the area of hills in Judea.

The one who tells the story is Luke, who follows the account of the annunciation. Mary had just accepted God's plan with humility. According to the context, the angel had spoken to her about her relative Elizabeth, who was also expecting a child. The name of the city is not given, and we cannot know with certainty which one it was. The text also does not explain why Mary went in haste; we may assume she wanted to share the news and to support Elizabeth.

For today: when God speaks to us and we respond in faith, we can act without delay. Also, seeking out someone we trust who shares our faith strengthens us.
exp.22:2:
Pilate asks Jesus a direct question: "Art thou the King of the Jews?" Jesus answers: "Thou sayest it." This phrase is neither a simple yes nor a simple no. Many understand that Jesus confirms that he is a king, but not in the political sense that Pilate imagined.

The chief priests and leaders brought Jesus before Pilate, the Roman governor, and accused him of rebellion and of forbidding people to pay taxes to Caesar. Pilate focused on the charge that was most serious for Rome: that Jesus made himself a king. Afterward Pilate declares that he finds no fault in him.

For today: Jesus did not defend himself with anger or with lies, but with truth and calm. When you are unjustly accused, try to answer with calm and honesty, trusting that God sees everything.
exp.16:23:
Jesus says that his coming will be like lightning: it appears at one end of the sky and lights up the other end, so that everyone sees it. "His day" refers to the moment when the Son of Man, the title Jesus uses for himself, will be revealed openly. The phrase "Here he is" means "look, he is here."

Jesus speaks to his disciples after answering the Pharisees about the kingdom of God. He warns them that difficult times will come, with people who will claim to have found the Messiah or who will point to hidden signs. Before his return, he must suffer and be rejected. Interpreters debate some details of how and when this will happen.

For today: do not be carried away by those who announce dates or claim secret knowledge about the return of Christ. Trust that it will be evident to all, and in the meantime live faithfully, in prayer and love, each day.
exp.6:48:
The explanation says that the other guests at the table, hearing Jesus forgive the woman, began to ask one another: "Who is this that forgives sins also?" The phrase "sat at meat with him" means they were eating together with him, and the word "meat" here means food in general, not only meat.

Jesus was in the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known for her sinful life came, wept at the feet of Jesus, and anointed them with perfume. Jesus told her that her sins were forgiven. The guests were amazed, because in their thinking only God could forgive sins. They ask the question, but the text does not record Jesus answering it in words at that moment.

For today: do not stop at the question of who Jesus is. Come to Him with humility, as that woman did, and trust that He can forgive you and give you peace.
exp.7:51:
The people in the house were weeping and wailing loudly for the girl. Jesus asks them to stop weeping and says that she is not dead but sleeping. "Wailing" means crying out with loud sounds of grief, as was done at funerals.

Jesus is speaking in the house of Jairus, the leader of the synagogue, whose daughter, about twelve years old, had just died. Jesus had encouraged the father to believe. Those present mock him because they know she is dead. Many understand that when Jesus speaks of sleep, he is referring to death because he is going to wake her, and that for him death does not have the final word. Some believe he also speaks of death as something temporary.

When a situation seems hopeless, do not let grief or mockery extinguish your trust. Bring it to Jesus and wait on him with simple faith.
exp.1:39:
It says that Jesus, as a child, kept growing in body and becoming stronger. He was also filled with wisdom, that is, with good understanding for living. The verse's wording about being "strong in spirit" and "filled" describes this same growth. Moreover, the grace of God, that is, his favor and kindness, was upon him.

The speaker here is Luke, the narrator of the Gospel. He summarizes the years of Jesus' childhood in Nazareth, after having told of his birth and his presentation in the temple. It is a brief pause before the account of Jesus at twelve years old in Jerusalem. Luke gives no further detail about those years, so it is not right to invent any.

For today: growing is a process, and God works in everyday life. We can ask him to help us grow patiently in wisdom, character, and dependence on his grace, including in ordinary and simple days.
exp.12:14:
Jesus answers the ruler of the synagogue firmly and calls him "thou hypocrite," meaning someone who appears to be devout but does not live with consistency. He reminds them that every one of them, on the sabbath, loosens his ox or his ass from the stall and leads him away to drink water.

Jesus is speaking in a synagogue, on a sabbath. He had just healed a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years. The ruler of the synagogue became angry and said that people should be healed on the other six days. Jesus shows that if a person cares for an animal on the sabbath, much more can a person be set free. Many rejoiced at this.

For today: let us not allow religious rules or customs to make us hard toward those who suffer. Ask yourself whether your faith leads you to help and to show compassion, or only to defend your standards.
exp.15:13:
The verse says that the Pharisees were listening to everything Jesus was teaching. They were covetous, that is, they loved money and wanted to have more and more. When they heard Jesus, they mocked him, meaning they treated him with contempt, as if his words were worth nothing.

Jesus had just told his disciples that no one can serve God and riches at the same time. The Pharisees felt the sting of his words, but instead of reflecting on them, they laughed. Then Jesus answered them that God knows the heart, even though they wanted to look good before the people.

For today: when God's word touches an uncomfortable area, such as our relationship with money, we can laugh it off or we can listen with humility. Let us ask God to show us whether our heart is attached to material things, and be willing to change.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that Jesus sent his twelve disciples with two tasks: to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. The word "sent" tells us they did not go on their own initiative but under Jesus' commission. To proclaim means to announce or preach, and to heal means to restore the sick to health.

Jesus had just gathered the twelve and given them power and authority over demons and diseases. Then he sends them out to travel with very little: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money. In this way they would learn to depend on God and on the hospitality of the people. His words and his deeds went together: they announced the kingdom and showed God's care.

Today we can speak about God and also help with concrete actions. This week, share a word of hope with someone and offer real help: accompany them, visit them, or pray with them.
exp.2:21:
It says that when Jesus was baptized and was praying, the Holy Spirit came down upon him in a visible way, like a dove. Then a voice was heard from heaven saying to him: "Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased."

The one speaking is God the Father. Luke recounts this just before Jesus begins his ministry. The passage shows the Father, the Son, and the Spirit together. The voice confirms Jesus' identity before the people. Some think the dove symbolizes peace or a new beginning, but the text does not explain this.

Today we can remember that the Father's love comes before our achievements. Jesus was approved before he performed any miracles. If we trust him, we can live and serve from that love, without having to earn it.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that all people, from every nation, will see the salvation that comes from God. The word "flesh" is an old way of saying "human beings." "Shall see" means that the salvation will be visible and known, not hidden.

Luke explains who John the Baptist was by quoting the prophet Isaiah. John was preparing the way for Jesus, and Isaiah spoke of leveling mountains and straightening crooked roads as an image of a heart ready to receive God. Luke closes the quotation by showing that this salvation is not only for Israel but for everyone. Right after this, John warns that being a descendant of Abraham is not enough; a genuine repentance is required.

For today: God's salvation is an open invitation for everyone, even for someone who feels far away. But it asks for a sincere heart. Today you can ask yourself what crooked path in your life needs to be made straight, and pray that God will help you change.
exp.23:47:
Jesus says to his disciples: "You are witnesses of these things." A witness is someone who saw or experienced something and can tell others about it. The "things" are what Jesus has just explained: his suffering, his resurrection on the third day, and the message of repentance and forgiveness.

Jesus speaks after his resurrection, on the same day he rose, to his disciples. He has just opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. He shows them that everything was part of God's plan and that they must now proclaim it, beginning in Jerusalem. Soon after, he promises them the Holy Spirit, the power from on high, so that they can carry out this mission.

For today: you do not need to be an expert to be a witness. You can simply tell what Christ has done in your life, trusting that God gives you the strength to do it.
exp.7:2:
This verse continues the list of women who accompanied Jesus. It mentions Joanna, the wife of Chuza, who was a steward or manager of Herod's affairs, and Susanna, along with many others. All of them served Jesus with their substance.

Luke is the one narrating as Jesus travels through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God. These women had been healed and, out of gratitude, supported the ministry with their resources. About Susanna we know nothing more than what this text says. That Joanna came from Herod's household shows that the gospel reached people of every social level.

For today: all of us can serve God with what we have, whether money, time, or talents. Giving with gratitude, even when it seems small, sustains the work of God and honors Christ.
exp.23:48:
Jesus says he will send "the promise of my Father" upon his disciples. He asks them to "tarry," that is, to stay in Jerusalem, until they are "endued with power from on high." To be "endued" means to be clothed or covered, as someone who receives a garment or an authority. "Power" means strength.

Jesus speaks after his resurrection. He has just explained to them that the Scriptures foretold his death and resurrection, and that the message of repentance and forgiveness was to reach all nations. They are witnesses, but they cannot carry out that mission by their own strength. Many Christians understand the promise to be the Holy Spirit, as explained in Acts 1 and 2.

For today: before rushing into service, we need to wait on God and depend on his strength. Set aside time to pray and ask him for direction before your decisions and your service.
exp.23:39:
This verse says that Jesus, after speaking with his disciples, showed them his hands and his feet. He wanted them to see his body for themselves.

The risen Jesus appears to his disciples, who are frightened and confused, because they think they are seeing a ghost. He shows them his hands and feet so that they can see that it is really him and that his body is real. Many people understand that the marks of the crucifixion were there, although this verse does not say so explicitly. Then he eats in front of them.

When we doubt or are afraid, Jesus does not rebuke us harshly, but gives us reasons to trust him. We can come to him with our honest doubts, asking him to strengthen our faith through his Word and his presence.
exp.18:21:
Jesus, in the parable, has the nobleman answer this servant with his own words. "Wicked servant" means a bad or lazy servant. "Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee" means: "by what you yourself have said, I will condemn you." "Austere" means harsh or demanding. The king does not admit that what the servant says is true; he only shows that, even if it were so, the servant should have acted differently.

Jesus tells this parable of the minas near Jerusalem, and the people thought that the kingdom of God was going to appear right away. Each servant was given money to trade with while the lord was away. This servant did nothing out of fear and a mistaken idea of his lord.

Today we can ask ourselves: what image do I have of God? If I see Him only as someone harsh, I become paralyzed. It is better to use what He has given me with faith and humility: time, gifts, opportunities, and to serve with them.
exp.11:28:
Jesus says that we should not go about anxiously seeking what we are going to eat or drink, nor live with a restless and divided mind. To "seek" here means to go after something with worry. The idea of "being of doubtful mind" speaks of a restlessness that leaves us unsure and without peace.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable of the rich fool. As an example, he points them to the lilies and the birds: if God takes care of them, he will also care for his children. Then he invites them to put the kingdom of God first, knowing that the Father already knows what they need.

Today we can make a simple prayer each morning, entrusting to God our needs for the day. And when anxiety comes, we can do what is within our reach and seek first what matters to God: to love, to serve, and to obey him.
exp.11:42:
It says that the servant is happy, or blessed, whose master, on returning, finds him doing his job well. "Blessed" means blessed or very fortunate. "Find" is the word used in the verse above, and "doing so" refers to what has just been described: giving food to the household on time, with faithfulness and wisdom.

Jesus speaks in a teaching about being watchful for his coming. Peter asks whether the parable is only for the disciples or for everyone. Jesus does not answer directly, but asks who the faithful and wise steward is. In this way he shows that responsibility belongs to the one who has been given a charge. Then he warns against the servant who takes advantage because he thinks his master is delayed.

For today: be faithful in what God has entrusted to you, such as caring for your family, working with honesty, and treating others well, no matter when He returns.
exp.21:67:
Jesus tells his accusers that even if he asks them questions, they will not answer, and they will not let him go free.

The explanation of the words "ye will not answer me" and "let me go" is not needed here, since those words appear in the verse above.

Jesus stands before the council, the group of Israel's religious leaders, at dawn. They ask him to say whether he is the Christ, the Messiah. He knows they are not seeking the truth with sincerity, because they have already settled on their course. For that reason he points out that they will neither believe his words nor answer with honesty. Some scholars see in this a criticism of their hardness of heart.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we listen to God with an open heart or only look for confirmation of what we already think. Let us ask him for humility to receive his truth, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.2:9:
Here the crowd that was listening to John the Baptist asks him a sincere question: "What shall we do then?" The crowds who had come out to hear him are the people in view here. The question shows that his message touched their hearts and that they want to know how to respond.

John had just warned them that it is not enough to say, "We have Abraham as our father." God expects fruit, that is, a changed life that shows a true repentance. That is why the people ask what concrete changes they should make. In the verses that follow, John answers them with practical examples of sharing and of acting justly.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, it is not enough to be moved or to feel that we agree. We can ask God with humility, "What should I change?" And then take a concrete step, such as sharing what we have with someone who needs it.
exp.7:18:
It says that Jesus' mother and his brothers came looking for him, but they could not get near him because there were too many people around him.

Luke tells this right after Jesus taught the parable of the sower and spoke about listening well. The crowd was pressing around Jesus to hear him. When he is told that his family is outside, he takes the opportunity to say that his true family is those who hear the word of God and do it. He is not rejecting his family; he is showing what matters most. Scholars understand in various ways exactly who these "brothers" were, but the text does not make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I only hear the word of God, or do I also put it into practice? Choose one teaching from the Bible today and obey it in one concrete step.
exp.0:72:
This verse says that God remembered the oath he swore to Abraham, our ancestor. The explanation of the old wording is not needed here, since the reader's verse uses "sware" and "oath," which are both in the verse above. The sentence continues into the next verse: what God promised to give is the ability to serve him without fear.

The one speaking is Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, filled with the Holy Spirit. He is praising God because the promised Savior is now coming. For him, this confirms the covenant God made with Abraham centuries earlier (Genesis 22:16-18). God keeps what he says.

For today: when your situation seems long or uncertain, remember that God is faithful to his promises. Trust in him and serve him today with honesty and with a heart free from fear, knowing that he upholds his word.
exp.20:36:
This verse tells us what Jesus' last days in Jerusalem were like. During the day he taught in the temple, and when night fell he left the city to stay on the Mount of Olives.

Luke is the one narrating, and here he summarizes Jesus' routine during that final week. He had just spoken about difficult times and the need to watch and pray. The text does not say in detail where he slept each night; it only mentions the mount. The next morning, the people came early to hear him.

For today: Jesus combined public service with moments of withdrawal. We can imitate him by setting aside a place and a daily time to be alone with God, especially when life is very full.
exp.20:9:
Jesus says that there will be conflicts between peoples and between governments. "Nation against nation" speaks of nations or ethnic groups that rise against one another, and "kingdom against kingdom" speaks of rulers who fight for power. This is no surprise to Him; He announces it in advance.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple in Jerusalem, when they ask him about the signs of what is coming. He warns them not to be deceived by false teachers or frightened by wars. These things must happen, but they do not yet mark the end. Some see them partly fulfilled in the year 70 A.D., and others also in the future.

When the news fills us with fear, let us remember that Jesus has already told us. We can pray, keep calm, and continue trusting in Him, without being carried away by voices that promise easy answers.
exp.18:5:
This verse tells how Zacchaeus climbed down from the tree right away, as soon as Jesus called him. The explanation of the old wording is handled by the verse itself: the reader sees that he made haste and came down quickly, and that he received Jesus into his home with joy.

The narrator is Luke. Zacchaeus was the chief of the tax collectors and a wealthy man, and the people saw him as a sinner. He had climbed the sycamore tree because he was short and wanted to see Jesus. To everyone's surprise, Jesus called him by name and decided to stay at his house. Zacchaeus responded with immediate obedience and sincere joy, even though the crowd was grumbling.

For today: when Jesus invites you to come closer, do not put it off. Answer him promptly and with gratitude, no matter what others think. A life that receives Jesus with joy begins to change on the inside, as it did with Zacchaeus.
exp.1:20:
This verse tells that, when the eight days after the birth were complete, the child was circumcised and received the name Jesus. That name was not chosen by Joseph and Mary as they pleased: the angel had already announced it before Jesus was conceived.

Luke is the one telling the story. After the visit of the shepherds, he shows that Joseph and Mary kept the law of Moses, which commanded that a boy be circumcised on the eighth day. In this way Jesus is placed within the people of Israel. In addition, the name "Jesus" means "the Lord saves," and it recalls what the angel announced to Mary (Luke 1:31).

For today: Joseph and Mary obeyed what God had told them, even in simple things. We can ask God to help us obey him also in the details of each day.
exp.22:11:
It says that Pilate and Herod, who had been enemies before, became friends that same day. "Made friends" means that they made peace. The reason for their earlier conflict is not explained in this passage.

Luke, the narrator, tells that Pilate, the Roman governor, sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, when he learned that Jesus was from Galilee. Herod mocked Jesus and sent him back to Pilate. That act of sending him and returning him may have helped them become reconciled, though the text gives no further details. Both had authority, and neither defended Jesus.

For today: unity is not always good. Two people can agree on something unjust. Let us seek peace, but a peace based on truth, respect, and the good of others, not at the expense of others.
exp.11:57:
Jesus says that if someone takes you before a judge over a debt or a dispute, the wisest thing is to settle matters with that person while you are still on the way. Otherwise, they will bring you before the judge, the judge will hand you over to the officer, and you will end up in prison. The officer was the one who carried out the sentence.

Jesus speaks to the crowd, and earlier he called those who could read the weather but did not recognize the decisive moment they were living through with his coming "hypocrites." He asks them to judge what is right for themselves. Some understand this as practical teaching, and others as a spiritual warning: be reconciled with God while there is still time.

Today: if you have an unresolved conflict, do not let it grow. Seek to speak with humility and make peace soon, before the problem becomes more serious.
exp.10:28:
Jesus speaks to a crowd that keeps gathering around him. He tells them that this generation is evil, because it asks for a miraculous sign before it will believe. But the only sign it will receive is the sign of Jonah. The phrase "the people were gathered thick together" means that the crowd was pressing in close around him. A "sign" is a proof or miracle that confirms who Jesus is.

Jesus has just said that those who hear the word of God and obey it are blessed. Shortly before this, some had asked him for a sign from heaven to test him. In the verses that follow he explains that Jonah was a sign to Nineveh, and that he will be one too. Interpreters often see here a reference to his death and resurrection, although in this passage Jesus mainly emphasizes his message.

For today: instead of demanding proof from God before we believe, we can listen to his word with humility and put it into practice. We already have enough light to obey today.
exp.7:24:
Jesus asks his disciples where their faith is. They are afraid and amazed, and they say to one another, "What kind of man is this, that he even commands the winds and the water, and they obey him?" Some words from the source are old-fashioned: the phrase for "afraid" means frightened, and the phrase for "wondered" means were amazed.

Jesus was crossing the lake with his disciples when a strong storm came up. He was asleep, and they woke him in fear that they would die. Jesus calmed the wind and the waves with his word. Then he speaks to them, not to shame them, but to lead them to think. His question shows that he hoped they would trust him more. Their amazement reveals that they were only beginning to understand who he was.

For today: when a storm comes into your life, remember who is in the boat with you. Before letting panic carry you away, speak with Jesus and trust that his power and his care are greater than your problem.
exp.21:47:
Jesus addresses Judas by name and asks him a question that hurts: will you betray me with a kiss? A kiss was a sign of affection and respect between friends or disciples, but Judas uses it as a signal so the crowd will know whom to arrest. The phrase "Son of man" is a title Jesus uses for himself.

Jesus speaks in the garden, after praying and finding his disciples asleep. The crowd arrives, led by Judas, one of the twelve. Jesus is not caught off guard; he knows what is happening. His question does not sound like a simple rebuke, but like a call for Judas to see what he is doing. Luke does not say whether Judas actually went through with the kiss.

Today we can examine whether we use religious or friendly gestures to hide a betrayal or a double heart. Jesus invites us to be sincere, and his treatment of Judas shows us that even in the face of betrayal he speaks with truth and with grief.
exp.23:37:
Jesus asks his disciples why they are frightened and why doubts rise in their hearts. "Troubled" means upset, filled with fear or confusion, so the sentence is rewritten to use the verse's own word. The phrase about thoughts rising inside them refers to doubts and reasoning that well up from within.

Jesus had already risen, and he suddenly appeared in the midst of them. They were still talking about the news of his resurrection, and when they saw him they thought he was a spirit. Jesus does not rebuke them harshly; he helps them believe by showing them his hands and his feet.

For today: when fear or doubt troubles you, bring them honestly to Jesus. He understands our doubts and gives us reasons to trust. Speak to him openly and seek his Word so that it strengthens your faith.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that Jesus saw two boats near the edge of the lake. The fishermen had already climbed out of them and were washing their nets. The word "saw" is in the verse above, and "boats" here refers to small fishing boats. The "lake" is the Sea of Galilee, also called the Lake of Gennesaret.

Luke, the author, tells us that a large crowd was pressing around Jesus to hear the word of God. The fishermen had finished their night's work and were cleaning their nets. That simple detail prepares what follows: Jesus will get into Simon's boat to teach from there and then will invite them to fish. Luke says nothing more about the fishermen's mood at this point.

For today: Jesus often comes into our common work, even when we are tired or finishing a task. We can make room for him in everyday life, offering him what we have at hand, and stay attentive to what he might want to do there.
exp.18:23:
He says that the king orders those standing by to take the pound away from the servant who did not use it and to give it to the one who already had ten. A "pound" was a considerable sum of money. The words "Take" and "give" are the commands here: the king is telling them to take it from him and give it to him.

Jesus tells this parable near Jerusalem, and the people thought that the kingdom of God was going to appear right away. A nobleman goes away far from home and leaves money with his servants so that they will put it to work. On his return, the fearful servant only kept what he had received. The king judges him by his own words. Interpreters discuss some details of the parable, but its central meaning is faithfulness while the Lord is not present.

For today: God has entrusted us with time, gifts, and opportunities. Let us not hide them out of fear; let us use them with faith, serving others, and God will rejoice in our faithfulness.
exp.15:6:
Here Jesus continues the story of a manager who was about to lose his job. He calls another of his master's debtors and asks him how much he owes. The man answers: a hundred measures of wheat. (A measure was a large unit, perhaps more than 200 liters; the exact calculation is debated.) The manager tells him to take his bill of debt and write eighty. In this way he reduces the account for him.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and Pharisees are nearby. He tells this parable about the use of money. The manager was dishonest, and the master praises his shrewdness, not his injustice. Scholars debate whether he reduced his own commission or altered the debts.

For today: use what you have with an eye to the future. Money, time, and talents are temporary, so invest in people and in what is eternal, with generosity and honesty.
exp.21:29:
Jesus tells his disciples that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom, and that they will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. The phrase "sit on thrones" can be understood as "sitting down" in the sense of taking their place, and "judging" can be understood as governing or guiding. Interpreters explain this in different ways: some see it as something for the future, others as a role of authority that begins with the church.

Jesus speaks at the last supper. The disciples have just argued about which of them was the greatest. Jesus shows them that true greatness is serving, and still he promises them a place of honor because they stayed with him in their trials.

For today: God sees and remembers our faithfulness, even when we fail. We can serve with humility today, trusting that he keeps his promises.
exp.19:28:
The verse says there were seven brothers. The first one married and died without having children. The phrases "took a wife" and "without children" in the original wording are rewritten in the reader's verse as "took a wife" and "without children", so no separate explanation of them is needed; the explanation of those phrases is removed. The point is simply that he married and died without leaving descendants.

The speakers are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They cite the law of Moses about levirate marriage: if a man died without children, his brother would marry the widow to continue the name of the dead man. They were not seeking to learn anything with this exaggerated story; they wanted to trap Jesus and make the resurrection seem absurd.

For today: sometimes we ask questions in order to argue rather than to seek the truth. We can approach God and his Word with humility, willing to listen and to be corrected, instead of using arguments to defend what we already think.
exp.23:21:
It says that certain women from the group of the disciples left them amazed, or very astonished. They had gone to the tomb very early, while it was still dark. The word "astonished" here does not mean fear, but a strong impression caused by unexpected news.

Cleopas speaks, one of two followers of Jesus who are walking toward Emmaus. They do not yet recognize that the stranger walking with them is the risen Jesus. They tell him what happened, and they are sad because they had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel. They mention the women's report, but they still cannot bring themselves to believe it.

For today: sometimes God is already at work, but our sadness or our doubts keep us from seeing it. When something does not add up for you, do not shut yourself off. Bring your questions to God honestly, and seek his Word to see with new eyes.
exp.0:58:
This verse tells that, eight days after the child was born, the family and the neighbors came to circumcise him. It was the time to give him his name, and they wanted to name him after his father, Zacharias. Circumcision is a sign that God gave to Israel as part of his covenant.

Luke tells what happened with the son of Zacharias and Elizabeth. The neighbors and relatives had rejoiced because of God's mercy. They followed the custom of the time, though it was not a law, of naming the child after the father or a family member. But earlier the angel had indicated another name: John (Luke 1:13). That is why what follows surprises everyone.

For today: sometimes customs and the opinion of others weigh heavily on us. But obeying what God has said is worth more than following what "has always been done." Ask God for the courage to obey him with simplicity.
exp.18:6:
It tells that, when they saw Jesus going to the house of Zacchaeus, all the people began to complain under their breath. "Murmured" means that they grumbled quietly. "Gone to be guest" means that he had gone to stay as a guest, to eat and to lodge there. For them, Jesus had gone with a man that is a sinner.

Zacchaeus was the chief of the tax collectors in Jericho, and he was rich. Many saw him as a dishonest man who worked for Rome. Those who murmured were the ones who witnessed the scene, perhaps both followers and curious onlookers. Jesus had just invited himself into his home, and this seemed scandalous to them.

Today, we can be careful not to judge those who seem far from God. Jesus drew near to Zacchaeus, and that nearness opened the door to a true change. Let us ask God for a heart that welcomes with love and without prejudice.
exp.19:29:
It says that after the first brother died without children, the second married the widow, and he too died without leaving descendants. The word for "took" here means "married her." The words for "seed" and "offspring" mean children or descendants.

The speakers are some Sadducees, a religious group that denied the resurrection. They put to Jesus an invented case, based on the law of Moses about marriage between brothers-in-law (Deuteronomy 25), which was meant to keep the dead man's name from being lost. Their purpose was not to learn but to make the idea of resurrection look ridiculous. Jesus will answer them later in the chapter.

For today: when someone asks us questions only to trap or mock us, we can imitate the calm of Jesus. We can answer with the truth of God's Word, without getting drawn into quarrels, and trust that God is greater than our doubts.
exp.8:4:
Jesus says that if a town does not welcome them, the disciples should leave that place and shake the dust from their feet as a witness against those people. The word "receive" in the verse means to welcome or accept, and "as a witness against them" signals that the townspeople rejected the message.

Jesus is speaking to his twelve disciples as he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. He asks them to go without resources, trusting in God. Shaking off the dust was a gesture of parting: they had already done their part, and the responsibility now rested with those who turned them away. Some scholars believe it also showed that they wanted to take nothing from that place.

For today: do your part with love and clarity, but do not carry the blame if someone rejects the message. Take your leave in peace, without bitterness, and keep moving forward, trusting that God is at work in every heart.
exp.20:17:
Jesus says that not a single hair of his disciples' heads will be lost. "Will perish" means it will be destroyed or ruined, in the sense that God looks after even the smallest details of the lives of his people.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple, shortly before his death. He warns them that they will be betrayed, hated, and even put to death for following him. It seems contradictory that he says not a hair will perish when some of them will die. Many understand this as referring to God's lasting care: the body may suffer, but nothing that we are to Him is lost. Others see it as protection in the middle of trial.

When you face difficulties because of your faith or feel forgotten, remember that God knows you and cares for you in the great things and in the small. Trust in Him and persevere with patience.
exp.22:51:
This verse says that Joseph of Arimathea went to Pilate, the Roman governor, and asked him for the body of Jesus so he could bury it. The word "went" here means that he presented himself before him, and "senator" refers to a member of the Jewish council.

The one telling this is Luke, who recounts what happened after Jesus died. Joseph was a good and righteous man who was waiting for the kingdom of God, and he had not agreed with the decision to condemn Jesus. Asking for the body was a risky act, because it meant approaching the very man who had authorized the crucifixion. The Bible does not say more about what Joseph felt.

For today: sometimes loving God calls for a brave and concrete step, even if it comes late or costs something. Ask Him to give you courage to do what is right and to serve others, even when it is not easy or popular.
exp.22:6:
This verse tells us that Pilate learned Jesus was from Galilee. Since Galilee was under Herod's authority, Pilate sent him to Herod. "Jurisdiction" means the territory where someone has authority. "Sent" means that he sent him over. Herod was in Jerusalem at that time.

The Jewish leaders were accusing Jesus before Pilate, the Roman governor. They said he was stirring up the people. When Pilate heard the mention of Galilee, he saw a way out: passing the case on to Herod Antipas. Some think he wanted to avoid responsibility, though the text does not say this in so many words. Luke shows that Pilate did not find a clear fault in Jesus.

For today: sometimes we want to avoid difficult decisions by passing them on to others. Pilate knew something was not right, but he looked for a convenient way out. Let us ask God for the courage to act justly, even when it costs us.
exp.22:7:
Luke 23:8 says that Herod was exceedingly glad when he saw Jesus. He had wanted to see him for a long time, because he had heard many things about him. He hoped to see some sign, that is, a miracle. The word "glad" describes his joy, and "a long season" means for quite some time.

Luke, the narrator, tells how Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, when he learned that Jesus was from Galilee. Herod was in Jerusalem at that time. His gladness did not come from faith or repentance, but from curiosity. According to the text that follows, Jesus gave him no answer.

We can seek Jesus only out of curiosity or for what he might do for us, and not out of love and obedience. This passage invites us to approach him with a sincere heart, ready to listen to him and follow him, and not merely to ask him for spectacles.
exp.13:31:
The explanation says that the king who sees that his army is smaller does not throw himself into battle. While the enemy is still far away, he sends messengers to ask for peace and to reach an agreement. "Asks for peace" means he requests a treaty of peace.

Jesus speaks to great crowds that were following him. With two examples, the unfinished tower and the king at war, he teaches them to count the cost before following him. He then makes clear that his disciple must give up everything he owns. He does not want followers who act on impulse, but people who understand what their decision involves.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: am I willing to put Jesus above my plans, my possessions and my comfort? Following him is not a passing enthusiasm but a full surrender. Let us speak with God today about what we find hard to let go of.
exp.8:33:
What it says: While Peter was still speaking, a cloud came and covered them all. The disciples were afraid as they entered into it. In this passage, the word for fear means a fear full of reverence before something holy. No one knows for certain whether the word for "they" refers only to Jesus, Moses, and Elijah, or to the disciples as well; the text seems to point to everyone.

Context: This is the account of the transfiguration. Luke tells us that Peter was speaking without fully understanding, wanting to make three shelters or tents for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. In the Bible, a cloud often signals the presence of God. Then God himself interrupts, and from the cloud he says that Jesus is his beloved Son and that people must listen to him.

For today: Sometimes we speak too quickly, especially when we do not understand what God is doing. Today you can pause, stay silent for a moment, and ask him: "Lord, help me to listen to you." Then read a passage from the Gospels and pay attention to what Jesus says.
exp.15:30:
Here Abraham says that if people do not listen to Moses and the prophets, that is, to the Scriptures of the Old Testament, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

Jesus tells the story of the rich man and Lazarus. The rich man, already suffering after death, asks that someone go to warn his five brothers. Abraham replies that they already have God's Word. The problem is not a lack of evidence, but a heart that does not want to listen. Many also see here an allusion to Jesus' resurrection and to how many did not believe, though this is an interpretation.

For today: do not wait for an extraordinary sign in order to obey God. Read the Bible with a humble heart and put into practice what you already understand.
exp.1:48:
Jesus answers Mary with two questions. He tells her there was no need for her to search for him anxiously, because he had to be about his Father's business. The phrase "about my Father's business" is the wording of the verse above, and some versions translate it as "in my Father's house"; the original can be understood in both ways.

Jesus is twelve years old and is in the temple in Jerusalem, among the teachers. Mary reproaches him because she and Joseph had searched for him for three days. Jesus, with respect, makes it clear that God is his Father and that he has a mission. His parents did not fully understand, but he went back with them and was obedient to them.

For today: put first what God asks of you, without ceasing to honor your family. And when you do not understand something about God, do as Mary did: keep it in your heart, with patience and trust.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that Satan entered into Judas, who was also called Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples closest to Jesus. The phrase "surnamed" in the King James Version is the same as "also called," which appears in the verse above as "surnamed Iscariot." "Iscariot" probably indicates where his family came from (a man of Kerioth), although not all scholars are certain.

Here Luke speaks as narrator. The religious leaders wanted to kill Jesus, but they feared the people. Just then Judas appears and offers them a way out: to hand him over in secret. Luke shows that behind this betrayal there was a spiritual force of evil. Even so, Judas acted by his own decision.

For today: do not give evil a place in your heart. Judas arrived there step by step. If you hold on to resentment, ambition, or disappointment, bring it to God in prayer and ask for help in time.
exp.18:27:
He says that, after finishing speaking, Jesus was walking ahead of his disciples, going up toward Jerusalem. The explanation notes that the verse uses an older spelling of the city's name, which is simply Jerusalem. It says "going up" because the city sits high, in the hills of Judea.

Jesus had just told the parable of the minas, about a nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom and then returns to call his servants to account. Luke says he told it because they were near Jerusalem and some thought the kingdom of God would appear right away. With this verse, the account moves from teaching to the road toward the cross.

Jesus does not move blindly or by force: he goes ahead, with determination, knowing what awaits him. Today you can trust that he knows the hard road and goes first. When you face something difficult that you must do, follow his steps with faith and obedience.
exp.4:23:
Jesus says that he wants to show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. Then he turns to the paralyzed man and commands him: rise, pick up your mat and go home.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees and teachers of the law, who believed that only God could forgive sins and that Jesus was speaking blasphemy. Earlier he had told the man, "Your sins are forgiven." Since they could not see forgiveness, Jesus healed the body, something visible, to show his authority. "Son of Man" was the title Jesus used for himself.

Jesus cares about our whole life: the soul and the body. If you carry guilt or shame, you can come to him with confidence. His forgiveness is real, and his word has the power to raise you up and give you a new life.
exp.2:27:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It says that Neri was the son of Melchi, Melchi the son of Addi, Addi the son of Cosam, Cosam the son of Elmodam, and Elmodam the son of Er. The phrase "which was the son of" means the same as "which was the son of" in the verse above; these are names of people who lived in successive generations, and of most of them we know very little.

Luke, the author of the Gospel, is the one who presents this genealogy of Jesus, right after his baptism. He traces it backward, from Jesus to Adam. This stretch falls roughly between Zerubbabel and David. Scholars discuss why it differs from the list in Matthew; some think Luke follows the line of Mary, others the line of Joseph, and there is no certainty.

For today: God pays attention to ordinary people who are little known. These almost forgotten names were part of his plan. Your faithful life, though it may seem quiet, also matters to God.
exp.6:36:
This verse tells of a woman who was known in the city as a sinner. When she learned that Jesus was eating in the house of a Pharisee, she brought an alabaster jar, a fine, smooth stone container, filled with perfume.

Luke tells this moment after Jesus had spoken about wisdom and about how many people rejected him. A Pharisee invited him to eat, and Jesus accepted. The Bible does not say what kind of sin the woman had committed, so it is better not to assume. What matters is the contrast between her, who comes forward humbly, and the host, who watches her with judgment.

For today: if you know you need God's forgiveness, do not wait until you are perfect before coming to Jesus. Come with simplicity and sincerity, just as you are.
exp.5:14:
This verse continues the list of the twelve apostles whom Jesus chose. It names Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon, who was called "the Zealot." The word "Zealot" here means "zealous" or "ardent." Some think it refers to a group that wanted to free Israel from Rome; others think it only describes his strong religious passion. It is not known for certain.

Luke tells us that Jesus spent the night praying and, at dawn, chose twelve of his disciples to call apostles, that is, sent ones. Luke is the one who narrates. Among them were men who were very different, such as Matthew, who had earlier been a tax collector, and Simon, whose past was marked by zeal. After choosing them, Jesus came down with them to a level place where a large crowd was waiting for him.

For today: Jesus did not choose people who were alike or perfect. Today too he calls very different people to serve him together. We can learn to value those who think differently in the church, remembering that Christ unites us.
exp.19:40:
Jesus asks the teachers of the law a question: how is it possible for them to say that the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, is David's son? By "son" he means a descendant. The question is meant to make them think more deeply.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, after the scribes and other leaders had tested him with difficult questions. Now he asks them a question. He quotes Psalm 110, where David calls someone "Lord" who would also be his descendant. Jesus makes clear that the Messiah is more than a simple human heir; some understand that he points to his divine nature.

For today: it is not enough to repeat what we have always heard about Jesus. Ask yourself honestly who he is to you, and give him the place of Lord in your daily life.
exp.19:24:
Jesus answers with a brief statement: give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God. Caesar was the emperor of Rome.

Jesus speaks before religious leaders who wanted to trap him with a question about paying taxes to the Roman government. If he said yes, the people could reject him; if he said no, they would accuse him before Rome. He asked for a coin bearing the image of Caesar and answered with wisdom. Those who were listening were amazed and fell silent.

For today: we can fulfill our responsibilities as citizens, such as paying taxes and respecting just laws, without forgetting that our whole life belongs to God. Many understand that just as the coin bore the image of Caesar, the human being bears the image of God.
exp.20:23:
Many of the people of Jerusalem, it says, would die by the edge of the sword, and others would be led away as prisoners into different countries. Jerusalem would be trodden down, that is, trampled underfoot and ruled by peoples who are not Jews. This would last until the time God has set for those nations is complete.

Jesus speaks this way in his teaching about the future, shortly before his death. He warns of judgment on Jerusalem, which many connect with the destruction of the city in 70 AD. Christians do not agree on exactly what the times of the Gentiles mean or how long they cover. Jesus says this so that his disciples will not be taken by surprise.

For today: God does not lose control of history, even in hard times. Trust his word, live with humility, and stay alert, without letting fear or predictions carry you away.
exp.11:55:
Jesus calls the people "hypocrites" because they know how to read the signs of the weather, such as seeing the cloud rise in the west and announcing rain, but they fail to recognize what God is doing right now.

Jesus speaks to the crowds, after first warning his disciples. His ministry, with his teaching and miracles, showed that God was at work, but many did not want to see it. That is why he calls them to decide wisely, and immediately speaks of settling accounts with the opponent before reaching the judge. It is a call to act with urgency.

Today, it is not enough to be clever about the practical matters of life. Let us ask God for sensitivity to recognize his voice, and let us respond quickly, settling what is pending with him and with others.
exp.20:2:
Jesus says that the poor widow put in more than all the others. The word "treasury" was the place in the temple where the offering boxes stood. The two small coins were pieces of very little value, almost nothing. "Cast in" means that she gave or deposited her offering.

Jesus was in the temple in Jerusalem and watched how the people gave. He saw the rich giving out of what they had to spare, and this woman giving everything she had to live on. He does not measure the offering by the amount, but by the sacrifice and the heart. In this way he teaches his disciples how God values what we give.

Today we can remember that God does not look at how much we give, but at the sincerity and trust with which we do it. Even if you have little time, money, or strength, what you offer with love and faith has great value to him. Give generously, and do not compare yourself with anyone.
exp.9:32:
It says that a Samaritan was traveling and came to where the injured man was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, that is, he felt deep pity and wanted to help him. Here the story changes: the other two passed by on the other side, but this one stopped.

Jesus is speaking, telling this parable to a teacher of the law who asked him who his neighbor was. Jews and Samaritans used to look down on each other. That is why Jesus surprises his listeners by holding up as an example of love someone many did not expect.

For today: compassion does not stay as a feeling, but leads us to act. Today you can ask God to open your eyes to see someone near you who has a need, and do something concrete for that person, even if it is uncomfortable or they are not from your group.
exp.21:1:
This verse says that the religious leaders of Israel (the chief priests, that is, the leading priests, and the scribes, who were teachers of the Law) were looking for a way to kill Jesus. But they did not dare to act openly, because they feared how the people would react, since the people listened to him with respect.

Luke is the one telling the story. The Passover was drawing near, when Jerusalem filled with pilgrims. The leaders saw Jesus as a threat to their authority and influence. Their fear was not of God or of doing something unjust, but of losing the support of the people. Soon, Judas will give them the opportunity they were looking for.

For today: examine what moves you to make decisions. These leaders cared more about their image and their position than about the truth. Ask God for a humble heart, one that fears him more than the opinion of others.
exp.23:49:
He led his disciples out of Jerusalem, as far as the nearby village of Bethany. There he lifted up his hands and blessed them. The word translated "led out" means to bring someone outside, and the name of the village is simply Bethany. Lifting up the hands was a gesture of blessing.

The one speaking here is Luke, the narrator. Jesus had already risen, and he had just told them that they would be witnesses and that the Father would send his promise, the Holy Spirit. He was about to take his leave. The verses that follow tell that, while he was blessing them, he was carried up into heaven, and the disciples returned to Jerusalem with great joy.

For today: Jesus left his followers with a blessing, not with sadness. When you face change, farewells, or waiting, remember that Christ cares for you. You can wait with confidence and joy, and you can also bless others with your words.
exp.2:15:
John the Baptist says that he baptizes with water, but that someone far more powerful than he is coming. So great is this person that John does not feel worthy even to untie the strap of his sandals, a task proper to a servant. This one will baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire.

The people were waiting for the Messiah and wondered whether John might be the Christ. John makes it clear with humility that he is only preparing the way.

About the fire, there are several interpretations: purification, judgment, or the fire of Pentecost. The next verse, which speaks of burning the chaff, suggests a sense of judgment and cleansing.

For today: follow John's example and place yourself before Jesus. Recognize that He is greater and that only He can transform you from within. Do not seek the first place; seek for Christ to occupy the center of your life.
exp.13:17:
All the guests began, as if they had agreed among themselves, to make excuses. The first one tells the host that he has bought a field and must go and see it, and he asks to be excused.

Jesus is the one speaking. He is eating at the house of a Pharisee and tells this parable about a great dinner. The guests had already been invited, and when the time comes they turn down the invitation. Many readers understand that Jesus is showing how the call of God can be refused, although scholars debate exactly who the guests were meant to represent.

For today: the excuses often come from good and ordinary things, such as work, shopping, or family. Ask yourself what good thing you are placing ahead of responding to God, and give Him some time today.
exp.21:51:
Jesus speaks to the chief priests, the captains of the temple guard, and the elders, who had come to arrest him. He asks whether they are treating him like a robber, the kind of man they would come out against with swords and clubs. The "temple officers" are the officials in charge of watching over the temple, and the "chief priests" are the leading priests.

It is the night of the arrest, in the garden of Gethsemane. Jesus had just healed the ear of the servant who was wounded by one of the disciples. With his question he makes clear that the arrest was not just: he had been teaching openly in the temple in broad daylight, and they seize him at night, away from the crowds. Even so, he does not resist.

For today: when we are treated unjustly, we can imitate the calm of Jesus. We can speak the truth with firmness, without answering with violence or revenge, and trust that God is still at work even in dark moments.
exp.22:12:
This verse says that Pilate, the Roman governor, gathered together the chief priests, the rulers (the leaders or authorities of the Jews), and the people. "Gathered together" means he called everyone to come together. It is the beginning of what Pilate is going to say to them.

Luke records this while Jesus is being tried. Herod mocked Jesus and sent him back to Pilate. Now Pilate brings together the accusers and the people to tell them, in front of everyone, that he finds no fault in Jesus deserving of death. Scholars debate why Pilate later gave in, but the text shows that he recognized Jesus' innocence.

For today: knowing what is right is not enough; we must have the courage to act. Let us ask God for firmness to defend the truth even when the pressure of the crowd is strong.
exp.5:35:
This verse asks us to be merciful, that is, to have compassion and help others even when they do not deserve it. The reason is that God, our Father, is like this toward us.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to a crowd, within what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has just taught us to love our enemies and to give without expecting anything in return. This verse sums all of that up: the model is God himself, who is kind even to the ungrateful. Then Jesus goes on to speak about not judging and about forgiving.

For today: think of someone who annoys you or who has let you down. This week, instead of responding harshly, do something concrete: a kind word, a help, or a sincere forgiveness.
exp.5:28:
Jesus says that if someone strikes you on the cheek, you should also offer them the other one. And if someone takes your cloak, which is the outer garment or coat, do not refuse them your tunic, which was the clothing worn underneath.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to the crowd that listens to him, in the Sermon on the Plain. Just before this, he asked them to love their enemies, to bless those who curse them, and to pray for those who mistreat them. This verse gives concrete examples of that love. Many read it as an invitation not to repay evil with evil, rather than as a literal rule for every situation.

Today we can apply it this way: when someone offends us, instead of responding with revenge or with hurtful words, we can choose a calm and generous response and pray for that person.
exp.9:38:
She had a sister named Mary. Mary sat at Jesus' feet and listened to what he taught. Sitting at someone's feet was the posture of a student before his teacher. To hear his word means to listen closely to his teaching.

The one telling the story is Luke. Just before this, Jesus told the parable of the good Samaritan and said, "Go, and do thou likewise." Then he comes to a village, and Martha welcomes him into her home. Luke does not name the village here. The verse sets up the contrast between Martha, who was busy serving, and Mary, who was listening.

For today: serving others is good, but it must not take away the time we spend with Jesus. Set aside a quiet moment each day, without rush or phone, to read his Word and listen to him. From there, your service will have more peace and meaning.
exp.6:18:
John the Baptist sends two of his disciples with a direct question for Jesus: Are you the one who was to come, the promised Messiah, or should we keep waiting for someone else? The phrase "the one who was to come" was a way of speaking about the Savior announced by the prophets.

John is in prison (Luke 3:20) and hears about the works of Jesus. We do not know for certain why he asks. Some think he doubted because of his situation or because he expected a different kind of Messiah; others believe he wanted to encourage his disciples to see Jesus for themselves. Jesus answers with deeds: he heals and gives sight to the blind.

When you have doubts, do not hide them. Bring them honestly to Jesus. He does not turn away someone who asks sincerely, and he knows how to answer with patience.
exp.2:3:
Luke says that what John the Baptist was doing had already been announced by the prophet Isaiah. To "prepare" means to get ready, and the paths are the roads. The voice crying in the wilderness calls for preparing the way of the Lord and making his roads straight, as people do when an important king is about to arrive.

Luke is the writer, and he quotes Isaiah 40:3. John preached in the wilderness near the Jordan, calling for a baptism of repentance, that is, a change of heart in order to receive the forgiveness of sins. His message prepared the people for the coming of Jesus. The verses that follow speak of leveling what is crooked and rough, and of all people seeing God's salvation.

For today: ask yourself what crooked way there is in your life, such as a grudge, a lie, or a bad habit. Bring it honestly before God, ask for forgiveness, and take one concrete step to make it straight this week.
exp.6:26:
Jesus says that John the Baptist is the one the Scripture speaks about. The Scripture passage is the promise that God would send a messenger to go ahead of the Lord and get the way ready. The word "prepare" in the verse means to make everything ready in advance.

Jesus speaks to the crowd who have just watched John's messengers leave, since John was in prison. He asks them what they went out to the desert to see: not a man dressed in fine clothes, but a prophet, and more than a prophet. Jesus quotes the words of Malachi 3:1 and applies them to John, who announced the coming of the Messiah.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are preparing our hearts to receive Jesus. John called people to repentance and humility. Setting aside pride, asking for forgiveness, and obeying God is a good way to clear the way for him in our lives.
exp.18:43:
Jesus says that Jerusalem will be completely brought down. The phrase about being cast to the ground means that the city will be destroyed, and the phrase about the people inside you refers to its inhabitants. The words about not leaving one stone upon another mean that it will lie in ruins. The time of your visitation is the moment when God drew near to his people. And because you did not know it means that they did not recognize it.

Jesus speaks as he approaches Jerusalem, and he weeps over the city. He is the Messiah who offers peace, but many do not receive him. His words announce a judgment that many see fulfilled in the destruction of the city by the Romans, in the year 70 A.D. Shortly afterward, Jesus enters the temple and cleanses it.

Today, God still draws near to us. Let us ask for an attentive and humble heart, to recognize his voice and respond to him without delay.
exp.20:16:
Jesus says that his followers will be hated, that is, disliked and rejected, by many people. The reason is clear: "for my name's sake," meaning because they belong to Christ and confess him. The word "all" probably speaks of a very wide rejection, not necessarily of every single person without exception.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. He warns them of the trials that would come, even betrayals within their own families. But he also promises to give them words and wisdom, and assures them that not a hair of their head will be lost. His care remains firm in the midst of suffering.

For today: if someone rejects you or mocks you for following Jesus, do not be surprised or discouraged. Respond with respect and gentleness, trust that God will give you words, and remain steadfast with patience.
exp.8:48:
John tells Jesus that the disciples saw a man casting out demons in Jesus' name. They forbade him, that is, they told him not to do it, because he did not follow with them, meaning he was not part of the group of followers. The title John uses for Jesus means "Lord" or "Teacher." The word "casting out" means driving out.

John speaks right after the disciples argued about who would be the greatest. Jesus had taught them, using a child, that true greatness lies in humility. Now John, perhaps somewhat uncomfortable, confesses that they guarded their "group." Jesus answers that they should not stop him, because whoever is not against them is for them.

Today we can rejoice when others serve Christ, even if they are not from our church or circle. Before we criticize, let us ask whether they honor Jesus, and let us value humility above rivalry.
exp.3:30:
This verse tells that Jesus went down to Capernaum, a city in Galilee. The word "went down" is used because Capernaum was at a lower elevation than Nazareth. There Jesus taught the people on the Sabbath days, which was the day of rest and gathering for the Jews.

The one who narrates is Luke, who writes like a careful historian. Just before, the people of Nazareth rejected Jesus with fury and tried to throw him off the hill, but he passed through the midst of them and went on his way. Now Jesus does not stop or lose heart: he takes his message to another place. What follows shows that in Capernaum the people were astonished at his teaching.

For today: when someone rejects your faith or your good intentions, do not remain trapped in the pain. Keep moving forward with humility and look for where you can serve and share the good that God has given you. There are open hearts waiting.
exp.0:45:
Here Mary begins a song of praise. "My soul doth magnify the Lord" means that she, from the depths of her being, recognizes and proclaims how great God is. She does not make Him greater than He is; she shows Him to be great through her words and her life.

Mary has just arrived at the house of her cousin Elisabeth. Elisabeth has told her that she is blessed, that is, happy, because she believed the word of God. Mary responds not by speaking about herself, but by praising God. This song is known as the Magnificat, a name that comes from the first word of the ancient Latin translation.

For today: when you receive a blessing or a compliment, follow Mary's example and give the glory back to God. Before going on with your day, thank Him in your own words, from the heart and with simplicity.
exp.11:20:
Jesus says that this is what happens to the one who gathers riches only for himself and is not "rich toward God." The old words in the source are rendered as follows: the phrase about storing up is accumulating possessions; the word about enjoying oneself means taking one's ease and having fun; and the word about being anxious means worried or overly concerned. To be rich toward God means to have a life that is precious in His sight.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples. A man asked him to step in on an inheritance, and Jesus warned against greed with the parable of the rich man who filled his barns and thought only of resting. God calls him a fool because he trusted in his goods and forgot that his life did not belong to him. Afterward, Jesus invites his disciples not to live in worry.

Today, before you save or spend, ask yourself how you can use what you have to serve God and help others. Trust Him with your needs.
exp.10:2:
It says we ask God for the food we need for each day. The old form of "give us" is removed, since the verse above reads "give us." "Bread" means food in general, not only bread. The word "day by day" invites us to trust God one day at a time, without worrying about tomorrow.

Jesus speaks with his disciples, who ask him to teach them to pray as John the Baptist taught his own followers. He gives them this model prayer. First God is honored: his name, his kingdom, and his will. Then come our needs: daily bread, forgiveness, and protection. After that Jesus tells the story of the friend who asks for bread at midnight, to encourage us to pray with persistence.

Today we can begin the day by thanking God for what we have and asking him for what we need for that day. This helps us live with trust, with gratitude, and with generosity toward those who have less.
exp.13:23:
Jesus ends the parable of the great banquet here. The master of the house says that none of the first invited guests, the ones who made excuses, will taste his supper. The verse above uses the word "taste" for this, so the sentence about the meaning of the quoted word can be rewritten: taste here means to partake of, or to share in, the meal. Whoever turned down the invitation loses the place they had.

Jesus is speaking to people who were at the table with a Pharisee and had just heard about the banquet of God's kingdom. The guests who make excuses stand for those who put their own affairs ahead of God. Many scholars see in the new guests the poor, the marginalized, and people from other nations, though there is debate about how much applies to each group. Right after this, Jesus speaks about the cost of following him.

For today: do not put off God's invitation. Ask yourself what respectable "excuse," such as work or family, is keeping you from answering him today. Give him your time now, with humility and gratitude.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem and that he went "through the midst of Samaria and Galilee." In other words, he traveled through the border area between those two regions.

Luke tells the story of Jesus' journey toward Jerusalem, where he would face the cross. Shortly before, he had taught his disciples about humble service. Now Luke sets the scene in a mixed place, between Jews and Samaritans, which prepares for the meeting with the ten lepers. Some scholars see an important detail there, because among those who are healed there will be a Samaritan. The exact route cannot be fully determined.

For today: Jesus did not avoid uncomfortable places or people who were different. We can ask him to help us serve with humility and to see with compassion those who are on the margins.
exp.1:44:
This verse says that Mary and Joseph, when they did not find Jesus among the relatives and acquaintances, went back to Jerusalem to keep looking for him. The verse's wording is "they turned back again to Jerusalem, seeking him," and the explanation of its meaning is simply that they returned to search.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking. Jesus was twelve years old, and the family had gone to Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover. On the way home they were traveling in a group, and Joseph and Mary assumed the boy was with other relatives. When they realized he was not there, they returned worried. The account prepares the moment when they find him in the temple.

For today: when we feel we have lost sight of Jesus, through carelessness or routine, we should not stay behind lamenting it. We can go back and seek him earnestly, praying and opening his Word, trusting that he allows himself to be found.
exp.10:11:
Jesus asks: if a son asks for an egg, would his father give him a scorpion? The obvious answer is no. An egg nourishes; a scorpion harms. This is the third comparison, after the bread and the fish, to show that a father does not answer what his child asks in real need with something harmful.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, after teaching them the Lord's Prayer and the parable of the friend who asks for bread at midnight. He wants to encourage them to pray with confidence. If imperfect parents give good things, God, who is perfect, will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

For today: pray simply and with confidence, like a child speaking with his father. Even when you do not understand his answer, you can believe that God is good and will not give you something that would destroy you.
exp.11:33:
This verse says that what we value most is what draws our heart. "Treasure" is whatever we consider of greatest worth, and "heart" is the center of our desires, thoughts and affections. Where we place what we love most, our attention goes there too.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, whom he calls a little flock. He asks them not to be afraid, for the Father gives them the kingdom. Therefore he invites them to be generous and to store up treasure in heaven, which no thief or moth can destroy. Right after this, he asks them to be ready for his return.

Today, we can ask ourselves how we spend our time, money and energy. One practical way: set aside something this week to help someone in need, and so train the heart to value what is eternal.
exp.22:52:
He took Jesus' body down from the cross, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid it in a tomb cut into the rock. That tomb was new: no one had ever been buried in it before.

The verse's wording is "took it down," and the explanation's point is simply that he removed the body from the cross.

Luke is the one telling the story, drawing on what was reported about what happened after Jesus died. Joseph was a member of the Jewish council, but he had not agreed with the decision to condemn Jesus. He asked Pilate for the body so that Jesus could receive a proper burial, and he acted quickly because the Sabbath was about to begin. The women saw all of it.

For today: Joseph acted with courage and love when others stayed silent. We can ask ourselves what concrete act of kindness or faithfulness to Christ God is asking of us today, even if it is uncomfortable or little noticed.
exp.14:21:
Jesus tells how the father orders his servants to bring out the best robe and put it on the son who came back. He also orders a ring to be put on his hand and sandals on his feet. The word "put it on him" is the meaning of the verse above, and "best robe" is the finest and most valuable clothing.

Jesus speaks in the parable of the lost son, within a series of stories about what was lost and then found. The son had already confessed that he was no longer worthy to be called a son. Even so, the father does not answer him with reproach but restores him fully. Many understand the robe, the ring and the sandals as signs of honor and of being received as a son, not as a servant.

Today, if you have turned away from God or feel unworthy, you do not have to earn your way back. Come back sincerely, trusting that God receives with grace and restores whoever draws near to Him.
exp.16:21:
Jesus tells his disciples that a hard time will come when they will long to see even one of the days of the Son of Man, that is, a moment of Jesus' presence or action, and they will not be able to see it.

Jesus speaks first to the Pharisees, who ask when the kingdom of God is coming, and then he turns to his disciples. He warns them that there will be times of longing and waiting. Interpreters understand this in different ways: as days of persecution, as Jesus' absence before his return, or as both. Then Jesus adds that they should not follow false announcements, because his coming will be visible like a lightning flash.

For today: if there are seasons when you feel God is far away, do not run after any voice that promises easy signs. Remain faithful, pray, and trust that Jesus will do what he promised.
exp.22:39:
One of the two criminals crucified beside Jesus rebukes the other, who was mocking him. He says, "Dost not thou fear God, seeing thou art in the same condemnation?" That is, even now, about to die, do you not fear God at all? Being under the same condemnation means that both of them were suffering the same punishment.

It is one of the criminals who speaks, perhaps moved by a change in his heart. The other had mocked Jesus and was asking him to save himself and them. This second man acknowledges his guilt and sees that Jesus is innocent. Shortly afterward he will ask Jesus to remember him in his kingdom.

For today: let us not wait until everything is in order before we draw near to God. Acknowledging our need with humility and reverence for God can open the door to his mercy, even in the most difficult hours.
exp.11:0:
Jesus is surrounded by a crowd so large that the people were trampling on one another. Even so, he begins by speaking to his disciples. He warns them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Leaven is a small amount of fermented dough that makes the whole batch rise.

The one speaking is Jesus, and his words that follow explain his warning: what is hidden will come to light. The Pharisees were religious teachers who were highly respected, but many put on a show of faith that they did not live out inwardly. Jesus wants his disciples not to copy that attitude, even though the crowd is watching them.

For today: ask yourself whether your faith is the same in public and in private. Ask God for sincerity, and seek to have your words, your actions, and your heart match, without pretending to be what you are not.
exp.21:62:
This verse says that the men who were guarding Jesus mocked him and struck him. The phrase "held Jesus" means that they had him under guard, as a prisoner. "Hitting him" means striking him.

Here it is not Jesus who speaks, but the narrator, Luke. Jesus had already been arrested and taken to the house of the high priest, waiting for morning so the formal trial could take place. In the meantime, the guards mistreat him. Shortly before, Peter had denied him three times and wept bitterly. Luke contrasts Peter's weakness with the humiliation that Jesus endures in silence. The Gospels show that this fulfills what Jesus had foretold about his suffering.

For today: when you are called to suffer mockery or injustice, remember that Jesus went through that first. You do not have to respond with revenge; you can ask him for strength to act with dignity and peace.
exp.4:36:
No one puts new wine into old wineskins. Wineskins are bags made from animal skin that were used to store wine. An old wineskin is already dry and stiff, and it does not stretch. The new wine keeps fermenting and builds up pressure, so the skin bursts, the wine spills out, and everything is lost.

Jesus is speaking to the Pharisees and the teachers of the law. They were asking why his disciples did not fast like the disciples of John. Jesus answers with parables: what he brings is something new, and it does not fit into old, rigid molds. He is the bridegroom, and his presence is a reason for joy.

For today: ask God for a flexible heart. If he shows you something new, do not confine it to habits or customs that no longer let you grow.
exp.21:65:
Luke says that at daybreak the religious leaders of Israel gathered: the elders of the people, the chief priests, and the scribes.
