They brought Jesus before their council, that is, the Sanhedrin, the Jewish court. The phrase "as soon as it was day" means that morning had already come, and the chief priests are the priests of highest rank.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened after Jesus was arrested and mistreated during the night. Many scholars think the morning meeting was meant to give the condemnation a legal appearance, since it was not customary to hold trials at night. Right away they ask Jesus whether he is the Christ, the promised Messiah.

For today: Jesus faced injustice with calm and truth. When you are treated unfairly or pressured by others, do not repay evil with evil. Trust God, who judges with justice, and stay firm and steady as Jesus did.
exp.16:36:
The disciples ask where all of that will happen: that some will be taken and others left. Jesus answers with a saying: wherever the dead body is, there the eagles gather. In this version, "eagles" can also be understood as vultures, birds that gather where there is carrion.

Jesus is speaking of his coming and of judgment, and the disciples want to know the place. He gives no map, but an image: just as the birds find the body without anyone telling them, his coming and the judgment will be obvious and cannot be overlooked. Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of the image, but the central idea seems to be that it will be unmistakable.

Today, instead of becoming preoccupied with dates and places, we can live each day ready, in faith and obedience, trusting that God will do everything with clarity in his time.
exp.4:29:
The explanation says that the scribes (teachers of the Law) and the Pharisees (a very strict religious group) grumbled quietly against Jesus' disciples. They complained about why they ate and drank with the tax collectors, who worked for Rome and were looked down on by the people, and with sinners, people regarded as far from God.

Levi, also called Matthew, had just left everything to follow Jesus and had held a great feast in his house. His fellow tax collectors and other people were there. The religious leaders believed that sharing a table with them meant approving of their way of life. Although the complaint was directed at the disciples, Jesus himself answered, as the following verse shows.

Jesus draws near to those who need God. We may ask ourselves whether we are willing to treat kindly those whom others reject, without giving up love for the truth, and to offer them friendship and hope.
exp.1:31:
It says that Jesus, the child Simeon holds in his arms, will be a light for the Gentiles, that is, for the peoples who are not Jews. At the same time he will be the glory of Israel, the people of God. The word "á" is an old form of "a", and "aparejado" means prepared.

Simeon, a righteous and devout man of Jerusalem, speaks. God had promised him that he would not die before seeing the Messiah. When Mary and Joseph present the child in the temple, Simeon takes him and praises God. His words recall promises of the prophet Isaiah about a servant who would bring light to the nations. Joseph and Mary marvel, for God's plan is greater than they had imagined.

For today: Jesus is a light for everyone, regardless of origin or culture. We can share his hope with kindness and without making distinctions, starting with someone close to us this week.
exp.14:24:
He says that the elder son was working in the field. When he was coming back and drew near the house, he heard music and dancing. The word "symphony" here does not refer to a modern orchestra, but to music made with instruments or singing. The "dances" were celebratory dancing.

Jesus is telling the parable of the prodigal son. The younger brother has already returned in repentance, and the father received him with a great feast. Jesus tells this because the Pharisees and scribes were criticizing him for welcoming sinners. The elder son probably represents those who consider themselves faithful and find it hard to rejoice at grace shown to others.

When God shows mercy to someone who does not deserve it, how do we react? We can ask him to give us a heart like the Father's, so that we rejoice with those who come home instead of approaching them with judgment or resentment.
exp.22:25:
It says that the soldiers were leading Jesus away to be crucified. On the way they seized a man named Simon, from Cyrene, who was coming in from the countryside, and they laid the cross on his shoulders so that he would carry it behind Jesus.

Luke is the one telling the story, recounting what happened after Pilate handed Jesus over to the will of the crowd. The explanation does not say why they chose Simon. Many think Jesus was very weakened by the beatings, but the text does not say so. Simon was not a known follower of Jesus; he was simply passing by.

For today: sometimes God places us in the path of someone who is suffering, without our having planned it. We can help with humility and patience, and carry a little of the weight of others, knowing that Jesus also carried ours.
exp.0:52:
He gives good things to those who are hungry, and sends the rich away empty-handed. The word "filled" in the verse is the same idea as "filled," so the sentence explaining an old form of it is removed. The good things here mean food, blessings, and what is good in general. It does not speak only of food; it shows how God acts in the opposite way from what the world expects.

These words are Mary's, in the song called the Magnificat. She had just learned that she would be the mother of the Messiah, and she praises God for his mercy. She speaks of what God does with the proud and the humble, and recalls his faithfulness to the promise made to Abraham. Interpreters debate whether she is speaking of material poverty, spiritual poverty, or both.

Today it invites us to draw near to God with humility, recognizing that we need him. It also encourages us to share what we have with those in need, instead of trusting only in our riches.
exp.6:46:
Jesus says that this woman's many sins have been forgiven, and that her great love shows it. By contrast, whoever feels that little has been forgiven loves little. The words "for which reason" point to what she has just done: her acts of affection are the visible sign of a forgiveness she has received.

Jesus speaks in the house of Simon, a Pharisee who invited him to eat. A woman of bad reputation came in, wept at his feet, and anointed them with perfume. Simon looked down on her and doubted Jesus. Earlier, the Lord had told the parable of two debtors who were both forgiven a debt, to show that whoever recognizes more forgiveness loves more. Some understand that her love is the fruit of forgiveness; others, that it shows a faith already present.

Today, remember how much God has forgiven you. That sincere gratitude will make you love him more and treat with compassion those who also need forgiveness.
exp.8:10:
The explanation says that the people found out where Jesus had gone and followed him. He did not turn them away but received them. He spoke to them about the kingdom of God and healed those who needed healing. Words to note: "knew it" means they found out; "the people" is the crowd; "those who needed healing" means they were sick.

Luke tells us that Jesus had withdrawn with the apostles to a secluded place near Bethsaida, after they returned from their mission. Their plan was to rest, but the crowd arrived. Before this moment, Herod wondered who Jesus was. Here we see the answer in action: Jesus teaches and heals with compassion. Soon the feeding of the five thousand will follow.

For today: when your plans for rest are interrupted by the needs of others, ask God for a heart like Jesus'. Receive the person with patience, listen, and offer them hope and concrete help.
exp.11:4:
Jesus says there is someone worth fearing: God. The old words are easy to clear up: "I will forewarn you" is the same as "I will show you," and what the verse calls "fear" means having a deep reverence for God. Jesus says that God has authority not only over physical life but also over eternal destiny.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, whom he calls his friends, while a huge crowd presses around him. He warns them against hypocrisy and encourages them to be sincere, even if they are persecuted. For this reason he reminds them that fear of people is small compared with God's authority. Right after, he shows them that this same God cares even for the sparrows.

For today: when fear of what others think keeps you from being faithful, remember that God has the final word, and that he also cares for you tenderly. Pray, and take the step with confidence.
exp.0:70:
It says that God gives salvation, that is, rescue, from our enemies and from the power of all who hated us. The word "hated" means that they despised them or held hostility toward them. It is part of a phrase from the previous verse: God raised up a "horn of salvation," an image of strength and power that rescues.

It is Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, filled with the Holy Spirit, praising God. He celebrates that God fulfills what he promised through the prophets and through the covenant with Abraham. The enemies in his mind were probably the nations that dominated Israel; some also see here a more spiritual deliverance. Both readings have been held.

For today: when you feel trapped by pressures, opposition, or fears, remember that God is faithful to his promises. Rest in him, pray with confidence, and seek to live without resentment, for he is the one who rescues.
exp.14:8:
She says that the woman, having found her lost coin, calls her friends and neighbors to celebrate with her. The phrase "Give me your congratulations" is an old way of saying "Rejoice with me." The coin was a small silver coin of little value, yet it was important to her.

Jesus speaks in this parable. The Pharisees and scribes complained that he welcomed sinners and ate with them. Jesus answers with three stories: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. He wants to show how God rejoices when someone returns to him. The next verse says it plainly: there is joy before the angels of God.

For today: if God celebrates when a person returns to him, we too can rejoice and welcome with kindness someone who is drawing near to faith, instead of judging them. You can pray for someone who has drifted away and celebrate their steps toward God.
exp.23:12:
This verse tells that, on the same day as the resurrection, two followers of Jesus were walking toward a village called Emmaus. It was about sixty furlongs from Jerusalem, roughly seven miles. The distance is given in furlongs, an old unit of measure.

Luke, the narrator, reports this right after the women announced the empty tomb and the disciples did not believe them. Peter went to see for himself and was amazed. These two were not among the eleven apostles; we only learn the name of one of them, Cleopas, later on. They were walking along, confused by what had happened.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening, keep walking with your doubts and talk about them with other believers. Jesus often draws near to those who seek him sincerely, even when they do not notice right away.
exp.8:60:
A third man tells Jesus he will follow him, but first asks to say goodbye to his family. "Say goodbye" here means to bid farewell. The man does want to follow Jesus, but he sets a condition before he begins.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem and has met several people who want to be his disciples. To each one he shows that following him requires total priority. This man does not ask for anything wrong in itself, but his heart seems divided. Jesus answers with the image of the plow: whoever looks back does not move forward straight. Some scholars see here a reference to Elisha's calling (1 Kings 19:19-21), though not everyone interprets it this way.

Today, we can ask ourselves what we put "first" before God: work, comfort, plans. Jesus invites us to obey him with an undivided heart, without putting it off for later.
exp.7:7:
Jesus says that another part of the seed fell on good ground. When it sprang up, it bore fruit a hundredfold, that is, a hundred grains for each grain sown. Then Jesus cried out loudly: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear," an invitation to listen carefully and understand.

Jesus teaches a crowd in parables. This is the parable of the sower. Afterward he explains to his disciples that the seed is the word of God and that the different kinds of ground represent different ways of receiving it. The good ground shows those who hear it and hold it fast with an honest and good heart (Luke 8:15).

For today: it is not enough to hear the word of God; we must receive it and obey it. This week, read a passage of the Bible calmly, ask God to speak to you, and decide on one concrete action to put it into practice.
exp.8:0:
Luke tells us that Jesus gathered his twelve disciples and gave them power and authority. "Power" means strength or ability, and "authority" means the right to act with command. That power and authority were for casting out all demons and for curing diseases.

Here the narrator is Luke. Jesus is the one who acts, and he is preparing the twelve for a mission. The verses that follow show that he sends them out to preach the kingdom of God and to heal. The power was not theirs; they received it from Jesus in order to serve others and to proclaim his message.

For today: everything we are and everything we can do to help others is a gift from God, not a achievement of our own. If God gives you an opportunity to serve, do it with humility and trust in him, not in your own strength.
exp.10:3:
Jesus teaches us to ask for forgiveness of our sins. The word "owe" refers to those who have offended us or who owe us something. We also ask not to be led into "temptation," which can mean trial or being drawn into falling, and to be delivered "from evil," which can be understood as the evil one or as evil in general. "We forgive everyone" is the same as "we forgive everyone."

Jesus speaks to his disciples, who asked him to teach them to pray. This prayer follows the request for daily bread: we ask for sustenance, forgiveness, and protection. Then Jesus tells the story of the friend at midnight, to encourage us to pray with confidence and persistence.

For today: before you pray, think about whether there is someone you need to forgive. Hand that resentment over to God and ask him for help in letting it go. Then ask him for strength not to fall into what makes you stumble, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.21:34:
Jesus reminds his disciples of the time he sent them out without a purse (for money), without a bag (a knapsack for carrying provisions), and without extra shoes or spare sandals. He asks whether they lacked anything, and they answer that they lacked nothing.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He has just announced that Peter will deny him. By recalling that earlier sending out, he shows that God took care of them. But now the situation changes: opposition is coming. The matter of the sword is interpreted in various ways; many believe it is an expression meaning that they will face difficult times, not a command to fight.

For today: remember the times God has sustained you. That past faithfulness gives you confidence to face hard times, and it also invites you to prepare with wisdom, without ceasing to trust in him.
exp.15:23:
Here the rich man, who is in the place of the dead and suffers greatly, cries out asking for help. He addresses Abraham, asks for compassion, and begs that Lazarus be sent to dip the tip of his finger in water to cool his tongue.

The word "hell" here translates the Greek word Hades, the place of the dead. The phrase "cried and said" means crying out loud.

Jesus tells this story to a group that included Pharisees, who loved money. The rich man speaks from his suffering. Earlier he ignored the beggar at his gate, and now he asks that same man to serve him. Many see here a teaching about the reality of judgment, and others point out that it is a parable. All agree on its warning.

Today we can pay attention to the people God places near us. Let us not wait until it is too late: let us help those who are in need, and live with humility and compassion from now on.
exp.0:15:
It says that the son who will be born to Zechariah and Elizabeth, John, will turn many of the children of Israel back to the Lord, who is their God. The word "turn" means to make someone change direction, turn around, and return to God. The verse as given here uses the word "turn" for this action.

The angel Gabriel speaks to Zechariah, a priest, inside the temple. He announces that his wife, although she is old, will have a son. That child will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord, as the prophet Elijah did with his message. Zechariah doubts and asks for a sign.

For today: God still desires that people return to Him. We can help with humility, speaking kindly and showing a sincere life, without thinking of ourselves as the center. Today you can pray for someone who is far from God and look for an opportunity to encourage them.
exp.17:21:
Jesus tells this man that he still lacks one thing: sell everything he has, give it to the poor, and so have treasure in heaven. Then he invites him to follow him.

A wealthy and prominent man asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life. He said he had kept the commandments since his youth. Jesus does not argue with that, but he touches what the man loved most: his money. The text does not say whether this command is for everyone or only for him. What is clear is that his riches kept him from following Jesus, and so he went away sad.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: is there something I find so hard to let go of that it keeps me from obeying Jesus? Ask God for help to surrender it and to give generously to those who are in need.
exp.1:14:
This verse tells us that, when the angels returned to heaven, the shepherds encouraged one another to go to Bethlehem. "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem" means "let us go on, then, all the way to Bethlehem." They wanted to see with their own eyes what God had announced to them. Notice that they call the message "this thing which is come to pass," as if it were already a fact.

These are the shepherds, who were watching over their flocks by night. An angel had given them the good news of the Savior's birth, and then a heavenly multitude praised God. The shepherds did not stop at excitement: they responded at once, and soon afterward they found the child just as they had been told.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, admiration is not enough. We can take a concrete step of obedience and, if possible, encourage one another to do so, as they did.
exp.3:34:
Jesus spoke to the evil spirit with firmness: "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." The word "rebuked" means that he commanded it with authority, and "hold thy peace" means "be quiet." The demon threw the man down in the middle of the crowd, and then came out of him. What matters is that the man was not harmed.

This takes place in a synagogue in Capernaum, on a Sabbath. The spirit had just cried out that it knew who Jesus was, "the Holy One of God." Jesus does not accept that testimony, nor does he want the demon to speak. He orders it to be silent and drives it out. The people are amazed because Jesus gives commands with authority, through his word alone.

For today: when you feel fear, guilt, or a burden that seems stronger than you are, turn to Jesus in prayer. His word has authority, and he cares for you, even in the midst of the struggle.
exp.18:25:
He says that whoever has will be given more, and whoever does not have, even what little they have will be taken away.

Jesus speaks in the parable of the minas. A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and leaves money with his servants to put to work. When he returns, he rewards the one who made it produce and takes the mina away from the one who kept it without using it. Jesus tells this near Jerusalem, when many thought the kingdom would appear at once. Interpreters differ on some details of the parable, but the central point is faithfulness while he is away.

Today: think of a gift, time, or opportunity that God has given you, and use it this week to serve someone, instead of holding onto it out of fear or comfort.
exp.5:32:
Jesus says that there is no special merit in doing good only to those who do good to us. The sentence "What thank have ye?" means "What reward or merit will you have?" Even sinners, that is, those who do not follow God, act this way. The word "do" in "if ye do good" is an older form of the modern word "do".

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to a crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Just before this, he asks them to love their enemies. Here he shows that the love of his followers must go beyond mutual exchange and reflect the goodness of God, who is kind even to the ungrateful.

Today, this week, do a concrete favor for someone who cannot or does not usually return it: a difficult neighbor, a coworker who treated you badly, or someone in need. Do it without expecting anything in return.
exp.14:3:
Jesus asks a question to make us think: if a shepherd has a hundred sheep and loses one, does he not leave the other ninety-nine to go looking for it until he finds it?

"Wilderness" here means open country or grazing land, not necessarily a place without life.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees and scribes, who criticized him for welcoming sinners and eating with them. He answers with this parable to show how God thinks: the lost person matters to him, and he seeks them with determination. Some debate whether the question suggests that the listeners would agree with the shepherd; in any case, the central point is the value of each person.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we have left aside. Let us ask God for a heart like his, and approach with kindness someone who feels far away, without judging them.
exp.1:7:
There were shepherds in that region of Bethlehem, awake at night. The verse says they were alert and not sleeping, and that they took turns watching over their sheep through the night. The sheep are the flock they cared for.

Luke, the narrator, has just told of Jesus' birth in a manger, in a humble place. Now he introduces the first people who will receive the news: not important people, but ordinary workers. Some think shepherds were looked down on socially, although the Bible does not state this clearly here. What is certain is that the angel's message comes while they are doing their daily work.

God can speak to us in the middle of everyday life. You do not have to wait for a special or perfect moment. Be faithful and attentive in what you do today, even if it is simple or tiring, and keep your heart open to hear God right there.
exp.21:17:
Jesus says that he will not drink again of the fruit of the vine, that is, of the wine, until the kingdom of God comes. "I say to you" means "I tell you," and the cup is the drinking vessel.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper of Passover, shortly before he is arrested. He knows that his death is near. With these words he tells them that this meal is a farewell, but also a promise: there will be a kingdom of God, and they will share the table again. Some understand that this fulfillment will come in the final restoration, and others connect it with the time that began after his resurrection. Christians have interpreted this in different ways.

Even in difficult moments, we can live with hope. Jesus looked beyond his pain toward God's promise. Today we can trust that God will fulfill what he has promised.
exp.23:23:
Here the text says that some of the disciples went to the tomb and found everything just as the women had reported: the tomb was empty. But they did not see Jesus. The phrase about finding it "even so" simply means they found it the same way the women had described, and the word "but" in the verse is the one that marks the contrast with what follows.

It is Cleopas who speaks, one of two disciples walking toward Emmaus, not knowing that the man walking with them is the risen Jesus. He tells him sadly what has happened. Notice that they had facts, but not faith: the empty tomb was not enough for them. Jesus answers them by explaining the Scriptures to them.

For today: sometimes we have evidence and good news, yet we remain discouraged. Instead of holding only to what we can see, we can open the Bible and ask Jesus to help us understand it. He may be closer than we think.
exp.9:12:
Jesus laments with sorrow what will happen to Chorazin and Bethsaida. He says that if the mighty works done there had been done in Tyre and Sidon, pagan cities, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples whom he sent out two by two to proclaim the kingdom. He warns them that some cities will reject them. Chorazin and Bethsaida, in Galilee, had seen his miracles and heard his teaching, but they did not change their hearts. Their responsibility was greater because they had received more.

For today: if we have heard the Word of God many times, let us not take it lightly. Let us ask God for a humble heart that responds with repentance and obedience, not merely with admiration.
exp.8:29:
This verse tells us that, while Jesus was praying on the mountain, two men appeared and were talking with him. Luke makes clear who they were: Moses and Elijah. The word "men" simply means men, and the phrase "behold" is a way of saying "look" or "notice."

Luke recounts the transfiguration of Jesus. Peter, John, and James were with him. Moses represents the law and Elijah represents the prophets, so many understand that the whole Old Testament bears witness to Jesus. According to the next verse, they were speaking of his departure, that is, his death and his work in Jerusalem. Some think the word also recalls Israel's exodus.

For today: the whole Bible points to Jesus. When you read the Scriptures, ask God to show you Christ in them, and make prayer a place where you meet him.
exp.18:45:
Jesus quotes two texts from the Old Testament: "My house shall be called a house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7) and "a den of thieves" (Jeremiah 7:11). He says that the temple was meant to be a place of prayer, but they had turned it into a hideout for thieves.

Jesus speaks after entering Jerusalem and weeping over the city. He drives out those who were buying and selling in the temple. Many understand that the trade had become abusive and was getting in the way of worship, although we do not fully know the exact details of the practices. His reaction shows love for the presence of God and concern for those who sought to draw near to Him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our hearts and our church are places of sincere prayer. Before seeking advantage, money, or recognition, let us give God first place with humility.
exp.8:35:
It says that when the voice from heaven stopped speaking, Moses and Elijah were no longer there and only Jesus remained. Peter, James and John kept quiet and, in those days, told no one what they had seen.

Luke is describing the transfiguration. The three disciples had just seen Jesus' glory and heard the Father speak. The text does not explain why they stayed silent. Some think it was from amazement or fear, and others think Jesus had asked them to wait (Mark 9:9 says he commanded them not to tell it until after his resurrection). The next day they came down the mountain and right away found the crowd with its needs.

For today: after a special moment with God, do not stay only in the emotion. Seek to listen to Jesus, who was found alone as the center, and then live out that teaching by serving those you meet along the way.
exp.22:45:
Jesus cries out with a loud voice and speaks to God as his Father. He says that he places his spirit into the Father's hands, that is, he hands it over with trust. Then he dies.

"Commend" in the verse means to entrust something into someone's care. The phrase "gave up the ghost" simply means that he stopped breathing, that he died.

He speaks from the cross, at the end of his suffering. Before this there were three hours of darkness, and the curtain of the temple was torn. His words are part of Psalm 31:5, which a Jew could pray when entrusting his life to God. Even in dying, Jesus trusts the Father. Afterward, the centurion recognizes that Jesus was righteous, and the crowd beats their breasts, a sign of grief and repentance.

For today: we can learn to entrust to God our worries, our fears, and even our future. When we do not understand what is happening, we can pray, "Father, into your hands I commit my life," trusting that he cares for us.
exp.14:10:
Jesus begins another parable. He says that a certain man had two sons. The word "had" is in the past tense, as when a story is starting. There are only a few words, but they set the scene for a story about a family and two different ways of relating to the father.

Jesus is speaking to a mixed crowd. The tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to hear him, and the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling about it (Luke 15:1-2). That is why he tells three parables: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and now the two sons. The first two end with joy over a sinner who repents. In this one, the younger and the older son seem to reflect the two kinds of listeners, though Jesus does not say it in those words.

For today: ask yourself how you relate to God as Father. Some turn away from Him, and others stay close but with a cold heart. Today you can come to Him with confidence and simplicity.
exp.19:7:
Jesus answers the religious leaders that he will not tell them by what authority he does these things. The word "authority" here means the power or right to act. The phrasing is a calm refusal, not an expression of anger.

Jesus is in the temple teaching, and the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders ask him who gave him his authority. He asks them whether John's baptism came from heaven or from men. They fear the people and say they do not know. Because they do not answer honestly, Jesus does not give them his answer. Then he tells the parable of the vineyard, which shows his rejection of God's messengers.

For today: God reveals himself to those who seek the truth with honesty. If we remain silent or evade questions out of fear of losing our reputation, we close ourselves to the light. Let us ask for a sincere heart.
exp.19:14:
The workers threw the owner's son out of the vineyard and killed him. Then Jesus asks: "What therefore shall the lord of the vineyard do unto them?" The question asks what the owner will do to the workers.

Jesus speaks in the temple to the religious leaders and the people. He tells this parable: the vineyard represents Israel, the workers represent its leaders, and the beloved son points to Jesus himself. Many understand that it foretells his death outside Jerusalem. With the question, Jesus leads them to recognize for themselves the judgment they deserve.

For today: God has entrusted us with things that are not ours, such as time, gifts, and faith. We can ask ourselves whether we manage them with gratitude or want to keep control. Receiving Christ with humility is the best response.
exp.3:40:
This verse tells that demons came out of many people, crying out, "You are the Son of God." Jesus rebuked them, that is, he sternly corrected them with authority, and he did not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ, the promised Messiah. "Rebuking them" in the verse above is the same word the explanation discusses, so no further note is needed.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke. That day Jesus had healed Simon's mother-in-law and many sick people. The demons were saying something true, but Jesus did not want that testimony. Some think he was avoiding misunderstandings about what kind of Messiah he was; the text does not fully explain this. Afterward he withdraws to a deserted place and says that he must proclaim the good news in other cities.

For today: knowing correct facts about Jesus is not the same as following him. Let us ask him to lead us from knowing about him secondhand to trusting him and obeying him.
exp.14:27:
It says that the older son, when he learned of the feast because of his brother's return, was filled with anger and refused to go into the house. Then the father went out to look for him and begged him to come in.

The fattened calf is a young cow raised for a special celebration.

Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees and scribes, who were criticizing him for welcoming sinners. The older son represents, for many interpreters, those who think of themselves as faithful and are bothered by grace shown to others. It is striking that the father goes out to look for both sons: first the younger, now the older. The parable ends without telling us whether he went in.

For today: if we feel resentment when God is kind to someone we consider unworthy, let us remember that the Father also invites us. We can ask him for a heart that rejoices with those who come home.
exp.5:8:
Jesus asks the scribes and Pharisees a direct question: Is it permitted on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil? To save life, or to destroy it? The word "lawful" means permitted by the law. The sabbath days refer to the Jewish weekly day of rest.

Jesus speaks in a synagogue, in front of a man with a withered hand. His opponents were watching him, looking for a reason to accuse him if he healed on the sabbath. He knew their intentions and confronts them with a question that exposes their hardness of heart. Then he heals the man, and they are filled with rage.

For today: true religion does not stop at avoiding evil; it actively seeks to do good. Ask yourself whether there is someone near you whom you could help, even if it is not a convenient time or easy for you.
exp.3:9:
God says he will send his angels to watch over and protect someone. The phrase "give his angels charge over thee" in the King James Version means that he will command them about you. This promise is quoted from Psalm 91.

The speaker is Satan, during Jesus' temptation in the wilderness. He takes Jesus to the highest point of the temple and asks him to throw himself down, using Scripture to do it. He quotes the words accurately, but he uses them to push Jesus into testing God instead of trusting him. Jesus answers with another text: the Lord should not be put to the test.

For today: trust that God cares for you, but do not put him to the test with reckless decisions. Read each verse within the whole message of the Bible, and do not use it to justify what you want.
exp.22:0:
It says that the whole crowd that had gathered against Jesus rose to its feet and led him before Pilate. The word "rose" means they stood up, and the phrase "led him" is simply the word "led" in the verse above. Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea.

Luke tells what happened after the council of Jewish leaders had questioned Jesus. They had already declared him guilty, but under Roman rule they needed Pilate's authority to seek a greater sentence. That is why they brought him to him. The verses that follow show the accusations they brought, which were political in nature, so that Rome would take them seriously.

For today: when we face injustice or false accusations, we can look at how Jesus kept his calm and trusted the Father. We can also examine our own hearts so that we do not join the crowd without thinking.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that Jesus returned to Galilee full of the power of the Holy Spirit. The word "power" here means strength or force. "Fame" means that people began to speak about him, and "the region round about" refers to the whole surrounding area.

The one who narrates is Luke, the physician and writer of the Gospel. He tells what happened right after Jesus resisted the devil's temptations in the wilderness. Jesus comes out of that trial without having given in, and he begins his public ministry. Luke shows that everything Jesus does is guided by the Spirit.

For today: after a difficult trial, we can keep going, trusting that God walks with us through his Spirit. We do not depend on our own strength but on his, and so our lives can speak of him to others.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that the devil took Jesus to Jerusalem and placed him on the highest part of the temple. There he said to him: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here." In other words, he challenged him to throw himself into the void to prove who he was.

It is Satan speaking, in the third temptation that Luke records. Jesus was in the desert, after fasting, and had already rejected the first two tests. Now the tempter quotes Scripture (Psalm 91) to pressure him into putting God to the test. It is not known with certainty which exact part of the temple this was; scholars have several ideas.

For today: be wary of anyone who uses isolated verses to justify reckless decisions. Trusting God is not demanding signs from him or taking pointless risks, but obeying him and understanding the whole Bible.
exp.19:1:
The religious leaders come up to Jesus and ask him by what authority he does "these things," and who gave him that authority. "These things" refers to what Jesus was doing in the temple: teaching the people and proclaiming the good news, and probably also driving out the sellers, as was told earlier.

The ones speaking are the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders, that is, the authorities of the temple. They felt responsible for what was happening there and had not given Jesus their approval. Their question seems more like an attempt to trap him than a sincere desire to know him. Jesus answers with a question of his own about John the Baptist, and in doing so reveals what was in their hearts.

For today: we can ask ourselves whether we come before Jesus with humility, willing to listen and obey, or only wanting to argue in order to defend our own position.
exp.21:25:
Jesus tells his disciples that they should not be like the kings of the world, who dominate others. Among them, the most important should act like the one who is least, the youngest, who in that culture did the humble tasks. And the one who leads should behave like the one who serves.

Jesus speaks during the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. The disciples had just been arguing about who was the greatest. He corrects that idea calmly and holds himself up as an example: although he is the Master, he is among them as one who serves.

For today: in your home, work, or church, if you have some kind of authority, use it to help others and not to be admired. This week, look for a simple task that nobody wants to do and do it gladly, without expecting recognition.
exp.6:12:
This verse tells that Jesus saw a woman who was weeping over the death of her son. He had compassion on her, that is, a deep sorrow for her suffering, and said to her, "Weep not." Here "the Lord" is Jesus.

Jesus was arriving at the city of Nain with his disciples and a large crowd. At the gate he met a funeral. The dead man was the only son of a widow, so she was left alone and without support. No one asked him for help; Jesus drew near out of his own compassion. Shortly afterward, he restored the young man to life and gave him back to his mother.

For today: when you suffer, remember that Jesus sees you and is moved with you. You can bring him your sorrow with confidence, and also imitate him by drawing near with tenderness to those who weep.
exp.5:21:
Jesus says that those who suffer rejection for following him are blessed. "Hate" means to despise or feel strong hostility toward someone. "Separate" means to exclude or cast someone out of their group. "Reproach" means to insult or speak of someone with contempt. "Cast out your name as evil" means to make their reputation be stained. All of this happens "for the sake of the Son of Man," a title Jesus uses for himself.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, after going up to pray and choosing the twelve. He teaches them that the kingdom of God is not measured the way the world measures things. Then he asks them to rejoice, because their reward is great in heaven, and he reminds them that the prophets suffered the same things.

Today, if people criticize you or leave you out because you live faithfully for Christ, do not be discouraged. Pray, respond with humility, and remember that God sees your loyalty and does not forget it.
exp.6:22:
The explanation says that the person who does not stumble or turn away from Jesús because of him is happy, or blessed. "Blessed" means very happy, favored by God. "Offended" here does not mean being upset by gossip, but stumbling in faith, doubting or rejecting Jesus because he does not respond the way one expected.

Jesus is the speaker. John the Baptist, who was in prison, sent messengers to ask him whether he was the one who was to come. Jesus answers them with his works: blind people see, sick people are healed, good news is preached to the poor. In this way he invites John to trust, even though his situation was difficult. Some believe John had doubts; others think he wanted to strengthen his disciples. It is not certain.

For today: when God does not act the way you expected, do not turn away. Remember what you have already seen of Jesus in his Word and in your life, and keep trusting him.
exp.19:36:
Jesus says that the resurrection of the dead already appears in the writings of Moses. When Moses speaks of the bush (the burning bush, in Exodus 3), he calls the Lord "the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." The words "even" and "shewed" are old forms of English; here "even" means "also," and the phrase "that the dead are raised" means that they will be raised.

Jesus answers the Sadducees, a religious group that denied the resurrection, who had asked him a difficult question about a woman married to seven brothers. They accepted above all the books of Moses, so Jesus answers them from that same ground. His argument is that God remains the God of those men, even though they had already died.

For today: death does not have the last word for those who belong to God. If today you feel grief for someone who has passed away, or fear about your own end, rest in the fact that God is faithful and keeps his own. Live today with that hope.
exp.18:12:
This verse says that the nobleman called ten of his servants and gave each one a mina, which was a sum of money. He told them to put the money to work, that is, to trade or do business with it, while he was away. The word "occupy" in this verse means to use something actively, to put it to work.

Jesus is speaking near Jerusalem. Some people thought that the kingdom of God would appear very soon, so Jesus tells this parable. Many understand that the nobleman represents Jesus, who would leave and return, and that the servants are his followers. Others see it with different nuances.

For today: God has entrusted us with gifts, time, and opportunities. Instead of hoarding them out of fear or neglect, we can use them faithfully to serve others and honor him while we wait.
exp.4:34:
Jesus says that a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away, that is, separated from his disciples. Then they will fast. "But" means "but," and "will be taken away from them" means that they will take him away.

Jesus is speaking with Pharisees and teachers of the law who ask him why his disciples eat and drink while others fast. He compares himself to the bridegroom at a wedding, and his presence is a reason for celebration. Many understand that he is announcing his death and departure. Then he tells parables about the new and the old.

For today: let us not live our faith as mere custom. There are moments of joy because of Christ's presence and moments of fasting and prayer, waiting for his return. Ask him that your devotion be born of love and not of appearance.
exp.22:1:
Here the Jewish leaders bring Jesus before Pilate and begin to accuse him. They say that he is perverting the nation, that is, that he is leading the people astray. They also say that he forbids giving tribute to Caesar, meaning that he prohibits paying taxes to the Roman emperor. And they say that he proclaims himself Christ, a King, the Messiah.

The ones speaking are the chief priests and the crowd that brought him to Pilate. Only the Roman governor could sentence someone to death, so they gave their accusations a political tone. The second accusation was false, since Jesus had said to give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar (Luke 20:25). Pilate does not focus on the accusations, but on whether Jesus is a king.

For today: when you are accused unjustly, remember that Jesus went through the same thing. Respond with truth and calm, and trust that God sees everything.
exp.23:35:
It says that while the disciples were still talking about the resurrection, Jesus suddenly appeared in the middle of them and greeted them with "Peace be unto you," which today we would say as "Peace be with you." It was a common greeting among the Jews, but here it carries a special weight. The word "while" is what is meant by this phrase.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus. The disciples were gathered together in Jerusalem, and some had just returned from Emmaus, telling how they had recognized him when he broke the bread. Others said that he had appeared to Simon Peter. Even so, when Jesus arrives, they are frightened, as the following verse shows. He greets them with peace to calm their fear and confusion.

For today: Jesus comes to us even when we doubt or are afraid. We can bring our worries to him in prayer and ask for his peace, knowing that he draws near with tenderness and not with reproach.
exp.5:6:
The explanation says that the scribes and Pharisees watched Jesus very closely. To watch in this way means to observe in secret, waiting for the right moment. They wanted to see whether Jesus would heal on the sabbath, not to rejoice in a healing, but to find a reason to bring a charge against him.

Luke tells this in a synagogue, on a sabbath. A man had a withered right hand, and Jesus had just said that he is Lord of the sabbath. The scribes were experts in the Law, and the Pharisees took great care in keeping it. According to the text, Jesus knew their thoughts and placed before them a question: whether the sabbath was for doing good or for doing harm.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our religion makes us more compassionate or more critical. Before judging someone, let us examine whether we are seeking to do good or only looking for faults.
exp.0:34:
Here the angel Gabriel answers Mary's question. He says that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and that the power of God, called "the Highest," will cover her like a shadow. Therefore the child will be holy and will be called the Son of God. "Power" is the word for strength, and "overshadow" suggests a protective presence of God.

Mary had just asked how it could be possible for her to have a child if she had not been with any man. The angel does not give a scientific explanation, but tells her that God himself will act. Then he gives her, as a sign, the pregnancy of her relative Elizabeth, who was advanced in years and had been called barren.

Today we can learn from Mary to bring honest questions to God, and also to trust when we do not understand everything. What seems impossible in your life is not beyond the reach of God.
exp.3:2:
Here the devil approaches Jesus after forty days without eating and makes him a proposal: "If you are the Son of God," command this stone to become bread. The word "command" in the verse above is the one used for giving an order.

The devil speaks. Jesus had just been baptized, and the Father had said he was his beloved Son. The Spirit led him into the wilderness, and there he grew hungry. The devil takes advantage of his real need to plant doubt and push him to act on his own, without depending on the Father. Jesus answers with Scripture.

For today: when need or weariness press in, we may feel pressure to solve things our own way. Instead, we can return to God's Word and trust that he sustains us, even in hard times.
exp.8:46:
This verse says that Jesus knew what was going through the minds of his disciples. No one had told him anything, but he could see their thoughts. Then he took a child and set him beside himself.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. Jesus had just announced his suffering, but the disciples did not understand it and were afraid to ask him about it. Instead, they were arguing about who was the greatest. Jesus answers with a gesture: a child, who in that culture had no standing or power, is placed in a place of honor.

For today: examine what you secretly think when you want to stand out or be recognized. Jesus sees the heart. Ask him to teach you to value and serve those who seem small or unimportant, because that is where he invites us to find him.
exp.20:22:
He says it will be very hard for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing when those days come. "Pregnant" means expecting a child, and "those who nurse" are mothers with infants at the breast.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He warns them of what would come upon the city. Many understand this to refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70 AD, though some also see a future fulfillment.

For today: Jesus notices those who suffer most in difficult times. We can imitate him by caring for the vulnerable around us, such as mothers, children, and the elderly, with concrete help and prayer.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that Simon and all who were with him were filled with amazement and awe at the huge number of fish they had caught. The word "catch" here means what was taken, that is, the fishing haul. The nets were so full that the boats were nearly sinking under the weight.

Luke tells what happened after Jesus taught from Simon's boat and asked him to put the nets out again. Simon, an experienced fisherman, had worked all night and caught nothing, but he obeyed. That fear was not fear of danger, but the amazement of someone who realizes he is standing before something holy and powerful. That is why Peter recognizes himself as a sinner.

For today: when we see the greatness of Jesus, we do not need to pretend we are perfect. We can come near with humility and sincerity, and obey him even when his word seems to make no sense. He responds with grace, as he later tells Simon: "Fear not."
exp.17:2:
That same city had a widow who kept coming before the judge again and again. She would ask him: "Avenge me of mine adversary." In other words, she wanted him to defend her against the person who was harming her or wronging her.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Luke explains that he tells this parable to teach that people ought always to pray and not lose heart, that is, not give up.

The widow represents someone without power or influence, who has only her persistence to rely on. Scholars often see a contrast here: if an unjust judge gives in, how much more will God, who is good, respond.

For today: when you are tired of waiting for an answer, keep praying with confidence. Bring your need before God with perseverance, and do not let discouragement silence you.
exp.4:13:
Jesus orders the healed man not to tell anyone. Instead, he tells him to go and show himself to the priest, and to present the offering for his cleansing, just as Moses commanded, "as a testimony to them." "Cleansing" means that he was no longer a leper. "Commanded" means "ordered."

Jesus speaks with a man who has just been healed of leprosy. According to the law of Moses (Leviticus 14), only a priest could declare a leper clean and allow him to return to normal life. That is why Jesus sends him there. The reasons for asking for silence are not explained; some think he wanted to avoid crowds who sought only miracles. The following verse shows this.

For today: when God works in your life, respond with obedience and order, not only with emotion. Do what is right with humility, and let your life be a testimony.
exp.17:40:
Jesus asks the blind man: "What do you want me to do for you?" He answers in a few words: "Lord, let me see." The word "Lord" shows respect and trust. His request is clear and direct: he wants to regain his sight.

First it is Jesus who speaks, and then the blind man, who had been sitting by the road begging. The people told him to be quiet, but he cried out all the more, asking for mercy. Jesus stopped, had him brought to him, and asked him, even though the need was obvious. With that question he treats him as a person, not as an obstacle, and gives him room to express his faith.

Today we too can approach God with sincerity and without pretense. He knows our needs, but he invites us to speak to him with confidence. Tell him today in prayer, in simple words, and do not let yourself be silenced by those who discourage you.
exp.19:32:
The Sadducees put a hard case to Jesus: a woman married seven brothers, one after another, and all of them died. Then they ask whose wife she will be in the resurrection.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They use this story, based on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25), not to learn anything, but to make the idea of rising from the dead look ridiculous. Jesus answers that the life to come is not a simple copy of the present one.

For today: when we have difficult questions about God or eternity, we should not use them to mock, but to seek the truth. We can trust that what God prepares is better and greater than what we imagine today.
exp.22:23:
Pilate decided, or passed sentence, so that what the crowd was asking for would be done. "Judged" here means that he resolved or ruled. In other words, he agreed that Jesus should be crucified.

Luke tells this as the narrator. Pilate, the Roman governor, had said three times that he found no guilt in Jesus. But the voices of the people and the chief priests kept growing and pressing on him. Pilate gave in, even though he knew Jesus was innocent. Afterward he released Barabbas, who was indeed in prison for insurrection and murder.

For today: we often know what is right, but the pressure of others pushes us to stay silent or give in. Let us ask God for courage to act with justice, even when it costs us, and not to be carried along by the crowd.
exp.11:3:
Jesus speaks to his disciples and calls them "my friends." He asks them not to be afraid of those who can kill the body, because their power ends there. In other words, physical death is the most that they can do.

Jesus is teaching his disciples while a great crowd gathers. He has just warned them against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and said that everything hidden will come to light. He encourages them to be sincere and brave when speaking about him. Then he reminds them that God cares even for the sparrows, and so cares much more for them.

Today, fear of rejection, mockery, or threats can silence us. This week, when you feel pressure to hide your faith or to act against your conscience, remember that God sees you and cares for you, and ask him for the courage to be faithful.
exp.19:30:
He says that the third brother also married the widow, and that the same thing happened with all seven: they all died and left no children. The explanation's old word for children or offspring is not needed here, and the phrase for marrying a woman simply means to marry.

The speakers are the Sadducees, a Jewish religious group that denied the resurrection. They put this case to Jesus, based on the law of Moses about a brother marrying the widow so as to raise offspring for the one who had died. Their intention was to make the resurrection seem absurd. Jesus answers them afterward that in the life to come things do not work as they do in this one, and that God is the God of the living.

For today: when someone uses tricky questions to cast doubt on God, do not be troubled. Bring your doubts to Scripture with humility, knowing that God's ways are greater than our reasoning.
exp.14:5:
This verse tells how the shepherd, on returning home, calls together his friends and neighbors to celebrate with him. The reason for the celebration is that he has found the sheep that was lost.

Jesus tells this parable because the Pharisees and the scribes complained that he welcomed sinners and ate with them (Luke 15:1-2). He answers by showing how God feels when someone who was lost returns: not with indifference, but with great joy. He then explains this by speaking of the joy in heaven.

For today: If God rejoices so much when someone returns to him, we too can celebrate, and not judge, when a person draws near to God. Today you can welcome with warmth someone who is coming back to faith.
exp.5:26:
Jesus speaks to those who truly listen and pay attention to him: love your enemies and do good to those who hate you. The word "hate" here points to a strong rejection of someone, not just a passing dislike.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to a crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Shortly before, he had given blessings and warnings. Now the tone shifts: after speaking of poverty, hunger, and rejection, he teaches how to respond when someone treats us badly. His command is to love with actions, not just with feelings.

For today: think of someone who has treated you badly and do something concrete and good for that person this week, such as praying for them, helping them, or speaking well of them, without expecting anything in return.
exp.6:32:
Jesus says that John the Baptist came living with simplicity and discipline: he neither ate bread nor drank wine, that is, he lived a stern life, set apart from ordinary pleasures. Even so, the people rejected him, saying, "He hath a devil," meaning that he was possessed or out of his mind.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to the religious leaders who doubted him. He uses the image of children playing in the marketplace who complain that no one follows their game, neither the game of celebration nor the game of mourning. In this way, that generation rejected John for being too severe and Jesus for being too close.

Today, we sometimes look for excuses not to obey God, and we criticize the way he speaks to us. Let us ask for a humble heart that listens to his truth, regardless of the messenger or the style.
exp.8:8:
Herod says that he himself ordered John the Baptist to be beheaded. Then he wonders who this Jesus is, about whom he hears such astonishing things. The word "beheaded" means that he ordered him to be executed by decapitation, and "desired to see him" means that he was looking for a way to see him.

Herod Antipas, the tetrarch, was a local ruler under Roman rule. The apostles had just gone out to preach and heal, and Jesus' fame was growing. People had different opinions, and Herod was confused. The texts do not fully clarify whether his desire to see Jesus came from simple curiosity, fear, or guilt. Luke only says that he was seeking to see him.

We can feel curious about Jesus without truly drawing near to Him. Today I encourage you to move beyond simple curiosity and listen to Him sincerely in His Word, letting Him speak to you and change you.
exp.11:17:
Here the rich man makes a decision: he will pull down his old barns and build bigger ones. The barns are the storehouses where the grain was kept. He wants to gather there all his harvest and all his riches.

Jesus tells this parable to a crowd, after someone asked him to step into a dispute over an inheritance. Before that, he warned: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness." Notice that the man speaks only to himself: he says "my fruits" and "my goods," and he does not think of God or of others. Then God calls him a fool, because his life would end that very night.

For today: planning and saving is not wrong, but it is good to ask ourselves whether our riches are drawing us away from God and from our neighbor. Today you could decide to share something with someone who needs it.
exp.19:33:
Jesus answers a hard question. He says that "the children of this world" marry and are given in marriage. Here "world" means the present age, that is, the life we live now. "Being given in marriage" was the custom of fathers handing over their daughters to be married.

Jesus is speaking with the Sadducees, a group that did not believe in the resurrection. They brought him the case of a woman who married seven brothers, one after another, to mock the idea of life after death. Jesus replies that the life of the resurrection is different from life now. The verses that follow explain that in that age there is no more death, and so marriage no longer has the same role.

For today: value your relationships and your marriage, but do not place your final hope in them. Our greatest hope is in God and in the life he promises.
exp.17:8:
This verse introduces a new parable from Jesus. It says he told it to certain people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, meaning people who were sure of their own goodness, and who despised others, meaning they looked down on them with contempt.

The one speaking is Jesus, and he has just finished teaching about praying persistently and trusting that God brings about justice. Now he shifts the focus: it is not enough to pray often; the attitude with which we come before God also matters. The parable that follows contrasts a proud Pharisee with a humble tax collector.

For today: before we pray, we can ask ourselves whether we are trusting in our own merits or in God's mercy. And if I compare myself with others in order to feel better about myself, it is a sign that I need to return to humility.
exp.0:29:
What it says: The angel calms Mary, who is frightened. He tells her not to be afraid, because God looks on her with approval and has shown her his favor. "Found favor" means she received a favor she did not earn. The phrase "before God" (or "in the presence of God") is about being close to God and in his sight.

Context: The speaker is the angel Gabriel, sent by God. Mary had been troubled by the unusual greeting she received. Before giving her the news that she would have a son, the angel first reassures her. Her favor does not come from her own merits, but from God's kindness in choosing her.

For today: When you feel fear in the face of the unknown, remember that God does not draw near to frighten you, but to give you his grace. You can tell him honestly what you feel and trust that his favor is with you.
exp.20:26:
Jesus says that, after strange signs in the sky and on the earth, everyone will see the Son of Man, that is, Himself, coming in a cloud. The words "with power" tell of His authority and strength, and "great glory" speaks of His splendor and greatness. He does not come in humility, as He did the first time, but as King.

Jesus speaks to His disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before His crucifixion. He had already spoken to them about the destruction of the temple and of hard times. Here He describes His return, using images from the prophet Daniel (7:13). Some believers see in this passage also the fall of Jerusalem; many see mainly His second coming.

For today: when the world feels confused or fearful, we can live with hope, trusting that Christ is coming back and has the final word. Today, bring your fears to Him in prayer.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that Joseph went to Bethlehem to be registered in the census together with Mary. She was his wife-to-be, that is, formally pledged to him in marriage, and she was pregnant. The word "espoused," which the source uses for her status, means she was formally betrothed to him, and the verse's phrase "great with child" is the old way of saying she was expecting a baby. Being "registered" means being entered on an official list of residents.

Luke, the author, tells the events of Jesus' birth in an orderly way. He explains that everyone had to register in their town of origin, and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem because he was a descendant of David. In this way Luke shows that Jesus is born in the place and the family that the Scriptures had announced. Some historical details of the census are debated among scholars.

For today: God carries out his plans even amid human orders, uncomfortable journeys, and difficult circumstances. You can trust that he is working also in your situations that seem beyond your control, and obey him step by step, as Joseph and Mary did.
exp.17:12:
The explanation says that the tax collector stood far off and would not so much as lift his eyes to heaven. He beat his breast, a gesture of grief and sorrow, and prayed, "God be merciful to me a sinner." The explanation says that this phrase means "have mercy on me" or "forgive me." In the original, the idea is connected with forgiveness and atonement.

Jesus tells this parable to people who trusted in their own righteousness and looked down on others (Luke 18:9). The Pharisee compared himself with others and boasted of his works. The tax collector, by contrast, had nothing to offer but his need. Jesus says that this man went home justified, that is, accepted by God.

For today: when you pray, do not compare yourself with anyone or present your merits. Come before God with sincerity and ask for his mercy. He welcomes the humble heart.
exp.16:0:
Jesus tells his disciples that it is unavoidable that stumbling blocks will come. The word translated as "stumbling blocks" here is an old one that refers to things that cause others to fall into sin or pull them away from the faith. But Jesus adds a serious warning: woe to the one through whom they come. In other words, the one who causes such a stumbling block bears a heavy responsibility.

Jesus is speaking as he teaches his disciples on the way to Jerusalem. In the verses that follow, he speaks of the little ones, who may be children or believers who are simple and weak in faith, and then he moves on to the subject of rebuking and forgiving a brother. Thus, caring for others and forgiving go together in his teaching.

For today: watch your words and your example, especially toward those who are new in the faith or younger than you. Before you act, ask yourself whether this will help others draw near to God or cause them to stumble.
exp.7:10:
Jesus begins to explain the parable of the sower. He says that the seed, that is, the grain the sower scatters, represents the word of God. The reader does not need to know any older form of the word; the verse itself says plainly that the seed is the word of God, and this statement gives us the key to understanding the whole story.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, who asked him what the parable meant. He explains that they have been given to understand the mysteries of the kingdom, that is, the truths that God is gradually revealing. Others hear in parables and do not always understand. Afterward Jesus describes four kinds of ground, which show how different people receive the message.

For today: when you listen to or read the Bible, ask yourself how your heart is. Ask God to prepare it, so that his word may take root and bear fruit in your daily life.
exp.3:39:
This verse tells that, when the sun was setting, the people brought to Jesus all their sick, with all kinds of diseases. Jesús laid his hands on each one, one by one, and healed them. The phrase "when the sun was setting" means at sundown; "brought" is simply what they did in carrying their sick to him.

Luke, the narrator, describes what happened in Capernaum, on the same Sabbath day when Jesus healed Simon's mother-in-law. It is likely that they waited until evening because the Sabbath ended at sunset, though the text does not say this directly. In this way we see the compassion of Jesus and his authority over sickness.

For today: Jesus never tires of receiving us. Bring to him in prayer those who are suffering, and yourself too, trusting in his care.
exp.2:23:
This verse is part of a list of Jesus' ancestors. The word "which was" here means "was the son of," that is, a descendant of. Five people are named: Matthat, Levi, Melchi, Janna and Joseph. This Joseph is not Mary's husband, but an ancestor with the same name.

Luke, the author, gives this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism, when the Father calls him "my beloved Son." Luke wants to show that Jesus truly belongs to human history. His list goes back all the way to Adam. Scholars explain in several ways why it differs from Matthew's; some think it follows Mary's line, others Joseph's.

For today: God works in the history of ordinary people, even those almost no one remembers. Your life and your family also matter to God, and He can use them.
exp.17:33:
This verse says that the twelve disciples understood none of what Jesus had just announced. The word "hid" means concealed or kept out of sight: the meaning of his words was hidden from them. Although they heard every word, they did not grasp what it meant.

Jesus took the twelve aside and told them about his suffering, his death, and his resurrection on the third day. Luke, the writer, explains here why they did not understand. Many people think they were expecting a victorious Messiah and not one who would suffer, though the text only says that the meaning was hidden from them. Right after this, a blind man appears who does cry out to Jesus.

For today: do not be discouraged if you do not understand everything in the Bible or in your life. The disciples took time to comprehend, and God gave them light in his own time. Stay close to Jesus, ask with humility, and ask him to open your eyes.
exp.4:38:
He says that the one who is already used to drinking aged wine (kept for years) usually does not want new wine, because he thinks: "The old is better." We are speaking of taste and habit, not of real quality.

Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and teachers of the law who asked him why his disciples did not fast as they did. He answers with examples: the patch on a garment and wineskins with new wine. This verse closes those images. Many interpret that Jesus points out how hard it is to accept something new when one clings to what is familiar, though some understand it in another way.

For today: check whether you cling to a religious custom only because it is comfortable. Ask God for an open heart to receive what Christ wants to do in you.
exp.10:5:
It tells of a man who goes to ask his neighbor for bread in the middle of the night. It explains his reason: a friend of his has arrived after a journey, and he has nothing to set before him. To serve a guest a meal at the table was, in that culture, a very important duty.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples, right after teaching them the Lord's Prayer. He tells this parable to show them how to pray. The man asks with persistence, and the story sets that neighbor in contrast with God: if even an annoying friend ends up helping, how much more will the good Father listen to his children. Some understand the persistence as insistence, others as shameless boldness.

For today: when you see a need, your own or someone else's, bring it to God with confidence and without growing weary. He is not bothered by your request; he invites you to ask as a child asks his Father.
exp.21:40:
This verse tells us that Jesus withdrew from his disciples about as far as a stone can be thrown. There he knelt down and began to pray. "About a stone's cast" is an old way of describing a short distance, although the exact measure is not known. "Kneeled down" means that he knelt.

It is the night before the crucifixion. Jesus is on the Mount of Olives, as he often did, and Luke narrates it. He had just asked his disciples to pray so that they would not fall into temptation. Then he moves a little away to pray alone, but without going far from them. In the verses that follow he prays to the Father with great anguish.

When you are going through a difficult time, look for a quiet place to speak with God honestly. You can tell him what you feel and, like Jesus, entrust your situation to him with confidence.
exp.10:23:
Jesus says that when an unclean spirit goes out of a person, it wanders through dry places, that is, deserts and lifeless ground, looking for rest. When it finds none, it decides to return to the house it came out of.

Jesus speaks after casting out a demon. Some accused him of doing it by the power of Satan, and he answers that his power is greater. Then he warns that there is no neutral ground: one is either with him or against him. Some scholars see here a warning to those who are cleansed on the outside but do not give themselves over to God.

For today: it is not enough simply to leave behind a bad habit or a harmful influence. That empty space must be filled with a life drawing near to Jesus, through prayer, his Word, and a community of faith.
exp.0:54:
This verse says that God fulfilled what he promised to the ancestors of Israel, to Abraham and to his descendants. The word "seed" means descendants, that is, his children and their families over time. "For ever" shows that God's promise does not come to an end. The verse's wording "spake to" can be understood as "said to" or "promised to."

The one speaking is Mary, in the canticle known as the Magnificat. She praises God after visiting Elisabeth. She closes her song by remembering that God remembered his mercy toward Israel, as he had said from the time of Abraham. For her, what God was doing in her life was part of a much larger story.

For today: when waiting becomes long, remember that God is faithful to his word. Read his promises in the Bible, write them down, and repeat them in prayer, trusting that he keeps them in his own time.
exp.22:34:
The verse says that the people stood watching the crucifixion, while the leaders mocked Jesus. They said: "He saved others; let him save himself, if he is truly the Christ, the chosen of God." The word "rulers" here means the authorities or leaders of the people. "Christ" means the Anointed One, the king promised by God.

The speakers are the Jewish leaders, who did not accept Jesus. They mock him as he suffers, and without realizing it they say a truth: Jesus had saved others. But he did not come down from the cross, because his mission was to give his life. Shortly before, he had prayed, "Father, forgive them," and yet he stayed there out of love.

For today: when someone mocks your faith, or when it seems to you that God is silent, remember that Jesus endured mockery without responding with hatred. Ask God for strength to respond with patience and forgiveness.
exp.13:32:
Jesus says that whoever wants to be his disciple must give up everything they have. To give up means to let go, to stop clinging to something. He is not speaking only of money, but of anything that takes first place in the heart.

Jesus was speaking to large crowds that followed him. Before this, he had told two examples: the man who counts the cost before building a tower, and the king who weighs whether he can win a war. With these, he wanted people to think carefully about what it means to follow him, and not to do so out of passing enthusiasm.

For today: honestly ask yourself which thing is hardest for you to surrender to God, whether it is your time, your money, your plans, or your pride. Bring it to him in prayer and choose to trust him, putting him first in your decisions this week.
exp.0:18:
What it says: The angel answers Zechariah and identifies himself by name: Gabriel. He says that he stands in God's presence, ready to serve him. He also explains that God sent him to speak to Zechariah and to bring him good news.

Context: Zechariah was an elderly priest who served in the temple. The angel told him that he would have a son, John, who would prepare the people for the Lord. Zechariah doubted and asked for a sign, because he and his wife were already advanced in years. Gabriel answers him by reminding him who sent him: this is not a human idea, but a message from God.

For today: When a promise from God seems impossible, remember who stands behind it. We can speak to him honestly about our doubts, but let us trust that his word will be fulfilled in its time.
exp.12:7:
Here the vinedresser, that is, the one in charge of looking after the vineyard, answers the owner. He asks that the fig tree not be cut down yet and that it be given one more year. He says he will loosen and dig the soil around the tree, and will put manure on it, which helps it grow.

Jesus tells this parable after calling the people to repentance. The owner represents God, who looks for fruit, and the vinedresser pleads with patience. Many understand that the fig tree speaks of Israel or of anyone who receives God's care. The parable does not say who the vinedresser is, so it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God is patient, but He expects a life that bears fruit. Do not leave the change for later. Use this time of grace to obey, to ask forgiveness, and to care for your relationship with God.
exp.16:18:
Jesus says to the man who came back: "Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole." The old wording is simple to follow: the word "made thee whole" can be understood as "healed," and the phrase "thy faith" points to the trust he had placed in Jesus.

Jesus speaks this after healing ten lepers. Only one, a Samaritan regarded as a foreigner, returned to thank him and give glory to God. The other nine did not come back. Jesus recognizes this man's faith. Some believe that his "salvation" goes beyond the body, because his gratitude led him into a relationship with Jesus; the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: do not take God's blessings for granted. Take a moment to return to Him, give thanks aloud, and acknowledge His work in your life. Sincere gratitude draws the heart closer to God.
exp.7:15:
It says that no one lights a lamp to cover it with a vessel or hide it under the bed. On the contrary, they put it on a lampstand, a tall support for lamps, so that those who come in can see the light. Here "torch" is understood as lamp, and "bed" was the place where one lay down to rest.

Jesus speaks to the crowds and to his disciples after the parable of the sower. He has just explained how the word of God is received: some lose it, and others bear fruit. With this image he teaches that the truth God gives is not meant to be kept hidden. Interpreters apply it in different ways: to Jesus' teaching, to the lives of his followers, or to both.

For today: do not keep your faith only for yourself. This week, let what you have learned from God show in the way you treat others, with honesty, patience, and kindness.
exp.8:3:
Jesus tells his disciples that, in whatever house they are welcomed, they should stay there and continue on their way from that same house. The old-fashioned phrasing carries the same sense as "any house," and the words for "enter" and "stay" mean simply to go in and to remain. They were not to keep moving from house to house looking for something better.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles when he sends them out to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. He asks them to go with very little, so that they would depend on God and on the hospitality of the people. Staying in one house avoided comforts and distractions and kept the focus on the mission. Interpreters often read it this way, though the text itself gives no further detail.
