Today, we can learn to be thankful and simple with what God gives us. Instead of complaining or always looking for something more comfortable, let us focus on serving and sharing the love of Christ wherever we are.
exp.23:45:
Jesus explains to his disciples that the Scriptures had already announced that the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, had to suffer and die, and that he would rise on the third day. The word "suffer" in the verse means to go through hardship and pain, and "rise" means to return to life. The phrase "had to" does not speak of an accident, but of God's plan.

The risen Jesus is with his disciples on the same day of the resurrection. They were confused and afraid. He opens their understanding so that they see that the cross was not a failure, but part of what God had announced in the law, the prophets, and the psalms. Afterward he sends them out to preach.

When pain or waiting leaves you confused, remember that God can work even in what you do not understand. Ask him to open your understanding as you read his Word, and trust that Christ is the key to understanding it.
exp.11:8:
It says that whoever denies Jesus before people, Jesus will deny before the angels of God. This is the opposite of the verse before it, where whoever openly acknowledges him is acknowledged by him. The word "deny" here means refusing or rejecting, and "will be denied" means that Jesus will not own that person as his own.

Jesus speaks to his disciples while a large crowd is gathering. He warns them that there will be pressure and persecution for following him. That is why, just before, he tells them not to be afraid, because God cares even for the hairs on their heads. Then he promises that the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say when they are brought before the authorities. Some see here a total and final refusal; others remember that Peter denied Jesus and was restored.

Today, we can ask God for courage to be honest about our faith at work or at school, with humility and without fear, trusting that he sustains us.
exp.6:5:
Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him with a message: "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should come under my roof."

The speaker is a Roman centurion, a commander of soldiers, whose servant was very ill. Jewish elders had asked Jesus to help him. Even so, the centurion feels unworthy. He was a foreigner, and at that time a Jew would usually avoid entering the house of a Gentile. His humility and his trust in Jesus are remarkable.

For today: come near to God with humility, without claiming merit of your own, but with full confidence that Jesus has the power and goodness to help you. You can pray this way: "Lord, I am not worthy, but I trust in you."
exp.9:13:
Jesus says that on the day of judgment, the cities of Tyre and Sidon will be treated with more mercy than Chorazin and Bethsaida. Here the word translated as "more tolerable" means a gentler treatment, less punishment. The "you" refers to those two cities in Galilee.

Jesus is speaking after sending seventy disciples to announce the kingdom of God. Chorazin and Bethsaida had seen his miracles, but they did not change their lives. Tyre and Sidon were pagan cities, known for their wickedness. Jesus shows that whoever receives more light has greater responsibility. How this applies in detail to the final judgment is something that is debated, but the central message is clear.

For today: if we have heard the Word of God many times, let us not take it as something ordinary. Let us ask God for a humble heart that responds with repentance and obedience, and not merely with curiosity.
exp.9:4:
Jesus says that when they enter any house, the first thing they should say is: "Peace be to this house." The old wording, which your reader doesn't see here, is only a matter of phrasing, so nothing needs to be explained about it. It was a common greeting, but here it is also a sincere blessing.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples he sends out two by two ahead of him. He warns them that they will go like lambs among wolves, that is, with real risks. For that reason they should not carry things with them or get distracted along the way. Their mission is urgent, and they begin by offering peace, not argument. Afterward, the peace rests on whoever receives it, or it returns to them.

For today: before you talk about your ideas or your reasons, enter each place, whether your home, your workplace, or your church, with a blessing. You can pray silently and greet people kindly, leaving it to God to open hearts.
exp.0:53:
He has helped his servant Israel, as he said he would, in remembering to be merciful, which means his faithful and compassionate love. He did this because he remembered his mercy. "Remembering" does not mean that God had forgotten something, but that he acts in keeping with what he promised.

The speaker is Mary, in the song usually called the Magnificat. She has just visited her relative Elizabeth, and she praises God because he has chosen her to be the mother of the Messiah. She sees in her own story a sign of how God keeps his promises to Israel, and she mentions them in the verses that follow, when she speaks of Abraham.

For today: when you feel forgotten or small, remember that God is faithful and merciful. You can trust that he keeps what he promises, even when it takes time. Write down one of his promises and thank him for it today.
exp.18:46:
He taught every day in the temple in Jerusalem. At the same time, the religious leaders, along with the teachers of the law and the leading men of the people, were looking for a way to kill him. The chief priests were the priests with the highest authority, and the scribes were the experts in the Law of Moses.

Luke, the narrator, tells this right after Jesus drove out the sellers from the temple and said that God's house should be a house of prayer. That action exposed those who were profiting from the temple, and so they felt threatened. However, they could not act, because the people were paying close attention to every word Jesus said.

For today: Jesus kept teaching the truth even under opposition. We can ask him for courage to keep doing what is right and to be steady in the Word, even when others are uncomfortable with it.
exp.11:47:
This verse says that the one who did not know what his master wanted, but still did wrong things, will receive a light punishment. Here, "beaten" means punished, and "required" means to be held accountable or made to give an account. The central point is that God asks more of the one who has been given more.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples with a parable about servants who wait for their master's return. He teaches them to live faithfully and watchfully, not knowing when he will come. The one who knows the master's will and does not carry it out has greater responsibility. How this applies in detail has been interpreted in several ways, but the principle of responsibility is clear.

For today: think about what God has given you, whether knowledge of his Word, talents, time, or resources. Ask yourself how you can use them with humility to serve others, trusting in his grace and not in fear.
exp.7:38:
Jesus tells the healed man: "Return to your house and tell how much God has done for you." The old wording is "return" (in the sense of go back), "tell" (in the sense of recount) and "went his way" (in the sense of went on his way). The man obeyed and announced throughout the whole city what Jesus had done for him.

Jesus speaks with the man who had been freed from the demons, in the region of the Gadarenes. The people, frightened, asked Jesus to leave. The man wanted to go with him, but Jesus gave him another mission: to be a witness among his own people. It is interesting that Jesus speaks of what God has done, and the man proclaims what Jesus has done, which suggests that both are united in this work.

For today: you do not need a great stage to serve God. Begin in your home, with your family and your neighbors, simply telling what God has done in your life.
exp.17:3:
He would not do so for a while, but afterward he said to himself, "Though I do not fear God, nor care about people,

The explanation says that the judge at first did not want to help the widow. After some time he thought to himself, "Though I do not fear God nor care what people think..." The phrase about not caring about anyone's opinion or dignity means that he was indifferent to what others thought of him or how they were treated. The words "to himself" mean that he thought it inwardly.

Jesus is telling this parable to his disciples to teach them that they should always pray and not lose heart. The judge is deliberately unjust, to create a contrast: if even such a judge ends up attending to a widow who keeps coming back, how much more will God, who is good, hear his children.

For today: when you feel that your prayer is getting no answer, do not give up. Keep praying with confidence, remembering that God is not like that judge; he hears you with love, even though his timing is not always ours.
exp.14:28:
Here the older son answers his father with anger. He says that he has worked for many years, that he never disobeyed a command, and yet he never received so much as a young goat (a young goat from the flock) to celebrate with his friends. "Broken" means violated or disobeyed, and "rejoice" means to enjoy or celebrate.

Jesus tells this parable of the father and his two sons. The younger one left, squandered the inheritance, and came back repentant; the father received him with a feast. The older son, who stayed at home, becomes angry. He speaks like a hired worker who is owed wages, not like a son. Jesus tells it to Pharisees and scribes who were criticizing his treatment of sinners.

We can serve God and still have a cold heart. If we compare ourselves with others or feel we deserve more, we lose the joy of grace. Let us ask God for a heart that rejoices when someone returns to Him.
exp.6:16:
The report of what Jesus had done spread throughout all Judea and the surrounding regions. The word "rumour" here means what people talk about and pass along concerning someone, that is, his reputation. It refers to the fact that Jesus had brought the widow's son at Nain back to life.

Luke, the author of the Gospel, is the one who tells the story. After this miracle, the people were filled with awe and praised God, saying that a great prophet had risen among them. The news even reached the disciples of John the Baptist, who, from prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come. Luke thus shows that many were talking about Jesus, though not everyone fully understood who he was.

Today we can ask ourselves what we say about Jesus. It is good that others speak well of him, but it is worthwhile to know him personally, to read the Gospels, and to trust in him. In this way, what we tell others will come from firsthand knowledge.
exp.6:1:
The explanation says that a centurion, a Roman officer who commanded about a hundred soldiers, had a servant who was sick, so gravely ill that he was about to die. This servant was very dear to him: the phrase means that he valued him highly.

The one who tells this is Luke, the writer of the Gospel. It comes right after the Sermon on the Plain, when Jesus enters Capernaum. Luke presents a man who is not Jewish, who has authority and power, yet who shows humility and concern for someone of lower standing. The verses that follow show that he asks Jesus for help through the Jewish elders.

For today: it reminds us that no person is unimportant to God. If the centurion cared so tenderly for his servant, we too can look with affection on those who work or serve beside us, and bring their needs to Jesus in prayer.
exp.15:0:
He also said to his disciples, and he told them a story. There was a rich man who had a steward, that is, a manager in charge of looking after his property. Someone accused that manager before his master of wasting his goods, of squandering and spending on himself what did not belong to him.

The one speaking is Jesus. He has just told the parables of the prodigal son and others about what was lost. Now he teaches his disciples with this parable, often called the parable of the unfaithful steward. It is a difficult story, and scholars interpret it in several ways, but here it begins by showing a manager who will have to give an account.

For today: everything we have, such as time, money and talents, is a trust from God. Ask yourself honestly whether you are taking good care of it, because one day we will give an account of it.
exp.10:0:
This verse tells us that Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples asked him: "Lord, teach us to pray." The words "aconteció" and "á" are old forms, and the explanation I was given for them is no longer needed, since the verse your reader sees does not use these words.

The speaker is an unnamed disciple, who probably saw Jesus pray and wanted to learn. John is John the Baptist, who gave his disciples some teaching about prayer, though the Bible does not spell out what that teaching was. Jesus answers right away with what we now call the Lord's Prayer.

For today: you do not need to know how to pray perfectly to begin. We can ask the Lord, simply, to teach us. Watching Jesus' life of prayer and using his example helps us speak with God as a close Father.
exp.16:6:
Jesus asks: which of you, if you have a servant who works plowing the field or looking after sheep, will tell him as soon as he comes in from the field, "Come and sit down to eat"? The expected answer is that no one would do it that way.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, who had just asked him, "Increase our faith." He speaks to them about a small but real faith, and then uses this everyday picture from his time. The verses that follow show that the servant does his duty before he rests. Not every detail is explained, but the central point seems to be a humble attitude of service.

For today: serve God and others with joy, without seeking applause or rewards. When you do what is right, do not do it to show off, but out of love and gratitude to God.
exp.11:34:
Jesus says that his followers must be ready. "Let your loins be girded about" refers to gathering up a long robe with a belt so that you can work or walk without being hindered. "Your lights burning" refers to lamps that are kept lit so that no one is left in the dark. In other words: be prepared and awake.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and earlier he taught them not to live anxious about material things, but to trust in God and to store up a treasure in heaven. Now he uses the image of servants who wait for their master when he returns from a wedding, without knowing the exact hour. He promises that the master, upon finding them alert, will serve them.

For today: live each day with a heart attentive to God. You can set aside a few minutes to pray, obey what you already know He asks of you, and be generous, without putting off what is important until tomorrow.
exp.7:40:
Luke 8:41 tells us that a man named Jairus came, and he was a ruler of the synagogue, meaning a leader in charge of order and the gatherings held in that place of worship. He fell down at Jesus' feet and kept begging him to come to his house.

Luke is the one telling the story. Jesus had just crossed back over the lake by boat, and the crowd was waiting for him. Just before this, he had healed a man freed from evil spirits, and that man was telling everyone what God had done. Jairus comes for an urgent reason: his only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying.

For today: when pain strips away your pride and your standing, follow Jairus' example. Come to Jesus with humility and tell him with trust what hurts you most, no matter who you are.
exp.14:4:
It says that when the shepherd finally finds the sheep that had been lost, he does not scold it or force it to walk. He lays it on his shoulders, and he does so with joy.

Jesus tells this parable in response to the Pharisees and scribes, who criticized him for welcoming sinners and eating with them. With this story he shows them how God thinks: he seeks out the one who has wandered away and rejoices greatly when he recovers them. The shepherd's shoulders show care and effort, not punishment.

For today: if you feel far from God or tired of your mistakes, remember that he seeks you and is ready to carry you. And if you know someone who has wandered away, treat them with patience and kindness, not judgment, and rejoice when they come back.
exp.21:16:
Jesus takes a cup of wine, gives thanks to God, and asks his disciples to share it among all of them. "Cup" is the word for "vessel," and "take" here means "receive" or "grab," and "divide it" here means to share it out among you.

Jesus speaks during the Passover supper, the feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. He knows that he will soon suffer and die, and so he says that he had longed very much to eat this meal with his friends. This cup comes before the bread, and many believe it was part of the Passover meal. Afterward, Jesus will give the bread and the cup a new meaning.

For today: sharing what God gives us, with thankfulness and in community. Before we eat or serve ourselves, we can give thanks and think about who needs to sit at our table.
exp.8:56:
While Jesus and his disciples were walking along the road, a man said to him, "Lord, I will follow you wherever you go." The phrase "wherever you go" means "to any place you go." It is a great and sincere promise.

Jesus had just been rejected in a village and was continuing his journey toward Jerusalem. The one speaking is an unnamed man in this account. Matthew tells a similar scene and calls the speaker a scribe, although not everyone is sure it is the same moment. Jesus answers him that following him means giving up comfort.

For today: before promising God "I will go wherever," think honestly about what you are willing to leave behind. Following Jesus is not only a good wish but a daily decision, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.18:14:
This verse tells that the nobleman returns after receiving the kingdom. Then he gives orders for the servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, because he wants to know how much each one had gained.

The word "trading" in the verse means doing business to make a profit. The amount of money he gave each servant was a considerable sum.

Jesus is speaking in a parable, near Jerusalem. The people thought the kingdom of God was going to appear right away. Jesus shows that the king goes away and comes back later. Many interpreters see in this an image of his return, though some also notice an echo of the story of Herod's heirs.

For today: God has entrusted us with things, such as time, gifts, money and opportunities. We can simply think about what he has given us and use it faithfully and with love, knowing that one day we will give an account with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.0:62:
Zechariah asked for a writing tablet, a small board for writing, and wrote: "John is his name." And they all marvelled. The word "asking" here means "requesting," and "marvelled" means that they were amazed.

Zechariah had not been able to speak since the angel Gabriel announced that he would have a son, because he doubted the message (Luke 1:20). His neighbours and relatives wanted to name the child Zechariah, after his father, but Elisabeth had already said he would be called John. Zechariah confirmed in writing the name that God himself had given (Luke 1:13). Soon afterward he recovered his voice and praised God.

For today: obeying God can go against the customs and opinions of the people around us. Zechariah learned to trust God's word even when others thought differently. Let us ask for courage to obey him with simplicity.
exp.8:54:
Jesus turns and firmly corrects his disciples. He tells them that they do not understand what kind of spirit is moving them. "Rebuked" means that he called them to account with seriousness.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem and passes through a Samaritan village, which does not receive him because his destination is that city. James and John, upset by the rejection, want to call down fire from heaven as Elijah did. Jesus stops them, since his mission is not to destroy but to save, as the following verse says. Some early manuscripts do not include this whole sentence, and scholars debate it.

When someone rejects or offends us, anger can seem justified. Before reacting, it is good to ask ourselves: Is it the spirit of Christ that is moving me? We can respond with patience, keep going, and seek that person's good.
exp.9:16:
This verse tells that the seventy disciples whom Jesus had sent came back very joyful. They were amazed because even the demons obeyed them when they spoke in the name of Jesus. "Even the devils are subject unto us" means that the demons submitted to them, obeyed them.

The one speaking is Luke, narrating the return of these disciples. Jesus had sent them out two by two to announce the kingdom of God, and had told them that whoever heard them, heard Him. Now they come back excited with their report. Jesus will answer that He saw Satan fall, but He will also teach them that their greatest joy should be something else: that their names are written in heaven.

For today: when God works something through you, rejoice and give thanks to Him, because the power is not yours but comes from the name of Jesus. And remember that your greatest joy is to belong to Him.
exp.5:10:
The explanation says that the Pharisees and the teachers of the law were filled with fury. The word "fury" here speaks of a strong anger, almost without reason. Afterward they talked among themselves about what they might do to Jesus. The word "to" is simply the form used before a name, and nothing more needs to be said about it.

Jesus was in a synagogue on the Sabbath. They were watching him to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath so they could accuse him. He asked them whether it was right to do good or evil on that day, and he healed the man's hand. Instead of rejoicing, they grew angry. Then Jesus prayed through the night and chose his twelve apostles.

We can take care that our rules or customs do not harden our hearts. When we see that someone receives help or healing, the right response is to rejoice and give thanks to God, not to become angry because it does not fit our way of thinking.
exp.11:51:
Jesus says that, from now on, in a family of five people there will be division: three will be against two, and two against three. "From now on" means "from this point forward," and "divided" means separated by disagreements.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd. Shortly before, he said he had to go through a baptism, that is, through his suffering and death. He makes clear that he did not come to bring an easy peace, but that his message would force people to decide. Some would follow him and others would not, and this could divide even the closest family members.

For today: if following Christ causes tension in your family, do not respond with pride or anger. Remain kind, honest, and faithful, and pray for those who think differently.
exp.19:9:
It says that, when the season of harvest came, the owner of the vineyard sent a servant to collect his share of the fruit. But the tenants (the workers who looked after the vineyard) beat him and sent him away with nothing.

The word "beat" here means that they mistreated him physically.

Jesus is teaching in the temple, and the religious leaders had just questioned his authority. He tells this parable to the people. Many understand that the owner represents God, the vineyard represents Israel, and the servants represent the prophets who were rejected. The tenants would be the leaders who did not want to answer to God.

Everything we have is a trust from God, not our own property. Today we can ask ourselves whether we respond with humility when He corrects us or calls us through others, or whether we become defensive and ignore Him.
exp.19:4:
What it says: The religious leaders were reasoning among themselves in secret. They thought: if we admit that John's baptism came from God, Jesus will ask us why we did not believe John.

Context: Jesus was teaching in the temple when the priests, the scribes, and the elders asked him by what authority he was acting. Jesus answered with a question of his own about John the Baptist. They found themselves trapped. They were not seeking the truth, but an answer that would protect them. In the end they said they did not know.

For today: Before you answer, ask yourself whether you are seeking the truth or only protecting your image. When God confronts our hearts, it is better to be honest and humble than to give calculated answers to avoid trouble.
exp.5:4:
Jesus declares that he, the Son of man, has authority over the Sabbath. The word "Lord" means he has the right to command and to decide how that day is to be lived. The word "also" stresses that his authority reaches even to something as respected as the day of rest.

Jesus is speaking with some Pharisees who were criticizing his disciples for picking heads of grain on the Sabbath. He reminds them of the time David, when he was hungry, ate the sacred bread of the Presence, bread reserved for the priests. By this he shows that human need and his own authority matter more than a rigid interpretation of the law. "Son of man" is a title Jesus uses for himself.

God gave rest for our good, not to burden us. Today we can rest and worship with gratitude, and treat others with compassion instead of judging them by external rules.
exp.0:12:
Here the angel calms Zacharias, who was frightened. He tells him that his prayer has been heard and that his wife Elisabeth will bear him a son. He also tells him that the child will be named John.

The one speaking is an angel of the Lord, who appeared to Zacharias, a priest, while he was serving in the temple before the altar of incense. Zacharias and Elisabeth were elderly and had no children. The text does not say exactly what the prayer was, but many think it referred to the desire for a child, and others think it also included hope for Israel. The angel announces the birth of John the Baptist.

For today: God hears our prayers, even when his answer comes late or in a way we did not expect. We can keep praying with confidence and wait for his timing.
exp.6:45:
Jesus says to Simon, a Pharisee who had invited him to eat, that he did not anoint his head with oil, which was ordinary oil. Instead, the woman anointed his feet with ointment, which was an expensive perfume. Anointing means pouring oil over someone as a sign of honor and care.

Jesus is in Simon's house, and a woman known as a sinner comes in weeping, washes his feet, and perfumes them. Simon judges him in his heart. Then Jesus compares the actions of the two: Simon left out the normal courtesies of hospitality, while the woman gave everything she had. Jesus teaches that her love comes from having received forgiveness.

For today: do not measure your faith by appearances or compare yourself with others. Remember how much you have been forgiven, and respond with sincere gratitude, serving and loving generously, not merely doing things out of obligation.
exp.0:69:
This verse says that God fulfilled what he had promised long ago. He spoke "by the mouth" of his prophets, that is, through them. He calls them "holy ones" because they were set apart for God. And "since the world began" means that these promises come from very ancient times. The word "as" here means "just as".

Zechariah speaks, the father of John the Baptist. He has just regained his speech, and filled with the Holy Spirit he praises God. He is celebrating that the promised Savior is coming, from the family of King David. For him, what is happening is not chance, but the fulfillment of God's Word.

For today: God is faithful and does what he says, even when it takes a long time. When waiting feels long, remember his fulfilled promises and trust that he will remain faithful to you.
exp.9:1:
Jesus says there is a great deal of work to be done, like a large harvest ready to be gathered, but there are few workers. So he tells them to pray to the Lord of the harvest, that is, to the owner of the harvest, that he would send out workers. A harvest is the crop of grain gathered from the fields, and the workers are the ones who do the gathering.

Jesus speaks to the seventy he had just appointed and sent out two by two to the towns where he himself intended to go. He explains the great need for people willing to announce the kingdom of God. Some manuscripts say "seventy-two," which is why translations differ. Then he warns them that their task will not be easy.

For today: before looking for solutions, pray sincerely for those who share the gospel in your community and in the world. And stay ready, because God may answer your prayer by sending you.
exp.6:23:
Jesus begins to speak to the crowd about John the Baptist, after John's messengers had already left. He asks them what they went out into the wilderness to see: a reed shaken by the wind? It is a rhetorical question. The expected answer is no.

John was in prison and had sent his disciples to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come. Jesus answered by pointing to his works, and then he defended John before the crowd. Some understand the reed as an image of someone weak or unstable. John was not like that: he was firm, even in prison.

Today, this question invites us to examine what we look for in our faith. We may prefer comfortable messages, but God honors those who stand firm in the truth. Let us ask him for steadfastness, so that we do not move with every wind of opinion.
exp.12:20:
It says that the kingdom of God is like leaven. A woman took it and mixed it into three measures of flour, and left it there until the whole dough rose. "Leaven" is what makes bread rise. "Hid" means she mixed it inside, so that it could not be seen. "Leavened" means the dough was filled with yeast and grew. "Three measures" was a large amount of flour, enough for many people.

Jesus speaks while teaching on the way to Jerusalem. He has just told the parable of the mustard seed, and now he adds another image like it. Both show that the kingdom begins small but grows. Some think the leaven also speaks of an influence that works quietly; others read it differently, but the main point is growth.

For today: do not despise what is small and quiet. A prayer, an act of kindness, or a word of faith can work little by little, even when you do not see results right away.
exp.17:36:
What it says: A blind man was begging beside the road and heard the sound of a large crowd. He asked what was happening, and they told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. The Nazareth detail points to where Jesus came from, the town where he grew up.

Context: Jesus was entering Jericho, near his road toward Jerusalem. The ones speaking are people in the crowd, who give the blind man a simple piece of news. But the blind man does not stop at the name alone: he immediately cries out to Jesus as the Son of David, a title that recognized Jesus as the promised Messiah. His faith goes further than what the people told him.

For today: Sometimes we hear that Jesus is passing by our lives in an opportunity, a word, or a moment of need. Do not let him pass by. Call out to him sincerely, even when others tell you to be quiet.
exp.10:24:
This verse says that the unclean spirit returns to the house it came out of and finds it swept and put in order, clean and tidy, but with no one living in it. The word "finds" in the verse above is the meaning of the word that was used here.

Jesus is the one speaking. He has just been accused of driving out demons by the power of Beelzebul, and he answers with this warning. Many understand the house to represent a person who has been freed from evil but is left empty. Jesus says there is no neutral ground: you are either with him or against him.

For today: it is not enough to simply give up a bad habit or a harmful influence. That empty space must be filled with something good. Set aside time each day for prayer, for reading the Bible, and for obeying Jesus, so that your life does not stay empty.
exp.21:54:
This verse tells us that some people lit a fire in the middle of the courtyard, and everyone sat down around it. Peter sat down with them too. The word "hall" here most likely refers to the open courtyard of the house, though some scholars understand it as an inner room or enclosed court.

Luke, the narrator, describes the night Jesus was arrested. They took him to the house of the high priest. Peter was following at a distance, afraid but wanting to know what would happen. By sitting down near the fire, he was exposed, and soon a servant girl recognized him.

When we are in surroundings that do not honor Christ, it is easy to blend in so that we go unnoticed. Peter reminds us that following Jesus from a distance leaves us weak. Let us ask the Lord for courage to draw near to him and to be honest about our faith.
exp.8:45:
The explanation says the disciples began to argue among themselves about who was the most important. Lucas writes this right after Jesus told them that he would be handed over to men, that is, that he would suffer. The disciples did not understand that message and were afraid to ask him about it. Instead, they argued about greatness. Jesus knew what they were thinking in their hearts, so he placed a child beside him and taught them that the smallest and most humble is the truly great one in the kingdom of God.

For today: when we feel the urge to compare ourselves with others or to want to stand out above them, we can stop and ask ourselves how we might serve someone simple or someone who goes unnoticed. Jesus values humility and service more than prestige.
exp.10:43:
Jesus says that the scribes and Pharisees are like graves that cannot be seen. People walk over them without realizing it. "Scribes" were the teachers of the Law, and "hypocrites" are those who appear to be good but are different on the inside.

Jesus speaks during a meal in the house of a Pharisee. He is rebuking the religious leaders who were careful about outward details, such as tithes, and neglected justice and love for God. According to the Law, touching a grave made a person unclean. So walking over a tomb without knowing it made a person unclean without their noticing. In this way, those leaders could affect others without their being aware of it.

For today: let us ask God to examine our heart. May our faith not be mere appearance, but may it be seen in honesty, justice, and love toward those around us.
exp.7:52:
The verse says that the people laughed at Jesus and mocked Him. They did this because they were certain that the girl had died. "Mocked" means they were scornful, and "the girl" is the young daughter of Jairus.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke. Jesus had just said that the girl was not dead but sleeping. Those present were weeping and mourning her death, so they did not understand His words. Many think Jesus was speaking of death as a sleep from which He could wake her, and the account confirms this when He raises her.

For today: sometimes our situation seems lost and others laugh at our hope. We can keep trusting Jesus, even when human reasoning says there is no remedy left. He can act where we see only an ending.
exp.5:27:
Jesus says we should bless those who curse us, that is, speak well of them and wish them good. He also asks us to pray for those who mistreat us, that is, for those who tell lies to harm us.

Jesus is teaching his disciples in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Shortly before, he told them they would be rejected and insulted for following him. Now he shows them how to respond: love your enemies, do good, and do not repay evil with evil. It is a love that acts, not just a feeling.

Today, when someone speaks badly about you, in person or online, avoid answering with insults. Pray for that person by name, asking God to bless them. This does not deny your pain, but it guards your heart against bitterness.
exp.10:48:
Jesus says that God, in his wisdom, announced that he would send his messengers, prophets and apostles, to speak to his people. He also announced what would happen: some of them would be killed, and others would be persecuted. The phrase "I will send" shows that God always takes the initiative in reaching out to people.

Jesus is speaking to the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, whom he has just rebuked. They decorated the tombs of the prophets, but by their attitude they resembled those who had killed them. Some scholars think Jesus is quoting a saying of divine wisdom, and others believe he is speaking of himself. Opinions vary.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly obey God's voice or only admire those who obeyed it before us. Respecting the past is not enough; we need to listen with humility to what God is saying to us now.
exp.17:16:
Jesus says that whoever does not receive the kingdom of God the way a child receives it will not enter it. "Truly I tell you" is an old way of saying "I assure you." "Whoever" here means "whoever receives." To receive the kingdom is to accept it as a gift, with trust and without trying to earn it.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Some people were bringing little children to him so that he would touch them and bless them, and the disciples were scolding them. Jesus corrects them and holds the children up as an example. Afterward, an important man asks him what he must do to inherit eternal life, which shows the contrast: he wanted to earn it through his own deeds. Many see here a call to humility, although one can debate which trait of the child stands out most.

Today we can come near to God without pretending to strength or merit. Ask him with simplicity, trust in his grace, and receive his forgiveness as a gift.
exp.12:16:
This verse tells how the people reacted after Jesus spoke. His opponents, those who were criticizing him, were put to shame. But all the people rejoiced over the glorious things, that is, the wonderful things, that Jesus was doing. The word "adversaries" means opponents.

Jesus was in a synagogue on a Sabbath and had just healed a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years. The ruler of the synagogue became angry because she was healed on the Sabbath. Jesus answered him that everyone unties their animals on that day to give them water to drink, and that all the more this woman, a daughter of Abraham, deserved to be set free.

For today: when doing good clashes with our habits or our pride, let us remember that God rejoices in compassion. Let us also rejoice in what God does in others, instead of criticizing.
exp.6:42:
Simon answers Jesus' question: he thinks that the one to whom the larger debt was forgiven loves more. Jesus says to him, "Thou hast rightly judged." Simon's answer, "I suppose," shows that he responds with some caution.

Jesus is dining in the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known as a sinner comes in, weeps at his feet, and anoints them. Simon despises her in his heart. Jesus tells this parable and leads Simon himself to recognize the truth. Then he shows him that the woman has shown more love than he has.

For today: let us not forget how much we have been forgiven. A heart grateful for God's grace becomes humble, and it is easier to love and to treat others with compassion, instead of judging them.
exp.22:17:
What it says: All the people shouted at the same time, as one voice. They demanded that Pilate take Jesus away, that is, get rid of him, and set Barabbas free for them. The phrase translated here as "shouted together" means they cried out together, with force.

Context: Pilate, the Roman governor, found no crime in Jesus deserving death, and he proposed to punish him and release him. It was the custom to release a prisoner at the Passover feast. But the chief priests and the crowd insisted on freeing Barabbas, a man imprisoned for insurrection and murder, as the next verse explains. The Gospels do not fully explain why the crowd changed its mind in this way.

For today: The pressure of a crowd can push us to reject what is right. Before joining a collective cry, let us ask God for wisdom and courage to act in truth, even if we stand alone.
exp.7:13:
Jesus explains that the seed that fell among thorns represents people who do hear the word of God. But as they go on with their lives, worries, riches, and pleasures of this life choke it, like thorns that smother a plant. For that reason they do not bring fruit to maturity.

Jesus is speaking to the crowds and then to his disciples, explaining the parable of the sower. He shows them that the word of God meets different kinds of hearts. This is the third kind, after the path and the rock, and before the good soil.

For today: check what things compete for your attention and your heart. Worries, money, or entertainment are not always bad, but they can choke your spiritual life. Set aside time each day to listen to God, and ask him to help you remove the "thorns."
exp.21:15:
Jesus tells his disciples that he will not eat this Passover meal again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. The word "to you" in the verse is the same as the word for "them" or "you all" in plain speech. "Fulfilled" means that it reaches its full completion and its full meaning.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, the night before his death, with his apostles. They were celebrating the Passover, which remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. He knew he was going to suffer, and so he tells them how much he longed to share this meal with them. Christians understand that Jesus is the true fulfillment of the Passover. Some think he is referring to a future banquet in the kingdom; others see something broader. The Bible does not spell out all the details.

For today: value moments of fellowship with other believers. Jesus desired to be with his own, and he reminds us that our final hope is to be with him.
exp.0:49:
This verse says that God's mercy never runs out or wears thin: it reaches one generation after another. Mercy here means his compassionate love and his kindness toward those who need it. Fearing God in this verse does not mean being afraid of him, but respecting him with reverence and trust.

The speaker is Mary, the mother of Jesus, in the song that many call the Magnificat. She has just learned that she will give birth to the Messiah, and she praises God. She moves from what God has done for her to what he does for all his people: he is faithful, he cares for the humble, and he brings down the proud.

For today: trust that God's mercy does not depend on your mistakes or your family history. Pray and live with reverence, and teach your children or those around you to know him, so that his kindness keeps being passed on.
exp.8:31:
It says that Peter, John and James were very sleepy, that is, they were heavy with tiredness. When they were fully awake, they saw Jesus's glory and splendor. They also saw the two men who were with him, namely Moses and Elijah.

This takes place on the mountain, while Jesus was praying and his appearance changed. Luke is the one who tells the story. Moses and Elijah were speaking with Jesus about his departure, which is his death and his journey toward Jerusalem. The disciples nearly missed this scene because of sleep, but they woke up in time to see the glory.

For today: sometimes tiredness distracts us from what is spiritual. Look for moments to pray and to listen to God with attention, and ask him to keep you awake to see what he wants to show you.
exp.6:0:
When Jesus had finished all he wanted to teach the people, while they were listening closely, he went on to the town of Capernaum. The phrase about finishing all his words means that he ended his teaching. The people listening to him means that they were paying attention to what he said.

Before this verse, Jesus had given the Sermon on the Plain, with teachings about loving your enemies, not judging others, and building your life on a firm foundation. Luke marks the end of that discourse here and the move to a new scene. In Capernaum, the encounter with a Roman centurion who asks for help for his sick servant will follow shortly.

For today: Jesus did not only speak, he also acted with compassion. After hearing the Word of God, try to put it into practice and be alert to the needy people God places in your path.
exp.16:20:
Jesus says that people will not be able to point to the kingdom of God as something located in one place, saying "Here it is" or "There it is." The word "Behold" in the verse above is the same kind of expression: it calls attention to something seen. The phrase "within you" can also be read as "among you," though many scholars think it means "in the midst of you."

Jesus is answering the Pharisees, who asked him when the kingdom would come. He was there in person, healing and teaching with authority, so the kingdom was already present in him. The Pharisees were looking for a visible and spectacular sign, but they did not recognize the King standing right in front of them.

For today: do not look for God only in great events, trends, or famous leaders. His kingdom advances wherever Jesus is received and obeyed. You can live it out today with faith, forgiving, serving, and following Christ in everyday life.
exp.9:18:
Jesus tells his disciples that he gives them authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, that is, to walk on them firmly, and to overcome all the power of the enemy. He promises them that nothing will harm them. Authority, not strength of their own, is what the word for it means.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples who have just returned from a mission, happy because even the demons obeyed in his name. He reminds them that he saw Satan fall like lightning. Many understand the serpents and scorpions as images of spiritual evil; others also add a literal meaning. He then makes clear that their greatest joy should not be power, but that their names are written in heaven.

Today, you do not have to live in fear of evil, because your authority comes from Christ. But do not place your joy in your spiritual achievements, but in the fact that you belong to God.
exp.6:20:
This verse tells us that, just as John's messengers arrived, Jesus healed many people. He cured those who suffered from diseases and afflictions (serious ailments, such as bodily sicknesses or pains), freed others from evil spirits, and gave sight to many who were blind.

Luke is the one who tells the story. John the Baptist was in prison and sent word to ask whether Jesus was the expected Messiah. Jesus did not answer with an argument, but with deeds. While the messengers were present, he healed the people, and then he asked them to tell John what they had seen and heard. In this way he showed that what the prophets had foretold was being fulfilled.

When we have doubts, as John did, we can bring them to Jesus with sincerity. He does not become angry at honest questions. Looking at what He has done, both in the Bible and in our own lives, can strengthen our faith.
exp.4:28:
This verse tells how Levi, also called Matthew, held a great feast at his house after leaving everything to follow Jesus. There were many tax collectors, that is, men who collected taxes, and other people reclining at the table with them. "Company" means a group or crowd, and "at the table" means they were eating together.

Luke is the one speaking here, recounting what happened. Levi had just been called and wanted to introduce Jesus to his friends and coworkers. Tax collectors were looked down on for collecting taxes for Rome, and many despised them. That is why the Pharisees complained, and Jesus replied that he came to heal the sick, not the healthy.

For today: if Jesus has changed your life, open your table and your heart to those around you, without judging them, so that they too may come to know his love.
exp.21:35:
Jesus tells his disciples that now, unlike before, whoever has a purse should take it, and likewise a bag for travel provisions. Whoever has no sword should sell his cloak and buy one.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. Earlier he sent them out without provisions and they lacked nothing, but now hostility will come against them. He quotes Isaiah: "he was numbered with the transgressors." When the disciples show him two swords, he replies, "It is enough." Many understand that he is not asking for an armed fight, since shortly afterward he rebukes the use of the sword in Gethsemane. Some see it as figurative language of warning; others take it as a literal caution. The question is debated.

For today: Jesus asks us to be watchful and prepared for difficult times, trusting God, but without using faith as an excuse to be careless or violent.
exp.5:12:
It says that when morning came, Jesus called together his followers and chose twelve from among them. He named these twelve "apostles," which means "sent ones."

Some older wording needs no comment here, since the verse reads plainly in modern English.

Luke is the one who tells the story. Before this, the religious leaders had become furious with Jesus because he had healed on the Sabbath. Then Jesus went up into the hills and spent the whole night praying to God. At daybreak he made this important decision. The twelve would be his close companions and the ones sent out to carry on his message. The text does not say what he asked for in that prayer, only that he prayed all night.

Before big decisions, it is wise to stop and pray. Jesus did this even in the middle of opposition. Today we can bring our decisions, work, and relationships to God, and give him time to guide us before we act in a hurry.
exp.16:13:
Jesus sees the ten lepers and tells them to go and show themselves to the priests. While they are on their way, they are cleansed, that is, healed of leprosy. Some older wording in the source has been adjusted here, and "clean" in this verse means healed.

Jesus speaks with ten sick men who asked him for mercy from a distance, as was the custom for lepers. According to the law of Moses, the priest had to confirm that a person was well before he could return to the community. That is why Jesus sends them before they see themselves healed: he asks them to trust his word. Afterward, only one returns to give thanks.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take a step of faith before we see the full answer. Obey with confidence, and when you receive his help, do not forget to return and give him thanks.
exp.2:36:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It says that Jesus, tracing his family line backward through history, comes from a line that includes Methuselah, Enoch, Jared, and Mahalaleel. The names appear in the spelling used in the King James Version your reader sees.

The one who wrote this is Luke, a physician and companion of Paul, who wants to present the life of Jesus in an orderly way. After Jesus' baptism, Luke includes this genealogy that goes back all the way to Adam, and he ends by saying "which was the son of God." Many understand that Luke is showing that Jesus is connected to all of humanity, not only to Israel.

For today: God acts in real history, generation after generation, and he also knows your name and your story. Trust that your life, though it may seem ordinary, has a place in his plan.
exp.14:6:
Jesus says that there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who acknowledges his sin and turns around than over ninety-nine "righteous" people who have no need to repent.

The word "joy" here means gladness. "Repent" means turning back to God with the heart.

Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and scribes, who complained that he welcomed sinners and ate with them. He tells them the parable of the lost sheep to show the heart of God. Many understand the "righteous" to be those who consider themselves righteous, like these critics, but others think it refers to those who are already with God. The text does not fully settle this. In either case, the central point is God's joy over the one who returns.

Today, rejoice when someone draws near to God, even if their past has been difficult. Receive that person with kindness, without judging them, as God does.
exp.22:53:
That day was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath. "Day before" means the day just before. The sabbath was about to begin, since for the Jews each day started at the coming of evening.

Luke, the narrator, explains why Joseph of Arimathea acted with such haste. Jesus had died, and little time remained before the sacred rest began. That is why he buried him quickly, and the women had to wait to finish preparing the body. It is understood that Luke wants to show that everything was done in keeping with the law.

For today: God works even in limited times and in times of waiting. When something is left unfinished, we can rest and obey him, trusting that he is still in control.
exp.10:35:
Jesus says that if your whole being is full of light, with no dark part in it, then you will be completely illuminated, as when a lamp lights you with its brightness.

Jesus speaks to the crowd that was asking him for signs. He has just said that the eye is the lamp of the body, and he warns that the light within can become darkness without one noticing. Shortly after, a Pharisee invites him to eat and is surprised that he does not wash first, which shows that a person can take care of the outside and neglect the heart.

For today: ask God to show you whether there is some corner of your life that you keep in the shadow, such as a grudge or a hidden habit. Open it to his light and let his Word heal it.
exp.21:44:
He got up from prayer and came to his disciples, and found them sleeping because of sorrow, that is, overcome by grief and exhaustion.

Luke tells this on the Mount of Olives, shortly before Jesus was arrested. He had just prayed with great anguish, and an angel strengthened him. The disciples, by contrast, could not stay awake. Jesus had asked them to pray so that they would not fall into temptation, and then he wakes them with that same call.

For today: when sorrow or tiredness leaves you without strength, do not condemn yourself. Go to God honestly, ask for his help, and seek out other believers who will pray with you. Jesus understands your weakness.
exp.1:26:
He says that Simeon came to the temple guided by the Holy Spirit. Just at that moment, Mary and Joseph were bringing the child Jesus to do what the law of Moses required for a newborn.

The phrase "after the custom of the law" means according to what the law commanded them to do. The word "devout" (in the previous verse) means that he honored God.

The narrator is Luke. He tells us that Simeon had received the promise that he would not die before seeing the Christ. Luke shows that the encounter was no accident: the Spirit led Simeon, and at the same time Jesus' parents were obeying the law. In this way God's promise is joined with the simple obedience of a family.

For today: if we seek to be attentive to God's guidance, He can meet us at the right moment, even in ordinary life. It is worth praying, waiting in faith, and obeying in small things, because that is where God often works.
exp.4:3:
Here Jesus finishes teaching the crowd from Simon's boat and gives him an instruction: "Launch out into the deep," and "let down your nets for a draught." In other words, Jesus asks him to go out into deeper water and fish.

The one speaking is Jesus. He has just been using the boat as a place to teach. Simon, who would later be called Peter, is a fisherman who had worked all night without catching anything. The command seems illogical, because fishing in the daytime with no previous results did not seem like a good idea. Even so, Simon answers with trust in Jesus' word.

For today: sometimes God asks us to try again where we have already grown tired or failed. Obedience is not always understood right away, but we can take a step of faith, trusting that his word can be relied on.
exp.5:25:
Jesus warns that there is a danger when everyone speaks well of a person. To speak well of someone means to praise them or to speak with approval. "Their fathers" are the ancestors of the people of Israel. They applauded the false prophets, who said what the people wanted to hear, and that is why Jesus says "Woe unto you," an expression of lament and warning.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, after the beatitudes in Luke. There he had said that those who are persecuted for his sake are blessed. Here he shows the opposite side: being admired by everyone can mean that someone keeps silent about the truth in order to please people. He then goes on to the command to love your enemies.

For today: do not live seeking everyone's approval. Strive to be faithful to the truth with love, even when it sometimes costs you to be criticized.
exp.8:55:
This verse says that Jesus, here called "the Son of man," did not come into the world to destroy people, but to save them. The word "destroy" in this verse means to ruin or bring to ruin. After saying this, Jesus and his disciples continued on their way to another village, that is, another small town.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after a village in Samaria refused to receive him. James and John, upset, wanted to ask that fire fall from heaven on them, as in the days of Elijah. Jesus rebuked them because that was not the spirit of his mission. He was on his way to Jerusalem, and his purpose was to give life.

For today: when someone rejects us or offends us, let us not respond with revenge or contempt. Let us ask God for a heart like Jesus', one that seeks the good and salvation of others, and let us move forward in peace.
exp.7:35:
This verse says that those who had seen what happened told the others how the man who had been possessed by demons had been healed. The word "saved" here means set free, rescued from his oppression. "Possessed" describes someone tormented by evil spirits.

Luke tells what happened in the region of the Gadarenes. Jesus had freed this man, and the pigs in the area had rushed down the slope into the lake. The herdsmen fled and reported it in the city. Now the witnesses, who saw the change, explain to the people what took place. Even so, the crowd reacts with fear and asks Jesus to leave.

For today: the power of Jesus can make us uncomfortable, because it changes things we thought were under our control. Let us not be afraid of his work in us. And, like the witnesses, let us simply tell what we have seen God do.
exp.21:14:
Jesus tells his disciples that he has desired very much to eat this Passover meal with them before he suffers. The phrase "with desire I have desired" means "I have longed deeply," and the word "suffer" refers to his suffering and death.

Jesus speaks while seated at the table with the apostles, on the night before his crucifixion. The Passover recalled Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Jesus knows what is coming, and yet he shows his affection for his friends. Soon he says that he will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God, and then he takes the cup.

For today: Jesus desired to be close to his own, even in his most difficult moment. This reminds us that God wants closeness with us. Today you can set aside a few minutes to be with him in prayer, without hurry, knowing that he desires it too.
exp.0:21:
What it says: Zechariah came out of the holy place, where he had been offering the incense, but he could no longer speak. The people waiting outside realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. He kept making signs to them with his hands and remained speechless.

Context: Luke tells what happened after the angel Gabriel announced to Zechariah that his wife Elizabeth would have a son, John. Zechariah doubted because they were both already advanced in years, and the angel told him he would be unable to speak until the promise was fulfilled. The people wondered at his delay, and seeing him unable to speak, understood that God had intervened.

For today: God can fulfill His promises even when they seem impossible to us. When we doubt, we can use silence to listen and to trust Him more, instead of speaking out of fear.
exp.14:12:
The explanation says that, a few days after receiving his share of the inheritance, the younger son gathered together everything he had and went off to a faraway country. There he spent his money without wisdom, living in a disorderly way. The verse tells us he wasted his substance with riotous living, which means he spent what he had recklessly and destructively.

Jesus is telling this parable to Pharisees and teachers of the law, who criticized him for welcoming sinners and eating with them. It is the third story about something lost that is recovered. Here Jesus shows that God waits with love for the one who wanders away. The distance described in the story speaks of more than geography; it speaks of the heart.

For today: when we think freedom lies far from God, we usually end up empty. Examine whether any decision is pulling you away from Him, and return soon, because His door is still open.
exp.0:19:
It says that Zechariah would be silent and unable to speak until the promised child was born. The reason is that he did not believe the angel's words.

The angel Gabriel speaks, sent by God. Zechariah, an elderly priest, was in the temple when he received the news that his wife Elizabeth, already advanced in years, would have a son. He asked for a sign because of his doubt. The silence was that sign, and also a consequence of his lack of faith. Some believe it was a correction, and others, a demonstration of God's grace.

For today: when God speaks to you through his Word, trust even when the promise seems impossible. He fulfills what he says, in his time and in his way.
exp.5:38:
Jesus tells a parable, that is, a simple comparison. He asks whether a blind man can guide another blind man, and he answers with another question: will they not both fall into the ditch? The idea is clear: someone who cannot see well cannot lead another person safely.

Jesus is teaching his disciples and a large crowd in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He had been speaking about loving your enemies, not judging others, and being merciful. Then he warns about leading others while spiritually blind, and he continues with the image of the speck and the plank: before correcting someone, we must examine our own lives.

Before you advise or correct others, ask God to show you your own mistakes. Learn from Jesus, the teacher who sees clearly, and help others with humility.
exp.5:43:
Jesus says that every tree is known by the fruit it produces. No one gathers figs from thorn bushes or grapes from brambles, which are shrubs with thorns. "Gather" means to pick, and to harvest grapes means to gather them in. What a plant produces shows what kind of plant it is.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has just warned against judging with hypocrisy, and now he teaches that a person's life reveals what is in his heart. That is why he ends by asking why they call him Lord and do not do what he says.

For today: do not look only at beautiful words, whether your own or other people's. Ask God to change your heart, and humbly examine your attitudes, your treatment of others, and your obedience.
exp.12:23:
Jesus calls us to strive to enter through the narrow gate. The word "strive" means to struggle earnestly and not give up. He warns that many will try to enter but will not be able. The idea in the word "seek" suggests a desire to enter without the serious commitment to do so in God's way.

Jesus is traveling toward Jerusalem, teaching as he goes. Someone asks him whether only a few will be saved. He does not answer with numbers but with a personal call. He then explains that the door will be shut, and some will say that they ate with him and heard him teach in their streets, but he did not truly know them. Being near Jesus is not the same as following him.

For today: do not put off your answer to Jesus. Today you can speak with him sincerely, trust him, and obey him, instead of being content to be merely someone who knows about religious things.
exp.21:63:
Luke 22:64 tells how the guards blindfolded Jesus, struck him in the face, and taunted him to guess who had hit him. The word "prophesy" in this verse means to guess or to name who did it. "Blindfolding" means they covered his eyes.

Luke tells this after Jesus was arrested, during the night, in the house of the high priest. The men guarding him mocked him because their leaders considered him a false prophet. Without knowing it, they were fulfilling Jesus' own words about his suffering. Luke places this next to Peter's weeping to show that Jesus was alone.

For today: Jesus endured mockery and blows without returning evil for evil. When someone mocks you for your faith, you do not have to answer with hatred. You can pray and trust that God understands your pain, because Christ experienced it first.
exp.14:11:
Here the younger son asks his father for the share of the inheritance that would fall to him. The word "goods" in the verse refers to the family's possessions and property. The father agrees and divides his property between his sons. It was a very bold request, because normally an inheritance was received when the father died.

Jesus is the one speaking. He tells this parable after saying that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. Before this, he told the story of the lost sheep and the lost coin. Now he shows, through a family story, how God receives the one who turns away and comes back.

For today: everything we have comes from God; it is not just ours. We can ask ourselves whether we use his gifts to live close to him or to move away from him. If we have wandered off, his door is still open.
exp.21:37:
Here the disciples show Jesus that they have two swords. He answers, "It is enough." Some readers take this to mean "that's enough" in the sense of "let's stop talking about this," but the wording itself shows only that he is closing the exchange.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. He had just told them that hard times were coming and that he would be counted among the lawless, as Isaiah said. Many understand that the disciples took his words literally, and that Jesus ended the conversation with "It is enough." Others believe the swords were a sign that he would be treated like a criminal. There are several interpretations. Later, he himself rebukes the use of the sword.

For today: when we do not fully understand what God says, let us listen with humility and ask for light. And let us remember that Jesus calls us to pray, not to defend ourselves with violence.
exp.3:43:
This verse says that Jesus kept proclaiming his message in the synagogues of Galilee. Synagogues were the places where Jewish people gathered each Sabbath to pray and hear the Scriptures. Here the word for "preached" means that he spoke and announced his message publicly.

Here Luke, the narrator, summarizes what Jesus was doing. Earlier, the crowds wanted him to stay in Capernaum, but he said that he had to announce the good news of the kingdom of God in other towns, because that was why he had been sent.

For today: Jesus prayed in a quiet place and then continued his mission without being stopped by comfort or by applause. We can ask God to show us whom we should serve or share his hope with today, and to obey him faithfully.
exp.7:3:
A very large crowd gathered around Jesus. People came to him from town after town, from every city, to find him. Then he spoke to them in a parable, that is, a simple story taken from everyday life to teach a deeper truth.

The speaker is Luke, the narrator, and he presents Jesus teaching as he traveled through towns with his disciples and with several women who supported him. Many came out of curiosity or out of need. Jesus uses the parable of the sower, which follows in the verses after this one, to show how people receive the word of God in different ways.

For today: it is not enough to come near Jesus or to hear a great deal about him. We can ask ourselves honestly how our hearts stand when we hear his word, and ask him to give us a attentive heart, ready to obey.
exp.4:11:
This verse tells that Jesus was in a city when a man came to him who was "full of leprosy," that is, with the disease at an advanced stage. Seeing Jesus, the man fell on his face on the ground and pleaded with him: "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean." "Clean" means healed and set free from that uncleanness.

Luke, the writer, relates this just after Jesus called his first disciples. In that time, leprosy (and other skin diseases) cut the person off from other people, according to the law of Moses. That is why this man humbles himself and trusts in Jesus' power, even though he does not know whether Jesus will want to help him.

For today: we can come to Jesus with sincerity and humility, telling him our needs. We trust that he is able, and we leave his will in his hands.
exp.14:29:
The older son speaks to his father here and complains. Where the explanation mentions the quoted phrase about the money being spent, it says that he squandered all the family's wealth and goods, which the reader can connect to the verse's "devoured thy living." The word for prostitutes (women who sell their bodies) can be explained as "harlots" in the verse above. The calf that is well fattened, reserved for a great celebration, is the fatted calf. Notice that he does not say "my brother" but "this thy son," as if he did not want to acknowledge him.

Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees and teachers of the law, who criticized him for welcoming sinners. The older son represents them: he keeps the rules, but gets angry when the father forgives. His accusation about the harlots is his assumption, since the story does not confirm it beforehand.

For today: when someone who has fallen away returns to God, let us rejoice instead of comparing ourselves or judging. Serving God is not a debt to be collected, but a relationship of love with the Father.
exp.12:12:
He says that Jesus laid his hands on the woman who was bent over, and at that very moment she stood up straight. The words "immediately" mean "at once," and "glorified" means that she praised and honored God. After eighteen years bent over, she was able to stand upright, and her first response was to give thanks.

Jesus is teaching in a synagogue on a Sabbath. He himself called the woman, without her asking him to, and told her she was free. Then he touched her. The one who tells the story is Luke. The leader of the synagogue became angry because she was healed on the Sabbath, but Jesus showed him that doing good and freeing someone is not breaking the day of rest, but rather honors its purpose.

When God relieves us of a burden, the first thing we can do is give thanks out loud. We can also notice those who carry heavy loads and help them, without waiting for a perfect occasion.
exp.21:66:
Jesus stands before the Jewish council, which asks him: "Art thou the Christ? tell us." Christ means "the Anointed One," the promised Messiah. Jesus answers that if he tells them, they will not believe.

It is the morning after Jesus' arrest. Elders, chief priests, and scribes gather together. Those who speak are not seeking the truth with sincerity; they were already mocking him. Jesus knows that their hearts are closed, and then he adds that they will not answer him either if he asks them a question. Then he declares that the Son of man will sit at the right hand of the power of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek God with humility or only want to confirm what we already think. An open heart truly listens and is willing to believe.
exp.8:41:
As the boy was still coming toward Jesus, the demon threw him to the ground and shook him violently. The word "threw down" here means to throw someone to the ground, and "tore" describes strong convulsions. Then Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, that is, he corrected it with authority. The boy was made well, and Jesus gave him back to his father.

The one who tells the story is Luke. A desperate father had asked the disciples for help, but they could not free his son. Jesus laments the lack of faith of that generation and asks for the child to be brought to him. Then the people are amazed at the greatness of God.

For today: when a situation seems greater than our strength, we can bring it to Jesus with confidence. He does not despair or delay, and he cares about our pain and the pain of our family.
exp.15:26:
The rich man, who is suffering in the place of torment, asks Abraham: "I pray thee therefore, father, that thou wouldest send him to my father's house." The word "pray" here means "ask," and "father" is how he addresses Abraham, as one of his descendants. The verse before mentions Lazarus, so "him" refers to him.

The rich man speaks within the parable that Jesus tells. He has now understood that there is no way to cross the great chasm that separates them, so he now pleads on behalf of his family. It is remarkable that he asks for help for others, although he still thinks of Lazarus as someone who could serve him. The text says nothing more about his motives.

For today: let us not wait for extraordinary signs to take God seriously. Today we can hear His Word and obey it, and also care lovingly for those near us, speaking to them of Him while there is still time.
exp.0:2:
Luke says that it also seemed good to him to write an orderly account of the deeds of Jesus. He first investigated everything carefully from the very beginning. The phrase "it seemed good to me" means "I decided." The idea of having "had perfect understanding of all things" means that he studied them with care. The word "orderly" suggests a well-organized account. "Most excellent" is a title of respect.

The speaker is Luke, the author of the Gospel, according to Christian tradition. He writes to Theophilus, whom we do not know for certain. He may have been a real man of high standing, and some think the name, which means "friend of God," has a broader meaning. Luke wants to give him a reliable account, supported by eyewitnesses.

For today: our faith rests on real events, not on mere ideas. Study the Bible with care and order, ask with sincerity, and keep growing in the truth you have received.
exp.18:8:
Jesus declares that salvation came to Zacchaeus's house that very day. He says that Zacchaeus too is a son of Abraham, that is, a descendant of God's people.

Jesus speaks in Jericho, after Zacchaeus, the chief tax collector, received Jesus into his home. The people grumbled because Jesus had gone in to stay with a sinful man. Zacchaeus responded by offering to give half of his goods to the poor and to repay four times anything he had cheated people out of. Jesus sees this change and calls it salvation. Then he explains that he came to seek and to save what was lost.

For today: no one is too far away for Jesus to seek them out. If he comes into your life, the change shows up in practical things, such as honesty and generosity. And we should look at others with the same grace.
exp.13:29:
This verse ends the story of the man who wanted to build a tower. The people who see him say with mockery: "This man began to build and was not able to finish." The word "build" here means to construct, as in the verse above. The man laid the foundation, but he ran out of what he needed to finish the work.

Jesus speaks to large crowds who were following him (Luke 14:25). Just before this, he had told them that following him requires putting God above everything, even family, and taking up the cross. With this comparison he asks them to think carefully about the cost before they decide. He is not trying to frighten them, but to make them sincere.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we follow Jesus out of the enthusiasm of the moment or out of a considered decision. One practical way is to identify something specific that is hard for you to obey, and to ask God for strength to persevere in that, without relying only on your own feelings.
exp.23:2:
They entered the tomb and did not find the body of Jesus. "Found" is the word used in the verse above, and "prepared" describes the spices and oils the women had brought to anoint the body, but the tomb was empty.

Here Luke speaks as narrator. He tells of what the women who followed Jesus experienced early on the Sunday morning. They came with sadness, thinking of a funeral, not a resurrection. Seeing the stone moved and the tomb empty left them confused and frightened. Shortly afterward, two men in shining clothes explained what had happened.

For today: sometimes we look for God where we believe He should be, and we are thrown off when He acts differently. If something does not turn out as you expected, do not close yourself off to the confusion. Ask God to open your eyes, because He may be doing something greater than you imagine.
exp.7:19:
Someone told Jesus that his mother and brothers were outside and wanted to see him. The message was passed on to him, and the crowd was so large that they could not get close to him.

This message comes right after the parable of the sower and the warning to be careful how you listen. The one speaking is someone from the crowd, who reports to Jesus. The brothers mentioned here are, according to the most common reading, the sons of Mary and Joseph, although some Christian traditions understand them differently. Jesus uses the moment to teach that his true family is made up of those who hear the word of God and put it into practice. He does not look down on his family; he widens the meaning of what family is.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only hear the Word or also put it into practice. Choose one of Jesus' teachings today and carry it out with a concrete action.
exp.9:0:
After these things, Jesus appointed seventy other disciples, in addition to the twelve. He sent them out two by two, going ahead of him, into every city and place where he himself was about to go. The words "appointed" and "chose" are the ones used for "designated" here. The phrase "also other" means "other ones too." Some early manuscripts say seventy-two, and scholars do not agree on which reading is original.

Luke describes here how Jesus, on the way to Jerusalem, was preparing the people for his visit. He had already sent out the twelve, and now he involves more followers. His purpose was to announce the kingdom of God before he himself arrived.

For today: God works through ordinary people to share his message. You do not have to do it alone; look for a fellow believer or friend and serve together, preparing the way for others to come to know Jesus.
exp.1:22:
This verse explains why Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple. The phrase "opens the womb" refers to the firstborn son, the first male child. The words "shall be called holy to the Lord" mean that he would be set apart and dedicated to God.

Luke, who is narrating, quotes the law of Moses (Exodus 13:2, 12). According to that law, the firstborn belonged to God, a reminder of Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
