Luke shows that Jesus' family faithfully carried out what God commanded. The parents present the child in Jerusalem, and this prepares the meeting with Simeon.

For today: God deserves the first and the best of our lives. We can begin the day by offering him in prayer our time, our decisions, and our family, with an obedient heart like that of Mary and Joseph.
exp.23:19:
This verse tells how the chief priests and the rulers of the Jewish people handed Jesus over to be condemned to death, and how they crucified him.

The word "rulers" here means leaders or authorities. A "sentence of death" is a judgment that condemns someone to die.

The one speaking is Cleopas, one of two disciples walking to Emmaus on the same day as the resurrection. They do not yet recognize Jesus, who is walking with them. They tell him what happened with sadness and confusion, because they had hoped that Jesus would redeem Israel. Their account is true, but it lacks the most important thing: the resurrection.

For today: sometimes we see our situation as the disciples did, only with the pain and what went wrong. You can honestly tell Jesus about your discouragement, and trust that he is still walking with you, even when you do not yet understand how he will act.
exp.23:7:
This verse says that the women who went to the tomb remembered what Jesus had told them before. "And they remembered his words" means that his teachings came back to their minds, especially what he had announced about his death and resurrection.

The two angels speak to the women at the empty tomb. They ask them to remember what Jesus said in Galilee: that he would be handed over, crucified, and would rise on the third day. They had not understood this before. But when they heard it again, everything made sense, and they went out to tell the apostles.

For today: the Word of God that we have heard can come back to our hearts just when we need it most. It is worth keeping verses in memory and going over what Jesus taught. That way, when doubt or pain comes, his truth will sustain us and give us hope.
exp.17:10:
The Pharisee stands and prays, but the explanation notes that his prayer is really to himself rather than to God. Although he begins by giving thanks, he quickly compares himself with others: robbers, unjust people, adulterers, and even with the tax collector standing nearby. A tax collector was a man often looked down on by the people.

Jesus tells this parable to those who trusted in their own righteousness and looked down on everyone else. The Pharisees were respected for their strict religious life. Jesus does not criticize their praying, but the attitude of the heart: feeling superior and not needing mercy.

For today: when we pray, let us avoid comparing ourselves with others in order to feel better. Rather, let us ask God to show us our own hearts, and thank him for his mercy with humility, without looking down on anyone.
exp.1:12:
Suddenly, along with the angel who was speaking to the shepherds, a great multitude of angels appeared. The word "suddenly" means that it happened all at once. The "heavenly host" are the beings of heaven, like a great company of God's servants. They were praising God and began to speak.

The angel had just announced to some shepherds that the Savior had been born, Christ the Lord. Then many more angels joined together to celebrate. What they say is found in the next verse: a song of glory to God and peace on earth. Luke shows that all of heaven rejoices over this birth.

Today we can learn that the coming of Jesus deserves praise. When we think about what God has done for us, we can pause to thank him, sing, or give thanks out loud, just as the angels did, without waiting for a special day.
exp.1:47:
What it says: When Mary and Joseph saw Jesus in the temple, they were amazed. Mary speaks to him with concern and asks why he treated them this way. The phrase "with sorrow" means with distress, with a heavy heart. "Said to him" is the plain way to say it.

Context: Mary, the mother of Jesus, is the one speaking. He was twelve years old and had stayed behind in Jerusalem after the Passover feast. His parents had searched for him for three days. When they found him, they saw him listening to and asking questions of the teachers of the law. She expresses both the relief and the anguish of a mother. Luke calls Joseph his father, since Joseph acted as his father in the home.

For today: God understands both our worries and our desire to seek him. When something troubles us, we can speak honestly, without losing respect, and listen patiently to what God wants to teach us.
exp.5:44:
This verse says that what a person keeps stored in their heart is what comes out of them. Someone with a good heart produces good things, and someone with a bad heart produces bad things. The words we speak show what is inside.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to the crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has just been teaching about loving enemies and not judging others. He uses the image of the tree and its fruit to say that conduct reveals what is within. Then he asks why people call him "Lord" without obeying him, which shows that pretty words are not enough.

For today: when you notice that you speak with anger, mockery, or complaint, don't stop at simply controlling your tongue. Ask yourself what is in your heart, and ask God to fill it with his truth, by reading his Word and praying every day.
exp.1:36:
This verse says that Anna was a widow and was about eighty-four years old. The phrase "about" can be understood as meaning she was that age, or that she had been a widow for that long; the text allows both readings. She did not depart from the temple: she spent her time there. "Serving" means worshiping God, and "fastings" are days without eating in order to seek God.

Luke is the narrator. Anna, a prophetess of the tribe of Asher, was in the temple when Joseph and Mary presented the child Jesus. Luke shows her life of devotion so that we understand why she recognized the Messiah and spoke about him, as the following verses say, to those who were waiting for redemption.

For today: set aside fixed times to pray and to be with God, even if they are brief. Someone who seeks God with constancy learns to recognize what he is doing and can encourage others.
exp.3:29:
He says that Jesus passed through the midst of the angry crowd and went his way. The words "went his way" are the older form of the phrase "went away." Those who wanted to throw him off a cliff, that is, to push him over a precipice, were not able to stop him.

Luke tells what happened in Nazareth, the town where Jesus grew up. He had said in the synagogue that the words of Isaiah were being fulfilled in him, and he reminded them that God had blessed foreigners in the times of Elijah and Elisha. This offended the people. The text does not explain how he managed to leave: some think of a miraculous event, others of his authority holding them back. What is certain is that his hour had not yet come.

For today: opposition, even from people close to us, does not stop God's plan. We can go on calmly and in obedience, trusting that he cares for our path.
exp.22:13:
Pilate speaks to the chief priests, the rulers, and the people. He reminds them that they brought Jesus to him, accusing Him of "perverteth the people," that is, of turning people away from their way or stirring them up against the authority. He says that he examined Him before them and found no fault in Him concerning the things they accused Him of.

This happens at Jesus' trial. Pilate, the Roman governor, had already examined Jesus and sent Him to Herod. Now he declares publicly that there is no cause to condemn Him. Even so, he later gives in to the pressure of the crowd. Luke emphasizes the innocence of Jesus.

For today: Jesus was declared innocent, yet He suffered unjustly for us. Let us ask for courage to defend the truth and not to give in to fear or to the pressure of others when we know what is right.
exp.18:26:
The explanation says that the king in the story orders his enemies, those who did not want him to reign, to be brought before him and put to death in his presence. Killing them with a sword is what the verse describes, so the explanation comments on it directly. The word "here" is also used in the source phrasing, meaning "bring them here," which the verse above already conveys with "bring hither," so no separate note is needed.

Jesus is speaking within the parable of the ten minas. A nobleman travels to receive a kingdom, and his citizens reject him. Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem, and the people thought that the kingdom of God would appear right away (v. 11). The parable shows that there will be a return and a judgment. Many understand that the king represents Jesus and that the passage warns about the consequences of rejecting him. It is harsh, figurative language, and not an instruction for believers to use violence.

For today: do not put off your response to Christ. Examine whether you truly let him reign in your life, and faithfully serve what he has entrusted to you.
exp.6:43:
Jesus turns toward the woman, but he speaks to Simon: "Seest thou this woman?" He reminds him that when he entered Simon's house, Simon gave him no water for his feet, as was the custom of hospitality. She, on the other hand, washed his feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.

Jesus is having a meal in the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known as a sinner came in and showed a deep love for Jesus. Simon judged her in his heart. Jesus has just told the parable of two debtors who were forgiven, and now he compares Simon's attitude with hers.

Many times we look down on others and forget how much we ourselves have been forgiven. Today you can respond to God with sincere gratitude and treat with compassion those who feel they have failed.
exp.11:52:
This verse describes a household divided in every direction: fathers against sons, mothers against daughters, mothers-in-law against daughters-in-law, and the reverse. The mother-in-law here is the mother of one's husband or wife, and the daughter-in-law is the wife of one's son.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd. He does not say that he wants family quarrels. He explains that his call requires a decision, and that not everyone will respond in the same way. Therefore, even within the same house, some will follow him and others will reject him. It is a warning, not a wish.

For today: if following Jesus brings tension with your family, do not lose heart or respond with harshness. Be faithful, speak with respect, and love with patience, asking God for wisdom. And do not seek division out of pride; seek peace as far as it depends on you.
exp.20:1:
It says that Jesus, while watching the people, also saw a very poor widow putting in two small coins at the treasury. The treasury was the place in the temple where offerings were placed, like a kind of storehouse or donation boxes. The coins were of very little value.

The one speaking is the narrator, Luke, who tells what Jesus was seeing in the temple in Jerusalem. Jesus had just watched the rich giving their offerings, and now he fixes his attention on this humble woman. Afterward he will say that she gave more than all of them, because she gave out of her need and not out of what she had left over.

God does not measure an offering by the amount, but by the heart and the sacrifice. Today we can give simply and confidently what we have, without being ashamed that it seems small or comparing ourselves to others.
exp.11:41:
Jesus answers with a question: who is the faithful and wise steward? A steward was the servant in charge of managing his master's household. Here, the master places him over his household (his servants) to give them their portion of food, their meat, in due season, that is, at the right moment.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He had just told them to be ready, because the Son of man will come when they do not expect him. Peter asked whether the parable was only for them or for everyone. Jesus does not answer directly but describes the responsible servant. Some think it points especially to leaders, though the teaching serves everyone.

For today: whatever God has entrusted to you, whether your family, your work or your service in the church, look after it faithfully and in due season, without waiting for someone to watch over you.
exp.1:5:
This verse tells us that Joseph and Mary were still in Bethlehem when the time came for the birth. The word "deliver" in the verse means to give birth. The phrase "the days were accomplished" means that the normal time of the pregnancy had been completed.

Here Luke speaks, carefully telling in order what happened. Joseph and Mary had traveled from Nazareth because of the census ordered at that time. Luke shows that, even in the middle of a journey caused by a government order, what God had announced was being fulfilled: that the Messiah would come from David's family and be born in Bethlehem.

For today: God works with patience and in his own time, even in the midst of uncomfortable circumstances or things we cannot control. Today you can trust that your waiting is not forgotten. Ask him to help you obey with faith, one day at a time.
exp.7:22:
This verse tells us that Jesus fell asleep while the disciples were crossing the lake in a boat. Suddenly a strong windstorm came down on the lake. The phrase "filled with water" means that the boat was taking on water as they sailed, and "in jeopardy" means they were in danger of sinking.

Luke is the one telling the story. Shortly before this, Jesus had said that his true family is made up of those who hear the word of God and put it into practice. Then he suggested they cross to the other side of the lake. They obeyed, and even so the storm came. His sleep shows that he was a real man, tired, and the disciples quickly woke him, frightened.

Obeying God does not always spare us from storms. When one comes, we can go to Jesus without fear, because He is in our boat and hears our cry.
exp.3:32:
In the synagogue at Capernaum there was a man with a spirit of an unclean demon. The word "unclean" means impure, opposed to what is holy. That spirit cried out with a loud voice. So while Jesus was teaching, that evil presence broke in with a shout.

Luke tells us that Jesus had just arrived in Capernaum and was teaching with authority on a Sabbath. The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke, and he presents the first encounter of Jesus with an unclean spirit in this Gospel. He does this to show that the authority of his word not only amazed people, but also overcame evil.

For today: you do not need to fear dark forces if you are with Christ. When you feel that something is oppressing you, turn to Jesus in prayer and trust that his word has power and that he cares for you.
exp.3:17:
Jesus says that the Spirit of God is upon him and that he has anointed him, that is, set him apart and equipped him for a mission. That mission is to announce good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, to give sight to the blind, and to set free those who are oppressed. The word "bruised" means wounded or broken to pieces, and "preach" means to announce something out loud.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue of Nazareth, his hometown, on a Sabbath. He reads a passage from the prophet Isaiah (chapter 61, with a touch of 58:6) and then sits down. Everyone looks at him because he is about to say that this promise is being fulfilled in him. Scholars debate whether the liberty and the sight are only spiritual, only physical, or both; the Gospels show both.

Today, Jesus invites us to follow his heart: to draw near to those who are wounded, alone, or in need, and to bring them comfort and hope through words and concrete actions.
exp.13:12:
Jesus says that when someone prepares a banquet, they should invite the poor, the maimed (people with a crippled hand or arm), the lame, and the blind. These were people who were usually left out of important tables and who could not return the invitation.

Jesus is speaking in the house of a prominent Pharisee, on a Sabbath, while he watched how the guests looked for the best places. He had just taught that whoever exalts himself will be humbled. Now he speaks to the host: do not invite only to receive something in return. He teaches them to live with generosity, expecting the reward of God.

For today: think of someone who almost never receives an invitation, and offer them a plate of food or a place at your table, without expecting anything in return.
exp.13:11:
Jesus tells the man who had invited him to a meal that when he prepares a lunch or a dinner, he should not invite only his friends, his brothers, his relatives or his rich neighbors. The reason is that they would also invite him back, and so he would already have his repayment, his reward in return.

Jesus speaks in the house of an important Pharisee, on the Sabbath. He has just watched the guests looking for the best places. After teaching about humility, he now turns to the host and questions the habit of inviting only those who can repay the favor.

For today: the next time you invite someone, think also of the person who cannot return the kindness, such as a lonely neighbor, an elderly person, or someone in need. Make a concrete gesture of generosity without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:27:
This verse tells how Levi, a tax collector, left everything, got up, and followed Jesus. The phrase "left everything" means that he walked away from his job and his possessions. "Followed" means that he became a disciple of Jesus, walking with him.

Luke tells this right after Jesus healed a paralyzed man and the people were amazed. Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth, a job that many people looked down on, and calls him with just one word: "Follow me." Levi responds at once. Afterward he holds a banquet, and the Pharisees complain that Jesus eats with sinners. Many believe that Levi is the same person as Matthew, although Luke's text does not say so here.

For today: when Jesus calls you to obey him in something, do not put it off. Ask him what is holding you back from following him, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.4:26:
This verse tells that Jesus, after healing the paralytic, went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting where taxes were collected. A tax collector was a man who collected taxes for the Roman government. The table or booth where the money was collected is what is meant by the place where he sat. Jesus said to him, "Follow me," an invitation to become his disciple.

Jesus speaks here right after showing his power to heal and to forgive sins. Tax collectors were looked down on by many, since they were associated with Roman rule and with unfair charges. Even so, Jesus called him. Levi, who is the same man we know as Matthew, left everything and followed him, and later he held a banquet in his house.

For today: Jesus calls people whom others reject, and he also calls you. If you feel his invitation, respond with confidence and obedience, even when it costs you something you must leave behind.
exp.8:23:
Jesus says that whoever wants to hold on to his life, that is, to protect it and live only for himself, will end up losing it. On the other hand, whoever gives up his life for Jesus' sake will find it and save it. The phrase "whoever will" means "whoever wants," and "lose his life" can include dying for the faith or setting aside one's own plans to follow him.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, right after announcing that he will suffer, be rejected, die, and rise again. He explains that following him means denying oneself and taking up the cross every day. He then adds that it profits a person nothing to gain the whole world if he loses himself.

For today: ask yourself in what area you are holding on to your life out of fear or selfishness, and give it to Jesus with one concrete step, such as forgiving, serving, or staying faithful even when it costs you.
exp.0:31:
This verse says that Jesus will be great and that he will be called the Son of the Highest, that is, the Son of God. It also says that God will give him the throne of David, his ancestor. The phrase "in the presence of God" is the same as "before God," and "the Highest" is a name for God.

The angel Gabriel speaks to Mary, a young woman who did not expect anything like this. She is frightened, and the angel calms her and announces that she will have a son. That promise recalls what God had promised David: that one of his descendants would reign forever. The verses that follow say that his kingdom will have no end.

Today we can trust that Jesus truly reigns, even when the world seems disordered. If something frightens you, remember the words "do not be afraid": God keeps what he promises. Today you can hand him a worry and ask him to help you trust Jesus as your King.
exp.11:21:
Jesus tells his disciples not to live anxiously about what they are going to eat or about the clothes they are going to wear. The word "anxious" in the verse means overwhelmed and worried to excess. "Your life" here refers to what is needed to live from day to day.

Jesus has just told the parable of the rich fool, who stored up riches for himself and did not think about God. Now he turns to his disciples and shows the other side: just as one should not trust in riches, one should not live consumed by worry over the basics. Then he points to the ravens, which God feeds.

For today: when worry about money or the future steals your peace, pause, pray honestly, and entrust that burden to God. Then take the responsible step that is yours to take today, without carrying tomorrow's weight.
exp.5:47:
Jesus speaks of a man who builds a house. He dug deep, cleared away the loose soil, and laid the foundation on rock. When a flood came, the stream struck the house with force, but it could not shake it or move it, because it stood firm on the rock.

Jesus is teaching his disciples and the crowd. He has just asked why they call him "Lord, Lord" but do not do what he says. With this picture he explains that hearing him is not enough; his words must be put into practice.

For today: choose a teaching of Jesus that you already know, such as forgiving or helping someone, and put it into practice this week. When trials come, that simple obedience can hold you steady.
exp.7:45:
Jesus says that someone touched him on purpose, because he sensed that power had gone out of him. Here "power" means a healing force. Jesus distinguishes between the crowd that merely surrounded him and a person who touched him with a purpose.

Jesus is on his way to Jairus's house, and a crowd presses in on him from every side. A woman who has suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, finding no cure, touches the edge of his garment and is made well. Peter does not understand the question, since there are many people around. Jesus does not seek to scold her but to bring her into an open relationship with him. How exactly that transfer of power happens is not explained in the text.

It is possible to be near Jesus without coming to him in faith. Today we can pray with simple trust, even when we feel weak or overlooked. He does notice the one who seeks him with a sincere heart.
exp.9:19:
Jesus tells his disciples not to put their greatest joy in the fact that the evil spirits obey them. The phrase "are subject to you" means that they submit to them. "Rejoice" here means "be glad." What should move them most is that their names are written in heaven, that is, that they belong to God and have a place with him.

Jesus speaks with the seventy disciples who have just returned from a mission. They come back happy because even the demons obeyed them in the name of Jesus. He does not dismiss that power, but he leads them to look at something greater: the salvation that God gives. Shortly after, Jesus himself rejoices and praises the Father.

For today: even though God may use us and we see good results, our greatest joy is not in what we achieve, but in God knowing us and having received us as his own.
exp.22:10:
The explanation says that Herod and his soldiers looked down on Jesus and mocked him. They dressed him in a splendid robe, probably to make fun of the idea that he was a king, and sent him back to Pilate.

Luke tells that Pilate sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, because Jesus was a Galilean. Herod questioned him at length, but Jesus kept silent, while the religious leaders accused him insistently. Herod was offended and mocked him. Afterward, Herod and Pilate were reconciled, although before they had been enemies.

For today: Jesus' silence reminds us that not everyone seeks the truth sincerely. When someone only wants to mock, we are not obliged to defend ourselves. We can respond with calm and trust in God, as Jesus did.
exp.18:18:
This verse tells that the lord of the story speaks to the second servant, the one who earned five minas. He gives him authority over five cities as his reward.

Jesus is telling the parable of the minas, near Jerusalem. A nobleman goes away far to receive a kingdom and leaves money with his servants to put to work. When he returns, he rewards each one according to what he did. Jesus tells it because people thought the kingdom of God would appear right away (v. 11).

For today: God values faithfulness, not comparison. This servant earned less than the first, but he was also rewarded. Serve with what God has given you, whether much or little, and trust that he sees your effort.
exp.13:28:
It says that someone who starts to build a tower, lays the foundation, and then cannot finish it, is left open to everyone who sees it mocking him. The source's glosses on individual words are not included here, since the reader's verse uses different wording.

Jesus speaks to the large crowds who were following him. He has just said that being his disciple means carrying the cross, that is, being willing to suffer and to put God above everything. With this comparison, he invites people to think seriously before committing, not to frighten them, but so that the decision is made honestly.

For today: before saying "yes" to following Jesus, or to a commitment of faith, reflect sincerely on what it involves. Pray, ask God for strength, and trust that he will help you persevere to the end.
exp.10:12:
This verse compares a human father with God. If parents, though imperfect ("evil"), know how to give good things to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. "Gifts" are what is meant by the word rendered "gifts" in the verse, and "ask" is the word used in the verse itself.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, after teaching them the Lord's Prayer. He explains how to pray with confidence and persistence. The examples of bread, fish and egg show that no careful father would deceive or harm his child. Then the account shifts to a scene where Jesus casts out a demon, and some criticize him.

For today: pray simply and with confidence, like a child speaking with his Father. You can ask him each day for his Spirit to guide you, comfort you and give you strength, knowing that God is good and wants to give you what you truly need.
exp.19:19:
The explanation says that the religious leaders kept Jesus under close watch. Since they did not dare to arrest him for fear of the people, they sent spies who pretended to be honest people. They were looking for a way to catch him. To watch him secretly, and to catch him in something he said that they could use against him, is what they wanted. The phrase about his authority refers to the power of the Roman governor.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened after the parable of the wicked tenants. The chief priests and the scribes understood that Jesus was speaking about them. Instead of reflecting on it, they looked for a way to silence him. Their plan was to get him into political trouble with Rome. The question about paying tribute to Caesar, which comes next, was the trap.

For today: appearances can deceive. We can use pleasant words and still have a crooked heart. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that our questions seek the truth and not the winning of an argument. And when the Word confronts us, let us respond with humility instead of hardening ourselves.
exp.12:27:
Here Jesus speaks of a place of pain and sorrow: "weeping and gnashing of teeth" expresses weeping, anger, and despair. Some will see Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets inside the kingdom of God, while they themselves are thrust out, that is, cast outside.

Jesus is responding to someone who asked him whether few people are saved. He speaks to people who heard him teach and even ate with him, but did not follow him from the heart. He warns them that the door is narrow and that being near Jesus is not enough. He then adds that people from all over the world will enter the kingdom.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only know things about Jesus or whether we truly trust him and follow him. Living close to religious things does not replace a sincere faith and a life that obeys his word.
exp.14:18:
It says the young man feels unworthy to go on being called a son. For that reason he plans to ask his father to treat him as one of his "hired servants," that is, a hired worker who is paid by the day.

The one speaking is the younger son in the parable Jesus tells. He has already spent his inheritance and gone hungry, and he has come to his senses, that is, he has recognized his mistake. He is rehearsing what he will say to his father. Notice that in the story, when he arrives, the father receives him with embraces, and the Bible does not say that the son gets to ask for the hired-servant request.

For today: when you fail, return to God sincerely, without excuses. You do not need to earn forgiveness; God receives you with love.
exp.17:7:
Jesus says that God will vindicate his chosen ones quickly, that is, those who trust in him. The word "speedily" means "quickly" or "without delay." Then Jesus asks a question that invites reflection: when he returns, will he find faith on the earth?

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, at the end of the parable of the persistent widow and the unjust judge. He wanted to teach them to pray always and not lose heart. If even a wicked judge ends up doing justice, how much more will God, who is good, do so. Some understand "speedily" to mean that God acts without delay when the time comes; others understand it to mean that his answer is certain.

Today, when the wait grows long and prayer seems to receive no answer, keep praying with confidence. Keeping faith alive, day after day, is a way of preparing ourselves for the return of Christ.
exp.5:29:
This verse says we should give to anyone who asks of us, and that if someone takes away something that belongs to us, we should not press them to return it. The words "á" and "vuelvas á pedir" are older forms; today we would say "a" and "no se lo exijas de nuevo," which in this verse correspond to the English words "ask" and "again."

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Shortly before, he told them to love their enemies. Here he describes how that love is lived out: with generosity and without revenge. Many scholars understand this as an attitude of the heart rather than a literal rule for every case, while others apply it more directly.

For today: the next time someone asks you for help or owes you something, ask yourself how you can respond with kindness and not with resentment. Ask God for wisdom to give generously and for peace.
exp.16:1:
It would be better for someone to have a millstone, a heavy stone used for grinding grain, hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea than to make one of these little ones stumble. To "offend" means to lead someone into sin or to cause them to stumble in their faith. The "little ones" may be children or simple, humble believers; the text does not specify.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He warns them that stumbling blocks are unavoidable in this world, but that whoever causes them carries a great responsibility. With this very strong image he shows how much God values those who are weak.

Today, watch your words and your example, especially before children and new believers. Ask yourself whether what you say or do brings them closer to God or gets in their way. And if you fail, seek to make it right with humility.
exp.0:39:
This verse tells that Mary arrived at the house of Zacharias and greeted Elisabeth. It is a simple gesture of courtesy and affection. The words "entered" and "greeted" are clear; just note that the verse itself uses "entered" and "saluted" as its key action words.

Luke, who narrates, tells how the angel had just announced to Mary that she would have a son by the work of God. She accepted in faith and hurried to visit her relative Elisabeth, who was also expecting a baby. Christian tradition places this town in the region of Judah, though the text does not give its name.

For today: after receiving great news, Mary sought companionship and support. We can do the same: visit someone of faith, greet them with love, and share what God is doing in our lives.
exp.0:56:
What it says: The time came for Elisabeth to give birth, and she had a son.

Context: Here Luke speaks as the narrator. He has just recounted Mary's song and her stay of about three months with Elisabeth. Now he returns to Elisabeth's story. She was older and had not had children. Her son will be John the Baptist. Luke shows that God fulfilled what he had promised through the angel to Zechariah.

For today: God keeps his promises in his own time, even when it seems late to us. If you are waiting for an answer, keep praying and trusting. The waiting does not mean that God has forgotten you.
exp.18:34:
The passage tells us that the two disciples brought the young donkey to Jesus. The phrase "they brought him" means the same thing as the verse's wording, and a young donkey is a colt, a foal of a donkey. They placed their garments, that is, their cloaks or outer robes, on the animal to serve as a saddle, and seated Jesus on top of it.

Context: Luke tells of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, shortly before his death. Jesus had sent two disciples for the colt, and they answered the owners that the Lord needed it. Many understand that this gesture, a king riding on a donkey and not on a warhorse, recalls the prophecy in Zechariah 9:9 about a humble king. Luke does not quote it here, but the scene fits with it.

For today: The disciples gave what they had, even their clothing, to serve Jesus without seeking attention for themselves. Today we can ask ourselves what simple thing we have, such as time, a talent, or an act of help, we can place humbly at his service.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that Jesus looked up and saw some rich people putting their offerings into the treasury. The treasury was the place in the temple where offerings and money were kept.

The narrator here is Luke, who tells what Jesus was doing. This happens in Jerusalem, in the temple, shortly before his arrest. Jesus had just been teaching the people, and now he pauses to watch how they were giving. The verse sets up the contrast with the poor widow who appears next.

For today: God looks not only at how much we give, but at the heart with which we give. Before you give your time, your money, or your help, ask yourself whether you are doing it sincerely and with love, without seeking applause.
exp.16:11:
It says that Jesus was entering a small village when ten men with leprosy came out to meet him. They stood at a distance, that is, far off. The phrase "from afar" is about the distance they kept, and the word "village" refers to a small town, and the phrase "came to meet him" means they went out to greet him.

Luke tells us that Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, passing between Samaria and Galilee. The law of Moses required that lepers live apart and not come close to other people (Leviticus 13:45-46). That is why they stop at a distance. Afterward they will cry out asking for mercy, and Jesus will heal them while they obey his word.

Today we can learn that we should not stay silent out of shame or from feeling unworthy. Even if we feel far away, we can call out to Jesus sincerely, trusting that he listens and has compassion.
exp.22:54:
They say the women who had accompanied Jesus from Galilee followed after Joseph of Arimathea. They saw the tomb and observed how the body of Jesus was laid in it.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened after the death of Jesus. It was the day of preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin. Luke emphasizes that the women were eyewitnesses: they knew where the tomb was and how the body had been placed. This prepares the account of the resurrection, when they would return to that same place.

For today: these women were faithful even in the saddest moment, when it seemed that everything had ended. We can imitate them by staying close to Jesus in difficult days, serving with love, and waiting on God even when we do not understand what is coming.
exp.6:44:
Jesus reminds Simon that when he arrived at his house, he did not receive the greeting of welcome with a kiss, something common among guests. Instead, that woman has not stopped kissing his feet since he came in.

Jesus is speaking in the house of Simon, a Pharisee who invited him to eat. A woman known for her sinful life came in weeping and honored him with great affection. Simon judged both her and Jesus unfavorably, so Jesus told them a story about two debtors and compared the attitudes of the two.

For today: do not minimize what God has done for you. When we remember his forgiveness, love and gratitude arise naturally. Today, thank God sincerely and in concrete ways.
exp.20:13:
Jesus tells his disciples to settle it in their hearts not to worry beforehand about what they will answer when they are accused. "Settle it therefore in your hearts" means to make the decision firmly within yourselves. This is not a call to be careless, but to avoid living in anxiety over preparing a defense.

Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives, before his crucifixion, warning of what would come. His followers would be arrested, brought before synagogues, prisons, kings, and governors because of their faith. He makes clear that this situation would be an opportunity to bear witness, and in the following verse he promises to give them words and wisdom.

For today: when you face pressure because of your faith, or a difficult conversation, pray and trust that God will guide you. Prepare yourself through a life of prayer and of the Word, but do not let the fear of failing paralyze you.
exp.2:7:
John the Baptist says that true repentance must be seen in everyday life, just as a tree is known by its fruit. He also warns that being a descendant of Abraham is not enough. He says "produce fruit" in the sense of "bring forth" real results, and that God is able to raise up children of Abraham even from stones.

John speaks to crowds who were going out to the Jordan to be baptized. Many trusted in their Jewish heritage as if it would shield them from God's judgment. That is why he calls them a brood of vipers and urges them to truly change. The people respond by asking what they must do, which shows that his message reached them.

For today: do not rest on your church, your family, or your spiritual history. Ask God to show you one concrete change, such as forgiving, being honest, or helping someone, and begin this week.
exp.11:26:
Jesus invites us to look closely at the lilies of the field. They grow without working or weaving clothes, and yet Solomon, the king famous for his wealth, was never dressed in such beauty. "Consider" means to observe and think calmly. "Toil" here refers to working, and "spin" to making thread to weave cloth. Scholars are not sure exactly which flower the "lily" was.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just warned against greed, and now he calls them not to live anxious about food and clothing. Earlier he said that worry cannot add even a single cubit to a person's life. Then he concludes that if God clothes the grass this way, he will care far more for his children.

For today: when worry about money or the future troubles you, stop for a moment, look at something in creation, and pray, handing that burden to God, trusting his care while you do what is yours to do.
exp.21:57:
This verse tells of Peter's second denial. Shortly after the first, another person sees him and says, "You are also one of them," meaning one of Jesus's followers. Peter answers, "Man, I am not." The word "man" here is simply a way of addressing someone, like saying "friend" or "sir."

Jesus had just been arrested and taken to the house of the high priest. Peter had followed him at a distance and sat down by the fire in the courtyard. There, surrounded by people, he became afraid of being recognized. Earlier, Jesus had told him that he would deny him three times before the rooster crowed, and now it was all coming true.

For today: all of us can fail out of fear, especially when it is hard to show our faith. Peter was not written off; Jesus forgave him and restored him. If we have failed, we can return to Christ with humility, and ask him for the courage to be honest about our faith.
exp.16:22:
Jesus warns his disciples that there will be people who say, "Look, here is the Messiah!" or "He is over there!" The phrase "here he is" is explained as "look, there he is." He clearly asks them not to go after those voices or follow them.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the Pharisees that the kingdom of God is among you, since the King himself was present. He announces difficult times, when they will long to see him again and there will be confusion. He gives them a sign so they will not be deceived: his return will be visible and obvious, like lightning, not something hidden that only a few discover.

For today: if someone claims to have Christ only in their group or announces dates and secret signs, be wary. It is better to remain firm in Scripture, in prayer, and in a simple faith, trusting that Jesus will keep his promise.
exp.0:44:
It says that the woman who believed is happy, or blessed, because what the Lord promised her will indeed take place. The sentence that explains the word "blessed" means that she is blessed and very happy. The sentence explaining "will be fulfilled" means that what was promised will become reality.

Here Elizabeth speaks, filled with the Holy Spirit, when Mary comes to visit her. Elizabeth recognizes that Mary will be the mother of the Lord, and she congratulates her because she believed the angel's message, even though it seemed impossible. After this, Mary responds with her song of praise to God.

For today: when God has shown you something in his Word and you do not yet see it fulfilled, trust him. You can pray, wait patiently, and keep obeying, knowing that he is faithful to what he promises.
exp.0:16:
John, the son who would be born to Zechariah, would go before the Lord with the same spirit and power as the prophet Elijah. His mission would be to reconcile fathers with their children and to bring rebellious people to think with the wisdom of the righteous. He would prepare a people ready to receive the Lord.

The angel Gabriel speaks with Zechariah, an elderly priest, while he was serving in the temple. He tells him that his wife Elisabeth will have a son. This statement echoes the promise of the prophet Malachi about a messenger who would come before the Lord. Zechariah doubts, and so he asks how he can know this will happen.

For today: God continues to work to heal broken relationships. Today you can take a step toward reconciliation with a family member, with humility and patience, and so prepare your heart for the Lord.
exp.7:5:
This verse describes another part of the seed that fell on the rock. It sprang up, but it dried out quickly because it had no moisture. In the original text the idea is rocky ground, with little soil, where the roots cannot reach deep.

Jesus speaks to a large crowd that gathered from several towns. He teaches them with a parable, a simple story with a spiritual message. Later in this same chapter, he explains that the seed is the word of God and that this ground represents those who receive it with joy, but do not take root and fall away when the test comes.

For today: it is not enough to be moved when you hear the Word. Ask that it take root in you. Read the Bible consistently, pray, and seek a community of faith, so that when difficulties come your faith has something to hold on to.
exp.13:0:
It says that on a sabbath Jesus went in to eat at the house of a leading Pharisee, that is, an important leader of that religious group. To share a meal is what is meant here. The verse says they were watching him closely, waiting to catch him in a mistake.

Luke tells this as the narrator. Jesus accepts the invitation, but those present do not receive him with sincere friendship, but with suspicion. In the verses that follow, a man with dropsy (swelling caused by a buildup of fluid) appears, and Jesus asks whether it is right to heal on the sabbath. This shows that the watching had to do with how he kept the law of the day of rest.

For today: sometimes we are watched or judged harshly. Jesus did not respond with fear or anger, but by doing good with clarity. Let us pray that our hearts will not be among those who watch in order to accuse, but among those who seek to help.
exp.15:19:
This verse introduces a beggar named Lazarus. He was lying at the gate of the rich man, his body covered with sores, that is, open wounds on the skin. Being "laid" there means he was stretched out, without strength to move. It is an image of extreme poverty and suffering.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and also to Pharisees who were mocking him, since they loved money (Luke 16:14). He tells this story to show how the rich man lived in luxury while a poor man suffered a few steps from his house. Some believe it is a parable; others, a true account. Lazarus is the only character with a name in Jesus' parables.

Today we can ask ourselves who lies at our gate without our having seen them. God invites us to notice the needy person near us and to help them with something concrete.
exp.0:79:
John, the son of Zacharias and Elisabeth, says the text, grew and became strong in spirit. He lived in lonely places, which the text calls the wilderness, until the day came for him to make himself known publicly to the people of Israel.

This verse closes the account of John's birth. Before this, his father Zacharias, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied, praising God for sending the Savior. The narrator, Luke, now summarizes John's childhood. He does not say in detail what John did in the wilderness; some think it was a time of preparation alone with God, but the text does not explain it.

For today: not every time of preparation is visible or quick. God can shape your character in silence, in simple or hidden stages. Trust that this time is not wasted, and seek to be strengthened in spirit through prayer, the Word, and patience.
exp.0:74:
He says that God delivers us from our enemies so that we may serve him in holiness and righteousness before him, that is, with a life set apart for God and upright in how we treat others. And this is not only in special moments, but all the days of our life. Living before him suggests living aware that God sees us.

The one speaking is Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, filled with the Holy Spirit. He is praising God because God fulfills the promise he made to Abraham and sends a Savior. The verses that follow speak of his son, who would prepare the way of the Lord. The freedom God gives has a purpose: to serve him.

For today: each morning you can ask God to help you live that day with integrity, being honest in your work and just in your home, remembering that salvation is not only getting out of trouble, but walking close to God every day.
exp.3:24:
Jesus reminds them that in the time of the prophet Elijah there were many widows in Israel. Then it did not rain for three years and six months, and there was a very great famine throughout the whole land. The word "fué" is an old spelling of "was," and the phrase "great famine" means "very severe hunger."

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Nazareth, his hometown. The people wanted to see there the miracles he had done in Capernaum. He answers them with examples from Israel's history: God at times blessed people from outside, while many of his own people were left without receiving. With this he shows them that God acts freely and that his grace is not earned by having a good background.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we take for granted that we know God. He draws near to those who receive him with humility and faith, not to those who think they have a right to his favors. Today, open your heart simply to what God wants to say to you.
exp.6:2:
This verse tells us that a centurion, a Roman officer, heard about Jesus. Because his servant was very sick, he sent some elders of the Jews, that is, respected leaders of the community. They were to ask Jesus to come and heal his servant. The phrase "sent unto him" means "sent to them."

Jesus had just finished teaching the people and entered Capernaum. Luke explains that the centurion valued his servant highly. Being a foreigner, he asked for help through Jewish elders. Later they will say that he loved their nation and had built a synagogue.

When someone we love suffers, we can come to Jesus with confidence. We can also ask other believers to pray with us and for us, without feeling ashamed of needing help.
exp.6:14:
This verse tells that the young man who had died sat up and began to speak. Then Jesus gave him back to his mother. "He sat up" means that he sat up or got up. The phrase "gave him" refers to Jesus handing him back to his mother.

Jesus is entering the town of Nain and comes upon a funeral. The young man is the only son of a widow, so she is left alone and without support. The Lord has compassion, tells her not to weep, touches the coffin, and commands the young man to rise. Luke thus shows Jesus' compassion and his authority over death.

For today: Jesus notices the pain others do not see and draws near. We can bring him our sorrows with confidence, and also imitate him by paying attention to someone who suffers in silence, through a visit, a phone call, or an act of help.
exp.17:41:
Jesus says to the blind man: "Receive thy sight: thy faith hath saved thee." The word "saved" here can mean healed, rescued, or both. It is like saying: "Your trust in me has brought you healing and life."

Jesus speaks with a blind beggar who was sitting by the road near Jericho. He had cried out for mercy, even though the people tried to silence him. When Jesus asked him what he wanted, he asked to see. His faith showed in that he did not give up and trusted that Jesus could help him. After being healed, he followed Jesus and praised God.

For today: faith is not having everything figured out, but coming to Jesus with sincerity and telling him what you truly need. Even when others discourage you, keep crying out to him with confidence.
exp.11:53:
Jesus reminds the crowd of something they already knew how to do. When they saw a cloud coming from the west, they said, "It's going to rain." And so it happened.

The word "crowds" here refers to the large groups of people gathered around him, and "west" is the direction from which the sun sets.

Jesus speaks to the crowd after teaching his disciples. He has just said that his coming would bring division, even within families. From the west, clouds heavy with rain would come in from the Mediterranean Sea. With this common example, he shows them that they could read the weather, but not what God was doing among them.

For today: let us not neglect attention to the spiritual. If we pay attention to the news, to our work, or to the weather, we should also stop to listen to God and ask ourselves what he is asking of us today.
exp.22:31:
This verse says that along with Jesus they were leading two other men to be executed. The word "malefactors" refers to people who had committed serious crimes. "To be put to death" means they were going to be executed. The spellings "also" and "to" in the source are old-style spellings from the 1909 edition, so no comment is needed on them.

The one who tells this is Luke, the author of the gospel, who follows Jesus on his way to the cross. Shortly before, Jesus had warned the women of Jerusalem about difficult times. Luke mentions the two men to show that Jesus was treated as just one more among the criminals. This matches what Isaiah 53:12 says about the servant of the Lord: he was counted with the transgressors.

For today: Jesus did not keep his distance from broken and guilty people, but walked beside them. If you feel unworthy, you can draw near to God with confidence, and also treat with compassion those whom others despise.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that this first census, or registration of the population, was taken when Cyrenius was governor of Syria. The word "taxing" in the King James Version is an older term for a census: counting and listing the names of the people.

Luke is the writer. He is a careful historian who wants to place the birth of Jesus in a real time and place, under the emperor Augustus. Scholars debate how to fit this detail together with other historical sources about Cyrenius, and there are several possible explanations. What is clear is Luke's purpose: Jesus was not born in a story, but within human history.

For today: God acts in specific times and in the middle of decisions made by governments that seem far away. If today you feel trapped by circumstances you cannot control, remember that God can work right there, in the ordinary.
exp.15:18:
Jesus begins a story about a rich man. "Purple" was clothing dyed with a very expensive dye, and "fine linen" was a soft and costly cloth. "Feasting in splendor" means he held lavish parties every day, holding nothing back.

Jesus is speaking here to his disciples, and Pharisees are also present, whom Luke describes as lovers of money (16:14). Earlier he taught about serving God or money. This story continues that theme. Many understand it as a parable, though some think it may have been a real account; the text does not make this clear.

For today: wealth is not the problem in itself, but living so focused on our own comfort that we stop seeing the person in need who is at our door. Ask yourself today: whom can I help?
exp.23:20:
The explanation says that two of the disciples had hoped that Jesus would be the one who would free Israel. The source's term for "free" (rescue or liberate) is not used in the verse above, so that sentence is deleted in favour of the plain meaning. They tell with sadness that it is already three days since the crucifixion, and their hopes seem broken.

Two followers of Jesus are walking toward Emmaus. They do not yet recognize that the stranger walking with them is the risen Jesus. They explain what happened in Jerusalem. Many Jews of that time expected a deliverer who would lead them out of oppression, and so the cross seemed to them a failure. They had heard the report of the empty tomb, but they did not yet understand it.

For today: when things do not turn out as we expected, we can trust that God is still at work, even when we do not see it. Let us bring our disappointment to Jesus honestly; He walks beside us.
exp.2:0:
This verse places in time and place the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry. It names the emperor Tiberius Caesar and several local rulers. A tetrarch was a regional ruler who governed part of the territory under Roman authority. The phrase "in the fifteenth year of the reign" refers to the period during which Tiberius held power. Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea.

Luke, the author, writes as a careful historian who wants to give his readers certainty. By naming these rulers, he shows that what he recounts took place in real history, not in legend. The verses that follow say that, in the midst of these powers, the word of God came to John in the desert.

For today: God acts in concrete history, including in times of unjust or powerful governments. You can trust that He is still at work in your own time and situation, and that His word reaches those who are willing to listen, even in humble places.
exp.6:41:
Jesus continues telling a short story. Two men owed money to a moneylender, and neither of them had a way to pay. The moneylender, out of pure kindness, canceled the debt for both of them. Then Jesus asks: "Which of them will love him most?" The one who lends is the creditor, and those who owe are the debtors.

Jesus is eating at the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known for her sinful life came in weeping and washed Jesus' feet. Simon was thinking poorly of her and of Jesus. With this parable, Jesus shows Simon, with great patience, how God sees forgiveness and love.

For today: we all need God's forgiveness, though we do not all notice it in the same way. Remembering how much we have been forgiven helps us love God with gratitude and treat others with mercy, without looking down on them.
exp.0:22:
The explanation says that when the days of Zechariah's service at the temple were over, he went back to his house. The verse uses the word "ministration" for his service as a priest, and the earlier forms of "came to pass" and "came" are older ways of writing those words.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. Zechariah had just received a visit from an angel who announced the birth of John. Because he doubted, he became unable to speak. Even so, he did not abandon his turn: he carried it through to the end, although he could no longer talk. Afterward he returned home, and there God's promise to him and his wife Elisabeth began to be fulfilled.

For today: sometimes God surprises us in the middle of our daily work. We can remain faithful in what is ours to do, even with doubts or limitations, trusting that God keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.10:45:
Jesus says "Woe to you" to the teachers of the law, that is, the experts in the law of Moses. He rebukes them for piling burdens on the people so heavy that no one could carry them, while they themselves won't lift a finger to touch them. "Woe" expresses warning and sorrow, not only anger.

Jesus is eating at the house of a Pharisee and speaks frankly. One of the teachers of the law feels insulted, and Jesus answers by addressing them as well. The "burdens" most likely refer to added rules and traditions that made life with God exhausting, without helping people keep them.

For today: if you teach, lead, or advise others, be careful not to require of them what you do not practice yourself. Help with humility, set the example, and walk alongside others with compassion, not with heaviness or pride.
exp.7:25:
The explanation says that Jesus and his disciples crossed the lake by boat and arrived in the region of the Gadarenes, on the opposite side from Galilee. Sailed across here means crossing by boat. The phrase "over against" in this verse means "facing" or "on the other side." Some ancient manuscripts read "Gerasenes" or "Gergesenes," so the exact name of the area is debated.

Luke is the one narrating. The disciples had just lived through a storm and seen Jesus calm it with his word. Now they arrive in territory that is mostly non-Jewish, and there Jesus will meet a man tormented by demons. It is as if Luke were saying: the one who commands the sea also has authority over evil.

For today: after a storm, Jesus does not only lead us to rest; sometimes he leads us to serve others. Trust that the one who sustained you in the crisis also accompanies you into the next task.
exp.2:1:
Luke says that, while Annas and Caiaphas were high priests, God spoke to John, the son of Zacharias, while he was in the wilderness. "The word of God came" means that God gave him a direct message. Speaking of two high priests is unusual, because normally there was only one; some think Annas kept great influence even though Caiaphas held the office.

Luke is the narrator. Before this, he names rulers of the world and of Israel to show that this happened in real history. With so much political and religious power in place, God did not speak from a palace or from the temple, but to a man in the wilderness. In this way the ministry of John begins, the one who prepares the way for Jesus.

For today: God does not depend on places or titles to speak. Seek times of silence, open his Word, and listen with humility, ready to obey.
exp.0:68:
This verse says that God has raised up a "horn of salvation" for us in the family of King David, his servant. In the Bible, the horn of an animal was a symbol of strength and power. So "horn of salvation" means a mighty savior. The word "raised up" means that God caused him to come forth or appear.

Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, is speaking. He is filled with the Holy Spirit and praises God because God has begun to fulfill his promises. Many understand that this savior is Jesus, a descendant of David, whose birth was near. Zechariah remembers that God had already announced this through the prophets.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a very long time. When you feel weak or are waiting for an answer, trust that he remains faithful. Praise him today for the salvation he offers in Jesus.
exp.11:29:
This verse says that people who do not know God spend their lives running after food, drink, and material things. But those who are children of God have a Father who already knows what they need.

"Peoples of the world" refers to the nations that do not know the God of Israel. "Seek" means they pursue these things with anxiety.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the story of a rich man who thought only about his possessions. He wants to free them from worry about their daily provision. He reminds them that God cares even for the birds and the flowers, and that they are worth far more to Him.

For today: when you worry about money or the future, pray a simple prayer and hand that burden over to God. Then take the next responsible step, trusting that your Father knows you and takes care of you.
exp.9:31:
This verse tells how a Levite, that is, a man from the tribe of Levi who helped in the service of the temple, arrived at the place where the wounded man was. He saw him, but he passed by on the other side, that is, he changed his path so as not to come near. Just like the priest before him, he did nothing to help him.

Jesus is telling a parable. A teacher of the law had asked him what to do to inherit eternal life, and then wanted to know who his neighbor was. Jesus answers with this story. The Levite and the priest were very religious people, and that makes their indifference stand out all the more. Then a Samaritan appears who does help.

For today: it is not enough to believe or to do religious things if we ignore the person who suffers near us. Today you can ask yourself whom you have seen in need and not stopped to help, and take one concrete step, even a small one.
exp.16:32:
Jesus says that whoever clings to his life and tries to secure it at all costs will end up losing it. On the other hand, whoever gives it up will save it.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about the day when the Son of Man will come. First he tells them not to go back for their belongings, and he reminds them of Lot's wife, who looked back (Genesis 19:26). Then he says that some will be taken and others left. Some interpret this as judgment and others as rescue; the text does not fully settle the question. The central idea is not to be attached to the things of this world.

For today: examine what it costs you to let go, whether money, comfort, or pride. Ask God for help to trust Him more than these things, and take one concrete step of surrender this week.
exp.8:27:
Luke says that about eight days after these words, Jesus took Peter, John, and James (also called Jacob) up a mountain to pray. The phrase "about eight days" is approximate. The verse above says "about an eight days," and the word "about" here means roughly, not exact.

Jesus had just spoken to his disciples about following him, taking up the cross, and not being ashamed of him. He had also promised that some would see the kingdom of God. What follows is the transfiguration, and many think it is a glimpse of that glory. Luke does not name the mountain, and it cannot be known for certain which one it was.

For today: before and after important moments, Jesus made a practice of prayer. If you are facing a hard decision or a difficult teaching, set aside a quiet time to pray. Do it with confidence, and perhaps with someone close to you in the faith.
exp.17:18:
Jesus asks an important man: "Why do you call me good?" Then he says that no one is good except God. Here "ruler" means a leader or official. A respectful greeting was "Good teacher."

A wealthy leader asks Jesus how to gain eternal life. Jesus does not deny being God; rather, he makes the man think about what the word "good" truly means. Some believe Jesus is inviting him to recognize who he is; others believe he is leading him to see that no person reaches perfect goodness on their own. Earlier, Jesus had spoken about receiving the kingdom like a child, with humility.

For today: let us not trust in our good conduct to feel secure before God. Let us humbly ask him to be the one who defines what is good, and let us follow him sincerely, not merely with kind words.
exp.17:37:
What it says: A blind man cries out loudly. The phrase "cried out" means he called out or shouted aloud. He calls Jesus "Son of David," a title for the Messiah, that is, the king God promised. And he asks for mercy, meaning compassion and help that he cannot earn or obtain on his own.

Context: The one speaking is a blind beggar who was sitting by the road near Jericho. Hearing that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he did not let the opportunity go. The crowd told him to be quiet, but he shouted all the more. His cry shows faith: he recognizes who Jesus is and trusts that he can help him.

For today: When you face a need you cannot solve, come to Jesus with sincerity and without shame. Speak plainly, ask for his mercy, and do not lose heart if others discourage you. He listens.
exp.11:49:
Jesus says that he has a baptism to be baptized with. "But" in the verse means "but," and "straitened" means that he feels a great pressure or distress. He speaks of a burden that weighs on him until what awaits him is fulfilled.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, on the way to Jerusalem. Here "baptism" is not the rite of water, but an image of his suffering and death on the cross, as if he were submerged in pain. He knows that his mission will bring fire, that is, judgment and division, and that its fulfillment passes through the cross. Some understand this in a somewhat different way, but most see it as his passion.

Jesus did not flee from the suffering that fulfilled God's will, and he truly felt its weight. Today we can be honest with God when something distresses us, and still remain faithful, trusting that he walks with us until his purpose is fulfilled.
exp.0:75:
Verse 76 says that John, the newborn child, will be called "prophet of the Highest", that is, a spokesman for God. He will go before the Lord to "prepare his ways", that is, to make the road ready so that someone can arrive.

Zechariah, John's father, speaks, filled with the Holy Spirit. He has just recovered his voice after months of being unable to speak, and he praises God for saving his people. Now he turns to his son and announces his mission: to prepare the people to receive the Lord, who brings forgiveness and mercy, as the following verses say.

For today: we can imitate John in small ways. Prepare the way for Christ in your family or workplace with humility, speaking the truth and showing a life that points to Jesus, not to yourself.
exp.11:58:
It says that someone who does not settle their debt or conflict in time will end up in prison, and will not get out of there until everything is paid.

Jesus speaks to the crowd after warning them to learn to read the present time. He insists that they do not judge what is right, and that they should be reconciled while there is still opportunity. Many understand the scene as a warning about making peace with God before judgment; others also see it as practical advice about human conflicts. It can be both.

For today: if you have an offense or an unpaid debt with someone, do not put it off. Seek to speak with that person soon, ask for forgiveness or offer to pay, and also return to God with humility while there is still time.
exp.1:33:
Simeon blesses Joseph and Mary, and tells Mary that this child will bring division in Israel. For some he will be a fall, for others a rising up. He will also be a sign that is spoken against, that is, a visible mark from God that many will reject and dispute.

Simeon was a righteous and devout man, who was waiting for the consolation of Israel. He took the child Jesus in his arms in the temple and praised God. Now he speaks to Mary with a warning: Jesus' path will not be easy or accepted by everyone. What follows, the sword that would pierce her soul, announces the pain she would feel.

Jesus leaves no one indifferent. We can honestly ask ourselves how we respond to Him: with humility and openness, or with resistance. Accepting Him, even when it disturbs our ideas, opens the door to being lifted up.
exp.10:22:
Jesus says there is no neutral position toward Him. Whoever is not on His side is against Him. And whoever does not gather with Him "scatters," that is, disperses and ruins what He gathers, like a shepherd whose sheep are scattered.

Jesus speaks this after casting out a demon. Some accused Him of doing it by the power of Beelzebul. He answers that His victory shows He is the stronger one who overcomes the strong man who is armed. So it is not enough to admire Him from a distance: a person must decide. Afterward He warns about a house that is swept clean but empty.

For today: do not settle for a lukewarm or undecided faith. Ask yourself where you are adding up with Christ: in your family, your work, and your church. Choose one concrete action today, such as forgiving, helping, or encouraging someone.
exp.0:65:
This verse says that everyone who heard about what had happened at John's birth kept it in their hearts, that is, they thought about it seriously and did not forget it. They asked, "What manner of child shall this be!" The text adds that "the hand of the Lord" was with him, an expression that speaks of God's power and favor.

The one telling the story is Luke. Zechariah had just regained his speech when he declared that the child would be named John, just as the angel had announced. The people of Judea were amazed and filled with reverent awe, and the news spread throughout the whole region. Soon afterward Zechariah would prophesy, filled with the Holy Spirit.

For today: when you see God at work, do not take it lightly. Keep those things in your heart, pray about them, and trust that God has a purpose, even when you do not yet understand everything.
exp.18:0:
Luke says that Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through the city. In other words, he was not staying there but was on his way. The phrase "having entered" is rendered here as "after he had entered," and this is a simple scene that prepares what comes next.

The one speaking is Luke, the narrator. Jesus is traveling toward Jerusalem, where he would be crucified. Jericho lay along that road. Luke includes this note about the journey to introduce the meeting with Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector. Although Jesus was only passing through, that passing became an opportunity for salvation for someone.

Today we can remember that God can work in the middle of everyday life. An ordinary journey, a brief conversation, or an unexpected moment can be an occasion to help someone or to draw closer to God. Let us ask for attentive eyes, like those of Jesus, to see the people who are near us.
exp.21:6:
This verse says that the day of the unleavened bread arrived, and that on that day the lamb of the Passover had to be sacrificed. The unleavened bread is bread made without yeast. The Passover lamb was the lamb the Jews ate to remember their departure from Egypt.

Here the narrator is Luke. Just before, Judas had agreed to take money to hand Jesus over in secret. Now Luke takes us to the Passover feast. While some were plotting evil, Jesus was moving toward the cross. Many Christians see here a sign that Jesus is the true Lamb of God, although Luke does not say this in this verse.

For today: even when everything seems to be going wrong, or when there are betrayals, God is still in control. Trust that his plan is moving forward, and seek Jesus with gratitude for what he did for you.
exp.22:5:
This verse tells that Pilate, the Roman governor, heard the accusers mention Galilee. Then he asked whether Jesus was a Galilean. "When Pilate heard of Galilee" means that on hearing that name, he took notice of it.

Pilate had already said that he found no fault in Jesus. But the religious leaders kept insisting on their accusations. When he learned that Jesus came from Galilee, Pilate saw a possible way out: sending him to Herod, who ruled that region. It is likely that Pilate wanted to avoid a difficult decision, although the text does not say so in these words.

For today: sometimes we know what is right, but we are afraid to bear the cost of doing it. Pilate tried to pass the responsibility on to someone else. Let us ask God for courage to act with honesty and not hide our decisions behind others.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that the whole crowd was trying to touch Jesus, because power came out of him and healed them all. The word "virtue" here means the power or strength of God. "Sought" means that they tried or strove to do it.

Luke tells this just before the Sermon on the Plain. Jesus had come down with his disciples to a level place, and a great crowd had come from Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre and Sidon. They came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases and of unclean spirits. Luke, who is telling the story, shows that Jesus cared for both the body and the soul of the people.

For today: when you are tired, sick, or hurt inside, come to Jesus with simple faith. Tell him in prayer what you feel, and trust that he hears you and has the power to help you, even though his answer does not always come the way we expect.
exp.18:33:
Jesús approaches Jerusalem and sends two disciples to untie a colt that no one had ridden. He tells them what to say if anyone asks. The owners question them, since it looked like theft, but they accept the answer. Luke shows that Jesus had everything under control, and the colt would carry him in his entry into Jerusalem. Some see here a previous knowledge of Jesus; others, an earlier agreement with the owners. The text does not clarify this.

For today: what we have, whether time, talent or resources, can be useful to Jesus. We can ask ourselves simply: what is he asking of me today, and am I willing to give it up with trust?
exp.21:30:
Jesus calls Simon by name twice, a sign of affection and urgency. He warns him that Satan has asked permission to shake all of them, the way wheat is shaken in a sieve to separate the good from the bad. The word "you" refers to all the disciples, although Jesus then speaks to Peter alone.

Jesus is speaking at the Last Supper. He has just promised a kingdom to the disciples, but He also knows they will soon face a hard test. He tells them that Peter will be shaken, but that He has prayed so that Peter's faith will not fail. Peter, confident, says he will go with Jesus even to prison and to death.

For today: trials can come even to those who love Jesus sincerely and deeply. Do not depend on your own strength; rely on the fact that Christ prays for you, and if you fall, return to Him and help others.
exp.9:35:
Jesus asks a teacher of the law: of the three men who passed along the road, which one acted as a neighbour to the man who had been attacked?

Jesus is speaking with an expert in the law of Moses, who had asked him who his neighbour was. Jesus told the story of the good Samaritan. A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side, but a Samaritan, from a people despised by the Jews, cared for the wounded man. With this question, Jesus changes the focus: it is no longer "Whom must I love?" but "How can I be a neighbour?"

For today: instead of asking whom we are obliged to help, let us look at who is near and in need of help. Today you can do something concrete, such as visiting a sick neighbour, giving food, or helping someone who is suffering, even if they are not from your group.
exp.17:17:
A man with authority comes to Jesus and calls him "Good Teacher." He asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, that is, to receive it as an inheritance. The word "ruler" here means a leader or chief, probably of a synagogue or of the people; the text does not say exactly what his position was.

Luke has just told how Jesus welcomed the children and said that the kingdom is received like a child: with trust, without any merit of one's own. Now this man appears, thinking in terms of "what shall I do." Jesus is going to lead him to examine his idea of goodness and of God.

For today: before asking what more we must do, it is worth asking ourselves whether we are willing to receive God with humility, like a child, and not to trust in our own good behavior.
exp.7:55:
Luke says that the girl's parents were amazed, deeply surprised by what Jesus had just done. He told them not to tell anyone what had happened. The word translated as "astonished" means so overwhelmed that they could hardly respond.

Jesus had just raised Jairo's daughter, the daughter of a synagogue leader, who was about twelve years old. Luke is the one who tells the story. Scholars offer several explanations for why Jesus asked for silence: perhaps to keep people from following him only for miracles, to avoid stirring up opposition too soon, or to give the family a moment of peace. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: not everything God does in us needs to be displayed. We can thank him quietly, take care of what he has done in our lives, and share it wisely, without seeking applause.
exp.7:11:
Jesus explains the parable of the sower. Those "by the way side" are people who do hear God's message, but the devil quickly comes and takes the word out of their hearts. His purpose is that they should not believe and should not be saved. Taketh away means snatches away or carries off.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, who have asked him what the parable means. He explains that the seed is the word of God and that hearts respond in different ways. The path is hard, trampled ground, where the seed lies exposed and cannot get in. Jesus presents the devil as a real enemy, but the scene centers on the condition of the heart.

For today: when you hear the Bible, do not let it pass you by. Stop for a few minutes, think about it, ask God to establish it in you, and put it into practice that same day.
