exp.17:28:
Jesus answers Peter with a solemn promise: "Verily I say unto you." He says that everyone who has left house, wife, brothers, parents, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God will receive a reward. The statement is completed in the next verse: they will receive many times more in this present time and, in the age to come, eternal life. The word "or" appears in the verse as a simple connector, and "age to come" means the future era.

Peter has just said that they left everything to follow Jesus. This happens after a rich young man went away sad, because he was not willing to give up his riches. Jesus had said that it is hard for rich people to enter the kingdom, and that what is impossible for men is possible with God. Now he encourages his disciples: their giving up is not in vain.

Following God sometimes costs relationships, comfort, or plans. Jesus does not ask us to abandon family on a whim, but to put God first. Today we can trust that nothing given to him is lost.
exp.13:30:
This verse tells the story of a king who is going to fight against another king. Before he acts, he sits down to think and calculate whether he can face an enemy coming with twenty thousand men using only ten thousand soldiers.

Jesus is speaking to large crowds who were following him. He has just said that following him requires putting God above family and above oneself. He uses two examples, that of the man building a tower and this king, to show that following him is a serious decision. Then he says that the disciple must give up everything he owns, that is, be willing to surrender it all to him.

For today: before saying "yes" to Jesus, think honestly about what it involves. This is not meant to discourage you, but so that you follow him with a heart that is resolved and trusting in his help.
exp.5:22:
Jesus invites his followers to rejoice and leap for joy on the day they are rejected because of him. The word "reward" means what is given back for faithfulness, and "insult" is what he means by being reviled. He says their reward in heaven is great, and that the ancient prophets were treated in the same way by their own ancestors.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and to a crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He explains that following him may bring rejection and mockery. He reminds them they are not the first: God's prophets also suffered for speaking the truth. The woes that follow show the contrast with those who seek only comfort now.

If you are criticized or set aside for being faithful to Christ, do not sink into bitterness. Remember that God sees your faithfulness and that his reward is certain. Ask him to give you peace and a joy that does not depend on the opinion of others.
exp.15:11:
It says that whoever does not take good care of what belongs to someone else cannot expect to be handed what would be his own. The word "another man's" means what belongs to another person. The phrase "have not been faithful" is a matter of how the verse reads, so I have left it as it stands. Jesus uses a question to make people think: if we fail with what is another's, who will give us what is our own?

Jesus is speaking to his disciples after the parable of the shrewd manager. He teaches that money and the goods of this world are not really ours, but that God entrusts them to us as stewards. The Pharisees, who loved money, were listening and mocked him. Many understand "that which is your own" as the true riches of God, though it is interpreted in several ways.

Today, treat your money, your time, and your responsibilities as something God has entrusted to you. Be honest and careful with small things, and also with the work of others.
exp.22:18:
This verse explains who Barabbas was, the man the crowd asked to have released. He had been put in prison for an uprising, a revolt against the authorities that took place in Jerusalem, and also for murder.

Luke, the narrator, pauses to clarify this detail in parentheses. Pilate was the Roman governor, and he customarily released a prisoner during the Passover feast. Rather than asking for Jesus, who had done nothing deserving of death, the crowd chose a man guilty of violence. The exact details about Barabbas outside the Gospels are not certain.

This scene reminds us that we often prefer easy solutions or the wrong people over the truth. It also shows the heart of the gospel: the innocent took the place of the guilty. Today we can thank God for that grace and ask ourselves whom we are following.
exp.6:17:
Luke tells us that John the Baptist's disciples reported to him everything Jesus was doing. Then John called two of them to himself. "Tidings" are news, and the word "á" is an old spelling of "a," so both of those comments are removed here.

The one who tells the story is Luke. Just before this, Jesus had raised the son of the widow of Nain, and the people were saying that God had visited his people. John was in prison, as Luke 3:20 and Matthew 11:2 report. That is why he learned about Jesus through his disciples. His next question, whether Jesus was the one who was to come, is understood in different ways: some see sincere doubt, others a desire for confirmation for his disciples.

When you have questions or doubts about Jesus, do not hide them. Bring them directly to him, as John did, and seek the answer with honesty and patience.
exp.0:10:
This verse tells that an angel sent by God appeared to Zechariah, a priest. The angel was standing on the right side of the altar of incense, the place inside the temple where incense was burned. The phrase "appeared to him" means that he suddenly saw the angel, without expecting it.

Luke writes to tell, in an orderly way, how the story of Jesus began. Zechariah had been chosen by lot to offer the incense, a very special moment that perhaps would not come again in his life. Outside, the people were praying. God chose that moment of worship to announce that he would give a son to Zechariah and Elizabeth, who would be John the Baptist.

God can speak to us and act in the midst of our daily lives and our prayer, even when we have almost stopped expecting an answer. Keep praying with faith and patience, and trust that God works in his own time.
exp.23:22:
The explanation says that the women went to the tomb and did not find Jesus' body. They returned telling that they had seen a vision of angels, and that the angels announced that Jesus is alive. The word "finding" in the verse is the same as "not finding," and a "vision of angels" is an appearance of beings sent by God.

The speaker is Cleopas, one of two disciples walking toward Emmaus on the same day as the resurrection. Without recognizing him, they tell Jesus what had happened. Their sadness shows: they had hoped for a deliverer, but the news of the empty tomb seems confusing to them, and they do not yet believe it. Jesus will answer them by explaining the Scriptures.

For today: sometimes we have the right information, but doubt or pain keeps us from believing. When something does not fit with your faith, do not walk away. Keep walking with Jesus, read his Word, and tell him honestly what you feel.
exp.22:49:
This verse introduces a new figure into the scene: Joseph. He is described as a "counsellor," an older word that here refers to a member of the Jewish council, the Sanhedrin. He is also called "a good man, and a just," meaning a man of integrity and uprightness.

Luke, who is writing the account, has just shown the death of Jesus, with the crowd beating their breasts in sorrow and those who knew him watching from a distance. At that moment Joseph appears, and he later asks for the body of Jesus in order to bury it. The verses that follow make clear that he had not agreed with the council's decision against Jesus and that he was waiting for the kingdom of God.

For today: one can do what is right even when surrounded by people who think differently. Joseph reminds us that faith is shown in concrete actions, even in difficult moments.
exp.23:8:
It says that the women, returning from the empty tomb, went to tell everything they had seen and heard. They told "the eleven," that is, the apostles (now without Judas), and also all the other followers of Jesus.

Luke is the one narrating. Those women had just heard the angels remind them of what Jesus had said: that he would be delivered up, crucified, and would rise on the third day. Then they remembered his words and ran to share the news. The verses that follow say that the apostles did not believe them at first.

For today: when God reminds us of his word and we understand something of his truth, we can share it simply, even when others doubt. We do not have to convince anyone; we only need to faithfully tell what we have seen and heard.
exp.7:30:
The explanation says that the demons were begging Jesus not to send them into the deep place. That word refers to a deep place where evil spirits would be shut up and punished.

The demons speak who were tormenting a man in the region of the Gadarenes. Jesus had just commanded them to come out of him. They recognize that Jesus has total authority over them, and so they do not demand but plead. The Bible does not explain in detail what the deep place is; other passages, such as Revelation 20, mention it, but interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: if even the dark powers recognize the authority of Jesus, we can trust that no force that oppresses us is outside his control. Bring him your chains with faith and hope.
exp.18:10:
Jesus tells a parable while the crowd listens. The text gives two reasons: Jesus was near that city, and the people thought the kingdom of God was going to appear right away, at once.

Jesus is speaking in the house of Zacchaeus, in Jericho, on the way to Jerusalem. His followers expected the kingdom to be revealed there immediately and with power. The parable of the ten minas corrects that expectation: the king goes away for a time, and his servants must work in the meantime. Scholars agree that this is the purpose Luke points to.

For today: instead of living only waiting for everything to be fixed soon, we can serve God faithfully in everyday life. Use today what He has entrusted to you, your time, your gifts, and your care for others, with patience and trust.
exp.8:20:
Here Jesus firmly orders his disciples not to tell anyone what Peter has just confessed: that he is the Christ of God. "Charged" means warning them seriously, almost with the authority of a command.

Jesus speaks after asking them who the crowds say he is, and who they themselves say he is. Peter gets it right, but many were expecting a Messiah of power and political victory. Jesus makes clear right away that he must first suffer, be rejected, die, and rise again. That is why he asks for silence: the popular idea of the Messiah did not match his mission. Some interpreters also see here a concern for the right moment.

For today: following Jesus is not just saying the right words about him, but accepting his way of self-giving and the cross. Ask him to help you know him as he really is, not as you would like him to be.
exp.8:51:
This verse tells us that Jesus sent messengers ahead of him, and they went into a village of the Samaritans.

Jesus had already decided to go to Jerusalem, where he would suffer and die. That is why his route passed through Samaria. There was an old hostility between Jews and Samaritans, and many people avoided that territory. Even so, Jesus did not go around it: he sought to give them a place on his way. What follows shows that they did not receive him, and that the disciples reacted with anger.

Today, when someone dislikes us or rejects us, it is easy to close ourselves off. Jesus teaches us to take the first step with respect and kindness, even when we do not know how others will respond. We can prepare the way with a greeting, a helping hand, or a prayer.
exp.21:43:
The verse says that Jesus was in deep anguish, and that because of it he prayed with even more force, with greater intensity. His sweat was like great drops of blood falling to the ground. The word "agony" here speaks of a very intense inner struggle.

Some scholars see here a comparative expression, meaning the sweat fell "like" drops of blood; others think real blood may have been mixed in. The text does not make this clear.

Luke describes Jesus on the Mount of Olives, the night before his crucifixion. He has just asked the Father that, if possible, the cup of suffering be taken from him, yet he submits to God's will. An angel comes to strengthen him. Afterward, he finds his disciples asleep from sorrow.

Jesus did not hide his pain or pretend to be strong; he carried it into prayer, with sincerity. When you are distressed, you can tell God what you feel, without pretense, and finish by entrusting the outcome to him, as Jesus did.
exp.7:31:
Verse 32 tells us that near that place there was a large herd of pigs feeding on the mountain. The demons that were inside the man begged Jesus to let them go into those animals, and Jesus allowed it. "Herd" means a group of animals together, and "feeding" means they were eating grass.

The one speaking here is the crowd of demons, who called themselves "Legion." They had already begged Jesus not to send them into the abyss, a place of punishment. This shows that they recognized Jesus' authority and could not act without his permission. Why Jesus allowed it is not explained in the text, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: even when evil sometimes seems strong, Jesus has authority over it. We can trust that nothing escapes his control, and come to him with confidence when we feel afraid or find ourselves bound.
exp.0:50:
This verse says that God acted with strength, and that his "arm" is a way of speaking about his power. "Scattered" means to disperse or throw into confusion. The "proud" are the arrogant, those who think themselves superior. God undid the arrogant plans and thoughts they held in their hearts.

The speaker is Mary, in the song we call the Magnificat. She has just learned that she will be the mother of the Messiah, and she praises God during her visit to Elizabeth. She speaks of what God does in history: he cares for the humble and opposes human pride.

For today: examine your own plans honestly. Ask God to free you from self-sufficiency and to teach you to trust him with humility, knowing that he cares for those who fear him.
exp.10:15:
This verse says that some people, to test him, demanded from Jesus a sign from heaven. "Tempting" here means putting him to the test, with doubt rather than sincere faith. A sign from heaven would be something spectacular that clearly showed God's backing.

Luke, the narrator, tells us that Jesus had just freed a man who could not speak, and the crowd was amazed. But some accused him of acting by the power of evil, and others asked for more proof. It is striking: they had already seen a miracle and still wanted another. Jesus immediately answers their thoughts, showing that he knows hearts.

For today: God invites us to trust what he has already shown us. We may ask him sincere questions, but we should take care not to demand proof every time we doubt, as if his goodness were never enough.
exp.18:39:
In this verse Jesus answers the Pharisees who wanted to silence the crowd. He tells them that if the people kept quiet, the stones themselves would cry out. The word "hold their peace" means "keep silent," and "cry out" means "shout" or "speak out loudly."

Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a donkey, and his disciples praise him as the King who comes in the name of the Lord. Some Pharisees are upset and ask him to rebuke his followers. Jesus does not stop them, because that moment deserved praise. Some understand this as a way of saying that all creation recognizes its Creator; the text does not explain more.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are holding back our gratitude to God out of fear, shame, or habit. Today you can thank God out loud, or tell someone about something good He has done in your life.
exp.13:14:
A man who was sitting at the table with Jesus heard what He said and exclaimed: "Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God." The word "blessed" means happy, fortunate, favored. Eating bread was a way of speaking about sharing a feast, a meal with God.

Jesus was dining at the house of a Pharisee leader and had just spoken about the reward at the resurrection of the righteous. The dinner guest responds with a pious and correct statement. However, some think he said it with an air of confidence, as if that place were already his. Jesus answers him right away with the parable of the great banquet, which shows that it is not enough to admire the kingdom: one must accept the invitation.

For today: do not be content with saying good things about God. Respond today to His invitation with obedience and gratitude.
exp.10:32:
Jesus says that no one lights a lamp to hide it in a corner or cover it with a box. It is set on a stand, a tall support, so that those who come into the house can see.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd that was asking him for a sign from heaven. He reminds them that the queen of the South and the people of Nineveh responded to less light than the light they already had, since now someone greater than Solomon and Jonah is here. The light is in plain view; the problem is that many do not want to see it. Some think the lamp is Jesus himself or his message; the text leaves this open.

If God has given you light, do not hide it out of fear or shame. And keep your heart open to it: live with sincerity, so that others may see in you something of its truth.
exp.22:46:
A centurion, a Roman officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers, saw everything that happened at the cross. Then he "gave glory to God," that is, he recognized that God was worthy of honor, and he declared that Jesus was "righteous." The word "righteous" can mean innocent, or also someone upright before God.

Luke is the one telling the story. Jesus has just died after the darkness, the torn curtain, and his prayer of surrender to the Father. The centurion was probably in charge of the execution. Luke stresses that a foreigner, not part of the Jewish people, recognizes Jesus' innocence. Other Gospels record slightly different words from the centurion, such as "Son of God"; Luke highlights his testimony about Jesus' righteousness.

For today: sometimes faith begins when we look at Jesus with sincerity and honor God for what we see. Today we can take a moment to read about the cross and thank God with simple words.
exp.12:15:
Jesus speaks of a woman he calls "a daughter of Abraham," that is, a Jewish woman who belonged to God's people. He says Satan had her bound for eighteen years. He asks whether it was not right to free her from that bond, even on the sabbath.

Jesus has just healed this bent-over woman in a synagogue. The leader of the synagogue became angry because she was healed on the sabbath. Jesus answers that everyone unties their ox or donkey on the sabbath to give it water. How much more, then, should a person be set free. His opponents were put to shame, and the people rejoiced.

For today: religious rules must never stand above compassion. Ask yourself whether there is someone you can help, encourage, or relieve, without letting customs or excuses hold you back.
exp.16:31:
Jesus asks his listeners to remember Lot's wife. According to Genesis 19, she was fleeing Sodom with her family, looked back, and was turned into a pillar of salt.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about the day when the Son of Man will be revealed. He has just said that, at that moment, no one should go back for their belongings. With this example he warns that a heart attached to what is left behind puts life at risk. Interpreters understand in various ways what that day will be like, but all agree on the urgency of the message.

Today we can ask ourselves what things tie us down and keep us from following Jesus with our whole heart. Ask God for help to let go of one of them today and to look ahead with confidence in him.
exp.20:34:
It says that day will arrive suddenly, like a snare or trap that catches an animal that is not expecting it. It will not be something limited to one place: it will reach all the people who live on the earth.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, in the last days before his cross. He explains things that are going to come, and Christians understand them in different ways: some think of the destruction of Jerusalem, others of his final return, others of both. His warning is clear: do not let yourselves be dulled by excess or by the anxieties of life.

For today: do not live distracted or weighed down. Set aside a moment each day to pray and place your worries in God's hands. In this way your heart stays awake, calm, and ready, without living in fear.
exp.14:19:
The explanation says that the son who had left home decided to return. While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, was deeply moved with compassion, and ran toward him. He embraced him tightly around the neck and kissed him.

Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees and scribes who were criticizing him for welcoming sinners. With this story he shows what God is like: a Father who waits and receives with joy the one who comes back. The father acts before hearing the son's confession.

For today: if you have moved away from God, do not wait until you feel perfect before returning. Take the first step with sincerity. God is already looking at you with compassion and receives you with open arms.
exp.0:43:
Elizabeth tells Mary that, as soon as she heard her greeting, the baby she was carrying in her womb leaped for joy. The word "greeting" means the same as the word "salutation" in the verse, and "baby" refers to the child who had not yet been born.

Elizabeth speaks filled with the Holy Spirit, according to verse 41. Mary, pregnant with Jesus, has just come to visit her. Elizabeth is expecting John, who would later prepare the way of the Lord. She recognizes that Mary is the mother of her Lord, and the leap of the baby is understood as a sign of joy at the presence of Jesus. Some see it as something supernatural and others as a poetic expression; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when we recognize the presence of God, joy can spring up with simplicity. Today we can stop, give thanks, and celebrate with others what God is doing, without holding back our joy.
exp.2:17:
This verse sums up the preaching of John the Baptist. The word "exhorting" means to warn firmly and kindly so that someone will change their way. Luke says that, in addition to what he had already recorded, John was preaching many other things to the people. In other words, his message was broader than what was written down.

Luke is the narrator. Earlier, John spoke of Jesus, who was mightier than he was, and of judgment, using the image of wheat and chaff. Then the text shows that John rebuked Herod for his wicked deeds, and because of this he was put in prison. So we see that John spoke the truth no matter whom it offended.

For today: good teaching includes both hope and correction. We can ask God to help us receive the warnings of his Word with humility, and to speak with truth and love when we need to encourage others to change.
exp.20:5:
Jesus says that the temple in Jerusalem, which everyone admired, will be torn down completely. "Stone upon stone" means that nothing will be left standing. "Destroyed" means thrown down and reduced to ruins. Today we would say: "Not one stone will be left on another without being brought down."

Jesus speaks to some people who admired the beautiful stones and offerings of the temple. Just before this, he had praised the poor widow who gave everything she had. He does not look at the beauty of the building but at the heart. Jewish writers and history record that the temple was destroyed in the year 70 AD. His disciples then ask about the sign, and Jesus warns them against deception.

For today: let us not place our security in what looks great and firm, whether a building, a position, or money. Let us trust in God and care for a sincere and generous heart.
exp.16:15:
He says that this man, now healed of leprosy, threw himself down on the ground, face down, at Jesus' feet, and gave him thanks. The explanation of the word "fell down" is removed here, since the verse your reader sees says "fell down on his face." The text makes clear that he was a Samaritan, that is, from a people the Jews often looked down on.

Luke tells us that ten lepers asked Jesus for help. He told them to present themselves to the priests, who were the ones who confirmed a healing, and as they went they were made clean. Only this man came back. Luke stresses that he was a foreigner, and Jesus later points out that the other nine did not return to give glory to God.

For today: let us pause to give thanks. It is easy to ask for help and forget to give thanks when it arrives. Think of something good God has given you this week, and thank him out loud, simply and from the heart.
exp.16:29:
This verse says that the day when Jesus, the Son of Man, is revealed will be like what happened in the time of Lot. "Is revealed" means he will be shown openly, so that everyone will see him. Jesus compares that moment to the sudden arrival of judgment on Sodom.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, after answering the Pharisees about the kingdom of God. Earlier he recalled the days of Noah and Lot: people went about their ordinary routines without thinking about God, and judgment came all at once. Christian interpreters understand this passage as a warning about his return, although they discuss some details of how and when it will happen.

For today: do not live distracted only by daily life. Working and eating are not wrong, but put God first. Today, find a moment to pray and set your heart in order.
exp.21:20:
Jesus says that the one who will betray him is sitting with him at the table. "The hand" stands for the person who betrays him. The phrase "But, behold" draws attention to what follows. The word "betrayeth" means handing someone over to their enemies.

Jesus speaks with his disciples during the Last Supper, just after he has broken the bread and shared the cup of the new covenant. Luke does not name the traitor here, but earlier he mentions that Judas had already made an agreement with the chief priests. Jesus is not surprised; he knows what is coming, and the disciples react by asking among themselves who it will be.

Today this verse invites us to examine our own hearts rather than point at others. We can be close to Jesus on the outside, in church or in prayer, and still drift away inwardly. Let us ask him for sincerity and faithfulness.
exp.16:26:
In the days of Noah, people lived their normal routines: they ate, they drank, and they got married. None of that was wrong in itself. But they carried on like this, paying no attention, until Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all. The phrase "they married wives" means that they got married.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about the coming of the Son of Man. First he announces that he would have to suffer and be rejected. Then he compares the future with the days of Noah and of Lot. His point is not to condemn ordinary life, but to warn that judgment would come suddenly, when many did not expect it.

Today we can live responsibly in our work, our family, and our rest, without forgetting God. A good question for each day is: am I living ready to meet him?
exp.22:4:
What it says: The religious leaders kept insisting forcefully on their accusation against Jesus. They said that he was stirring up the people with his teaching, and that he had done so throughout Judea, from Galilee, where he began, all the way to Jerusalem. The word "stirreth up" in the verse means that he agitates or disturbs the people.

Context: The chief priests and the crowd are speaking before Pilate. He had just said that he found no fault in Jesus. So they raised the pitch of the accusation, since a threat of revolt was something a Roman governor would be concerned about. Mentioning Galilee ended up leading Pilate to send Jesus to Herod.

For today: When the truth does not fit what we want, it is easy to exaggerate or twist the facts. Let us ask God for honesty when we speak about others and for the courage not to accuse without reason.
exp.18:19:
It says that another servant came and gave back to his lord his mina, that is, an amount of money that had been entrusted to him. He did not use it: he kept it wrapped in a napkin, which is a small cloth or piece of linen. He did no harm with it, but he also did nothing useful.

Jesus tells this parable as he makes his way toward Jerusalem. A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and leaves a mina to each servant to put to work. The first two multiplied it and were rewarded. This third one makes excuses, saying that he was afraid. Jesus teaches that faithfulness to God means acting, not merely keeping things safe.

For today: God has given us gifts, time, and opportunities. Fear or a mistaken image of God can leave us paralyzed. Today, take a small, concrete step to serve with what you have, trusting that God is good and walks with you.
exp.0:66:
Luke 1:67 says that Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, was filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke words inspired by God. The verse uses the word "was," and "prophesied" means that he spoke on behalf of God, not only from what he himself thought.

Zechariah had been unable to speak for nine months or more, because he did not believe the angel's announcement about the birth of his son. When John was born and was given the name God had indicated, Zechariah was able to speak again. The first thing he does is praise God. His song, which continues in the following verses, celebrates that God keeps his promises and sends salvation to his people.

For today: after a time of silence or doubt, God can still fill us with his Spirit and put praise in our mouths. When God fulfills what he promised, let us respond with gratitude and speak of his faithfulness.
exp.3:23:
Jesus says with great seriousness that no prophet is welcomed in his own country. The word "accepted" in the verse means received, welcomed, valued. In other words, the one who speaks on God's behalf is often rejected precisely among the people who know him best.

Jesus is in the synagogue in Nazareth, the town where he grew up. At first the people marvel at his words, but then they begin to doubt, asking whether this is not Joseph's son. Jesus knows they want miracles to prove who he is. For this reason he reminds them that Elijah was sent to a foreign widow, not to the widows of Israel.

For today: let us not allow habit or familiarity to close our hearts. Sometimes God speaks to us through someone close to us or through a message we already know. Let us listen with humility and without prejudice.
exp.8:22:
Jesus says that whoever wants to be his follower must deny himself, that is, stop putting his own desires first. He must also take up his cross daily and follow him. To come after him means to go behind Jesus as a disciple.

Jesus speaks to everyone, not only to the twelve. He has just announced that he will suffer, be rejected by the religious leaders, and die, but that he will rise again. For his hearers, the cross was a symbol of execution. He makes it clear that following him means a path of self-giving, not of comfort.

For today: each morning you can ask yourself what God wants from you that day and be willing to obey him, even when it costs you. For example, forgiving someone, telling the truth, or serving without expecting recognition.
exp.10:14:
Some of those who saw the miracle said that Jesus drove out demons by the power of Beelzebub, whom they called "the chief of the demons." Beelzebub is a name used to refer to Satan.

Jesus had just cast out a demon that had made a man unable to speak, and the man spoke. The crowd was amazed, but some refused to acknowledge that the power came from God. Some of those present spoke up, and Jesus answered them at once, showing that their accusation made no sense.

For today: sometimes, even in the face of something good, the heart resists believing and looks for excuses. Let us ask God for a humble and open heart, to recognize his work without prejudice, and to be thankful for it.
exp.8:16:
It says that all the people ate until they were satisfied. Afterward the disciples gathered up what was left over and filled twelve baskets with the broken pieces. "They were filled" means they ate until they were well fed, with no hunger left. "Took up" means they gathered it.

Luke tells this miracle after Jesus taught a crowd and healed the sick. There were about five thousand men, according to verse 14. Jesus took the little that was available, prayed, and distributed it through his disciples. Many see in the twelve baskets a sign of abundance, and some think they point to the twelve disciples, although the text does not say this clearly. Right after this, Jesus asks who people say he is.

When we give Jesus the little we have, he can do far more than we imagine. Offer him today, with confidence, your time, your strength, or your resources.
exp.9:23:
Jesus says that many prophets and kings of the past longed to see and hear what the disciples were seeing and hearing, but were not able to. The disciples had the privilege of seeing Jesus and hearing his words up close.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in private, after they returned from their mission and rejoiced. He has just said that the Father and the Son know each other in a unique way, and that the Son reveals the Father to whomever he chooses. The prophets of the Old Testament announced the Messiah, but they did not see his coming.

For today: value what God has already made known to you in Christ. Read his Word with gratitude and attention, because what many waited for across centuries is, today, within your reach.
exp.8:12:
Jesus says to his disciples, "Give ye them to eat." They reply that they have only five loaves and two fish, and that to feed so many people they would have to go and buy food. The word "meat" in that verse means food in general, and "all this people" refers to the crowd.

Jesus had spent the day teaching the people about the kingdom of God and healing the sick. As evening approached, the twelve asked him to send the crowd away, because they were in a deserted place. Jesus gives them the responsibility back, perhaps to test their faith and to teach them to depend on him. The disciples see only what they lack.

Often we look at the little we have and think it is not enough. We can offer Jesus what we have, even when it seems insufficient, and trust that he can do far more than we imagine.
exp.4:33:
Jesus answers with a simple question: can the guests at a wedding be made to fast while the bridegroom is still with them? The obvious answer is no. The guests of the wedding feast are the ones who attend the celebration with the groom.

Some people asked him why his disciples ate and drank, while the disciples of John and the Pharisees fasted. Jesus presents himself as the bridegroom, and his presence is a reason for celebration. Then he says that a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast. Many understand this as a reference to his death.

There are times to celebrate God's presence and times to fast with sorrow or longing. What matters is that fasting and joy come from a living relationship with Jesus, not from mere custom or outward appearance.
exp.16:8:
Jesus asks whether a master thanks his servant for doing what he was commanded. And He Himself answers: "I suppose not." The old words in the source are not needed here, so the comments about them are left out, and the quoted phrases are rendered in plain English: "I suppose not" and "unworthy servants," meaning servants with no special merit, who do not deserve an extra reward.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, right after teaching them about forgiveness and faith. He draws on the everyday life of that time, when a servant worked all day for his master. With this example He wants them to understand that serving God is not a way of earning His debt or His favor.

For today: serve God and others with humility, without expecting applause or feeling that God owes you anything. Obedience is a privilege, and everything good we do comes from His grace.
exp.4:7:
Peter sees the great catch and falls down at Jesus' feet. He says, "Depart from me, O Lord, for I am a sinful man." The word "fell down" here means that he threw himself to the ground, and "when he saw it" refers to what had just happened: the nets nearly breaking and the boats about to sink.

Peter speaks after a miracle. He had fished all night and caught nothing, and Jesus asked him to let down the net again. Seeing Jesus' power, Peter felt his own smallness. He does not ask Jesus to leave because he rejects him, but because he feels unworthy to be near someone so holy. Jesus does not walk away: he tells him, "Fear not."

For today: there is no need to hide our failings before God. We can acknowledge them honestly, and Jesus answers with closeness and purpose, not rejection. Today you can tell him in prayer what you truly feel.
exp.6:13:
Jesus approaches the bier, which was a stretcher or board on which the dead were carried, and touches it. Those who were carrying the body stop. Then Jesus speaks to the dead young man. He tells him "Young man," and commands him, "Arise."

Jesus speaks near the city of Nain. A widow was taking her only son to be buried, and she was left without support. Before acting, Jesus had compassion and said to her, "Do not weep." His word restores life, and the people recognize that God has visited his people.

For today: Jesus stops before people's pain and does not pass by. We can imitate him by approaching those who suffer with compassion, and trust that Christ still has power and care in our darkest situations.
exp.17:23:
Jesus sees that the man has become very sorrowful and comments on how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God. "With great difficulty" means with much difficulty. "Kingdom of God" refers to living under God's rule and receiving his salvation.

Jesus speaks with a leading, very wealthy man who wanted to inherit eternal life. Jesus asked him to give up everything and follow him, and he could not. Jesus does not say that wealth is sin, but that it can bind the heart. The listeners are amazed and ask who then can be saved; Jesus' answer shortly after is that what is impossible for people is possible for God.

Today you might ask yourself: is there something I find hard to let go of if God asks me to: money, comfort, or security? Bring it honestly before God and ask him for a heart free to follow him.
exp.19:18:
The explanation says that the chief priests and the scribes wanted to arrest Jesus at that very moment. They realized the parable was about them. But they did not do it because they feared the people. "Lay hands on" means to seize him; the phrase "chief priests" refers to the high priests.

Jesus was teaching in the temple in Jerusalem, a few days before his death. He had just told the parable of the wicked tenants, who mistreat the servants and kill the son of the owner of the vineyard. Many understand that the tenants represent the religious leaders, and the son represents Jesus himself. They understood the message, but instead of repenting, they wanted to silence him.

When the Word of God confronts us, we can harden ourselves or allow ourselves to be corrected. Let us ask God for a humble heart that listens, even when it hurts, and that changes rather than defends itself.
exp.6:25:
Jesus asks the crowd what they expected to find when they went out into the wilderness to see John. A prophet? Yes, and even more than a prophet.

Jesus is speaking. John the Baptist's messengers, who was in prison, had just left with Jesus' answer to his doubts. So Jesus makes clear to the crowd who John was: not a weak man swayed like a reed by the wind, nor an elegant courtier, but the messenger foretold in Scripture to prepare the way of the Lord.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are looking for when we listen to God or to those who speak to us about Him. Jesus invites us not to settle for what is comfortable or eye-catching, but to value the truth, even when it is plain or demanding, and to respond to it with faith.
exp.16:24:
Jesus says that before the Son of Man appears in glory, he must suffer greatly and be rejected by this generation. The word "rejected" means turned away and treated as worthless. The phrase "must" shows that this was part of God's plan and was not an accident.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, after answering the Pharisees about when the kingdom of God would come. He warns them that his return will be visible and unmistakable, like a flash of lightning, so they should not believe those who say, "Look, here!" or "Look, there!" But before that, there would be the cross. Jesus announces this in advance, and the disciples did not yet fully understand it.

For today: the way of Jesus went through suffering before glory. If you face rejection or pain for following him, do not think that God has abandoned you. Trust that he also passed through this, and that he remains with you.
exp.10:21:
He says that a strong man, fully armed, guards his house and his belongings are safe. But if someone stronger comes, he overcomes him, takes away the armor he trusted in, and divides what he had taken. The word "spoils" refers to the goods taken from the defeated one. "Coming upon" means arriving suddenly.

Jesus is speaking. Some were accusing him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul. He answers with this short parable. Many understand that the "strong man" represents Satan and the "stronger one" is Jesus, whose authority over the demons shows that the kingdom of God has already arrived. The verses that follow insist that no one can remain neutral before him.

For today: if Christ is stronger than whatever enslaves you, you can come to him with confidence. Do not depend on your own "armor," such as pride or your own strength. Take your place on his side and ask him to take control of your life.
exp.7:14:
Jesus says that the good ground represents those who have an honest and good heart. They hear the word of God, hold on to it firmly, and bear fruit with patience. "Holding on" means they keep it and do not let it go. "Patience" here speaks of perseverance: continuing forward without giving up.

Jesus is explaining the parable of the sower to his disciples. Earlier he spoke of those who hear and fall away in the time of trial, and of those who are choked by worries and pleasures. This is the fourth kind of ground, the one that responds well. Then he speaks to them about the lamp, which is not hidden but set up to give light.

For today: hearing a good message is not enough. Choose one teaching from the Bible, write it down, and put it into practice this week. Be steady, even when the fruit takes time to appear.
exp.13:33:
It says that salt is something valuable, but if it loses its flavor, there is no way to restore it.

Jesus is speaking to large crowds that were following him. Shortly before, he told them that being his disciple costs everything, and that a person should think it through carefully, like someone who calculates before building a tower. Salt is an image: a disciple who does not give himself truly loses his usefulness. Some explain the salt in different ways, but the general sense is the seriousness of the commitment.

Today, examine whether your faith is still alive and shows in how you treat others, in your honesty, and in your service. Ask God to renew your commitment, and practice it today in one concrete act of love.
exp.2:10:
It says that whoever has two tunics should give one to someone who has none, and whoever has food should share it in the same way. The tunic was the garment worn close to the body, under the cloak. "Do likewise" means that he should also share his food with the one in need.

John the Baptist is speaking to the crowd that was coming to the Jordan. He had just warned them that it was not enough to say, "We have Abraham as our father"; they had to bear "good fruit." Then the crowd asks, "What shall we do?" His answer shows that true repentance is seen in concrete acts of generosity. Then he gives similar advice to the tax collectors, the publicans.

For today: look at what you have in excess, clothing, food, or money, and share it this week with someone who needs it, whether a neighbor, a relative, or a church that helps others.
exp.15:29:
Here the rich man, who is in the place of torment, contradicts Abraham. He says that his brothers will not pay attention to Moses and the prophets alone, but that if someone from the dead goes to them, then they will repent.

It is part of the parable of the rich man and Lazarus. The rich man speaks with Abraham and asks for help for his five brothers. Abraham answers that they already have the Scriptures, that is, the Law and the prophets. The rich man thinks a more spectacular sign is needed. Jesus shows that the Word of God is already sufficient.

For today: do not wait for an extraordinary experience in order to obey God. Read the Bible carefully and respond with a willing heart, today, to what it already shows you.
exp.10:38:
Jesus tells the Pharisee that they carefully clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of greed, taking advantage of others, and wickedness.

Jesus is eating at the house of a Pharisee, who was surprised that He did not wash His hands before eating, as religious custom required. Jesus answers with a comparison: they cared a great deal about outward cleanness, but neglected the heart. Then He calls them foolish, because God made both the outside and the inside, and He invites them to give generously.

For today: it is not enough to care only about how you appear to others. Ask God to examine your heart, and look for one concrete act of generosity this week, so that your life, inside and out, honors God.
exp.12:11:
What it says: Jesus sees a bent-over woman and calls her to himself. She did not ask for anything. He says to her, "Woman, you are set free from your sickness." The phrase "when he saw her" means "when he saw her," and "you are set free" means "you have been released," like someone who is untied from a bond.

Context: Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on a Sabbath. This woman had been bent over for eighteen years, unable to straighten herself. The text says she had a "spirit of infirmity," and gives no further detail. Jesus takes the initiative and heals her with words and with his hands. Afterward, the leader of the synagogue becomes upset because the healing happened on the Sabbath, and this shows a tension between rules and compassion.

For today: Jesus notices those whom others overlook. Today we can pay attention to tired or burdened people who are near us, listen to them, and help them, without waiting for them to ask first.
exp.14:26:
He says that a servant gives the older brother the news: his younger brother has come home, and the father ordered the fatted calf killed, that is, the young calf that was kept fattened for a great feast. The reason is that he received him "safe and sound," that is, healthy and well.

The speaker is one of the servants, answering the question of the older son, who was coming from the field and heard the music and dancing. Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees and scribes who criticized him for welcoming sinners. The servant only reports the facts, but the joyful news provokes the older brother's anger, as what follows shows.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we rejoice when someone draws near to God, even if their past was disastrous. Let us ask God for a heart that celebrates with Him, without comparing merits or holding onto resentment.
exp.21:0:
It says that the feast of unleavened bread was drawing near, which was also called the Passover. The word for unleavened bread here refers to bread made without yeast. The Jews ate it for several days to remember that God brought them out of Egypt in haste.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking, and he is about to tell of the last days of Jesus. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims during this feast. The verses that follow show the religious leaders looking for a way to kill Jesus, but fearing the people. Luke points out that all of this happens just when the deliverance of Israel was being remembered.

For today: God works even in the middle of twisted plans and difficult moments. When everything seems to go against you, trust that God still guides history and has a purpose, as he did at the cross.
exp.17:32:
Jesus says that he will be whipped and then killed, but that on the third day he will rise again. "To whip" means to strike with a lash, a cruel punishment the Romans used before executing someone. The verse's wording makes plain that this is what happens to him before he dies. Jesus speaks clearly about his suffering and about his victory over death.

Jesus speaks to his twelve disciples as they go up to Jerusalem. He explains that all of this fulfills what the prophets had announced. However, the text says that they understood nothing, because the meaning was hidden from them. They expected something very different from a Messiah who suffers and dies.

For today: sometimes we do not understand God's plans, and that is all right. Jesus knew what was coming and still went forward out of love. We can trust him when the path seems hard, remembering that after the pain God has the last word: the resurrection.
exp.7:8:
This verse tells us that Jesus' disciples did not understand the parable of the sower, so they asked him what it meant. A "parable" is a simple story that uses familiar things to teach a deeper truth. Here, the word "asked" simply shows that they were putting the question to him.

Jesus had just told the story of the seeds that fall on different kinds of ground, and he ended with a call: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." The disciples took that call seriously and came to ask him. Then Jesus explains to them that the seed is the word of God.

For today: if something in the Bible is not clear to you, do not keep the doubt to yourself or set the passage aside. Ask God humbly in prayer, and also ask a pastor or a mature brother or sister in the faith. Wanting to understand is a good sign of an open heart.
exp.19:23:
Jesus asks them to show him a coin and asks whose face and name are engraved on it. They answer that it belongs to Caesar, the emperor.

Jesus speaks with some spies sent by the religious leaders. They wanted to trap him with a difficult question: if he said yes, paying the tax, the people would be upset; if he said no, they would accuse him before Rome. Jesus, knowing their cunning, uses the coin to answer them wisely and leaves them with no arguments.

For today: we can fulfill our civic responsibilities, such as paying taxes and respecting the laws, without forgetting that our whole life belongs to God. Ask yourself today: am I giving God first place in my heart?
exp.17:14:
This verse tells that some people were bringing their little children to Jesus so that he would touch them, that is, so that he would place his hands on them and bless them. When the disciples saw this, they rebuked them, or in other words, they scolded them and tried to stop it.

Luke is the one who narrates. Just before this, Jesus told the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, and he ended by saying that whoever humbles himself will be exalted. The children, small and unimportant in the eyes of that society, illustrate that humility. Afterward Jesus corrects the disciples and says that the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, without meaning to, we block others from access to Jesus. Let us welcome children and the simple with patience, and learn to receive God with humble trust.
exp.9:24:
It says that a teacher of the law of Moses stood up to test Jesus. He asked him what he had to do to receive eternal life. Here, "testing him" means probing or examining him, not necessarily trying to make him fall. "Inheriting" simply means receiving something as an inheritance.

Jesus had just rejoiced with his disciples over what God was revealing to them. Then this expert in the Scriptures asks him a question, perhaps to measure his teaching or to see whether he would answer well. Jesus does not give him a speech, but leads him back to the law he already knew. The man answers with love for God and for neighbor, and from there Jesus will go on to the parable of the good Samaritan.

For today: we can know a great deal of the Bible and still ask questions without a willing heart. Approach God with humility, not only to have answers, but to obey them by loving.
exp.0:60:
They said that the neighbors and relatives who were at the ceremony were surprised when Elizabeth said the boy would be named John. They asked her why, since no one in the family had that name.

The relatives and neighbors present at the boy's circumcision, eight days after his birth, are the ones speaking. It was customary to give the name at that moment, and the usual practice was to use the father's name or that of some relative. But the angel had told Zechariah that the boy would be named John (Luke 1:13). Elizabeth states it firmly, and Zechariah, who could not speak, will confirm it in writing.

Obeying God sometimes puts us against the customs and expectations of the people we love. When we know what God has shown us, we can act with humility and firmness, even when others do not understand right away. In time, obedience often bears fruit that even the doubters come to recognize.
exp.11:45:
This verse says that the master of that wicked servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know. Then he will cut him in sunder, and he will place him with the unbelievers, that is, with those who are neither faithful nor trustworthy.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and also to the crowd around him, using a parable about a servant put in charge of the household. If he is faithful while his master is away, he will be rewarded. But if he thinks the master is taking his time and abuses his position, he will have to give an account. The theme is being prepared and being faithful, because Christ will return when we do not expect him.

For today: live each day with responsibility and honesty, taking good care of what God has entrusted to you, your family, your work, and your gifts, without waiting for someone to watch over you.
exp.12:3:
Jesus speaks of eighteen people who died when a tower fell in Siloam. He asks whether they were worse than the other people living in Jerusalem. With this question, he makes it clear that the answer is no.

Jesus is responding to people who told him about the death of some Galileans at the hands of Pilate. Many believed that a tragedy was a punishment for some special sin. Jesus corrects that idea, and we do not know more historical details about that tower. Then he calls everyone to repentance and tells the parable of the fig tree.

For today: when you hear of a disaster, do not judge the victims as worse than you. Instead, use that moment to examine your own heart and turn to God today, without waiting until tomorrow.
exp.18:29:
Jesus sends two disciples to the village across from them. He tells them that when they enter, they will find a young colt, that is, a young donkey, tied up. No one has ever ridden it. They are to untie it and bring it to him.

Jesus speaks while he is going up toward Jerusalem, near the Mount of Olives. He is preparing to enter the city riding on this animal. Many believers see here the fulfillment of the prophecy in Zechariah 9:9 about a humble king who comes on a donkey. The fact that the animal had never been used suggests something set apart for a sacred purpose, though the text does not fully explain this.

For today: Jesus knows what is coming and cares about every detail. You can trust that he knows your path. And if he asks you to do something simple, obey with confidence, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.6:24:
Jesus asks the crowd what they expected to find when they went out to the wilderness to see John the Baptist. A man dressed in fine, soft clothing? Jesus answers his own question: those who dress in luxury and live in comfort are found in kings' palaces, not in the desert. Here "delicately" means living in pleasure and ease.

Jesus is speaking after John's messengers, who had been sent while John was in prison, have gone away with their answer. Jesus wants the people to recognize who John really was: not someone weak who changes his mind like a reed moved by the wind, nor someone who sought comfort. He was a firm and simple man, sent by God.

For today: we can ask ourselves what we look for in those who speak on God's behalf. Rather than fame, style, or comfort, let us value truth, steadfastness, and faithfulness to God.
exp.22:48:
It says that all of Jesus' acquaintances, together with the women who had followed him from Galilee, were standing at a certain distance, watching what was happening at the cross. The word "but" in the verse is the one the explanation refers to, and "acquaintances" means the people close to him, such as friends and those near to him.

Luke is the one narrating, and he does so right after Jesus' death. Before this, the centurion had recognized that Jesus was righteous, and the crowd was beating their breasts in grief. This verse shows the faithful witnesses who did not leave. Luke does not give all their names here; other gospels mention some of those women. Their presence prepares the account of the burial and the resurrection.

Today we can learn that, even when we do not understand everything or know what to do, staying close to Jesus in difficult moments has value. Sometimes accompanying someone faithfully, even from a distance and with sorrow, is an act of love.
exp.21:42:
It says that while Jesus was praying, God sent him an angel from heaven to strengthen him. The word the older text uses is not just about comforting him with words; it means giving him strength and courage, so the sentence needs no further explanation of that word.

Luke tells this moment on the Mount of Olives, shortly before Jesus was arrested. He has just asked the Father to take away the cup of suffering that awaits him, yet he submits to God's will. Some early manuscripts do not include this verse or the next one, and scholars debate it, although many Bibles keep it.

For today: when you are exhausted or afraid, you can pray honestly, as Jesus did. God does not always remove the trial, but he can give you strength to go through it, sometimes through other people.
exp.22:22:
They kept on insisting, shouting loudly, and demanding that Jesus be crucified. The crowd did not calm down. They pressed their demand without stopping, and their voices grew louder and gained the upper hand, along with those of the chief priests, the leading religious officials.

Pilate, the Roman governor, had declared three times that he found no guilt in Jesus deserving death. Even so, the pressure from the leaders and the crowd proved stronger than his sense of justice. The next verse shows that he gave in and handed Jesus over.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are carried along by group pressure or by the noise of popular opinion. Before deciding, it is good to stop, seek the truth, and act with courage, even when many shout the opposite.
exp.7:50:
Jesus arrives at the house of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, and does not let all the people go in. He allows only Peter, James, and John to accompany him, along with the child's father and mother. The word for the girl here means a young girl.

Jairus had asked for help for his sick daughter, and now he is told that she has already died. Jesus said to him: "Do not be afraid; only believe." Then, inside the house, there was much weeping and also mockery. Jesus chooses a calmer setting, with few witnesses. The Bible does not explain in detail why he chose those three disciples, although they appear other times near Jesus at important moments.

When we are in the middle of a painful situation, we can ask Jesus to be with us and step away from the noise and the voices that steal faith. Let us seek the calm of his presence and people we trust who will pray with us.
exp.23:28:
The verse says that the two disciples urged him strongly to stay with them. They pressed him with great insistence, telling him that it was already late and the day was almost over. So Jesus went in to stay with them.

It is the day of the resurrection. Two disciples are on the road to Emmaus, sad and confused, not knowing that the one walking with them is Jesus. He has explained the Scriptures to them, and their hearts have been moved. When they arrive, Jesus acts as if he is going on ahead, and they, wanting to hear more, ask him to stay.

Today we can invite Jesus to enter our everyday life, not only in religious moments. If the heart longs for more of his Word, say to him simply, "Stay with us." He draws near to those who seek him.
exp.7:26:
Luke tells us that, when Jesus stepped out of the boat onto land, a man from the city came to meet him. He was controlled by demons for a long time. He wore no clothes, did not live in a house, and lived among the tombs, which were caves or graves where the dead were buried.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking. Jesus has just calmed the storm, and the disciples were asking who he was. Now they arrive in the region of the Gadarenes, on the other side of the lake. The scene shows that Jesus also has authority over the evil that destroys people. Some manuscripts name a different region, but the account is the same.

For today: Jesus does not turn away from the one who is broken and cast out, but goes to meet him. If you feel alone or bound to something, you can come near to Him. And look on those who suffer with compassion, not fear.
exp.18:4:
This verse tells how Jesus came to the place where the tree was, looked up, and saw Zacchaeus. He called him by name and told him to hurry, which means to be quick, and to come down, and that he would stay at his house. Jesus says that today he must do this.

Jesus is speaking as he travels through Jericho. Zacchaeus, according to the account, was a small man who wanted to see him, so he climbed a tree. Jesus takes the initiative and invites himself to his house. The people grumble because Zacchaeus was seen as a sinner. The text does not explain why Jesus says "must"; many understand it as part of his mission to seek out the lost.

For today: God seeks us even when we think we do not deserve his attention. Respond to his call quickly and with joy, opening your home and your life to him without waiting to be perfect.
exp.8:19:
Jesus asks his disciples directly what they themselves think of him. Peter answers, "The Christ of God." The word "Christ" means "Anointed One," the promised Messiah whom God would send.

Jesus was praying alone, and the disciples were with him. First he asked them what the people were saying: some thought he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, or another of the prophets. Then he asked them for their own answer. Peter speaks for the disciples. Afterward Jesus commands them not to tell this yet, and explains that he must first suffer, be rejected, die, and rise again.

Repeating what others think about Jesus is not enough. He invites us to answer personally: who is he to me? Today you can stop, pray, and tell him honestly what you believe about him, trusting that he also guides you on the way.
exp.3:35:
And they were all amazed at this scene in the synagogue. They spoke among themselves and asked what kind of word this was, one that carried such authority and power that it commanded the unclean spirits, and the spirits obeyed.

We are in Capernaum, on a Sabbath, in the synagogue. Jesus had just ordered a demon to come out of a man, and the demon obeyed without harming him. The ones speaking are those present, who had watched the whole event. They noticed that Jesus used no rituals or formulas, only his spoken word. That is why his fame spread quickly.

For today: the word of Jesus has real authority over whatever binds us. When something overwhelms you, draw near to him in prayer and trust what he says, not your own strength.
exp.8:40:
Jesus answers with a loud lament: he calls those around him "faithless and perverse generation," and asks how long he will have to be with them and "suffer" them. Here "suffer" means to endure or bear with patience. Right away, without delay, he tells the father: "Bring your son here."

A desperate father tells Jesus that his son suffers terrible fits and that the disciples could not free him. Jesus speaks with sorrow at the lack of faith, and it is not clear whether he is addressing mainly the crowd, the disciples, or everyone. Even so, his rebuke does not shut the door: he calls for the boy and heals him.

For today: when our faith fails us or we feel we cannot go on, we should not walk away. Let us bring our need to Jesus just as it is, trusting in his power and his patience.
exp.13:13:
This verse says that the one who invites those who cannot repay the favor will be happy and blessed by God. The source's quoted terms for "blessed," "repay," "rewarded," and "resurrection of the righteous" are not in the verse your reader sees, so the explanation of them is rewritten here in plain terms: "to repay" means to give something back in return. The verse's promise of reward means that God himself will give the payment, and the phrase about the resurrection refers to the time when God will raise up his people to give them their reward.

Jesus is speaking in the house of an important Pharisee, on a Sabbath, where everyone was watching Jesus and looking for the best seats. After speaking to the guests about humility, he now turns to the host. He teaches them that true generosity does not seek to be paid back or to gain status.

For today: think of someone who cannot repay you at all, such as a lonely neighbor, an elderly person, or someone in need. Invite them to a meal or help them this week, without expecting anything in return, trusting that God sees and rewards.
exp.19:5:
The religious leaders were calculating in their minds. If they answered that John's baptism came from men, the people would stone them. The sentence about the old word meaning "let us say" and the word meaning "convinced" must be rewritten or removed, since those words are not in the verse. The people were certain that John was a prophet of God.

Here the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders speak among themselves. They had asked Jesus by what authority he acted. He turned the question back to them about John. They were not seeking the truth, but an answer that would protect them. That is why they said they did not know.

For today: before you answer, examine your heart. Are you seeking what is true, or only what suits you? God invites us to be honest, even when the truth costs us, and not to hide our position behind fear of what others think.
exp.18:11:
He said a man of an important family went to a distant country to receive from a higher authority the right to be king, and afterward return. The phrase "to receive for himself a kingdom" means to receive authority to rule. "A far country" means a place that is very distant.

Jesus tells this parable near Jerusalem. His listeners thought the kingdom of God was going to appear right away. With this story, Jesus teaches them that there will be a period of waiting before the king returns. Many Christians see here a reference to his departure and his return, although some interpret it with different nuances.

For today: if the King will return, the waiting is not wasted time. It is time to serve him faithfully in everyday life: at work, in the family, and in the church, using what God has entrusted to us, without anxiety and without carelessness.
exp.14:1:
The Pharisees and the scribes, who were teachers of the law, complained quietly among themselves. "Complained" here means they criticized with irritation. What bothered them was that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them.

Luke tells this right after saying that tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to hear Jesus. Tax collectors collected taxes, and many people looked down on them. In that culture, sharing a meal was a sign of friendship and acceptance. That is why the Pharisees were scandalized. Jesus answers with the parable of the lost sheep, to show how God thinks about those who wander away.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we look down on those we consider far from God. Jesus invites us to draw near with love, to listen, and to treat people with dignity, without approving of sin, but wishing that they be found.
exp.13:25:
Jesus says that whoever wants to follow him must "hate" his family and even his own life. The word "hate" sounds very harsh, but here it does not mean hating with resentment. It was a way of speaking that expressed preference: loving less in comparison. A "disciple" is a learner or follower.

Jesus is speaking to large crowds who were walking with him on the road. He had just told the parable of the great banquet, where the invited guests made excuses. Now he wants people to understand that following him demands total commitment, not just passing enthusiasm. Right after this he speaks of carrying the cross and of counting the cost.

For today: ask yourself what thing or person holds first place in your decisions. Following Jesus means that, when a choice has to be made, his voice carries more weight than any other, even though you continue to love and care for your family.
exp.21:12:
What it says: Peter and John (as verse 8 names them) went into the city and found everything just as Jesus had told them. So they made ready the passover, which means they prepared the Passover meal: the lamb, the unleavened bread, and everything needed for the table.

Context: Luke tells what happened shortly before the Last Supper. Jesus sent two disciples with very precise instructions about where to celebrate the Passover. Everything happened as He said, which shows that Jesus knew what was coming and was in control, even as His suffering drew near.

For today: We can trust the word of Jesus, even when His directions seem small or unclear. The disciples obeyed step by step and found that He had gone ahead of them. Obey today what you already know He is asking of you, and trust that He takes care of the details.
exp.18:16:
Here the king says to his servant, "Well done, good servant. Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you will have authority over ten cities." The word "authority" means the power or right to rule. The "coin" was a sum of money, and "doing business" means working with that money to earn more.

Jesus tells this parable as he travels toward Jerusalem. The people thought the kingdom of God would appear right away. The nobleman who leaves and later returns as king represents Jesus, and the servants are those who serve him while he is away. Some interpreters see in this an invitation to live responsibly until his return.

For today: God values faithfulness in small things. Do not wait for great opportunities; be honest and steady in your daily tasks, using carefully what God has entrusted to you, such as your time, your talents, and your money.
exp.22:29:
Jesus says that a time will come of such terror that people will beg the mountains to fall on them, and the hills (the small mountains) to cover them. The old spelling "á" is the form of writing "a" used in older texts. In other words, they would rather be crushed than face what is coming.

Jesus is walking toward the cross, and some women of Jerusalem are weeping for him. He warns them about a future judgment. Many believe he is speaking of the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, though others also see a reference to the final judgment. His words repeat an image from the prophet Hosea (10:8).

Even in his suffering, Jesus thinks of others. Today we can take his warning seriously, not live with indifference toward God, and seek refuge in him now, rather than flee from him later.
exp.8:14:
The disciples obeyed Jesus and had all the people sit down, just as he had asked them to. Their doing so meant they managed to seat the whole crowd.

Luke describes the scene in which Jesus feeds about five thousand men. The disciples had only five loaves and two fish, and even so Jesus asked them to get the people organized before the miracle happened. They still could not see how the food would reach everyone, but they did what they were told.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take a step of obedience before we understand how he will meet the need. We can do what is within our reach, with the little we have, and trust that he will do what we cannot.
exp.5:40:
Jesus asks why someone notices a small flaw in another person but fails to notice a much bigger one in themselves. The "speck" is a tiny splinter or dry fragment; the "plank" is a large beam used in construction. The exaggeration is meant to make clear how absurd the situation is.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He had just been talking about loving your enemies and not judging others. With the parable of the blind man leading another blind man, he warns that whoever does not examine himself cannot guide others well.

Before correcting someone, honestly examine your own heart. Ask God to show you your faults, and if you must speak with another person, do so with humility and love, not with pride.
exp.8:47:
Jesus says that whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives God the Father, who sent me. The sentence that follows says that the one who is least among you all is the one who will be great.

The disciples were arguing about who would be the greatest. Jesus knew what they were thinking in their hearts. So he set a child beside him. In that time, a child had no social importance and no power. Jesus teaches that greatness in his kingdom is not measured by rank, but by humility and service.

Today we can treat with respect and attention those whom people usually overlook: children, the elderly, ordinary people. Doing so is a way of honoring Christ. This week, set aside time to serve someone without expecting recognition.
exp.11:22:
This verse says that life is worth more than food, and that the body is worth more than clothing. The phrase "is more than" means "is more important than." Jesus reminds us that food and clothing serve life, but they are not the purpose of it.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable of the rich fool, a man who piled up riches but was not rich toward God. That is why he tells them not to be filled with anxiety, that is, with worry about what they will eat or wear. Then he points to the ravens, whom God feeds, to show that the Father cares for them.

For today: when worry about money, food, or clothing takes away your peace, stop and pray. Hand that weight over to God, and remember that your life is worth more than your daily needs, and that He cares for you.
exp.6:21:
Jesus tells John's messengers to report back what they have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor, that is, the gospel, the glad tidings.

John the Baptist was in prison and sent two of his disciples to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come. Jesus does not give a simple yes, but points to deeds that recall Isaiah's promises about the Messiah. Why John asked, the Bible does not say; some think he had doubts, others that he wanted to strengthen his faith.

When we doubt, we can bring our questions to Jesus with sincerity. He does not scold us, but invites us to look at what He has done and to trust in Him.
exp.2:35:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. The phrase "which was the son of" means "who was the son of," or a descendant of. Here the line is named that runs from Lamech back through Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Cainan, and Shelah. Some of the names are spelled in older forms: Shelah is written as Sala in some editions, and Lamech is written as Lamec. The name Cainan appears here, but not in the Hebrew text of Genesis. It does appear in the ancient Greek translation, and scholars explain this in different ways.

Luke, the author of the Gospel, presents Jesus' genealogy right after his baptism. The list goes back as far as Adam, and so it shows that Jesus is not only for one people, but comes for all of humanity.

For today: God keeps his promises across many generations, even through people who are little known. Your life and your faithfulness also count in his story.
exp.21:39:
Jesus arrives at the place where he used to pray, the Mount of Olives, and says to his disciples: "Pray that you may not enter into temptation." The words "á" and "fué" are old spellings of "a" and "fue." "Temptation" here can mean a strong trial that tests faith.

Jesus speaks with his disciples shortly before he is arrested, on the night of the Last Supper. He knows what is coming: his suffering and their flight. For this reason he invites them to pray. Afterward he withdraws a little and prays to the Father, accepting his will. Some understand that the temptation would be abandoning him out of fear.

For today: before facing a trial, do not rely only on your own strength. Pray in advance, asking God for the strength to remain faithful.
exp.11:56:
Jesus asks: "Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?" That is, why do you not use your own judgment to see what is correct?

Jesus speaks to the crowd and calls them hypocrites. They knew how to read the weather, but they did not recognize that a decisive moment had come with Jesus. Right after this, he speaks of settling accounts with your opponent before reaching the judge. Many understand this as an urgent invitation to be reconciled with God and with others while there is still time, although it is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: what do I know is right and am I still putting it off? If there is a broken relationship or an unpaid debt, take the first step today to repair it.
exp.22:41:
This verse records the request of one of the two criminals crucified beside Jesus. He asks Jesus to remember him when he comes into his kingdom. He asks for no miracle and does not ask to be taken down from the cross; he only asks to be remembered.

The second criminal is the one speaking. Shortly before, he acknowledged that he deserved his punishment and defended Jesus' innocence. In this he shows repentance and faith: he sees in the crucified man a king with a real kingdom. Jesus answers him with an immediate promise that he will be with him in paradise.

For today: you do not need a settled life or many words to draw near to God. With humility and trust, you can acknowledge your need and ask Jesus to receive you. He responds with grace to those who come to him sincerely.
exp.2:33:
