This verse continues the list of Jesus' ancestors, going backward in time: Judah, son of Jacob; Jacob, son of Isaac; Isaac, son of Abraham; Abraham, son of Terah; and Terah, son of Nahor.

Luke, the author of this Gospel, presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. Unlike Matthew, who starts with Abraham, Luke goes back all the way to Adam. In this way he shows that Jesus is connected to all of humanity and to the promises made to Abraham. Scholars explain the differences between the two lists in several ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: God works across generations, through imperfect people. You can trust that he also counts on you and your family in his plans.
exp.1:29:
Simeon says that his eyes have already seen God's salvation. He is referring to the child Jesus, whom he holds in his arms. The phrase "mine eyes have seen" is simply the verse's wording, so it can be translated directly in the reader's verse as "mine eyes have seen thy salvation." Salvation here is the rescue that God sends, and in this verse it is joined to the person of Jesus.

Simeon is a righteous and devout man from Jerusalem. Luke tells us that the Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ. When Joseph and Mary bring the child to the temple, Simeon recognizes him, takes him in his arms, and praises God. With this, he feels ready to depart in peace.

For today: salvation is not a distant idea but a person, Jesus. Like Simeon, we can trust that God keeps what he promises, even when it takes time. Today you can give thanks for Jesus and rest in that peace.
exp.10:33:
Jesus says that the eye is like the lamp of the body. "Lamp" is the word for the light-giving object here, and the verse says "light of the body." "Single" means sincere, without duplicity, focused on one thing. "Evil" speaks of an eye damaged by envy, greed, or hardness. If the eye is single and healthy, the whole body receives light; if it is evil, everything is in darkness.

Jesus speaks to a crowd that was asking him for a sign from heaven, even though they were already seeing his works. He has just said that something greater than Jonah is here. The light is in plain view, but the problem is not that light is lacking; it is how one looks. Many interpreters understand the eye as the inner attitude of the heart.

For today: before you read the Bible, ask God for a sincere heart, ready to obey. Examine whether what you look at and desire is drawing you toward the light or gradually darkening you.
exp.23:33:
The verse says that the disciples gathered in Jerusalem were confidently declaring: the Lord is indeed risen, and he appeared to Simon. Simon is Simon Peter. The word "appeared" means that Jesus let himself be seen.

The ones speaking are the eleven apostles and their companions. The two disciples coming from Emmaus arrive excited with their own news, but they find that the group already had news of its own. Peter, who had denied Jesus, received a personal appearance. The Bible does not give the details of that encounter here; Paul mentions it briefly in 1 Corinthians 15:5.

For today: Jesus seeks out those who have failed, as he did with Peter. If you feel far from God because of your mistakes, remember that the risen Lord goes looking for people; he does not cast them aside. And when you come to know him better, share him with others, as they did.
exp.17:6:
Jesus asks a question to encourage his listeners: if even an unjust judge ended up granting justice to a persistent widow, how much more will God do so for his chosen ones, that is, for those who belong to him? The word "patient" means that God is slow to act. In this way, God seems to delay, but he is not indifferent.

Jesus tells the parable of the widow and the judge to teach that we must always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Here he compares and contrasts: God is not like the unjust judge but a Father who listens. The verses that follow speak of the coming of the Son of Man and of faith. How to understand "soon" (quickly, or suddenly) has been interpreted in several ways.

When you feel that God is slow to answer, keep praying with confidence. His patience is not forgetfulness, and your faith grows strong while you wait.
exp.13:5:
This verse says that the people who were present had nothing to say in reply to Jesus' words. The word "reply" here means to answer back or argue against what someone says. "These things" refers to what Jesus had just said and done. His argument was so clear that no one could contradict it.

Jesus was eating in the house of a leader of the Pharisees, on the Sabbath. A man suffering from swelling caused by illness was there, and those present were watching to see whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath. He questioned them, healed the man, and asked whether they would not pull their animal out of a well on that day. They were silent, because their own custom showed that doing good should not wait.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we guard the rules more than we care for people. When someone is suffering, compassion should not wait. And if the truth leaves us without an answer, it is better to listen to it with humility than to defend ourselves with pride.
exp.10:27:
Jesus answers a woman who praised his mother. He says "Yea rather," which here means "on the contrary" or "rather." Blessed, that is, truly happy and favored, are those who hear the word of God and keep it, meaning they obey it and put it into practice.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd, just after speaking about the danger of an empty life without God. A woman called out a blessing on Mary. Jesus does not despise it, but he turns attention to what matters most: admiring is not enough, one must obey. Then he warns the people who are looking for signs.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I only hear the Bible, or do I also practice it? Choose a teaching you have read this week and decide today on one concrete step to live it out, such as forgiving someone, being honest, or helping someone in need.
exp.11:40:
Peter asks Jesus a question: he wants to know whether the parable about being ready for the Lord's coming was meant only for the disciples or for all people. The Greek-style phrasing here is not something your reader sees, so the explanation's note about old wording is set aside; the verse itself reads "Lord, speakest thou this parable unto us, or even to all?"

Jesus had just taught that people must be prepared, like a homeowner who would stay watching if he knew when the thief would come. Peter speaks on behalf of the disciples. Jesus does not answer with a direct yes or no, but with another question about the faithful steward. In this way he shows that the teaching touches everyone, and especially those who have responsibility over others.

For today: instead of asking whether a teaching is meant for others, ask yourself what it asks of you. Be faithful in what God has entrusted to you, whether that is your family, your work, or your church, and live each day ready to meet Him.
exp.21:45:
Jesus finds his disciples asleep and asks them why they are sleeping. He tells them to get up and pray so that they do not fall into temptation.

Jesus is speaking on the Mount of Olives, shortly before he is arrested. He had just prayed with deep anguish. Luke says the disciples were sleeping from sorrow, that is, worn out by grief. Soon Judas arrives with the crowd. Jesus knows a hard trial is coming, and he wants them to be spiritually awake.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to pray. If you feel tired or sad, still seek God simply. Prayer strengthens us before the trial, not only after.
exp.11:5:
Jesus asks whether five sparrows are not sold for two farthings, coins of very little value. Even so, he says that not one of them is forgotten by God. Sparrows are small birds, and "before God" means in God's sight, under his watchful eye.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, although a great crowd surrounded him. He warns them that there will be opposition and persecution for following him. He asks them to fear God more than men, but he also shows them that God cares even for the smallest things. If he does not forget a sparrow, how much less will he forget those who confess his name.

When you feel afraid or think you are insignificant, remember that God sees you and knows you. Pray with confidence, hand over today's worry to him, and remain faithful to Jesus, even when others do not understand you.
exp.19:42:
God the Father invites the Messiah to sit in the place of honor and authority, at his right hand, until all his enemies are made subject to him. The phrase "footstool" for your feet was the stool beneath a king's feet; placing someone there meant defeating them completely.

Jesus speaks in the temple, surrounded by religious leaders who were testing him. He quotes Psalm 110:1 and asks them how the Christ can be the son of David if David himself calls him "Lord." Jesus does not give the full answer here. Many Christians understand that he is pointing to the fact that the Messiah is more than a human descendant: he is also divine.

For today: you can rest in the knowledge that Christ reigns and that his final victory is certain. When you feel that evil is advancing, trust that God has the last word, and keep living with hope, patience, and faithfulness.
exp.10:34:
Jesus warns: "Take heed," that is, "be careful," "examine yourself." The "light" is the light within us, what guides us from the inside, such as the way we understand and judge things. Jesus says that this light could be switched off or twisted without our noticing, and that what is really there is darkness.

Jesus speaks to a crowd that was asking for a sign from heaven. Shortly before, he spoke of the light that must be seen and of the eye, which lets light into the body. An eye that is sincere and without duplicity is one thing; an eye that is full of envy or hardness is another. Soon after, a Pharisee invites him to eat, and Jesus confronts the Pharisees over their hypocrisy.

For today: ask God to examine your heart. Before you believe you are right, ask yourself whether you are guided by truth or by pride, and open your mind to the Word.
exp.23:10:
This verse says that the apostles thought what the women reported was nonsense, and they did not believe them. The word "nonsense" here refers to foolish talk, to something without sense.

The women had just come back from the empty tomb. They had heard the angels say that Jesus had risen, and they ran to tell the eleven and the others. Luke, who tells the story, shows with honesty that the disciples were not expecting the resurrection, even though Jesus had already announced it. Shortly afterward, Peter went to check for himself.

For today: sometimes we find it hard to believe what God does, especially when it sounds too good. Instead of dismissing something right away, we can do as Peter did: approach with humility, search sincerely, and ask God to help us in our unbelief.
exp.4:25:
This verse tells how the crowd responded after seeing the paralyzed man healed. The people were all amazed, almost speechless. They praised God, felt a deep sense of awe, and said, "We have seen strange things today," meaning they had witnessed extraordinary things they had never seen before.

Luke is the one telling the story. Jesus had just told the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven, and to show that he had authority to do so, he healed him in front of everyone. Some of the teachers of the law had doubted him, but the crowd responded with wonder and worship. Shortly afterward, Jesus called Levi, a tax collector.

For today: when you see God's work in your own life or in the lives of others, do not walk past it. Stop, give thanks to him, and acknowledge his power with humility and joy.
exp.3:28:
The passage says that the people in the synagogue rose up, drove Jesus out of the town, and led him to the high edge of the hill on which the city was built. They meant to cast him down headlong, that is, to throw him off a cliff to kill him.

Luke tells what happened in Nazareth, where Jesus had grown up. He had just reminded them that God had shown his favor to foreigners, such as the widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian. This wounded their pride, because they expected special privileges. They were filled with rage. Yet the account says that Jesus passed through the midst of them and went on his way. The text does not explain how he did this.

For today: let us examine our hearts with humility when the Word makes us uncomfortable. Instead of becoming angry or defensive, let us ask God to correct us and teach us, even when the truth touches our pride.
exp.11:7:
Jesus says that whoever openly acknowledges him before others, he will also acknowledge before the angels of God. "Acknowledge" here means publicly declaring that you belong to Christ. "Son of man" is the title Jesus uses for himself.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, surrounded by a crowd, and warns them about pressure and persecution. Just before this, he told them that God cares even for the sparrows and has counted every hair on their heads. For that reason he asks them not to be afraid. He then adds that denying him will have serious consequences.

For today: you do not need perfect speeches to acknowledge Jesus. It can be a prayer before a meal, an honest word about your faith, or an upright decision at work. Do it with confidence, knowing that God cares for you.
exp.4:19:
This verse tells us that Jesus saw the faith of the men who brought the paralyzed man to him. Then he said to the sick man, "Man, your sins are forgiven you." The word "Man" was a direct and respectful way of addressing someone.

Jesus was speaking in a house full of people, where there were also scribes and Pharisees, teachers of the law. The paralyzed man's friends had opened the roof to bring him to Jesus. He responded first to the forgiveness of sins, something the leaders considered blasphemy, because only God can forgive sins. In this, Jesus showed his authority.

Today we can bring others to Jesus through prayer and concrete help. And if anyone needs forgiveness, Jesus still offers it to those who trust in him.
exp.17:22:
He says that this man, after hearing what Jesus asked of him, became very sorrowful. The reason the text gives is that he was very rich. The sentence that explains the old wording is removed, and the phrase "very sorrowful" speaks of deep grief, not a simple annoyance.

An important man asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life. He said he had kept the commandments since his youth. Jesús, with love, pointed out what he still lacked: letting go of his riches, helping the poor, and following him. His sorrow showed that his money held a very strong place in his heart. The text does not say what he decided afterward.

For today: ask God whether there is something you find hard to let go of that competes with following Him. It may be money, comfort, or security. Hand it over to Him with trust, because Jesus offers something better.
exp.7:49:
Jesus hears the news that Jairo's daughter has already died. He says to the father: "Do not be afraid; only believe, and she will be made whole." The word "made whole" here means healed and restored to life. "Only believe" means trusting in Jesus, without adding anything else.

Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairo, a leader of the synagogue. Along the way he had healed a sick woman and stopped to speak with her. Then a messenger arrived with the bad news and said they should no longer trouble the Teacher. Jesus speaks directly to the father to support him in that moment of grief.

When news arrives that seems to close every door, Jesus invites us not to let fear have the last word. Trusting in Him does not take away the pain at once, but it allows us to take the next step knowing that He is present and has power.
exp.19:15:
He says the owner of the vineyard will come, will punish those tenants, and will give the vineyard to others. When they heard this, the people answered: "God forbid." The words "destroy" and "inheritance" refer to a serious punishment and to the son's inheritance.

Jesus speaks in the temple to the religious leaders and the people. He tells a parable where the vineyard represents Israel, the tenants represent its leaders, and the son represents Jesus himself. Many understand that he is announcing his rejection and its consequences. The people's reaction shows that they understood the message, although it is not clear how many of them accepted it.

For today: God entrusts us with responsibilities, such as family, work, or the church. They are not ours but are on loan. Ask yourself with humility whether you are listening to Christ or resisting his voice, and respond today with obedience.
exp.19:12:
Here the owner of the vineyard asks himself what to do after his tenants mistreated three servants. He decides to send his beloved son, thinking that perhaps they will respect him. The phrase "when they see him" is the same as "when they see this one," and "will treat with respect" means they will honor him.

Jesus tells this parable in the temple, before the religious leaders and the people. The vineyard represents Israel, and the servants recall the prophets sent by God. The beloved son points to Jesus himself. The word "perhaps" shows the patient hope of the owner, not that God ignores what will happen.

For today: God remains patient and gives us opportunities to turn back to Him. Ask yourself whether there is some message or correction you have been ignoring. Listen humbly to Christ today, before hardening your heart.
exp.13:4:
Jesus asks a simple question: if someone's donkey or ox falls into a well, would they not pull it out at once, even on the Sabbath? The word "at once" is what this rendering uses in place of the older wording. A "well" is a deep pit, sometimes with water in it. Some ancient manuscripts say "son" instead of "donkey"; the traditional reading followed here is "donkey."

Jesus is eating in the home of an important Pharisee, on the Sabbath. In front of him is a man suffering from dropsy, that is, with a swollen body from an excess of fluid. The teachers of the law were watching him. Jesus healed the man and then showed them that helping someone who is suffering does not break the meaning of the Sabbath. They had no answer.

For today: do not let religious customs harden your heart. When someone needs urgent help, do good with compassion, without waiting for the perfect moment.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that Jesus often withdrew to solitary places to pray. "Withdrew" means that he went away from the crowds. "Solitary places" does not necessarily mean sandy deserts, but places that were uninhabited and quiet. The wording of the verse, "withdrew" and "prayed," suggests something habitual, not something that happened only once.

Luke tells this after Jesus healed a man with leprosy and asked him not to spread the news. Even so, his fame kept growing and large crowds came looking for him. Right in the middle of all that demand, Luke highlights that Jesus sought out moments alone with the Father. Then comes a scene of teaching and healing.

For today: even if you have a lot of work or many people who depend on you, set aside some time alone to speak with God. Choose a quiet place and a fixed time, even if it is only ten minutes. Praying is not wasting time; it is receiving strength for everything else.
exp.17:31:
Jesus says that the Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles, that is, to those who are not Jews, to the Romans. There he will be mocked, insulted and treated with contempt, and spat on.

Jesus speaks to the twelve disciples while they are on the way to Jerusalem. He tells them for the third time what awaits him, and says that this fulfills what the prophets had written. He then adds that they will kill him, but that he will rise on the third day. The disciples did not understand this, because they did not expect a Messiah who would suffer.

For today: Jesus was not caught off guard by pain; he accepted it out of love. When you suffer mockery or injustice for your faith, remember that he knows that path and that suffering does not have the last word.
exp.9:26:
It says the most important thing is to love God with everything we are: the heart (our desires and emotions), the soul (our whole life), the strength (our energy) and the mind (our understanding). Then it adds loving our neighbor, that is, the people near us, as we love ourselves.

The one speaking here is a teacher of the law, an expert in the Jewish Scriptures. He wanted to test Jesus, and Jesus turns the question back to him. The man answers by quoting the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18). Jesus will say he answered well, but the man then asks who his neighbor is, and that is where Jesus tells the parable of the good Samaritan.

Today, love God and your neighbor with concrete actions: today help someone close to you who needs it, without choosing whether you like them or not.
exp.11:43:
Jesus says that the master, when he returns, will find his faithful servant doing his work well, and he will reward him by putting him in charge of all that he owns. The words "all that he hath" refer to the master's possessions or riches. Jesus is speaking with great certainty about this promise.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and Peter had asked whether the parable was meant for them or for everyone. Jesus teaches them to be ready for his return. A steward was a servant responsible for managing his master's household. Many understand that the master represents Christ, although the text does not describe in detail what the reward will be.

Today, each of us can ask: how am I caring for what God has entrusted to me, such as my family, my time, and my work? Serve faithfully and steadily, even when no one sees you, trusting that God does see.
exp.5:24:
Jesus says that those who are now "full," meaning well fed and satisfied, will come to hunger. And those who laugh now are waiting for mourning and weeping. "Woe" expresses sorrow and warning more than a curse.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and the crowd, after declaring blessed the poor and those who weep. Here he makes a contrast: he warns those who already have their comfort in the present and do not seek God. Some understand that he is speaking of material wealth; others, also of an attitude of the heart. What follows, loving one's enemies, shows the kind of life he desires.

For today: examine whether your security and joy depend only on what you have or enjoy. Give thanks for what is good, but share with those who are in need, and place your hope in God.
exp.21:41:
Jesus prays to God and calls him "Father." He asks that, if it is possible according to your will, the cup be taken away from him. Here "cup" refers to a cup, and in the Bible it sometimes stands for a burden or a painful suffering. Jesus ends by surrendering himself: that what he wants will not be done, but what the Father wants.

Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives, shortly before he is arrested. He withdraws a little from his disciples and prays on his knees. Earlier he had asked them to pray so that they would not fall into temptation. Facing the cross that is drawing near, he openly expresses his anguish, and yet he chooses to trust in the Father's plan. The text that follows shows his great agony.

You can be honest with God about your fear or your pain, and ask him for what you desire. Then, with God's help, learn to rest in the truth that his will is good, even when you do not yet understand it.
exp.9:41:
Jesus says that only one thing is truly needful, and that Mary chose the better part. The word "but" in the verse is the connecting word that marks the contrast with Martha's busyness. The phrase "the good part" refers to what is most valuable, and "taken away" means snatched away or lost. No one will take from Mary what she has chosen.

Jesus is visiting the home of Martha and Mary. Martha was busy preparing everything, and she became upset because her sister was sitting and listening to Jesus. She asked Jesus to tell Mary to help her. He answered her with affection, repeating her name, and showed her that her worries were troubling her. Some think that "one thing" is simply listening to Jesus; others, that it means putting what is essential first.

Today we can set aside a few minutes each day, unhurried and without a phone, to listen to Jesus in His Word and in prayer. Serving is good, but first we need to be with Him.
exp.17:25:
The explanation says that those who heard Jesus were astonished and asked: "Who then can be saved?" The word "saved" means rescued, that is, freed from sin and received by God into his kingdom. The question shows surprise and even discouragement.

Jesus had just spoken with a rich and prominent man who went away sad, because he would not give up his possessions to follow him. Then Jesus said it is very hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom, like a camel passing through the eye of a needle. In that time, many people saw wealth as a sign of God's blessing, so if even they could not be saved, who could? Jesus answers that what is impossible for people is possible for God.

For today: do not trust your own effort or what you own to be saved. Recognize that you need God and trust in his grace.
exp.8:5:
This verse tells us that the twelve disciples set out and went from town to town. The word "went through" means they moved about among the places, and "towns" refers to small villages. Everywhere they went they proclaimed the gospel, that is, the good news of the kingdom of God, and they healed the sick.

Jesus had just sent the twelve out with power and authority, and he gave them simple instructions: to depend on God for their provision, to stay in the house that welcomed them, and not to press themselves on places that refused them. Here Luke shows that they obeyed. Soon after, Herod hears about everything that was happening, which shows that the work was becoming known.

For today: God uses ordinary people who obey step by step. It is not necessary to have everything figured out; it is enough to share the good news in words and in acts of kindness toward those around us, and to trust that God is with us.
exp.6:33:
Jesus says that he, the Son of Man, came eating and drinking like any other person, and people criticized him for it. They called him "a gluttonous man," someone who eats too much, and "a winebibber," a drunkard, and "a friend of publicans and sinners," that is, a friend of the tax collectors, who were looked down on by everyone, and of sinners.

He speaks this to the crowd right after praising John the Baptist. He compares that generation to spoiled children: they rejected John, who lived in strict self-denial, for being too serious, and they rejected Jesus, who mixed freely with people, for being too easygoing. Nothing pleased them, because they did not want to believe.

For today: when someone does not want to accept the truth, they always find excuses. Examine whether you set conditions on God to suit your own convenience, and remember that Jesus draws near in love to those whom others despise.
exp.18:42:
Jesus says that difficult days will come upon Jerusalem. Her enemies will surround her with a wall or trench (a fortification), lay siege to her, and press her in from every side, leaving her no way out. "They will hem you in" means that the distress will be complete.

Jesus speaks as he draws near to Jerusalem, shortly before entering the temple. He wept when he saw the city, because its people did not recognize the moment when God was visiting them with peace in the person of Jesus. Many believe this was fulfilled when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in the year 70 AD. That is the most common interpretation, though some also see a broader meaning.

Today, this text invites us not to let pass the moment when God speaks to us. If we sense his call, let us respond with humility and not postpone it.
exp.9:37:
This verse tells us that Jesus was on his way and came to a village. There a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home. "Happened" means "took place," and "welcomed him" means that she received him as a guest.

The one telling the story is Luke, who recounts a moment in Jesus' journey. Shortly before, Jesus had told the parable of the good Samaritan and had said, "Go and do likewise." Now a concrete example of hospitality appears. The village is not named here; another Gospel connects Martha and Mary with Bethany, but Luke does not say so in this passage.

Today we too can open the door of our home and of our time to Jesus and to other people. A good deed begins with something simple, such as welcoming someone warmly, listening to them, and caring for them with a willing heart.
exp.3:33:
A spirit that was unclean, speaking through a man, cries out to Jesus. The explanation says the words "let us alone" mean "leave us alone." What have we to do with thee means, roughly, "What do we have in common? Don't meddle with us." The spirit asks whether Jesus has come to destroy them, and it acknowledges that he is the Holy One of God. The title "of Nazareth" indicates that he came from Nazareth.

We are in the synagogue at Capernaum, on a Sabbath. The people had just been amazed at the teaching of Jesus, who spoke with authority. The demon speaks in the plural ("us"), perhaps because it includes other evil spirits. It recognizes who Jesus is, but it does not repent or follow him. Jesus silences it and casts it out with a single command.

For today: Knowing correct facts about Jesus is not the same as trusting him. Ask him to be Lord of your life, not merely someone you respect. And if something oppresses you, remember that his word has authority.
exp.15:5:
The manager asks the debtor how much he owes, and he answers: one hundred measures of oil, a large amount. Then the manager tells him to take his bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty. In this way he cuts the debt in half.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples. A manager is about to lose his position, and he acts quickly to make friends who will receive him afterward. Scholars debate whether the reduction cut into his own profit or was a kind of fraud. What the master praises is his shrewdness in planning for the future, not his dishonesty.

For today: God entrusts us with money, time, and opportunities. Use them wisely and generously, with thought for what lasts forever, and not only for what is immediate.
exp.1:19:
What it says: The shepherds went back to their fields and did not keep quiet. They gave glory to God and praised him for everything they had heard from the angel and seen with their own eyes in Bethlehem. The words "glorifying and praising" show joy and gratitude. "As it was told unto them" means that everything matched the angel's message.

Context: Luke is the narrator. The shepherds had just found the child Jesus lying in the manger, just as the angel had told them. Earlier, others were amazed when they heard the shepherds, and Mary kept all these things in her heart. Now Luke shows the shepherds' response: simple worship, from people who were not important in the society of that time.

For today: When God speaks to you through his Word or shows you his help, do not keep it to yourself without giving him thanks. Praise him sincerely and tell others what you have seen of him, even if you feel like an ordinary person.
exp.7:16:
It says that nothing that is hidden today will stay that way forever. Everything that is concealed will come out into the open and be known. "Manifested" means made known, and "come into light" means becoming visible to everyone.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, right after the parable of the sower. He has just spoken about the lamp that is set up high to give light. His teaching, which many do not yet understand, will become clearer over time. Some interpreters see here also a warning: what is hidden in the heart will be revealed. That is why he adds: "Take care how you listen."

Today we can hear the Word with attention and sincerity, without pretending before God or before others. If there is something hidden in our heart, it is better to bring it to God now, with confidence, because he forgives and transforms.
exp.20:29:
The explanation says that when the trees put out their buds, people see it and know for themselves that summer is already near. No one needs to explain it to them. The quoted phrase about seeing it and understanding for yourselves is simply rendered as "when they now shoot forth, you see and know of your own selves."

Jesus speaks in Jerusalem, near the end of his teaching before the cross. He tells his disciples that hard signs will come. He uses this parable of the fig tree to tell them to learn to recognize the times. The verses that follow say that in this way they will know that the kingdom of God is near. Some understand this as the fall of Jerusalem and others as his return; Christians have interpreted it in several ways.

For today: live alert and with hope, not with fear. Ask God for wisdom to discern the times and remain faithful each day.
exp.14:20:
Here the younger son comes before his father and admits his wrong. He says he has sinned against heaven, that is, against God, and also against his father. He acknowledges that he does not deserve to be treated as a son.

Jesus tells this parable. The young man had asked for his inheritance, spent it on a reckless life, and came back hungry and ashamed. His father saw him from afar, ran to him, and embraced him before hearing his confession. Notice that the son does not get to finish his plan to ask to be made like one of the hired workers; the father receives him as a son.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or try to pay for your mistake with effort. Confess honestly and return to God, trusting that his mercy is greater than your shame.
exp.8:53:
James and John, two of Jesus' disciples, see that the Samaritans do not want to receive him. Then they ask him whether he wants them to call down fire from heaven to destroy them, as the prophet Elijah did. "Consume" means "destroy completely."

Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem, and his messengers were looking for a place to stay. The Samaritans rejected him for that reason. Jews and Samaritans had an old enmity. James and John reacted with anger and wanted to punish. Jesus rebuked them, because he came to save and not to destroy. What they ask recalls an episode involving Elijah in 2 Kings 1.

When someone rejects or offends us, we may feel like taking revenge. Jesus teaches us to respond with patience and mercy. Today we can pray for the one who treated us badly and move on without holding a grudge.
exp.16:25:
Jesus says that what happened in the days of Noah will serve as a comparison for the time when he returns. "Son of man" is the title Jesus uses for himself.

Jesus speaks with his disciples about his coming. First he reminds them that he must suffer and be rejected by that generation. Then he compares those days with the days of Noah: people lived ordinary lives, eating, drinking, and marrying, without paying attention to the warning, until the flood came suddenly. What is emphasized is the carelessness, not that those things are wrong.

Today we can carry on with our work, our families, and our meals, but without forgetting God. A good practice is to set aside a few minutes each day to pray and ask yourself: "Am I living ready to meet Jesus?"
exp.9:2:
Jesus says to his disciples: "Go your ways: behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves." He compares them to lambs, defenseless animals, and the people who oppose them to wolves, which are dangerous.

Jesus himself speaks when he sends out seventy followers, two by two, to the towns he would visit later. He has just told them that the harvest is large and the workers are few. He honestly warns them that they will be rejected. Some believe that "seventy" also appears as "seventy-two" in other manuscripts; scholars have not fully settled the question.

For today: if you share your faith, do not go with pride or with violence. Trust that Jesus sends you and takes care of you, offer peace, and accept that not everyone will respond well.
exp.12:31:
Jesus responds to some Pharisees who warn him that Herod wants to kill him. He sends a message to Herod, whom he calls a "fox." "I cast out devils and do cures" means that he keeps on driving out evil spirits and healing people. "Today and tomorrow" and "the third day" are not exact dates, but a way of saying that his work follows a plan. "I shall be perfected" means that he will reach his goal, that his mission will be fulfilled.

Jesus speaks while on the way to Jerusalem. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee. It is not known for certain why the Pharisees gave him the warning; some think it was a sincere caution, others that they wanted to get him out of the region. The "fox" suggests cunning, and Jesus is not frightened: his mission depends on God, not on human threats.

For today: when fear or pressure try to stop you, keep doing the good that God has given you to do, trusting that he directs your times.
exp.18:37:
This verse tells what the crowd of disciples was shouting as Jesus drew near to Jerusalem. They call him "the King who comes in the name of the Lord," that is, sent with God's authority. "Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest" speaks of the highest heaven, where God dwells. They say there is peace and glory up there.

The ones speaking are Jesus' followers, glad because of all the miracles they had seen. They were coming down the Mount of Olives, and they spread their cloaks on the road as people did to honor a king. Their words recall Psalm 118:26. Some of the Pharisees were displeased and asked him to silence them, but Jesus did not stop them.

Today we can praise Jesus with joy and without shame, remembering what he has done in our lives. If he is our King, it is worth saying so out loud, even when others do not understand.
exp.20:11:
Jesus says that before the wars, the earthquakes and the signs in the sky take place, his followers will be arrested and persecuted. They will be handed over to the synagogues, which were places of gathering and also of judgment, and to prisons. They will be brought before kings and governors. Being arrested is the meaning of the phrase "lay their hands on you," and the cause is one alone: "for my name," that is, for being followers of Jesus.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, near the end of his ministry, when he warns them about the future. He does not want to frighten them but to prepare them. Many understand that this was fulfilled in part in the time of the apostles, though some also see a broader fulfillment in the future. The verses that follow say that these trials would be an opportunity to give testimony.

For today: if you are criticized or rejected because of your faith, do not be surprised. Jesus already announced it. Trust that he is with you, and ask him for courage to respond with gentleness.
exp.23:51:
It says that the disciples, after worshipping Jesus, returned to Jerusalem with great joy. The word "worshipped" means that they recognized Him as Lord and God, and bowed before Him with reverence.

Luke, the author, tells the ending of his Gospel. Jesus had just blessed them and ascended into heaven from near Bethany. Before that, He had explained to them that everything written about Him had been fulfilled. That is why they do not leave sad, even though Jesus is no longer with them in sight. Their joy comes from knowing that He lives and reigns. Then they gather in the temple, praising God.

For today: worship and joy go together. When you face uncertain days, stop to worship Jesus, remembering that He is alive and keeps His promises. That can give you a joy that does not depend on circumstances.
exp.15:22:
Jesus tells that the rich man, after he died, lifted up his eyes in the middle of his suffering and saw Abraham far off, with Lazarus beside him. The word for the place of the dead is rendered here as hell, the place of the dead. The image of resting in Abraham's bosom is a picture of rest and honor, like reclining beside him at a feast.

The one speaking is Jesus, and he addresses some Pharisees who loved money (Luke 16:14). Many scholars see this story as a parable, others as a real account; the Bible does not make this clear. Its central teaching is plain: the situations are reversed, and the rich man, who ignored the poor man, now suffers.

Today, ask yourself who is at your door with a need. Do not put off compassion: use what God has given you to help today.
exp.4:24:
He stood up at once in front of everyone. He picked up the mat he had been lying on and went home, giving thanks and praise to God.

Jesus was teaching in a house full of people. Some friends lowered this man through the roof. Jesus forgave his sins, and some teachers of the law were upset. Then Jesus healed the man to show that he has authority to forgive. The narrator, Luke, tells how the man responded.

When God works in our lives, the natural response is gratitude. Today you can take a moment to thank God, aloud or with someone else, for something specific he has done for you.
exp.8:17:
It says that Jesus was praying in a place apart, though his disciples were near him. Then he asked them a question: "Whom say the people that I am?" The word "people" in this verse refers to the crowds, the multitudes. Jesus does not ask because he does not know, but to lead them to think.

He speaks just after feeding more than five thousand people with five loaves and two fish. Many had seen his miracles and held different ideas about him. Luke shows that prayer comes before this key moment. After hearing what the people think, Jesus asks the disciples, and Peter answers: "The Christ of God."

For today: before deciding what matters most, set yourself apart to pray. And remember that what others think of Jesus is not enough; each person must answer for themselves who he is for their own life.
exp.22:38:
This verse tells us that one of the two criminals crucified beside Jesus was insulting him. He said: "If you are the Christ, the Messiah, save yourself and us." The word "malefactors" refers to people who have done wrong, and "railed" means that he was speaking with mockery and scorn.

It is one of the condemned men speaking, who is suffering on the cross just as Jesus is. Earlier, the leaders and the soldiers had also mocked him. This man repeats those words, but with a different desire: he wants to be freed from the pain. Afterward, the other criminal rebukes him and admits that they deserved that punishment, but Jesus did not.

For today: sometimes we ask God only to take us out of suffering, without acknowledging who he is. We can learn to come to Jesus with humility and trust, not to demand from him, but to seek his forgiveness and his company.
exp.1:45:
This verse tells how, after three days of searching, Mary and Joseph found Jesus in the temple. He was sitting among the teachers, who were men who taught the law of God. He was listening to them and asking them questions.

The one who tells the story is Luke. Jesus was twelve years old, and the family had gone to Jerusalem for the Passover feast. On the return journey, his parents thought he was with other travelers, and they did not notice he was missing until later. So they went back anxiously to look for him. The verses that follow show how amazed people were at his understanding.

For today: Jesus teaches us the value of listening and asking questions with humility. Learning God's Word requires a willing heart. Whether through the Bible or through wise people, let us seek to learn with simplicity.
exp.3:20:
He begins to speak to the people in the synagogue. He says that the Scripture they have just heard, the one that speaks of good news for the poor and freedom for the captives, is fulfilled "this day." The word "ears" means that they are hearing it at that very moment.

Jesus is in Nazareth, his hometown. He has just read the passage from Isaiah 61 and sits down, as a teacher customarily did. Everyone looks at him intently. With these words he presents himself as the one of whom the prophet spoke, the messenger sent by God. At first the people are amazed, but then they doubt, because they know him as the son of Joseph.

God does not speak only of the past. His Word reaches you today. When you read it, do not ask only what it meant then, but also: what is Jesus asking of me today? Respond with faith and simple obedience.
exp.11:9:
Luke 12:10 says that speaking a word against the Son of Man, that is, against Jesus, can be forgiven. But speaking against the Holy Ghost, which means speaking wickedly against the work of God, will not be forgiven. To blaspheme means to insult or despise God with words and with the heart.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, with many people around them, and encourages them not to deny him out of fear. Just before, he speaks of confessing him or denying him; afterward, he speaks of the Spirit helping them before the authorities. Many believe this blasphemy is a stubborn and final rejection of the work of the Spirit, who leads people to Christ. Interpreters explain the detail in several ways.

If you worry that you have committed this sin, remember that the Spirit invites you to return to God. That desire to repent is a good sign. Today, respond with humility to his voice.
exp.5:17:
This verse says that the people who were troubled by unclean spirits, that is, evil spirits, were made well. "Vexed" speaks of strong and constant suffering. "Healed" means that they were set free and restored.

Luke tells that Jesus came down from the mountain with his twelve apostles and stopped on a level place. There a great crowd was waiting for him, from Judea, Jerusalem, and the coast of Tyre and Sidon. They had come to hear him and to be healed. After this scene, Jesus begins to teach his disciples with the beatitudes.

For today: Jesus did not turn away from those who suffered in the deepest darkness, but received them and healed them. We can draw near to him honestly, without hiding our struggles, and also treat with compassion those who today carry pains that cannot be seen.
exp.15:14:
Jesus tells the Pharisees that they present themselves as righteous before people, but God sees what is really in the heart. "You justify yourselves" means that they declare themselves good. "Highly esteemed" means greatly admired or valued, and "abomination" is something God rejects. What people applaud may be worth nothing to God.

Jesus speaks after teaching that one cannot serve God and money. The Pharisees, who according to the text loved money, mocked him. Jesus responds by showing that their apparent piety hid a divided heart, although God knew it well.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I do good things so that people will see me, or to please God? Today, before acting, pray with sincerity and ask him to examine your motives and cleanse your heart.
exp.17:1:
He says that Jesus began the parable by speaking of a judge in a city. This judge had no fear of God and no regard for people. In other words, he did not care about what God thought or about what people needed.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Luke had already told us the reason: to teach them that they must always pray and not lose heart. Jesus uses an unjust judge as a contrast. If even such a man ends up attending to a widow who keeps insisting, how much more will God, who is good, hear his children.

When we pray, we are not speaking to someone indifferent like that judge. God is a Father who listens. If today you are tired of praying for something, do not give up. Keep speaking with God with confidence, knowing that he hears you and loves you.
exp.9:33:
The explanation says that the Samaritan came near the wounded man and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he lifted him onto his own animal, that is, his beast, brought him to an inn, which was a lodging place for travelers, and took care of him personally.

Jesus tells this parable in response to a teacher of the law who asked him, "And who is my neighbor?" Earlier, a priest and a Levite saw the wounded man and passed by on the other side. The Samaritan, from a people despised by the Jews, was the one who acted with mercy. Jesus shows that loving your neighbor means helping through deeds.

Today, compassion is shown through concrete actions, even when they cost time or money. We can ask ourselves: who near me needs help, and what can I do for that person today, no matter who they are?
exp.20:24:
It says there will be strange signs in the sun, the moon and the stars. On the earth, the nations will feel anguish and bewilderment because of the roaring of the sea and the waves. The word for "nations" here means peoples, and the sentence about the noise that confuses and frightens refers to a sound that disorients people and fills them with fear.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. First he announces the fall of the city, and then he looks ahead to his return. Christians understand in different ways how these themes fit together, but all agree that Jesus wants to prepare his followers, not frighten them.

When the world feels insecure and the news fills people with fear, we can remember that Jesus had already said this and that he remains in control. Today you can respond with prayer, trust and a watchful life, without letting panic take over.
exp.9:10:
If a town does not welcome Jesus' messengers, they are to shake the dust of their feet off as a sign that they are leaving. "The dust has clung to us" means that the dust stayed stuck to them. Even so, they must make one message clear: the kingdom of God had come near to those people, whether they accepted it or not.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples whom he sends out in pairs to the towns he himself planned to visit. Shaking off the dust was a gesture showing that they were free of responsibility, and interpreters understand it as a serious warning: rejecting the message has consequences.

For today: share your faith with kindness and without pressure. If someone does not want to listen to you, leave them in peace, without bitterness or anger, and trust that God is still at work in that person.
exp.19:37:
He says that God is not a God of the dead, but of the living, because to him all people live.

Jesus speaks with the Sadducees, a group that denied the resurrection. They had put a difficult case to him about a woman who married seven brothers. Jesus answers them by using what God said to Moses at the burning bush: God presented himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who had died long before. For Jesus, this shows that they are still alive before God. The scribes had no more questions.

For today: if you have lost a loved one who trusted in God, you can rest in the knowledge that God does not forget them. And your own life with him does not end with death, so you can live with hope and with less fear.
exp.14:2:
This verse is a short introduction. It says that Jesus told them a parable, that is, a simple story with a deeper message. The word "spake" means that he told it or spoke it. The "them" refers to the Pharisees and scribes who had just criticized him.

Jesus speaks because the religious leaders were complaining when they saw him welcome and eat with tax collectors and sinners. Eating with someone was a sign of acceptance and friendship. Instead of arguing, Jesus answers with a story. The parable that follows, the lost sheep, shows how God thinks about those who have wandered away from him.

For today: before we judge those who seem far from God, let us remember that God seeks them out with love. We can ask ourselves who near us needs a kind word or an invitation, and take the first step with patience and without contempt.
exp.10:30:
Jesus says that the queen of the South, that is, the queen of the south, will rise up in the judgment together with the people of that generation and condemn them. She traveled from a very distant place ("the utmost parts of the earth") to hear the wisdom of Solomon. And Jesus declares that here is someone greater than Solomon.

Jesus speaks to crowds who were asking him for a miraculous sign, even though they were already seeing his works and hearing his teaching. He calls them an evil generation because they kept asking for more proof instead of believing. The queen of the South is often identified with the queen of Sheba, although the text does not give her name. She made a great effort to listen, and they had Jesus right in front of them.

Today, God has spoken clearly to us in Christ. Instead of asking for more proof, we can come to Jesus with humility, listen attentively to his Word, and obey it without putting it off for later.
exp.22:35:
The explanation says that the Roman soldiers who were guarding Jesus also mocked him. "Mocked" means they ridiculed him with scorn. They would come up to him and offer him sour wine, a cheap, sharp drink that soldiers commonly carried. Rather than helping him, the gesture seems to be part of the mockery.

Luke tells of the crucifixion. Earlier, Jesus had prayed for those who were crucifying him. Now the leaders, the people, and the soldiers challenge him to save himself if he is really the King. According to the account, they did not understand that his path was to give his life for others.

When someone mocks your faith or treats you with contempt, remember how Jesus responded: he did not return mockery for mockery. Ask God for help to respond with patience, and even to pray for those who offend you.
exp.19:44:
While all the people were listening, Jesus turned to his disciples to say something. This is a short introduction to the warning that follows.

Jesus is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. He has just silenced the religious leaders with a question about the Messiah and David. Now, in front of the crowd, he addresses his disciples with more personal teaching: that they should not imitate the scribes, who sought honor and appeared pious while taking advantage of the weak.

For today: Jesus speaks in public, but he cares that his followers learn to tell sincere faith from mere appearance. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking applause or serving God with humility, caring especially for the vulnerable.
exp.16:3:
Jesus says that if a brother wrongs us seven times in a single day, and seven times comes back saying "I'm sorry, I repent," we must forgive him. "Seven" speaks of forgiveness without limit, not of an exact count.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Earlier he had warned them strongly about causing the little ones to stumble, and now he teaches them to correct with frankness and to forgive when there is repentance. The apostles respond by asking for more faith, perhaps because forgiving in this way seemed very hard to them.

For today: if someone who failed you asks your forgiveness sincerely, do not keep count of the times. Ask God for help to forgive from the heart, and if necessary, speak clearly and lovingly about what happened.
exp.2:32:
This verse continues the list of Jesus' ancestors: Aminadab, Aram, Esrom and Phares. These names are written in an older style (today we would say Fares rather than "Phares"). Each "son of" in the list links one generation to the one before it.

Luke, the author of the Gospel, presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. He goes backward, from Jesus to Abraham and beyond. These names belong to the line of Judah and David. Matthew gives a different list, and scholars explain it in several ways, with no single certain answer. Luke shows that Jesus has real roots in the history of Israel.

For today: God works across generations, including those that almost no one remembers. Your faithfulness each day, though it may seem small, can be part of what God is doing beyond what you can see.
exp.17:30:
Jesus takes the twelve disciples aside and tells them that they are on their way to Jerusalem. There, everything that the prophets wrote about the Son of man will be fulfilled, a title Jesus uses to refer to himself.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, who have just heard that leaving everything for the kingdom has its reward. Now he makes clear that his own path goes through suffering, death, and resurrection. The verses that follow spell this out. Luke says afterward that they did not understand this (v. 34).

For today: God carries out his plans even when we find them hard to understand. When something does not make sense, we can keep trusting him, as Jesus trusted the Father, knowing that God is faithful to his Word.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells us that Zacharias, a priest, was greatly frightened when he saw the angel. The phrase "he was troubled" means he was startled and left confused, and "fear fell upon him" means that fear completely overcame him.

Luke tells us that Zacharias was serving in the temple and had the duty of offering the incense, while the people prayed outside. Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared to him beside the altar. His reaction is very human: meeting what is holy and supernatural is overwhelming. Right away the angel calms him and announces that God has heard his prayer and that he will have a son, John.

For today: when God surprises you or something frightens you, do not stay in fear. Listen to what He wants to tell you. Very often God comes with a word of comfort just when we feel smallest or most uncertain.
exp.21:59:
Peter answers, "Man, I know not what you are saying," and this is the third time he denies knowing Jesus. While he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. The word "Man" here is simply a way of addressing someone, like calling a person "friend" or "sir."

Jesus is being tried, and Peter had followed at a distance into the courtyard of the high priest. There, by the fire, several people recognize him as a follower of Jesus because of his Galilean accent. Peter, afraid, denies it. Earlier, Jesus had warned him that he would do this three times before the rooster crowed. The crowing of the rooster marks that this word was fulfilled.

For today: all of us can fail, especially under pressure. Do not rely on your own strength alone; ask God for courage. And if you fall, remember that Peter wept with repentance, and Jesus did not abandon him.
exp.2:19:
The explanation says that Herod, besides all his wickedness, did something even worse: he put John the Baptist in prison. The phrase "added yet this above all" means that this act was added to a long list of evil deeds. "Tetrarch" was a ruler over part of the territory, under Roman rule.

Luke, as the narrator, summarizes what happened to John. John preached boldly and rebuked Herod for taking Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, and for other wrongs. Herod answered by silencing the messenger instead of correcting his life. Luke tells this before Jesus' baptism, to close the account of John.

For today: when someone corrects us with truth, we can choose between repenting and silencing the voice that makes us uncomfortable. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen, and for courage to speak the truth with love.
exp.12:5:
Jesus tells a parable. A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. He went to look for fruit on it and found none. A vineyard is a piece of land where grapes and other fruit trees are grown. The phrase "went to look" means he went to check whether the tree was already bearing fruit.

Jesus is speaking to people who had been talking to him about some tragic deaths. He tells them that those people were not worse than others, and that everyone needs to repent. With this parable he shows that God is patient, but expects to see fruit from a changed life. Many think the fig tree represents the people of Israel, although it can also apply to each person.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: what fruit is my life producing, such as love, honesty, and service? We should not postpone change, because God's patience is an opportunity to turn back to him now.
exp.22:3:
Pilate says to the chief priests and the crowd that he finds no fault in Jesus. The word "fault" here means a crime or a reason to condemn him. The chief priests are the leading priests. The word "find" means to discover or determine.

The Jewish leaders had just accused Jesus before Pilate, the Roman governor, of misleading the people, of opposing payment of taxes to Caesar, and of calling himself a king. Pilate questioned him and, after hearing his answer, concluded there was no legal basis for condemning him. The accusers, however, kept insisting.

For today: Jesus was declared innocent, and this reminds us that he suffered unjustly for us. When someone accuses us without reason, we can trust God, who knows the truth. We can also ask ourselves whether, like Pilate, we know what is right but lack the courage to act on it.
exp.11:25:
Jesus says that if you cannot do even something as small as adding a little to your height, there is no point in worrying about the bigger things. "Anxious" means worried to an excessive degree. A cubit was a short measure, roughly half a meter, and here it is used as something minimal.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and there was a crowd nearby. He teaches them not to live ruled by anxiety about food and clothing. He gives the ravens and the lilies as examples, which God takes care of. Some scholars say that "height" could also be understood as "length of life"; the text allows both readings.

Today we can notice when worry tries to control what is not in our hands. Do what is yours to do, with responsibility, and leave the rest to God in prayer, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.12:8:
Here the vinedresser asks the owner for one more year to care for the fig tree. If after that time it bears fruit, good; if not, then he will cut it down.

Jesus tells this parable right after speaking about the need to repent (Luke 13:1-5). The owner represents God, who looks for fruit. The vinedresser asks for patience. Many understand that it speaks of Israel, though it also applies to each person. The parable does not say what happened afterward, and that invites us to respond today.

God is patient, but his patience is no excuse for putting off change. Today you can ask yourself: what area of my life needs repentance and obedience? Make use of this time of grace to bear fruit: love, justice, humility and service.
exp.7:39:
He says that when Jesus came back, the people welcomed him gladly, because they had all been waiting for him. The word "received" in the verse means he was welcomed, and "returned" means he was coming back from the other side of the Sea of Galilee.

The one telling the story is Luke, who recounts what happened after Jesus healed the man freed from demons in the region of the Gadarenes. There the people asked Jesus to leave, but now, on his return, a crowd is waiting for him. The contrast is clear: some rejected him, and others longed for him. Soon Jairus will come, asking for help for his daughter.

For today: Jesus welcomes those who seek him with hope. We can come to him with confidence, without waiting until everything is in order, and bring him our needs with expectation, like those people who were waiting for him.
exp.6:27:
Jesus says that, among all human beings, no one has been a greater prophet than John the Baptist. But he adds that the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John. The phrase "among those that are born of women" is an old way of saying "all human beings." "Prepare" is the meaning of the word in the verse above that prepares the way.

Jesus speaks to the crowd after John's messengers have left. He praises John because he was the messenger announced by God to prepare the way for the Messiah. In saying that the least in the kingdom is greater, Jesus does not belittle John; many understand that he is speaking of the privilege of living in the salvation that Christ would bring. Some interpret it in other ways.

For today: if you belong to Christ, your worth does not depend on your achievements or your fame, but on the grace you have received. Live thankfully and with humility.
exp.17:39:
Jesus stopped when he heard the blind man's cry. Instead of continuing on his way, he gave orders for the man to be brought to him. When the man came near, Jesus asked him a question. The word "stood" in the verse means stopping, and "commanded him to be brought unto him" means he gave orders for the man to be brought to his side.

The narrator here is Luke. He tells of a blind man sitting by the road, crying out for mercy. The people told him to be quiet, but he shouted all the more. Jesus did not ignore his voice. He called him, brought him close, and treated him as a person of worth, not as a nuisance.

For today: when your need feels very great, or when others do not seem to listen to you, come to Jesus honestly and keep praying. He stops to listen, and he also invites us not to silence the cries of others.
exp.17:26:
Jesus answers that what is impossible for people is possible for God. The phrase "with men" here means "from a human point of view" or "for people." In this passage, the impossibility is entering the kingdom of God, that is, being saved, by one's own effort.

Jesus has just spoken with a rich man who was unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. Then he said it is very hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom, using the exaggerated image of the camel and the needle. The listeners were astonished and asked who could then be saved. Jesus makes clear that salvation does not depend on human ability, but on the power of God.

For today: do not trust in your money, your achievements, or your goodness to earn God's favor. If you feel that your situation or your heart is beyond help, ask God for help, because he can do what you cannot.
exp.6:40:
Jesus begins a short story. A certain creditor, that is, someone who had lent money, had two debtors. One owed him five hundred pence and the other fifty. A pence was roughly the pay for a day's work, so the first debt was huge and the second was much smaller.

Jesus is having a meal at the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known as a sinner came up to Jesus, and Simon thought badly of her and of Jesus as well. So Jesus tells him this parable to help him see his own heart. The story sets up a question about who will love the one who forgives more.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to make yourself feel better. All of us need God's forgiveness, even though our debts may seem different. Recognizing this leads us to love God more and to treat others with compassion.
exp.10:13:
This verse tells that Jesus was driving out a demon that had left a man unable to speak. When the demon went out, the man was able to talk, and the crowd was amazed. "Casting out" means driving out, and "the people" refers to the crowd that was present.

Luke is the one telling the story. Just before this, Jesus taught his disciples to pray and encouraged them to ask the Father with confidence, since the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Now his power is seen in action. But the reaction is divided: some marvel, others accuse him of acting by an evil power, and others ask for a sign. The texts do not say more about the man's condition.

Faced with the work of God, we can respond with wonder and gratitude, or with doubt and criticism. Today we can choose to humbly recognize what God does in our lives and in the lives of others, and to give thanks aloud, like someone receiving a new voice.
exp.8:57:
Jesus says that foxes have holes to live in and birds have nests, but he, called "the Son of man" (a title Jesus uses for himself), does not even have a place of his own to rest his head. In other words, he lived without a fixed home.

Jesus is on the road toward Jerusalem, and a man promises him: "I will follow you wherever you go." Jesus answers him with this image so that he will think carefully about what he is saying. Following him could mean discomfort, rejection, and a lack of security. Shortly before, a village had not welcomed him.

For today: before saying "I will follow you," ask yourself what you are willing to let go of, whether comfort, security, or your own plans. Following Jesus is a gift, but it is also a commitment that is lived out with humility and trust in God.
exp.15:8:
Jesus says that we should use money, called here "mammon of unrighteousness," to make friends. "When ye fail" means when money no longer serves us, that is, at death. Then those friends may "receive" us into the eternal dwellings, that is, into God's home forever.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after the parable of the shrewd manager. That man used what he had with wisdom to secure his future. Jesus does not praise his dishonesty, but his foresight. Some explain that the "mammon of unrighteousness" is so called because money is often stained by the selfishness of this world. Interpreters debate the exact details of this passage.

Today we can use our money generously: helping someone in need, supporting the church, or sharing with someone in trouble. In this way we invest in what is eternal and not in what passes away.
exp.10:46:
Jesus says that the teachers of the law build beautiful tombs for the prophets, but it was their ancestors who killed them. "Woe" expresses a serious and sorrowful warning. The words that name the people Jesus is speaking to and the words for "build" are rendered in the verse above as "you" and "build the sepulchres."

Jesus is eating in the house of a Pharisee and speaking with the teachers of the law. One of them feels offended. Jesus answers that honoring the dead prophets seems like a good thing, but they reject God's message today, just as their fathers did. Many understand that by approving what their fathers did, they were following the same path.

For today: it is easy to admire the heroes of faith of the past and, at the same time, to resist what God is telling us now. Let us ask him for a humble heart that obeys his Word, not only one that admires it.
exp.21:22:
The disciples began to ask one another which of them it was who would betray Jesus. The word "á" is the preposition "a" written with an old accent mark, and "do this thing" refers to the betrayal Jesus had just announced.

This moment takes place during the Last Supper. Jesus said that one of those eating with him would betray him. Luke, who tells the story, shows that no one was pointed out with certainty: everyone was left troubled. Soon after, the text tells us they also argued about who was the greatest, which stands in contrast to the seriousness of the moment.

For today: instead of looking only at others, we can examine our own hearts with humility. They asked "which of them it was," and other Gospels show that each one doubted himself. Ask God to show you whether there is anything in you that needs to change, and trust in his mercy.
exp.6:38:
This verse tells what the Pharisee thought when he saw the woman touching Jesus' feet. He was the one who had invited Jesus to eat. Seeing her, he said in his heart that if Jesus were a prophet, he would know who she was and what kind of woman she was: a sinner.

The one speaking here is Luke, the narrator, who lets us see the thoughts of Simon, the host. He judges the woman and also doubts Jesus. But Jesus answers right away with the parable of the two debtors, showing that he did know both the woman and the heart of Simon.

For today: before we judge someone by their past, let us remember that God looks at the heart and offers forgiveness to everyone. We can come to Jesus with humility, without feeling better than others.
exp.22:19:
Pilate spoke to the crowd again because he wanted to set Jesus free. Setting free means letting someone go from custody.

Pilate was the Roman governor and had the authority to decide the case. He had already declared that he found no fault in Jesus. The crowd, however, was asking for Barabbas to be released, a man imprisoned for an uprising and for murder. Pilate tries to persuade them once more, but the pressure of the people is strong. The text shows his desire to let Jesus go, though afterward he fails to hold to that intention firmly.

For today: it is not enough to know what is right or to desire it; courage is needed to act. Let us ask God for the firmness to defend truth and justice, even when the majority pushes in another direction.
exp.6:39:
Jesus speaks to Simon, the Pharisee who invited him to eat. He tells him that he has something to say to him, and Simon replies with respect: "Say on," that is, "Speak, I am listening." The word "Master" means "Teacher."

Simon had thought in his heart that Jesus could not be a prophet, because he let a sinful woman touch him. No one had said anything to Jesus, but he answered that hidden thought. In this way he shows that he knows the hearts of people. Next he will tell Simon a parable about two debtors who were forgiven, to teach him something about love and forgiveness.

For today: before judging others, let us let Jesus speak to our hearts. We can say to him with humility, as Simon did: "Speak, Lord," and be ready to see our own faults and to treat others with compassion.
exp.8:61:
It says that whoever starts plowing and keeps looking back is not fit for the kingdom of God. Here "fit" means suitable or useful. A plow is the tool used to break open the soil for planting. To plow a straight furrow, you have to look forward.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, and some people tell him they will follow him. One man asks first to say goodbye to his family. Jesus does not look down on family; with this image he teaches that following him requires a firm, undivided decision. Some understand that the problem is a divided heart, not the farewell itself.

For today: if God has called you to something, do not let the past, comfort, or indecision hold you back. Ask him for steadiness, and take one concrete step forward in your faith today, trusting in his grace.
exp.8:34:
It says that from a cloud a voice was heard that presented Jesus as "my beloved Son" and asked that people listen to him. The phrase "hear him" is an older way of saying "listen to him."

Jesus is on the mountain with Peter, John and James, and Moses and Elijah appear. Peter speaks without really understanding what is happening and wants to place the three of them on the same level. Then the voice, which is understood as the voice of God the Father, makes clear that Jesus is the Son and that he is the one to be listened to. When it ends, Jesus is left alone.

For today: before following opinions, customs, or voices that compete for our attention, we can return to the Gospels and ask ourselves, "What does Jesus say?" Listening to him each day, with humility, puts our decisions and priorities in order.
exp.0:59:
Elizabeth, the child's mother, answers firmly the neighbors and relatives who wanted to give him his father's name, Zechariah. She says no, that he will be called John. The phrase "will be called" means that this will be his name.

We are on the day of circumcision, eight days after the birth, when it was customary to give the child a name. Elizabeth speaks because the angel had told Zechariah that the child would be named John (Luke 1:13). Zechariah could not yet speak. The Bible does not say how Elizabeth knew the name; some think Zechariah had communicated it in writing, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: obeying God sometimes means standing firm, with kindness, even when tradition or the opinion of people says otherwise. Let us ask God for wisdom and courage to follow what He has shown us.
exp.17:13:
Jesus says that the tax collector went down to his house "justified," that is, accepted and forgiven by God, rather than the Pharisee. Lifting oneself up means thinking yourself superior; being brought low means God will put you in your place. Rather than the other can be understood as "instead of the other."

Jesus tells this parable to people who trusted in themselves as righteous and looked down on others. The Pharisee boasted of his works, while the tax collector only asked for mercy. Then the children come to Jesus, and He shows that the kingdom belongs to those who come with humility and without merits of their own.

Today, before you compare yourself with others, come before God with sincerity. Say to Him with confidence: "God, have mercy on me." His forgiveness is not earned by merit; it is received with a humble heart.
exp.14:7:
Jesus speaks of a woman who has ten silver coins, called drachmas. If she loses one, she lights a lamp (a small oil lamp), sweeps the house, and searches with great care until she finds it.

Jesus tells this to Pharisees and teachers of the law, who complained that He welcomed sinners and ate with them. It is the second of three parables about lost things: the sheep, the coin, and the son. A drachma was of little value, but to her it was important. Jesus shows that God seeks out the lost and rejoices when He finds them.

For today: never think that you are too small or too lost for God. And if you belong to Him, take on His heart: pray, draw near with patience to those who are far away, and rejoice when someone returns to Him.
exp.12:30:
That same day some Pharisees came to Jesus and told him to leave that place, because Herod wanted to kill him. The phrase "get out of here and go" is simply "leave here and go." The old spellings "á" and "Fariseos" are simply older ways of writing "to" and "Pharisees."

Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem, teaching and healing. Herod Antipas ruled the region of Galilee. We do not know for certain whether those Pharisees meant it kindly or were trying to pressure Jesus into stopping his teaching; the Bible does not make this clear. Jesus answers firmly: he will not turn aside from his mission.

For today: when others try to frighten you or pull you away from what God has entrusted to you, do not act out of fear. Pray, listen to God, and confidently follow the path he shows you.
exp.11:30:
Jesus says that, instead of living worried about food or drink, we should make the kingdom of God the first thing we seek. "Seek" means to pursue earnestly. "Added" means that God will give us what we need as a gift, without it being our main aim.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after telling the parable of the rich fool who kept everything for himself. He reminds them that the Father knows their needs. Then he calls them "little flock" and assures them that the Father is pleased to give them the kingdom, so they can live without fear and with generosity.

For today: when worry about money or the future comes upon you, pray and ask yourself what you can do today to live according to God, for example, helping someone or being honest at your work. Trust that the Father cares for you.
exp.23:27:
They drew near to the village where they were going, and Jesus gave the impression that he would go on farther. The two disciples have now reached Emmaus, the town they were heading for. The word "village" in the verse means a small town. Jesus, whom they did not yet recognize, acted as though he were going to continue on his way.

The one who tells the story is Luke. It is the same day as the resurrection. Jesus had walked with them and explained that all the Scriptures spoke of the Christ.
