He did not force them to do anything but let them decide. Some understand this gesture as an invitation for them to show their desire to have him near.

For today: Jesus draws near, but he waits for us to invite him. After reading his Word, say sincerely: "Stay with us." Give him time and a place in your home and in your day.
exp.19:3:
Jesus asks them a question: was the baptism that John preached from heaven, or only from people? [Note: this sentence explains archaic/unusual wording from the source translation and must be rewritten or deleted per instructions.]

The religious leaders, in the temple, had asked Jesus by what authority he taught and acted. Instead of answering right away, Jesus returns another question. In this way he leads them to show what was really in their hearts. They were not seeking the truth, but protecting their position and their image before the people, and that is why they argued among themselves instead of answering honestly.

For today: before we answer hard questions about God, it is good to ask ourselves whether we truly want the truth or only want to protect ourselves. Let us ask God for a humble and sincere heart, ready to acknowledge what He has already made known.
exp.11:13:
Jesus answers a man who asked him to get involved in a dispute over an inheritance. He says to him: "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" The word "divider" means someone who shares out or splits up property. Jesus does not reject the man harshly, but he makes clear that he did not come to settle that kind of legal matter.

Jesus is speaking while he teaches a crowd. Someone interrupts with a request about money, even though Jesus was talking about spiritual things. Then Jesus uses the moment to warn against greed and tells the parable of the rich fool. In this way he shows that the real problem was not only the inheritance, but the heart.

For today: before asking God to fix a conflict over money, let us examine whether there is greed in our hearts. Let us seek peace and a contented life first, rather than winning the argument.
exp.7:54:
It says that, when Jesus spoke, the girl came back to life: her spirit returned, that is, her life came back into her body, and she got up at once. Then Jesus asked that she be given something to eat. The word for "then" means "immediately", and "commanded" here means that he gave an instruction.

The one acting is Jesus, in the house of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, whose daughter of about twelve years had died. The people were mocking him, but Jesus took the girl's hand and called her. Asking for food shows that she was truly alive and well, and it reveals Jesus' practical and tender care. Afterward he asked the parents to be discreet; interpreters explain the reason in several ways.

For today: Jesus has power over what seems lost, and he is also concerned with simple needs. You can entrust to him your great sorrows and your everyday details.
exp.16:12:
The ten lepers cried out loudly, from a distance, asking Jesus for help. They call him "Master," a word of respect, and they ask him for "mercy," which here means compassion and help for their need. They do not say exactly what they want, but it is understood that they are asking to be healed.

Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem, between Samaria and Galilee. Lepers were kept apart from other people because of their illness, and that is why they stayed far away, as the law required. All ten speak together, and among them was a Samaritan, as the story shows later. Their cry comes from desperation and from the hope that Jesus will hear them.

When you are in a need you cannot solve, do not wait until you have the perfect words. Cry out to Jesus with sincerity, just as you are, and trust that his compassion reaches you.
exp.1:28:
Simeon says that God can now let his servant depart in peace, as he had promised. The verse's word "lettest" means that God releases him or allows him to leave, much like a master giving a servant permission to rest. The phrases "according to thy word" show that everything happens as God has said.

Simeon is a man in the temple in Jerusalem, guided by the Spirit. When Mary and Joseph bring the child Jesus to fulfill the law, he takes him in his arms and praises God. According to the account, God had promised him that he would see the Messiah before he died. Many understand his words to speak of departing in peace, perhaps of death, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when we trust God's promises, we can wait with calm. If we have come to know Jesus, our hearts can rest, even in times of uncertainty or farewell.
exp.22:26:
This verse tells us that, as Jesus was going toward the cross, a large crowd of people followed him. Among them were women who wept and mourned over him. "Lament" means to express grief with cries or sorrowful words.

Luke is the one narrating. Pilate has just handed Jesus over to be crucified, and Simon of Cyrene is carrying the cross. The text does not say that everyone in the crowd loved him; some may have gone out of curiosity. But the women showed sincere compassion. Jesus will respond right away, and his words point to the hard days that would come upon Jerusalem.

For today: compassion is good, but Jesus invites us to go beyond feeling sorrow. We can look at his sacrifice with a humble heart, examine our own lives, and respond to him with faith and obedience.
exp.0:27:
What it says: The angel enters where Mary is and greets her. The old greeting used here corresponds to saying "Hail" or "Rejoice." "Highly favoured" means God looked on her with kindness and gave her a special favor. "The Lord is with you" assures her of God's presence. "Blessed are you among women" means she receives a very great blessing.

Context: Gabriel, sent by God, speaks to a young woman from Nazareth who is engaged to Joseph. He comes to tell her she will be the mother of Jesus. That is why the next verse says Mary was troubled, and the angel tells her not to be afraid, because God has given her his grace.

For today: Mary did nothing to earn this favor; God gave it to her. Remember that your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on the grace of God. When you feel fear about what He asks of you, trust: if God is with you, you are not alone.
exp.3:22:
He tells them that they will surely quote to him a popular saying: "Physician, heal yourself." With that, the people would be asking him to do in Nazareth, his hometown, the same miracles they have already heard about from Capernaum.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Nazareth, after reading from Isaiah and saying that this prophecy was being fulfilled in him. The people admired his words, yet they doubted: "Is this not Joseph's son?" Jesus perceives that they want signs in order to believe, not sincere faith. Scholars understand the saying in several ways, but all of them see a demand for proof.

For today: let us not place conditions on God before we believe him. True faith receives Jesus for who he is, even when we have known him for a long time and he seems very familiar to us. Today we can ask him for a humble heart, willing to listen to him.
exp.1:24:
What it says: There was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon. He was "just," meaning he lived uprightly, and "devout," meaning devoted to God. He was waiting for the consolation of Israel, the coming of the comfort and salvation God had promised to his people. And the Holy Ghost was upon him, meaning God guided him in a special way.

Context: Luke, the narrator, tells how Mary and Joseph took Jesus to the temple to fulfill what the law required: presenting the firstborn and offering a simple sacrifice of turtledoves or young pigeons. At that moment Simeon appears. Nothing is said about his age or occupation; only what matters is stated: his faith and his relationship with God.

For today: Simeon teaches us to wait for God with confidence and to be attentive to his guidance. We can ask the Spirit to keep us sensitive to his voice, even when the waiting is long.
exp.2:11:
The tax collectors were collectors of taxes for the Roman rule. They came to John to be baptized, and they addressed him as "Master," with respect. They asked him what they should do. Here "publicans" is an old word; today we would say tax collectors.

John the Baptist preached repentance to prepare the way for the Messiah. Many people had already asked him what to do. Tax collectors were looked down upon, because many of them collected more than was owed and grew rich. Even so, they came near with humility. John did not turn them away, but gave them a concrete instruction: do not collect more than what is owed.

For today: true repentance does not stay in words, but changes daily conduct. We can sincerely ask God, "What must I change in my work or in my dealings with others?" And then obey with honesty.
exp.0:57:
It says that Elizabeth's neighbors and relatives heard that God had shown her great kindness, and they rejoiced together with her. Here "mercy" means God's loving and generous care. Her "cousins" are her relatives. Elizabeth was advanced in years and had not been able to have children, so the birth of John was seen as a gift from God.

The one speaking is Luke, the narrator, who tells what happened after John was born, the one who would later be called the Baptist. Mary's visit has just taken place, and now comes the scene of naming the child. Luke shows that the community recognized the work of God and celebrated it.

For today: when God blesses someone close to you, rejoice truly with that person. Thank God with them, and avoid envy or comparison.
exp.17:24:
Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. It is a deliberately exaggerated image: the camel was a large animal, and the eye of a needle is a tiny opening. He means that, for human beings, it is impossible.

Jesus speaks this after a rich and prominent man has gone away sad, because he was not willing to give up his possessions to follow him. Jesus sees his sadness and warns how hard it is for someone who trusts in their riches. The listeners are astonished and ask who then can be saved. Jesus answers that what is impossible for people is possible for God.

Today: examine where you place your security, whether it is money, work, or achievements. Hand it over to God, and remember that salvation is his gift to you, not something that can be bought.
exp.5:5:
This verse tells that, on another Sabbath, Jesus entered the synagogue and began to teach. There was a man there whose right hand was withered, that is, paralyzed or shrunken, without strength or normal use.

Luke is the one who narrates. Just before, Jesus defended his disciples for picking heads of grain on the Sabbath, and he said that he is Lord of the Sabbath. Now the scene sets up another confrontation: the scribes and Pharisees were watching him closely to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so they could accuse him. Jesus knew their thoughts, and yet he acted in full view of everyone.

For today: Jesus pays attention to a person's need even when others see only rules or an opportunity to criticize. We can ask him to help us see and care for those who suffer near us, without letting pride or religious routine harden our hearts.
exp.13:19:
He says that a third guest who had been invited to a great dinner also excused himself. His reason was that he had just gotten married, and so he said that he could not come. Note that he does not even ask to be excused as the other two did; he simply takes it for granted that he cannot come.

Jesus is eating in the house of a Pharisee and tells this parable. A man invites many people to a great dinner, but all of them make excuses. The excuses are not bad things in themselves: land, work, and marriage. But they become more important than the invitation. Jesus shows that many reject God's call, and that the invitation is then opened to the poor, the lame, and the blind.

For today: review which good things, such as work, family, or rest, are taking the place that God is asking of you. Respond to his invitation today, without putting it off until later.
exp.4:31:
Jesus says that he did not come to invite the righteous, but sinners, so that they would change their heart and their life. "Repentance" means turning back to God, leaving sin behind. The word "call" here is like inviting or summoning. The older spellings are simply the spelling of 1909.

Jesus speaks after Levi, a tax collector, followed him and held a banquet for him. The scribes and Pharisees criticized Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners. He answers with the image of the doctor: he goes where the sick are. Some see in "righteous" a gentle irony, since the Pharisees considered themselves healthy, although the text does not say this directly.

Today, instead of judging those who live far from God, we can approach them with friendship and compassion. And we can recognize that we too need the Physician.
exp.19:26:
This verse tells us that some Sadducees came up to Jesus, a Jewish religious group that did not believe in the resurrection of the dead. They had come to ask him a question. "Came to him" simply means that they approached him, and "there is any resurrection" means that the dead would come back to life.

The one telling the story is Luke. Jesus was teaching in the temple, and his opponents had already tried to trap him with questions about taxes. When that failed, the Sadducees now come forward with a complicated case about a woman and seven brothers. Their aim seems to be to make the idea of the resurrection look foolish and to put Jesus in a difficult position.

For today: we may bring our questions to God and to his Word, but with a sincere heart that seeks the truth, not with a desire to argue or to mock what we do not understand.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that God knows each person in complete detail, so much so that even the hairs of our head are all numbered. That is why Jesus says, "Fear not." The small birds are little sparrows, of low price, and yet God does not forget them. We are worth far more to Him.

Jesus speaks to his disciples while a great crowd surrounds them. He warns them that there will be opposition for following him. He asks them to fear God, who has final authority, and not those who can only harm the body. Then he encourages them: the Father cares for them. This prepares the call to confess Jesus without shame.

For today: when fear or the pressure of your faith troubles you, remember that God knows you and cares for you. Pray with confidence and take a step of courage today, even a small one.
exp.4:9:
It says that James and John, the sons of Zebedee, were also amazed at the catch. They were partners with Simon, that is, business partners in the trade. Jesus speaks to Simon and tells him: "Fear not." Then he adds: "from now on you will catch men."

Jesus has just asked Simon to let down the nets, and the catch was enormous. Simon felt unworthy and told him to go away because he was a sinful man. Jesus does not reject him; he calms his fear and gives him a new mission. Catching men is usually understood as leading others to follow Jesus.

Today, Jesus does not call us because we are perfect, but because he accepts us just as we are. If you feel fear or unworthiness, bring it honestly to him and offer him your willingness to serve.
exp.7:44:
Jesus asks who touched him. Everyone denies it, and Peter, together with those who were with him, tells him that the crowd is pressing in on him and crowding him on every side. The question seems strange to them. "Throng" here means a crowd or the people surrounding him. "Press" means that they push against him and squeeze him.

Jesus was on his way to the house of Jairus, and a crowd was pressing against him. A woman who had been sick for twelve years, and who had spent everything on physicians, came up to him from behind and touched the edge of his garment. She was healed at once. Jesus knows that someone touched him in faith, and this is not a simple jostle in the crowd. Peter speaks with common sense, but he does not see what Jesus sees.

For today: coming close to Jesus is not the same as merely being near Him. Many people surrounded him, but only one touched him in faith. Today we can come to Him with sincere trust, even in our weakness, and He notices us.
exp.6:35:
One of the Pharisees asked Jesus to come and eat with him. Jesus accepted, went into his house and sat down to eat. "Invited" here means "urged" or "asked earnestly," and the phrase about sitting down to the meal means that he took his place to eat, probably reclining, as was the custom of that time.

Just before this, Jesus had said that people criticized him for eating and drinking with tax collectors and sinners, while they criticized John the Baptist for not doing so. Now Jesus accepts the invitation of a Pharisee, a group that tended to distrust him. Luke does not say clearly why this man invited him; it may have been curiosity or sincere interest.

Jesus reaches out to everyone: to those who are labeled as sinners and also to those who consider themselves righteous. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are open to sharing the table with people different from us, without prejudice, letting God work in every encounter.
exp.5:9:
Jesus looks around at everyone gathered there, one by one, and says to the man with the withered hand, "Stretch out your hand." The man obeys, and his hand is made well.

It is the Sabbath, in a synagogue, and the teachers of the law and the Pharisees are watching him closely to see whether he will heal on that day so that they can bring a charge against him. Jesus knows what they are thinking and does not hide: he brings the man into the middle and asks them whether it is lawful to do good or evil on the Sabbath. They keep silent, and then they are filled with rage.

Today, Jesus invites us not to let rules or customs harden our hearts in the face of a real need. This week, do one concrete good for someone, even if it is not comfortable. And if something in you feels withered, obey his word in faith.
exp.23:44:
This verse says that Jesus "opened their understanding," that is, he opened their minds, so that they could understand the Scriptures.

The risen Jesus speaks with his disciples on the very day of the resurrection. He has just eaten in front of them to show them that he is not a ghost. He reminds them that what was written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms spoke about him. Even after living with Jesus, they needed him to give them light so they could comprehend.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to open your understanding before you open the book. Reading with humility and looking for Jesus in its pages changes the way you grasp what it says.
exp.5:37:
Jesus says that whoever gives will receive. The picture is that of a merchant filling a measure of grain: he presses it down, shakes it, and still it overflows, so that the grain spills into the fold of the garment where what is received was carried. The words that rewrite the old wording are reflected in the verse above: "good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over" and "with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again" describe the same idea, that God and people will treat us with the same measure we use.

Jesus teaches his disciples in the Sermon on the Plain. He has been speaking about loving enemies, being merciful, not judging, and forgiving. Giving here includes generosity, but also kindness in how we treat others. Many understand that the reward comes from God, although it does not say when or how.

Today: this week, be generous with someone, whether with your time, your forgiveness, or your help, without expecting anything in return. Trust that God cares for the one who gives with an open heart.
exp.3:6:
Here the devil says to Jesus: "If you worship me, all this will be yours." The phrase "bow down before me" means to bow before him and offer him worship. "They will all be yours" refers to all the kingdoms he had just shown him.

The devil speaks during Jesus' temptation in the wilderness. He offers power and glory without going through the cross, in exchange for worship. He claims that this authority has been handed to him, but the Bible does not present his word as trustworthy, and it is not clear how far his dominion actually extends. Jesus rejects the offer by quoting Scripture: only God is to be worshiped.

Today, sometimes a shortcut is offered to us: success, approval, or advantage in exchange for giving up what we believe. Before accepting it, let us ask ourselves: whom am I really serving? God deserves first place.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells us that while Zechariah went into the temple to offer the incense, the whole crowd of people waited outside, praying. "At the time of incense" refers to the moment when the priest burned incense in the holy place. The sentences explaining the old spellings of the words "á" and "viéndole" are removed because they do not apply to the verse your reader sees.

The narrator is Luke, who writes an orderly account of the story of Jesus. Here he sets the scene for the announcement of the birth of John the Baptist. Zechariah had been chosen by lot, and the people prayed while he carried out his service. Many think the incense symbolized the prayers of the people, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: before God acted, there was a people praying. We can support those who serve with prayer and wait in faith for God to work, even when we do not yet see what He will do.
exp.3:12:
He says that when the devil had finished testing Jesus with all his temptations in the desert, he left him, but only "for a season." There is an old word here: "se fué," which is now written "se fue," and it means he withdrew. The phrase shows that the devil did not give up for good; he would try again later.

Luke, the writer, sums up here the end of the three temptations: turning stones into bread, receiving the kingdoms of the world, and throwing himself down from the temple. Jesus answered each time with Scripture, and the last answer was: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." Luke does not say when the devil returned; some connect it with the passion of Jesus, but the text does not specify.

For today: a victory over temptation does not mean there will be no others. Stay alert, and like Jesus, keep the Word of God in your heart so that you can resist with it.
exp.9:36:
Jesus ends the parable of the good Samaritan with a question, and an expert in the law answers: "He that shewed mercy on him." To show mercy means to treat someone with compassion and help them. Then Jesus tells him: "Go, and do thou likewise." That is, it is not enough to understand; one must act.

A teacher of the law had asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life and who his neighbor was. Jesus told the story of a wounded man, ignored by a priest and a Levite, but helped by a Samaritan, someone despised by the Jews. The teacher does not even say "the Samaritan," but he recognizes that mercy was what made the difference.

Today, Jesus invites us to help without considering who the person is. This week, think of someone with a nearby need, such as a neighbor, a coworker, or a family member, and do something concrete for them, even if it costs you time or money.
exp.21:4:
The explanation says that the chief priests and the officers were very glad when Judas offered to hand Jesus over. The word "were glad" in the verse above is the word the explanation means. "Covenanted" means that they came to an agreement and committed to paying him money.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. He tells that the religious leaders were looking for a way to get rid of Jesus without causing an uproar among the people. Judas, one of the twelve disciples, gave them the opportunity. Luke says that Satan entered into him, but does not explain all of Judas's reasons, and the text gives no further detail about how that process unfolded. The money appears as part of the deal.

For today: let us guard our hearts against greed and against being glad about what harms others. Let us ask God to keep us faithful to Jesus, even when something promises easy gain.
exp.4:32:
This verse records a question put to Jesus. They tell him that the disciples of John the Baptist and the disciples of the Pharisees fast often and offer prayers, while his disciples eat and drink. The phrase "often" means frequently.

The ones asking are the Pharisees and the teachers of the law, who had just criticized Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners. Now they compare religious customs. Jesus answers with the picture of a wedding: while the bridegroom is present, it is a time to celebrate. He speaks of himself, and announces that days of fasting will come when he is no longer with them.

For today: before judging the faith of others by what can be seen, let us ask what God wants in this moment. Fasting and prayer are valuable, but they should arise from a living relationship with Christ, not from a comparison with others.
exp.21:58:
This verse tells us that about an hour passed since Peter's second denial. Then another person insisted firmly: "Surely this man also was with him, for he is a Galilean."

Peter is in the courtyard of the high priest on the night Jesus was arrested. Those around him notice something about him, probably the way he speaks, since the Galileans had an accent of their own. Peter is afraid and denies knowing his Master, just as Jesus had foretold. Shortly after, the rooster crows, and Jesus looks at him.

Peter fell, but his story does not end there. If you fail today out of fear or shame, do not hide. Remember that Jesus looks at you with truth and also with mercy. Return to Him with humility and ask Him for strength to follow Him with courage.
exp.12:29:
It says that some who now seem to be in front will end up at the back, and others who now seem to be behind will end up in front. "Last" means the ones who come at the end. "Behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "pay attention." Jesus uses this contrast to draw attention to a surprise in God's kingdom.

Jesus speaks while he is on the way to Jerusalem, teaching those who had asked whether few people are saved. He has just warned that many who felt secure, because they belonged to the people of Israel or had been close to him, would be left outside. People from all over the world would sit at God's table. Many understand "the last" to mean the Gentiles or those who were looked down upon.

For today: do not take your spiritual standing for granted just because of your background, your titles, or your religious habits. Examine your heart, respond with humility to Jesus' call, and rejoice when God welcomes those you did not expect.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that John the Baptist rebuked Herod the tetrarch for two things: for taking Herodias, who was the wife of his brother Philip, and for many other evil things he had done. A tetrarch was a ruler over a fourth part of a territory, under the authority of Rome. To be rebuked means to be corrected firmly.

Luke is summarizing John's preaching. Earlier he showed that John called the people to repentance and announced the one who would come after him. Now he tells us that John did not speak only to ordinary people, but also to the ruler. For this reason Herod put him in prison, as the next verse says.

For today: telling the truth in love can cost us dearly, but it is part of being faithful to God. And when someone corrects us, we can choose to listen with humility, instead of becoming angry and closing our hearts.
exp.0:32:
He says that Jesus will be king forever. "The house of Jacob" is another way of naming the people of Israel, the descendants of Jacob. The idea that his rule will never end is repeated in the words "forever" and "there shall be no end." The word "reign" means that he will rule as king.

The angel Gabriel speaks to Mary, a young woman from Nazareth, to announce that she will be the mother of Jesus. This promise recalls what God promised King David: that one of his descendants would have an eternal throne. Christians understand that Jesus fulfills that promise. After this announcement, Mary asks how this will be possible, since she is not yet married.

For today: the governments and powers of this world come and go, and at times they fill us with unease. This verse invites us to trust that Jesus reigns and that his kingdom does not end. We can rest in him when the future seems uncertain and live with hope and peace.
exp.6:3:
The Jewish elders came to Jesus and urged him earnestly and with effort to help the centurion's servant. The phrase "they besought him instantly" means that they pleaded with him with great earnestness. Their argument was that the man was "worthy", that is, he deserved to have this favor granted.

The elders speaking here are leaders of the people, sent by a Roman centurion. He loved his servant and wanted to save him, but he did not dare to come to Jesus himself. The elders supported his cause because he had shown affection for their nation and had helped build the synagogue. Later, the centurion himself will say that he does not consider himself worthy.

Today we can learn to intercede for others with persistence and care. But let us also remember that before God we do not approach on the basis of our merits, but by his grace. Let us pray for others with humility and perseverance.
exp.8:18:
The disciples tell Jesus what the people were saying about him. Some said he was John the Baptist, others said he was Elijah, and others said that one of the old prophets had come back to life. The word "risen" here means that he had returned from death.

Jesus had just been praying alone and had fed a large crowd. Then he asks them what people say about him. The ones who answer are the disciples. Herod also wondered who Jesus was (Luke 9:7-9), and people compared him to great figures from the past. These were respectful opinions, but they fell short. Jesus uses their answer to lead to the key question: "But who do you say that I am?"

For today: it is not enough to repeat what others think of Jesus. Today there are many ideas about him. Take a moment to answer honestly who he is to you, and talk with him about it in prayer.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that, besides the twelve disciples, Jesus was accompanied by some women whom he had healed of evil spirits and sicknesses. Among them was Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had come out. "Healed" means made well, and "Magdalene" probably indicates that she came from a place called Magdala.

Here Luke speaks, recounting how Jesus traveled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God. Luke adds that these women went with him and, according to the next verse, served him with their possessions. The mention of "seven demons" shows that her suffering had been serious. The text says nothing more about her past, so it is best not to assume anything else.

For today: when Jesus heals us or sets us free, our gratitude can be shown through service. Think about what God has given you and how you might use it to help others.
exp.9:30:
The explanation says that a priest was going down the same road where the wounded man lay. He saw him, but he moved away and passed by on the other side. The word that is translated as "by chance" means "happened," and the phrase "passed by on the other side" means he veered off so as not to come close.

Jesus tells this parable to an expert in the law who wanted to justify himself and asked, "And who is my neighbor?" The road from Jerusalem to Jericho went down through lonely areas. Scholars debate why the priest did not help; some think he feared becoming ritually unclean by touching a dead man, but the text does not say so.

We can have reasons that are very religious or very reasonable for not helping, and still fail in love. Today, God invites us not to turn our eyes away when someone close to us is suffering. This week, do something concrete for a person in need whom you come across on your path.
exp.6:4:
This verse is part of what the Jewish elders say about a Roman centurion. They say that he loves our nation, meaning that he wishes well toward the Jewish people, and that he has built us a synagogue, that is, that he paid for the building where the Jews gathered to pray and to hear the Scriptures.

The ones speaking are the elders of the Jews. The centurion sent them to ask Jesus to heal his servant, who was sick. They defend the centurion by saying that he deserves help because of what he has done. However, the centurion himself, shortly afterward, says that he is not worthy for Jesus to enter his house. He trusts in Jesus' grace, not in his own merits.

For today: we can show love through concrete deeds, such as helping our community, but without thinking that this gives us a claim before God. We serve with generosity and humility, trusting in his goodness.
exp.6:34:
God's wisdom is shown to be right by those who follow it. "Justified" means recognized as true or good. "Children" here does not refer to family by blood, but to those who accept and practice that wisdom. Their fruits prove it.

Jesus speaks to the crowd about John the Baptist and about himself. John lived a simple, austere life, and they called him demon-possessed; Jesus ate with people, and they called him a glutton and a drunkard. Many, especially religious leaders, rejected both of them, each with different excuses. Some understand "wisdom" to refer to God's plan; others, to God's action in both messengers.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we look for excuses not to listen to God. A sincere person looks at the fruits: love, humility, and changed lives. Let us ask for a heart willing to learn, even when God uses people or ways we did not expect.
exp.10:10:
Jesus asks which father would give his son a stone when he asks for bread, or a serpent when he asks for a fish. The obvious answer is that none would.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples after teaching them the Lord's Prayer and telling them the parable of the friend who keeps knocking at midnight. He wants them to trust that God hears prayer. He compares imperfect human parents with the heavenly Father, who is good and gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

Today we can pray with confidence and simplicity, knowing that God is a good Father. He does not always answer as we hope, but he never gives us anything that would harm us. Ask him sincerely for his guidance and his presence, and rest in his care.
exp.19:16:
Jesus looks steadily at those who are listening and asks them a question about Scripture. He quotes Psalm 118:22: the stone that the builders rejected became the chief stone of the corner, the one that holds up and joins the whole building together. The word "rejected" here means refusing or throwing away. The phrase "the head of the corner" means that it became the most important stone.

Jesus is speaking in the temple, shortly before his crucifixion. He has just told the parable of the wicked tenants who kill the owner's son in the vineyard. The religious leaders respond with an emphatic "God forbid!" because they understand that the story is about them. Jesus shows them that their rejection had already been foretold in Scripture.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are letting Jesus be the foundation of our lives, or whether we set him aside when he makes us uncomfortable. Building on him gives us firmness.
exp.22:24:
This verse says that Pilate released a man who had been imprisoned for rebellion against the authority and for murder. He was the man the crowd had asked for. Instead, Pilate handed Jesus over so that they could do with him what they wanted. The word for rebellion means an uprising against the government, and the phrase about being imprisoned means that he was held in jail.

Luke tells the end of the trial before Pilate. The religious leaders and the crowd kept shouting louder and louder that Jesus should be crucified. Although Pilate had tried to set him free, he gave in to the pressure. Other Gospels identify the man who was released as Barabbas.

For today: Pilate chose the pressure of the people over justice. We can ask ourselves where we give in out of fear of looking bad. Jesus took the place of a guilty man, and that reminds us of his love for us.
exp.21:3:
Judas went out and spoke with the chief priests and with the captains. These captains were the officers in charge of the temple guard. Judas wanted to reach an agreement with them about how he would hand Jesus over to them.

Luke is the one telling the story. The leaders wanted to kill Jesus, but they feared how the people would react. Luke says that Satan entered into Judas, and so he presents this betrayal as part of a spiritual struggle. The Bible does not fully explain Judas's motives; the text that follows mentions money, though there are other views about what he was thinking.

For today: betrayal usually does not begin with one big step, but with small decisions made in the heart. Let us ask God to examine our intentions and keep us faithful to Jesus, even when something else would be more convenient for us.
exp.7:53:
He took her by the hand and spoke in a loud voice: "Maid, arise." The word "called" means that he spoke with a strong, clear voice. "Maid" is a tender way of saying girl or young woman.

Jesus is in the house of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, whose daughter, about twelve years old, had died. Everyone was weeping, and they mocked Jesus when he said she was sleeping. He speaks with authority, without any complicated ritual. Some understand that "sleeping" describes death as something temporary before his power; others, that he announces what he is about to do.

For today: when a situation seems lost and others see only the end, we can bring it to Jesus in faith. He takes our hand, speaks to us with tenderness, and can give life where there seems to be no hope.
exp.7:27:
He says that the man, when he saw Jesus, cried out and fell down before him. In a loud voice he asked what Jesus had to do with him, called him "Son of the Most High God," and begged him not to torment him.

It is the man who speaks, the one who was controlled by many demons, and through him they speak. He lived naked, without a home, among the tombs, in the country of the Gadarenes. The spirits recognize who Jesus is and his authority, and they fear the judgment that awaits them. Jesus had already commanded them to leave the man.

For today: Jesus has authority over everything that dominates and destroys us. If something has you bound, come to him with humility and sincerity, without hiding. He does not come to torment, but to free and restore dignity.
exp.10:41:
Jesus says that the Pharisees gave a tenth of their produce, even from small plants such as mint and rue, which are kitchen and medicinal herbs. But they neglected what mattered most: justice and the love of God. "Love" here translates the word the verse renders as "love of God." Jesus does not reject tithing, since he says it was necessary to do it, but they should not have left the other things undone.

Jesus speaks while invited to eat at the house of a Pharisee. He confronts them because they were careful about every outward religious detail, while their hearts were far from compassion and justice. That is why he continues with other "woes" against their pride and their outward appearance.

For today: do not use your religious acts as an excuse for neglecting people. Ask yourself this week: whom can I treat with more justice, patience, or kindness, in addition to keeping my practices of faith?
exp.20:32:
Jesus says that heaven and earth, everything that seems firm and lasting, will one day come to an end. But his words will never fail to be fulfilled or lose their worth. "Shall pass away" means that they will come to an end or disappear.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in the temple in Jerusalem, shortly before his death. He has just spoken to them about difficult signs and the end of the age. Some scholars understand "this generation" in different ways, and there is no single agreement. With this phrase Jesus assures them that what he said is worthy of trust.

Today we can build our lives on what Jesus taught, and not on what changes. This week, choose one of his promises or commands, read it slowly, and ask God for help to obey it.
exp.6:47:
Jesus says directly to the woman: "Your sins are forgiven." In this older wording, the phrase that appears in the verse as "to her" is rendered as "to her," and the phrase that means "are forgiven to you" means "God has forgiven you." The sentence is in the perfect tense, which suggests a forgiveness already granted and one that remains.

Jesus is eating in the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known for her sinful life came in, wept at his feet, and anointed them with perfume. Simon despised her in his heart. Jesus explained to him that the one who is forgiven much loves much. Then he spoke to her with authority, and this is why the guests were amazed, since only God forgives sins.

For today: you do not need to make yourself presentable before coming to Jesus. Come with honesty and humility, trust in his forgiveness, and respond with gratitude, loving him and others.
exp.5:48:
This verse speaks of someone who hears Jesus' words but does not put them into practice. Jesus compares him to a man who built his house on the ground without a foundation. When the river rose and struck the house with force, it collapsed at once, and the destruction was great. "Ruin" here means total destruction.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to a crowd, at the end of what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Before this example, he had taught them how to live: to love their enemies, to be merciful, and not to judge. With this comparison he shows them that it is not enough to admire his teachings; they must obey them. The difference between the two houses is not in the storm, but in the foundation.

For today: do not be satisfied with only reading or hearing the Bible. Choose one of Jesus' teachings, for example forgiving someone, and this week do something concrete to obey it. In this way your life will have a firm foundation when the trials come.
exp.1:18:
What it says: Mary kept in her memory everything that was happening with her son. She did not forget them or let them pass by.

Context: Luke, who writes the account, tells that the shepherds had reported what the angel had announced about the child. Everyone was amazed, but Mary responded in a different way: more quiet and reflective. Some believe Luke may have learned these memories from her, although the Bible does not state this directly.

For today: when you do not fully understand what God is doing in your life, do not rush to draw conclusions. You can keep what you have seen of Him, pray, and think about it calmly, trusting that God will bring light in His time.
exp.5:23:
Jesus says: "Woe to you who are rich!" The word "woe" expresses sorrow and warning, like a painful notice, not simple anger. "Consolation" here means relief or reward. In other words, the rich are already receiving now all the comfort they will get, if they place their trust only in their riches.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Just before, he blessed the poor, the hungry, and those who are persecuted. Now he presents the contrast: whoever lives secure in material things can forget about God. Some think he is referring to the rich in general, others to those who trust in their money.

Today we can ask ourselves: in what do I rest my heart? Let us use what we have with generosity and trust in God, not in our bank accounts.
exp.21:48:
The disciples who were with Jesus saw that the crowd was coming to arrest him, and they understood what was about to happen. Then they asked him, "Lord, shall we smite with the sword?"

It is the night Jesus was arrested, in the garden. Judas had just come near with a kiss to point him out. The disciples, frightened and loyal, want to defend their Master, but they ask before they act. However, one of them does not wait for the answer and strikes a servant. Jesus stops the violence and heals the one who was hurt.

For today: when we feel that something unjust is happening, it is natural to want to react with force. Before we act, we can ask God what he wants from us. Jesus shows us that his way answers evil with mercy, not revenge.
exp.15:17:
It says that whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman who has been put away by her husband also commits adultery. "Putteth away" means sending the wife away and breaking the marriage. "Committeth adultery" means being unfaithful to the marriage covenant.

Jesus speaks to the Pharisees, whom Luke describes as lovers of money (v. 14). He says this right after affirming that the law still stands. Some interpret that Jesus gives an example of how God's law should not be bent by excuses. Others think he is correcting the relaxed way divorce was understood in his time. Christians understand in different ways how this applies in cases such as abuse or abandonment, and other passages (such as Matthew 19 and 1 Corinthians 7) are usually considered as well.

For today: take your promises of faithfulness seriously. Care for your marriage through prayer, dialogue and forgiveness, and treat with compassion those who have lived through a divorce.
exp.20:28:
Jesus tells them a simple comparison: he asks them to look at the fig tree and at all the other trees as well. "Parable" here means teaching through an example from everyday life. Words such as "said" mean "told them."

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He has just spoken of difficult signs and of his coming in glory. With this example he wants them to learn to read the times: just as new leaves announce summer, certain events announce that the kingdom of God is near. Christians understand in different ways exactly which events he means.

For today: learn to stay alert and not live distracted. Set aside time to pray, read the Bible, and live with hope, trusting that God will keep his promises, without anxiety or trying to guess dates.
exp.10:31:
Jesus says that the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment together with the people of his own time and will condemn them. The reason is that they repented when Jonah preached to them, and here there is someone greater than Jonah. "Will stand up in judgment" means they will serve as witnesses against them. "This generation" refers to the people of that time.

Jesus is speaking to crowds who were asking him for a sign from heaven. He answers that the only sign will be the sign of Jonah, and he compares it to the queen of the South (the queen of Sheba), who traveled from very far away to hear Solomon. Some understand the sign of Jonah as a reference to the resurrection; others, to his preaching. Perhaps both ideas are joined together.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are asking God for more proof, when we already have the word of Jesus. A humble response would be to listen to him carefully and repent today.
exp.0:41:
Elisabeth speaks with a loud voice, full of emotion. She tells Mary that she is "blessed among women," meaning that God has shown her special favor. She also calls blessed the "fruit of your womb," that is, the child Mary is expecting. Saying she spoke "with a loud voice" means she said it out loud, with enthusiasm.

Elisabeth is Mary's older cousin, and she is also pregnant, with John the Baptist. When Mary comes to visit her, the baby leaps in her womb and she is filled with the Holy Spirit. That is why she speaks this way: by the work of the Spirit, she recognizes that Mary will bear the Messiah. Her praise is a testimony of joy and faith.

For today: let us learn to rejoice sincerely in what God does in others, without envy. We can encourage someone this week with words that recognize God's work in their life.
exp.11:35:
Jesus says that his followers should be like servants who wait for their master when he returns from a wedding feast. The phrase "like unto" means "like." The idea is to be ready, so that as soon as the master arrives and knocks at the door, they open it at once and without delay.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the middle of teaching about not living anxiously for riches and trusting in God. Just before, he spoke about treasure and the heart. Then he promises that the Lord will bless the servants he finds watchful, and that he himself will serve them. Many understand this to refer to his return, although the exact time is not revealed.

For today: live each day with your heart attentive to God. Ask yourself which duty of obedience, forgiveness, or service you should not leave for later, and do it today with joy.
exp.20:19:
Jesus says that when his disciples see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, they should understand that its destruction is near.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple, a few days before his crucifixion. He warns them of what is coming upon the city and gives them a sign so they can act in time: to flee to the mountains rather than stay. Many understand this to refer to the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70 AD. Some also see a broader meaning pointing toward the future. Interpreters do not fully agree on this.

Jesus does not want his followers to be taken by surprise or to freeze in fear. Today we can take his words seriously, stay alert, and trust that God cares for us even in difficult times, obeying him with wisdom when he shows us the way.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that the things told about Jesus were passed on by people who saw them with their own eyes from the beginning. Those witnesses were also "ministers of the word," that is, servants who devoted themselves to proclaiming the message. "They delivered them unto us" means that the readers received these accounts from them.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of the Gospel, although the text itself does not name him here; this has traditionally been understood. He writes to Theophilus and explains that others had already tried to put these accounts in order. Luke relies on direct witnesses and wants to give a careful and trustworthy account.

For today: our faith does not rest on vague stories, but on a testimony passed on with care. Be encouraged to read the Gospels with confidence and gratitude, and share what you have received with honesty and simplicity, as those witnesses did.
exp.11:1:
It says that everything hidden will someday come into the light. What is secret will not stay secret forever. Everything hidden will eventually be exposed, sooner or later, and everything will be known.

Jesus speaks to his disciples while a large crowd gathers around him. He has just warned them to beware of the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy: appearing one way on the outside while being another way on the inside. Just as yeast spreads through dough, hypocrisy can spread. Then he encourages them not to fear people, because God sees everything.

Today it invites us to live with sincerity. What we are in private should match what we show in public. If there is something hidden that weighs on you, you can confess it to God and seek the truth, without living in fear of being found out.
exp.3:31:
Luke says that the people in Capernaum were astonished at how Jesus taught. "Teaching" simply means what he taught, and "authority" means the power that stood behind it. His words did not sound like mere opinions; they carried weight and firmness.

Luke, the writer, tells what happened when Jesus came to Capernaum, in Galilee, after being rejected in Nazareth. He taught in the synagogue on the Sabbath. The people were amazed, and right away Luke shows that authority: an unclean spirit recognizes Jesus and has to obey him. Many believe this contrasts with other teachers of the time, though the text here speaks only of the people's amazement.

Today we can come to the Bible without trying to set conditions on it, but with a willingness to obey what Jesus says. His word is not just information to know; it is an authoritative voice that can guide and transform our lives.
exp.0:25:
This verse says that when Elisabeth was already in her sixth month of pregnancy, God sent the angel Gabriel to Nazareth, a village in the region of Galilee.

Here Luke is speaking, the writer who tells the beginning of Jesus' story. The "sixth month" refers to Elisabeth's pregnancy; she is the mother of John the Baptist. Luke joins the two stories: first the announcement of John's birth, and now the announcement of Jesus' birth. Nazareth was a small and simple place, and God chose to begin there.

For today: God does not depend on famous places or important people to act. If you feel small or little noticed today, remember that God sees you and can work in your everyday life. He pays attention to the simple things.
exp.10:20:
The explanation describes a strong man, fully armed, who guards his courtyard or the entrance of his house or palace. While he keeps watch, his possessions are secure and at peace. No one dares to rob him.

Jesus speaks to the crowd that accused him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of demons. He answers with a comparison: the armed strong man represents the rule of evil, and the one stronger who comes afterward is Jesus himself. If he sets the oppressed free, it is a sign that the kingdom of God has already arrived.

For today: if something dominates you, such as fear or an addiction, do not be left without hope. Ask Jesus to set you free, and walk with him each day.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low. Crooked paths will be made straight, and rough roads will be made level.

The word "filled" here means that the valley will be made full, or raised up. The phrase "rough ways" refers to roads that are full of stones and holes.

Luke quotes the prophet Isaiah to explain the work of John the Baptist. John preached by the Jordan River that the people should repent and be baptized. These images speak of preparing the way for the coming of the Lord. Most readers understand that they do not refer to a road of earth, but to the heart: setting aside pride, lifting up the humbled, and correcting what is crooked.

For today: ask God to show you which mountain of pride or which crooked path in your life you need to straighten, and take one concrete step of repentance this week.
exp.9:22:
Jesus turns and speaks only to his disciples, without the crowd. He tells them they are blessed, meaning very happy and favored by God, because their eyes see something very precious. The word "privately" means apart from others, in private. What they see is Jesus himself and the work of God being fulfilled before them.

Jesus has just praised the Father because he has revealed himself to the humble and not to those who think themselves wise. The seventy disciples had returned from their mission with joy. Now Jesus tells them, in private, that they are living through a moment that many prophets and kings longed to see and did not see.

Today we can give thanks that God has made himself known to us in Christ, above all through his Word. Instead of growing accustomed to it, we can read the Bible with wonder and humility, like someone receiving a gift that others waited their whole lives for.
exp.3:25:
It says that although in Israel there were many needy widows during the great famine, God did not send the prophet Elijah to any of them. He sent him to a widow in Zarephath, a town in the region of Sidon, outside Israel. "Was sent" means that God commanded him to go there. "Welcomed" means well received.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue in Nazareth, his own hometown. His neighbors doubted him, and he reminds them of two stories from the Old Testament (1 Kings 17). With them he shows that God sometimes blesses those who stand outside the expected circle. That is why the people became so angry.

For today: let us not assume that God acts only as we expect. Let us ask him for a humble heart to receive his word, even when it comes through means or people we did not expect, and to love those we consider "outsiders."
exp.1:16:
This verse says that, after seeing the child Jesus, the shepherds told others what the angel had said to them about him. The words "when they had seen it" mean that they saw him with their own eyes. The phrase "made known abroad" means that they spread the news, that they made it public.

The account is from Luke. The shepherds had received the announcement from the angels about the birth of the Savior. They went quickly to Bethlehem and found everything just as they had been told. So, once they had confirmed it, they did not keep quiet. The verses that follow say that those who heard them were amazed.

For today: when we have seen God's faithfulness in our lives, we can share it simply. It is not necessary to be experts or to have long speeches. It is enough to honestly tell what God has shown us, as these shepherds did.
exp.23:18:
Jesus, without them recognizing him, asks them: "What things?" They answer that it concerns Jesus of Nazareth, whom they describe as a prophet, mighty in deed and in word, that is, strong in what he did and in what he taught, and acknowledged by God and by the people.

Two disciples are speaking, one of them named Cleopas, who are on their way to Emmaus after the crucifixion. They are sad and confused. The risen Jesus walks with them and asks them on purpose, so that they will express what they feel. They see Jesus as a great prophet, but they do not yet understand that he is much more than that.

We can bring our doubts and sorrows to God with sincerity. Jesus hears our pain even when we do not perceive him near, and from there he guides us to know him better.
exp.0:4:
This verse introduces Zechariah, a priest who lived when Herod ruled Judea. His wife, Elizabeth, also came from a priestly family, since she was a descendant of Aaron. The phrase "of the course of Abia" means that he belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, one of the groups that took turns serving in the temple.

Here Luke is speaking as the narrator. After explaining to Theophilus that he wants to write with order and care, he begins his account with events set in a real time and place. In this way he shows that the story of Jesus is not a myth but something that happened in history. He starts with a simple and faithful family.

For today: God often works through ordinary people who serve him faithfully day after day. You do not need to be famous to be useful in his plans. Serve God steadily where you are, and trust that he knows how and when to use your life.
exp.1:50:
The explanation says that Jesus, at twelve years old, went back with Mary and Joseph to Nazareth and lived in obedience to them. The phrase "was subject" means that he obeyed and respected them. Mary "kept" meant that she treasured up and carefully pondered in her memory everything that had happened.

Luke recounts what happened after Jesus stayed behind in the temple in Jerusalem and his parents searched for him in anguish. He spoke of being in his Father's house, and they did not fully understand. Even knowing who he was, Jesus returned home and lived in humility. Luke is the one who narrates, and he highlights Mary's quiet reflection.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, do not rush to explain it. Keep his words in your heart, remain faithful in everyday life, and trust that he will make the meaning clear over time.
exp.3:42:
Jesus responds to the people who wanted to keep him in Capernaum. He says that he must also proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to other cities, because that is what he was sent for. "Gospel" means good news, and "must" expresses that this is part of his mission, not a mere preference.

Jesus is speaking after a day of healing the sick and casting out demons. In the morning he withdrew to a lonely place, and the crowd searched for him to stay with them. He does not reject the people, but he does not let his popularity change the purpose for which the Father sent him. His central message is the kingdom of God.

For today: when there are many voices asking you for good things, stop to pray and ask God what your main calling is. This way you can serve with clarity, without losing your way.
exp.18:22:
Here the king says to the servant: "If you really thought I was so demanding, why didn't you put my money in the bank?" That way, on his return, he would have received his money back with interest.

Jesus tells this parable as he is on the way to Jerusalem, and the crowd believes the kingdom of God will appear right away. A nobleman goes away far off and leaves a mina (a sum of money) to each servant so they can put it to work. This servant did nothing out of fear. The king uses the servant's own words to show that his excuse does not hold up. Interpreters see Christ and his return in this.

For today: God entrusts us with gifts, time, and opportunities. Do not wait until you feel perfect; take a small step today, serving with what you have, instead of letting fear paralyze you.
exp.12:2:
Jesus says "No" to the idea that those Galileans suffered because they were worse sinners than others. "Nay" in the verse means "rather," and it is not the word that needs explaining here; the phrase "except ye repent" means "unless you repent," that is, unless you change direction and turn back to God. "Ye shall all likewise perish" means that everyone will face a similar ruin.

Jesus is speaking to people who told him about some Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. Many thought that a tragedy was a punishment for special sins. Jesus corrects that idea and calls everyone to repent. Interpreters debate whether "perish" refers to physical death, to the ruin of Jerusalem, or to the final judgment; perhaps it includes several of these things.

For today: when you hear of someone else's misfortune, do not judge those who suffered. Instead, examine your own heart and ask God to help you turn back to Him today, without leaving it for later.
exp.9:11:
It says that on the day of judgment, it will go better for Sodom than for the city that rejects Jesus' message. Here "remission" means something like relief, or a more bearable punishment. "That day" refers to the day of final judgment.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples he sends out two by two to announce that the kingdom of God is near. If a town rejects them, they are to shake off the dust as a solemn sign, but still keep proclaiming the message. Sodom was notorious for its wickedness (Genesis 19). Jesus teaches that rejecting the light one has received is more serious. Scholars debate how the degrees of judgment apply, but the central point is responsibility.

Today: if we have heard much about God, let us not take that grace for granted. Let us respond with humility and obedience, and share his message with kindness, without pressuring or despising anyone.
exp.22:50:
This verse finishes introducing Joseph of Arimathea. It says that he did not agree with the decision or the actions of the other leaders against Jesus. He was from Arimathea, a town in Judea, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God. The "council" refers to the group of Jewish leaders, the Sanhedrin, of which Joseph was a member. "Waited" means that he longed, in faith, for what God had promised.

Luke, who writes the account, wants to show that Jesus was condemned unjustly. Even within the group that judged him there was a good man who did not support that injustice. After Jesus died, Joseph took a brave step: he asked Pilate for Jesus' body so he could bury him with respect.

For today: we can follow Joseph's example. Sometimes it is hard not to be carried along by the majority. Let us ask God for the courage to say no to what is unjust, even when we are surrounded by people who think differently.
exp.9:29:
Jesus begins a story: a man was traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho, and robbers attacked him. They took everything from him, beat him, and left him half dead, that is, nearly without life. The verse's word "stripped" means taking away his clothing and belongings.

A religious law expert had asked Jesus, "Who is my neighbor?", wanting to justify himself. Jesus does not give him a definition but tells him this parable. The road from Jerusalem to Jericho went down through a desert area, and it was known to be dangerous. Here begins the famous story of the good Samaritan.

For today: love for our neighbor does not start by asking "whom do I have to help?", but by opening our eyes to the need around us. Today, ask God to show you someone who is suffering, and do something concrete for that person.
exp.8:36:
Luke tells us that the next day, when Jesus and his three disciples (Peter, John, and James) came down from the mountain, a large crowd came out to meet them. The word "crowd" in the verse above is the same as the sense of "multitude," meaning a large group of people. The phrase "came down" means they were already going down from there.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke. He has just told about the transfiguration, when the voice of the Father said to listen to Jesus. The disciples kept silent about what they had seen. Now the account moves from the glory of the mountain to the need of the valley, where a father waits for help for his sick son.

For today: moments of closeness with God are not meant for us to stay apart, but to return to daily life with more faith and compassion. After prayer or a time of peace, God may send us to serve someone who is suffering.
exp.6:29:
The explanation says that the Pharisees and the teachers of the law rejected God's plan or purpose for them, and that they did so to their own harm, because they were not baptized by John. The experts in the law of Moses are the ones meant here. "Rejected" means they despised it. "Counsel" here means God's will or purpose.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd and explaining the reaction to John the Baptist. The verses before this one say that the people and the tax collectors accepted John's message and were baptized. This verse appears as a comment within Jesus' words (some interpreters see it as a note by Luke). Then Jesus compares that generation to capricious children whom nothing pleases.

Today, when God speaks to us through his Word and calls us to change, let us not harden our hearts out of pride. Accepting his call with humility is the best path.
exp.18:44:
This verse tells that Jesus entered the temple in Jerusalem and began to drive out those who were selling and buying there. The phrase "drive out" means to expel with firmness. "Began" shows that this was the start of an action that continued with his words.

Luke records this right after Jesus wept over Jerusalem and announced its destruction, because the city did not recognize the time when God was visiting it. Jesus acts with authority and with grief. The temple was meant to be a place of prayer, but it had become a place of business. The texts do not detail everything that went on there, but Jesus calls it a "den of thieves," and that harshness led the leaders to want to kill him.

For today: examine your heart and your life in the church. Ask God whether anything, such as the pursuit of money, outward appearance, or routine, is taking the place of prayer and sincere worship.
exp.9:28:
This verse says that a man, who wanted to show that he was already doing what was right, asked Jesus: "And who is my neighbour?" The word "justify" here means to come out looking good, to prove that one is in the right. "Neighbour" is the person near us whom we are called to love.

The one speaking is a teacher of the law, who had asked how to inherit eternal life. Jesus had him answer from the law, and the man quoted the love of God and of one's neighbour. Hearing "do this, and you will live," he perhaps felt he had to set a limit on who counts as a neighbour. Jesus answers him with the story of the good Samaritan.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, instead of looking for excuses or limits to love, we are willing to help whoever God places in our path, even when it is inconvenient or they are not from our group.
exp.9:6:
Jesus tells his disciples that when a house receives them, they should stay in that house. They are to eat and drink whatever they are offered, because the worker deserves his wages. The word for "stay" means to lodge or to be a guest, and the phrase for "give" means to hand over what is offered. He also asks them not to keep moving from house to house.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples whom he sends out two by two to announce the kingdom of God. He gives them simple instructions: bring peace, depend on the hospitality of others, and do not look for better comforts. Avoiding a change of house protected their witness and showed that their mission was not about seeking luxuries.

For today: if you serve others, be thankful and humble with what you receive, without looking for something better. And if you benefit from the work of someone who serves, acknowledge it and support them generously.
exp.11:27:
Jesus says that if God clothes the grass of the field with such beauty, grass that is green today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven (it was used as fuel to heat the oven), then how much more will he care for his children. "Little faith" describes people who believe in God but doubt that he will provide for them. "Clothe" here means to care for and provide.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, and earlier also to a crowd, after warning against greed. He wants to free them from worry and anxiety about food and clothing. He reminds them that the Father knows what they need, and that they should not live like those who do not know God.

Today, when worry about money or the future robs you of peace, stop and look at something created, like a flower or a bird. Then tell God your need with confidence, and faithfully do what is yours to do today.
exp.13:27:
Jesus asks who, wanting to build a tower, does not first sit down to work out how much it will cost and whether they have what it takes to finish it. "Counteth the cost" means doing the reckoning before starting. The idea is simple: the wise thing is to think before you commit.

Jesus is speaking to great crowds who were going along with him on the road. He has just said that following him means putting everything else second, even family. Here the word "hate" is a strong way of speaking that expresses giving Christ a greater love than anything else. With this comparison, he wants people to follow him with their eyes open, not out of the enthusiasm of the moment.

For today: before saying "yes" to Jesus, or renewing your commitment to him, reflect honestly on what it involves: your time, your plans, your attachments. Then ask him for help to persevere, because it is not a matter of trusting your own strength.
exp.15:21:
It says that both men died, the poor man and the rich man. The beggar Lazarus was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom, a way of speaking about a place of rest and closeness to the great father of Israel. Of the rich man it says only that he was buried.

Jesus tells this story to his listeners, among them Pharisees who loved money (Luke 16:14). Up to this point we have seen the contrast: a rich man without needs and a poor man covered with sores at his door. Death completely changes the situation of both. Christians understand in different ways how much of this account is a literal description of the afterlife and how much is teaching in the form of a parable.

For today: pay close attention to the needy people God places near you, and do not put off compassion and generosity.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that the angels of God rejoice when one single person who has turned away from God repents. "Repent" means changing one's attitude and direction, turning back to God. The phrase "joy in the presence of the angels" is understood as the joy that exists in their presence, that is, in heaven.

Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and teachers of the law, who criticized him for welcoming sinners and eating with them. He answers with three stories: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. In this one, a woman carefully searches for her coin and celebrates when she finds it. In the same way, God celebrates when someone returns to him.

For today: if God rejoices over each person who returns to him, we too can welcome with kindness, without judging, the one who wants to change. And if you have wandered away, remember that your return brings joy to God.
exp.5:45:
Jesus asks a probing question. Calling him "Lord, Lord" is a way of acknowledging him as authority, but he points out that it does no good to call him that if one does not do what he says.

Jesus is teaching his disciples and a large crowd in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has just spoken about a tree being known by its fruit and about the mouth reflecting the heart. Now he shows that words of respect must be accompanied by an obedient life. He then illustrates this with the man who builds on the rock.

For today: it is not enough to say that we believe in Jesus, or to sing and pray with fervor. Today you could choose one specific teaching of Jesus, such as forgiving someone or helping someone in need, and put it into practice simply.
exp.20:18:
It says that if we hold firm under trials, we will keep what is most valuable: our inner life and our faithfulness. "Patience" here means perseverance, not simply giving in to what happens. "Gain" means to win or secure. "Souls" can be understood as life or the whole person.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He warns them that they will be persecuted and hated for following him, but he promises that God will care for them. Right after this, he announces the destruction of Jerusalem. Some scholars see that announcement fulfilled in the year 70 AD, and others also see a future fulfillment. Interpreters explain in several ways how the promise of care and the possibility of martyrdom fit together.

For today: when a difficulty wears you down, do not give up at the first blow. Ask God for strength to take one more step of faithfulness today, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.3:26:
In the time of the prophet Eliseus, it says, there were many lepers in Israel, but none of them was cleansed except Naaman, who was from Syria. "Was cleansed" means he was healed of his leprosy. The Syrian was a foreigner and an enemy of Israel.

Jesus is speaking in the synagogue at Nazareth, his own town. He had told them that no prophet is accepted in his own land. To explain this, he recalls two cases from the Old Testament, Elijah with the widow of Zarephath and Eliseus with Naaman, in which God showed his help to foreigners. His hearers became so angry that they wanted to throw him off a cliff.

For today: God is free to bless whom he chooses, and his grace does not belong to any one particular group. Examine your heart: does it cost you to accept that God loves and heals people you consider distant? Respond with humility and joy, ready to listen to his voice.
exp.11:38:
What it says: Jesus teaches that if the owner of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would stay awake and would not let his house be broken into through the wall. "Breaking in" here means digging through the wall to make an opening. "Staying awake" means keeping watch and being alert.

Context: Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and then Peter asks whether the parable is only for them or for everyone. Earlier, Jesus praised the servants who faithfully wait for their master. Now he uses the image of a thief to show that his coming will be unexpected. He is not comparing Jesus to a thief in character, but only in the unexpectedness of the hour.

For today: This is not about living in fear, but about living each day faithfully. Ask yourself today: if Christ were to come now, what matters pending with God or with others should I put right? Start with one.
exp.23:1:
This verse tells that the women came to Jesus' tomb and saw that the large stone that closed the entrance had already been moved. The verse says the stone had been rolled away, so it is easy to picture a stone that was pushed aside. The women did not move it themselves; they simply found it that way.

The one telling the story is Luke, who writes what witnesses had told him. The women had gone very early on Sunday to anoint Jesus' body with the spices they had prepared. They expected to find a closed tomb and a dead body. So seeing the stone moved left them confused and frightened, as the following verses show.

For today: sometimes God removes obstacles that seemed impossible before we arrive. The women went with a worry, but the stone was already moved. We can keep obeying and serving in faith, trusting that God is preparing the way even when we cannot yet see it.
exp.11:39:
Jesus tells his disciples to be ready, that is, prepared and alert, because the Son of man will come at an hour when no one expects him.

Jesus is teaching his disciples about staying watchful, like servants waiting for their master. Earlier he spoke of the blessing of those who are found faithful, and he gave the example of a homeowner who would keep watch if he knew when a thief would come. Then Peter asks whether the parable is only for them or for everyone, and Jesus answers by speaking about the faithful steward.

For today: live each day faithfully, without putting off what matters most. Be reconciled, serve, pray, and do your work as someone who knows God sees it, living not in fear but in hope.
exp.13:34:
The explanation says that salt which has lost its taste is no longer good for anything: not for fertilizing the soil, nor for throwing on the dunghill. That is the place where it is cast out. Then Jesus adds: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear," an invitation to listen carefully and obey.

Jesus speaks to large crowds that were following him. He has just explained the cost of being his disciple: putting God above everything a person owns. The salt represents the disciple. If one's commitment becomes empty, it loses its usefulness. Scholars explain in several ways how salt loses its flavor, but the sense of the warning is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we follow Jesus with real devotion or only in word. Ask God to renew your commitment, and look for one concrete act of obedience today, such as serving, forgiving, or being honest.
exp.4:20:
What it says: The scribes, who were teachers of the law, and the Pharisees began to reason within themselves. They thought Jesus was blaspheming, that is, speaking with disrespect against God. They asked who he was to forgive sins, since that belongs to God alone. "Began to think" means they started turning it over in their minds.

Context: Some men had lowered a paralyzed man through the roof to where Jesus was. Seeing their faith, he told the man that his sins were forgiven. The religious leaders reacted in silence. They were right that only God forgives sins, but they did not recognize who Jesus was. Then he knew their thoughts and answered them.
