For today: It is good to defend what we believe about God, but we should keep our hearts open. Before we judge others or Jesus, let us ask ourselves whether we are truly looking with humility at what God is doing.
exp.21:18:
Jesus takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and hands it to his disciples. He tells them that this bread is his body, given for them, and asks them to do this in remembrance of him.

Jesus speaks at the Last Supper with his twelve disciples, during Passover, shortly before he is arrested. He is giving new meaning to the meal: his body will be given and his blood poured out, and so a new covenant is established. Christians understand this moment in different ways (symbolic, spiritual, or of real presence), but all agree that it remembers his sacrifice.

For today: when you take part in the Lord's Supper, or simply pray, take a moment to truly thank God for what Jesus gave up for you. Let that remembrance move you to live with gratitude and to serve others with love.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that the axe is already ready, placed at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. "Is already laid at the root" means that judgment is very near. The fruit stands for a life that shows by its actions that a real change has taken place.

The speaker is John the Baptist, addressing the crowds who came to the Jordan to be baptized. He warns them that it is not enough to be descendants of Abraham or to carry out a ritual. God expects true repentance. Then, when they ask him what they should do, John answers with concrete examples: sharing clothing and food with those who have none.

For today: authentic faith shows in actions. Today you might think of one concrete act of kindness or generosity toward someone in need, as a simple sign that your repentance is real.
exp.3:36:
It says that the news about Jesus was spreading everywhere. "Fame" here means reputation or news, and the phrase "the region around" refers to the area nearby. In other words, people throughout that whole district were talking about what Jesus had done.

Luke, the author of the gospel, is the one who tells this. Jesus had just taught in the synagogue in Capernaum and freed a man tormented by an unclean spirit. People were amazed because Jesus gave commands with authority, and that is why his fame grew. Right after this, Luke reports that Jesus healed Simon's mother-in-law.

For today: when God works in your life, do not keep the story to yourself. Tell it simply to a family member or friend. A humble and sincere testimony can encourage others to come to know Jesus.
exp.23:36:
This verse says that the disciples were filled with fear and great surprise, and believed they were seeing a spirit, that is, a ghost. "Terrified" means frightened, and "affrighted" means very startled, not knowing what to think.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened the evening of the resurrection. The disciples from Emmaus had just recounted how they recognized Jesus when he broke the bread, and suddenly Jesus himself appeared and said to them, "Peace be with you." Even with the testimonies they had already heard, they still found it hard to believe. Jesus reassures them by showing them his hands and his feet.

For today: when doubt or fear shakes us, we can bring them to Jesus honestly. He does not scold us for being confused; he gives us peace and reasons to believe.
exp.16:34:
Jesus says that two women will be doing the same work, grinding grain together with a millstone. One will be "taken" and the other "left." Grinding was a daily and ordinary task, so the scene shows that two people can look exactly alike on the outside.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about his coming and about the day of the Son of Man. Earlier he warned that this day will arrive suddenly, as in the days of Noah and Lot. Interpreters disagree about what "taken" means: it can mean being rescued or being carried away in judgment. What is clear is the unexpected separation.

For today: do not live preoccupied with appearances, and do not feel secure just because you do what others do. Cultivate a personal and sincere faith in God, and live each day prepared, with your heart at peace with him.
exp.10:17:
Jesus asks a simple question: if Satan fights against himself, how can his kingdom last? Those who accused him said that Jesus cast out demons by the power of the prince of the demons, Beelzebub. Some sources describe a name for the chief of the demons.

Jesus speaks to a crowd. After healing a man who could not speak, some accused him of using evil power, and others asked him for a sign from heaven to test him. Jesus knew their thoughts and showed that their accusation made no sense. He then explains that if he casts out demons by the finger of God, the kingdom of God has already come near.

For today: let us be careful not to attribute to evil what is the work of God simply because we do not want to believe. Let us ask for a humble and sincere heart to recognize his work, even when it does not fit what we expected.
exp.5:1:
Here some Pharisees challenge Jesus' disciples. They ask why they are doing what is not permitted on the sabbath, that is, what the law, according to their interpretation, did not allow. The disciples were plucking heads of grain and rubbing them in their hands to eat the kernels.

The Pharisees are the ones speaking. They were passing through a grainfield, and the disciples were hungry. The law allowed people to take grain from someone else's field to eat (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the Pharisees regarded this as work, like harvesting and threshing, and so they saw it as a breach of the day of rest. Jesus will answer them with the example of David.

We may take great care with our religious rules, but it is worth asking whether they help us love God and other people. Before judging others, let us better understand the purpose of what God commanded: mercy matters.
exp.20:37:
The explanation says that all the people would get up early and come to Jesus in the temple to listen to him. The verse's wording is "came early in the morning to him in the temple, for to hear him," so the phrasing here follows it.

Luke tells this at the end of Jesus' days in Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. During the day Jesus taught in the temple, and at night he went out to spend it on the Mount of Olives. This verse summarizes what had happened in those days: the people were eager to hear him. Shortly before, Jesus had spoken about staying alert and praying, and here we see a people who sought his word with constancy.

For today: we can give the Word of God first place in the day. Before noise and tasks fill our minds, let us set aside a few minutes to read, pray, and listen to Jesus with attention.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that the fame of Jesus kept growing. Large crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their illnesses. The word "but" at the start of the verse shows the contrast with what came just before, and "gathered" means that the people came together.

Here Luke, the narrator of the gospel, speaks. He tells what happened after Jesus healed a man with leprosy and asked him not to tell anyone. Even so, the news spread. Luke shows that people sought out Jesus in their needs, and that Jesus received them. Then the text says that he withdrew to pray.

For today: even when our life is full of responsibilities and of people who depend on us, let us do as Jesus did and seek moments alone with God. There we receive strength to serve others without growing weary.
exp.8:2:
Jesus tells the twelve to go out on their mission without taking anything extra. A "staff" is a walking stick; a "scrip" is a travel bag for carrying food or personal belongings. Nor bread, nor money, nor a spare tunic ("two coats").

Jesus has just given them power over demons and diseases, and he sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God. By asking them to travel light, he teaches them to depend on God and on the hospitality of those who receive them. The Gospels recount this sending with small differences in the details, such as the staff, and there is no single way to explain them.

For today: this text does not oblige everyone to live without provisions, but it invites us to ask what things give us false security. We can serve God with more confidence when we let go of excess and depend on Him.
exp.14:30:
Jesus tells that the father answers the older son tenderly, calling him "son." He reminds him of two things: that he has always been at his side, and that everything the father has belongs to him.

The parable is about the prodigal son. The older son became angry because his younger brother, who had wasted his share of the inheritance, was welcomed with a great celebration. Jesus tells this in front of Pharisees and teachers of the law, who criticized him for welcoming sinners. Many see in the older son a reflection of them.

For today: we can serve God and still feel forgotten, or fill ourselves with comparison and resentment. This verse invites us to remember that we already live close to the Father and that He gives us all we need. Then we can rejoice when He welcomes others with joy.
exp.23:32:
As soon as they recognized Jesus, the two disciples got up at once, that very hour, meaning immediately. They went back to Jerusalem and found the eleven apostles gathered together, along with others who were with them.

Luke tells us what happened that first Sunday after the resurrection. The two disciples had been walking toward Emmaus, sad and confused, when the risen Jesus explained the Scriptures to them. When they recognized him, they could no longer stay still. The road back was probably several kilometers long, and still they did not wait until morning. They wanted to share the news with the other believers.

When God opens our eyes and touches our hearts, it is not meant to be kept to ourselves. Think of something God has recently shown you and tell it today to a brother or sister in the faith, or to a friend. Faith grows when it is shared in community.
exp.17:34:
This verse tells us that Jesus was approaching the city of Jericho. There, by the side of the road, sat a blind man who was asking people for money as they passed by.

Luke is the one telling the story. Just before this, Jesus had announced his death and resurrection, but the disciples did not understand. Now a man appears who could not see with his eyes, but who, as the following account shows, would recognize who Jesus was. Some see here a contrast between the blindness of the disciples and this man's faith, although the text does not say it in those words.

Today we can ask ourselves what we may be failing to see or understand, and approach Jesus with humility, as this man did. Asking him sincerely for light is a good place to begin.
exp.17:29:
This verse completes Jesus' promise: whoever has left something for the kingdom of God will receive "many times more" in this present time, and in the coming age, that is, the age to come, will have eternal life. The word "age" here means an era or period of time, not a hundred years.

Peter had just said that he and the disciples had left everything to follow Jesus. Earlier, a rich man had gone away sad because he would not let go of his riches. Jesus responds with a promise: no one loses by serving God. Some understand the "many times more" as the new family of the church and God's care; the text gives no further details. Right after this, Jesus announces his suffering in Jerusalem.

For today: when obeying God costs you something, trust that he cares for you. Take the next step of faith, and seek support in your Christian community.
exp.20:3:
It says that the rich gave offerings out of what was left over, that is, from what they did not need. By contrast, this widow, though poor, gave everything she had to live on.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem while he watches people putting their offerings in. He wants his disciples to learn that God does not measure giving by the amount, but by the heart and the sacrifice. Shortly afterward he announces the destruction of the temple, which makes this woman's faith stand out even more.

For today: God values sincere generosity, not outward appearances. You might ask yourself what you can give with trust in him, whether time, help, or money, even if it seems small. And do not compare yourself with others.
exp.5:42:
Jesus says that the quality of a tree shows in what it produces. A healthy tree gives good fruit, and a sick one gives bad fruit. In this verse, "bad" means damaged or of poor quality, and "fruit" stands for what a person says and does.

Jesus is teaching his disciples and a crowd during what is called the Sermon on the Plain. He has just warned against judging others with hypocrisy when we ourselves have bigger faults. Now he tells them that a person's life shows what their heart is like, as he explains in the verses that follow.

Today we can ask ourselves what fruit we are bearing: our words, attitudes, and decisions. Instead of only trying to look good on the outside, it is wise to ask God to change our hearts, so that what is good comes out naturally.
exp.8:52:
The explanation says that the Samaritans of that village did not receive Jesus. The reason is that his purpose, that is, his direction or intention, was to go to Jerusalem. "Did not receive him" means that they did not welcome him or give him lodging.

Luke tells us that Jesus had set his face firmly, that is, he had resolutely decided to go to Jerusalem, where his departure from this world would be fulfilled. He sent messengers ahead to prepare lodging. Between Jews and Samaritans there was an old enmity, and many understand that the rejection came from that conflict. James and John became angry, but Jesus rebuked them.

Today, when someone rejects us or does not welcome us, we may feel like responding with anger. Jesus teaches us to keep going with firmness and gentleness, without returning evil for evil.
exp.4:5:
They did what Jesus told them, and the catch was so large that their nets were nearly breaking. The verse says they "inclosed" many fish, which means they caught or surrounded a great number of fish inside the net. Here "fish" simply means fish, in large quantity.

Luke tells this moment after Jesus had taught the crowd from Simon's boat. Then he asked Simon to go out into deeper water. Simon, an experienced fisherman, was tired and had caught nothing, but he trusted Jesus' word. The result led him to recognize his sinfulness and to see who Jesus was.

For today: sometimes God asks us to obey even when we are tired or discouraged, and even when we do not fully understand. We can take that step of trust, without knowing how it will turn out, remembering that He is faithful and knows what He is doing.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that Judas agreed to the deal with the religious leaders and then kept waiting for the best moment to hand Jesus over to them. He wanted to do it "in the absence of the multitude," that is, away from the crowd and without people noticing. "And he promised" means he committed himself to carry it out. "To deliver him unto them" means to put him into their hands.

The one telling the story is Luke. The chief priests feared the people, who listened to Jesus with delight, and so they needed a quiet moment. Earlier, Luke says that Satan entered Judas (22:3). The Bible does not fully explain what Judas was thinking in his heart, but it does show that he betrayed Jesus for money.

For today: let us guard our hearts against the small decisions made in secret. If there is something we could not do in the open, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God to keep us faithful to Christ.
exp.0:37:
Here Mary responds to the angel's message. She calls herself "the handmaid of the Lord," that is, a servant who places herself at God's disposal. "Be it unto me according to thy word" means: "Let it happen as you have said." Then the angel departed.

She speaks, a young woman from Nazareth. The angel Gabriel had announced to her that she would have a son, Jesus, by the work of the Holy Spirit. To encourage her, he spoke to her of Elisabeth, her relative, who was also expecting a child in her old age. Then Mary went to visit her in haste.

Today we can imitate Mary's trust: she did not understand everything, but she said yes to God. We can offer Him whatever worries us and pray, "Lord, let your will be done," and take the next step of obedience that we see clearly.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that Jesus, whom it calls "the Son of man," came into this world with a clear purpose: to seek and save those who were lost. The phrase "came into" reflects "vino a," and "lost" describes someone who is far from God and cannot find the way back.

Jesus speaks in Jericho, in the house of Zacchaeus, a tax collector who was looked down upon by his own people. Zacchaeus had just promised to give back what he had taken and to help the poor. Jesus explains in this way why he drew near to a man whom others despised: he had come precisely for people like him.

For today: no one is too far from God. If you feel lost, Jesus is searching for you. And if you know someone whom others have rejected, follow Jesus' example: approach them with kindness and without prejudice.
exp.19:2:
Jesus answers the leaders' question with a question of his own. He says that he will also ask them one thing, and he asks them to give him an answer.

Jesus is teaching in the temple when the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders interrupt him. They demand to know by what authority he acts and who gave him that authority. Jesus does not avoid the issue. With his question about John the Baptist, he shows them that their hearts are not sincere, since they are not seeking the truth but a reason to accuse him.

For today: before we demand answers from God, let us honestly examine whether we truly want to obey him. Let us ask him for a humble heart, ready to receive the truth even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.11:2:
Jesus says that what has been said in secret, in the dark or in a low voice inside the rooms, will one day be made known and proclaimed in public. The flat roofs of houses, from which announcements were once made to everyone, are where it will be announced. Whispering something privately into someone's ear refers to telling something in private.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples while a large crowd gathers around him. He has just warned them against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who showed one thing on the outside and lived another way on the inside. Then he tells them not to fear people, but to fear God, who sees everything.

For today: live with sincerity, without a double life. If there is something hidden that does not let you rest, bring it to God in prayer today and ask for his forgiveness and his help to walk in the light.
exp.23:41:
This verse tells that the disciples gave Jesus a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. A honeycomb is the wax structure where bees store honey. It was simple, ordinary food.

Luke relates that the risen Jesus appeared to his disciples, who were frightened and full of doubts. He showed them his hands and his feet, and then asked for something to eat. By eating in front of them, he showed that he was not a spirit or an illusion. Afterward he led them to understand that the Scriptures spoke of him. Some believe this scene emphasizes that his body was real, though glorified.

Today we can remember that Jesus draws near in everyday life. If you have doubts, you can speak to him honestly, and sharing a simple meal can be a moment to remember that he is alive.
exp.13:24:
It says that a great crowd was walking along with Jesus. At that moment he turns, that is, he stops and addresses all those people to tell them something important. "People" means persons, and "turning" means that he turned around to look at them face to face.

Jesus is speaking, on his way to Jerusalem. He has just told the parable of the great banquet, where many invited guests refuse the invitation. Now he sees many people following him and wants them to know what being his disciple truly involves. It is not enough to walk behind him out of curiosity or habit; following him requires a sincere commitment.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we are only near Jesus, accompanying the crowd, or whether we truly follow him. Today you can give Jesus first place in one concrete decision of your day.
exp.19:13:
The explanation says that the farmers, seeing the son of the owner of the vineyard, reasoned among themselves: "This is the heir." Instead of respecting him, they decided to kill him so that they could keep the inheritance.

Jesus tells this parable in the temple to the religious leaders and the people. The vineyard represents Israel, the servants who were sent are the prophets, and the beloved son points to Jesus himself. With this he shows them that he knows their intentions and that their rejection has consequences. They understood that he was speaking about them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we want to control our lives without answering to God. Everything we have is a gift from him. Receiving Jesus with humility, and not with pride, is the best response.
exp.0:14:
It says that John will be great in the eyes of God, not of people. He will not drink wine or strong drink, which is a strong beverage made from fruit, different from our cider today. And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit from before he is born, that is, from his mother's womb.

The angel Gabriel speaks to Zechariah, a priest, while he was serving in the temple. Zechariah and Elisabeth had no children and were already advanced in years. The angel tells him that God has heard his prayer. Not drinking wine or strong drink recalls the vow of the Nazirite, although the text does not use that word. Many see it as a life given entirely to God.

For today: true greatness does not depend on fame or applause, but on living devoted to God and guided by his Spirit. We can ask him every day to fill us and help us say no to whatever pulls us away from his purpose.
exp.9:3:
Jesus tells his disciples to go out without a purse (for money), without a bag (a traveling pouch or knapsack for provisions), and without extra sandals. He also asks them not to stop to greet anyone along the way.

Jesus speaks to the seventy-two whom he sends out two by two to the towns where he himself intended to go. Their mission is urgent, and they must trust in God and in the hospitality of others. As for the greeting, it is not a lack of courtesy: in that time, greetings could be long and take up a great deal of time. Some believe it simply emphasizes the urgency of the message.

For today: serve God with confidence and focus. Ask yourself what things distract you or give you false security, and let them go so that you can devote yourself to what God asks of you.
exp.0:24:
Elizabeth says that the Lord did this for her, that is, He allowed her to conceive. She says that God "looked on" her to take away her "reproach," which is the shame or contempt she had felt. "Thus hath the Lord dealt with me" means that He made her pregnant. "In the days wherein he looked on me" refers to the time when God turned his attention to her with kindness.

Elizabeth is speaking; she is the wife of the priest Zechariah. She was older and had had no children, something that in her culture was seen as a disgrace. After the angel announced to Zechariah the birth of John, she conceived and kept herself secluded for five months. The text does not explain why she kept herself hidden; some think it was out of quiet reflection and gratitude.

God sees people who carry shame or silent pain. We can bring those wounds to him in prayer, trusting that He looks on us with kindness and, in his time, can bring comfort. And when He helps us, let us give him thanks.
exp.16:16:
Jesus asks two questions. First he recalls that ten men were cleansed of leprosy, and then he asks where the other nine are. The word "cleansed" here means healed of their disease. Jesus does not scold them in anger; he expresses sadness and surprise that only one came back to give thanks.

Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem when ten lepers ask him for mercy. He tells them to present themselves to the priests, and while they are going, they are made well. Only one returns, and he was a Samaritan, a foreigner whom many Jews looked down on. The Bible does not say why the other nine did not return; it only points out the contrast.

Today we can ask ourselves how many times we receive something from God and simply walk on. A simple practice is to stop each day and thank God for something specific, aloud or in writing, without waiting for everything to turn out perfectly.
exp.12:28:
Jesus says that people from all over the world, from the east, the west, the north, and the south, will come and take their places at the table in the kingdom of God. Sitting at the table speaks of fellowship, joy, and a banquet. Two words from the original text need a comment: the word for "south" here appears in the older wording as "midday," meaning south, and the verbs that express "will" and "come" speak of something certain.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd as he travels toward Jerusalem. Someone asked him whether only a few will be saved, and he warns that many who thought they were secure will be left outside. His Jewish listeners expected Abraham to be waiting for them in the kingdom, but Jesus announces that people from other nations will also enter, and that the order of importance will change.

For today: do not trust your name, your church, or your family to make you right with God. Respond honestly to his invitation, and welcome with joy every person whom God calls, no matter where they come from.
exp.11:50:
Jesus asks whether people think he came to bring peace on earth, and he answers that no, he came to bring division and disagreement instead.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd. He has just said that he came to cast fire on the earth and that he must go through a baptism, which many understand to mean his suffering and death. He knows that his message will force people to make a choice, and that not everyone will accept it, not even within the same family. He is not speaking of looking for fights, but of what happens when the truth confronts people.

For today: if following Christ brings tension with someone close to you, do not be surprised. Respond with humility, love, and firmness, without seeking quarrels.
exp.22:8:
This verse tells us that Herod asked Jesus many questions, one after another, but Jesus did not answer him at all. The phrase "he questioned him in many words" means that Herod talked at length and insistently. Jesus' silence was complete.

Pilate had sent Jesus to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, because Jesus was from Galilee. Herod had wanted to see him for some time, but more out of curiosity than faith, since he hoped to witness a sign or miracle. Meanwhile, the chief priests accused him vehemently. Jesus did not defend himself or put on a show for him. Many Christians connect this silence with Isaiah 53:7.

God is not obliged to answer those who seek him only out of curiosity or for entertainment. Let us come to Jesus with a sincere heart, ready to listen to him and obey him, and not only to ask him for things or for proof.
exp.14:13:
He says the younger son spent everything he had. Just then a severe famine struck that country, and he began to be in need. "Spent all" means he wasted it without wisdom. "Land" is the region or country where he was. "He began to be in want" means he started to run out of even the basics.

Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees, teachers of the law, and sinners who were drawing near to hear him. He tells it to show God's love for those who are lost. Here the young man reaches his lowest point: no money, far from home, and facing a crisis he could not control. This moment prepares his return to the father.

For today: when the things that promised us happiness run out, we do not have to remain in shame. We can see that emptiness as an invitation to return to God, who receives us with grace.
exp.8:26:
Jesus says solemnly that some of those who were listening would not die before they saw the kingdom of God. The phrase "taste death" is an old way of saying "die," so in the King James wording it appears as "taste of death." The words "I tell you of a truth" stress that this is a firm promise.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, right after announcing his suffering and calling people to follow him by taking up the cross. He speaks of glory and of shame, and he wants to encourage them. Christians understand this promise in several ways, but many connect it with the transfiguration, which takes place about eight days later, when three disciples see his glory.

Today we can follow Jesus with courage, without being ashamed of him, trusting that his kingdom is real and worth more than anything in this world.
exp.0:26:
This verse introduces the young woman to whom God sent the angel Gabriel. The word translated "virgin" refers to a woman who has not had relations with any man. The word "espoused" means betrothed to be married; at that time a betrothal was very serious and legally binding, even though the couple did not yet live together. Joseph was a descendant of King David, and the young woman's name was Mary.

The one speaking here is Luke, the author, who sets out in order what happened. After narrating the announcement of the birth of John the Baptist, he now introduces Mary. She was a humble person from Nazareth, a town in Galilee. By mentioning the house of David, Luke prepares the reader to understand that Jesus would come from that promised royal line.

For today: God does not look for famous or powerful people, but for willing hearts. If you feel ordinary and small, remember that God can speak to you and use you right where you are.
exp.18:38:
What it says: Some Pharisees who were in the crowd ask Jesus to make his disciples stop. They call him "Master," and they tell him to rebuke them, that is, to sharply correct them or order them to be quiet. The word "company" refers to the crowd that was with him.

Context: Jesus is approaching Jerusalem, coming down from the Mount of Olives. His disciples praise him loudly and call him "the King who comes in the name of the Lord." The Pharisees speak because those words recognize Jesus as King, and they did not accept that. Some think they were also worried about disorder or about how the authorities would react, but the text does not state this clearly. Jesus answers that if they keep silent, the stones would cry out.

For today: Do not let the criticism or discomfort of others quench your gratitude toward God. Praise him sincerely, at home, in church, or wherever you are, remembering what he has done for you.
exp.8:25:
Jesus says that whoever is ashamed of him and of his words, that is, whoever denies him or keeps quiet out of fear of what others will say, will also be disowned by the Son of Man when he comes in his glory, with the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.

Jesus speaks to his disciples shortly after Peter recognized him as the Christ. He has just announced that he will suffer, and he calls them to follow him by carrying their own cross. On that path there would be rejection and mockery, and he reminds them that what matters most is faithfulness to him, even when it costs them.

For today: be brave and simple in showing that you follow Jesus. It can mean praying before a meal in public, not laughing at a joke that offends God, or answering kindly when someone asks you about your faith.
exp.14:23:
Here the father explains why he throws a party. His younger son had gone far away and spent everything; to the father it was as if he had died. Now that he has come back, it is as if he has come back to life.

Jesus tells this parable to Pharisees and scribes who were criticizing him for welcoming sinners. The father speaks to his servants and represents the heart of God, who rejoices when someone returns to him. Soon after, the older son appears, who does not share that joy.

Today we can remember that God welcomes with joy anyone who comes back to him in humility. If you are far away, you can return. And if you are already close to God, ask him for a heart that rejoices when others are restored, instead of judging them.
exp.4:12:
This verse tells that Jesus stretched out his hand and touched a man who had leprosy. He said, "I will: be thou clean," and at that very moment the leprosy left him. "Immediately" means "at once," and "departed from him" means that the disease left him completely.

The man had begged Jesus, "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." At that time, the law of Moses required that people with leprosy live apart from others, and almost no one touched them. Jesus responds with both power and compassion: he does not only speak, but he also touches him. Afterward he asks the man to show himself to the priest, as the law prescribed, so that his healing would be confirmed.

Today we can come to Jesus with sincerity, even when we feel rejected or unclean inside. He listens to us and does not despise us. We can ask him for help, trusting in his goodness and his power.
exp.12:0:
Here, some people came to Jesus with sad news. They told him about certain Galileans whom Pilate had ordered killed while they were offering their sacrifices, so that their blood was mixed in with the blood of the animals.

The ones speaking were ordinary people who were with Jesus. Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea. The Bible gives no further details about this event, and outside the Bible we have no reliable information about it. They probably wanted to know whether those victims had suffered because they were greater sinners. Jesus answers in the following verse, and calls them to repentance.

For today: when we hear of a tragedy, let us not judge those who suffer it. Instead, let us examine our own hearts and return to God with humility.
exp.16:14:
This verse tells us that of ten men healed of leprosy, only one noticed that he was clean and came back. He returned praising God in a loud voice. To glorify means to recognize and honor God for what he has done. Speaking with a loud voice means speaking with a strong voice, without shame.

Luke narrates this moment as Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem. The ten lepers had asked for mercy, and Jesus told them to present themselves to the priests, who were the ones who confirmed a healing. As they went in obedience, they were cleansed. This man, as is seen afterward, was a Samaritan, that is, someone despised by many Jews.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. Let us pause, turn back to Him, and give thanks openly, also with words, for what He has done in our lives.
exp.1:6:
This verse tells that Mary gave birth to her first son, Jesus. She wrapped him in swaddling clothes, which were strips of cloth used to wrap newborn babies. Because there was no room for them in the inn (a lodging place where travelers stayed), she laid him in a manger, the trough where animals ate.

Here the narrator is Luke, who carefully investigated the events. Joseph and Mary had traveled to Bethlehem because of the census. Some think the birth took place in a house or in a stable; the text gives no further details. What is clear is that the King was born without luxuries, and soon the announcement came to some simple shepherds.

For today: God draws near to us in humility. If you feel small or without a place, remember that Jesus knows that experience. And you too can make room for him in your daily life.
exp.9:21:
Jesus says that the Father has placed everything into his hands. No one truly knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one truly knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. The word "delivered" in the verse means given or entrusted.

Jesus speaks full of joy after his seventy disciples return from their mission. He tells them that the greatest thing is not the power they had, but that their names are written in heaven. He praises the Father because he reveals himself to the humble, not to those who presume to be wise.

For today: we cannot know God through intelligence or effort alone; it is a gift that Jesus gives. Come to him with humility, ask him to show you the Father, and read the Gospels with a simple and open heart.
exp.6:37:
What it says: A woman stands behind Jesus, at his feet. She weeps so much that her tears wet his feet. She dries them with her hair, kisses them, and pours perfume on them. "Wet" here means to moisten, and "perfume" is a fragrant oil, kept in an alabaster jar.

Context: Luke tells us that Jesus is eating at the house of Simon, a Pharisee. The woman comes in, known in the town as a sinner. The text does not say what her sin was. Her gesture expresses humility and gratitude, and Simon looks on her with contempt. Jesus will respond with a teaching about forgiveness.

For today: We do not need to come to God with pretense or with pride. We can draw near with sincerity, acknowledging our failings and thanking him for his forgiveness. And when we see others, let us avoid judging them quickly: God looks at the heart.
exp.23:3:
The verse tells us that the women who went to Jesus' tomb were greatly perplexed at not finding his body. Suddenly, two men stood beside them. Their clothes were shining with great light. "Perplexed" means confused or puzzled, and "men" refers to the two figures themselves.

Here Luke is speaking as the narrator. The women had come early on Sunday to anoint the body of Jesus. They found the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. In this verse Luke does not call these two men "angels," but the shining clothing suggests they were messengers from God. Later Luke presents them as the ones who announce the resurrection.

For today: sometimes God works in ways that leave us bewildered, and we come to him with doubts and fear. Even so, he meets us with words of hope. You can bring him your confusion with confidence, because he knows how to answer.
exp.2:24:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Jesus, in his family line, comes after Mattathias, who was the son of Amos, and this one was the son of Naum, and this one was the son of Esli. The phrase "which was the son of" means "son of" or "descendant of." These are ancestors of Jesús, named one after another.

The one who writes is Luke, the doctor who carefully investigated the facts for his friend Theophilus. He presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. These names are hardly mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. Some scholars think the list follows the line of Mary, others the line of Joseph; there is no certainty.

For today: God pays attention to people the world forgets. These almost unknown men were part of his plan. Your faithful and simple life also counts for God, even though no one remembers it.
exp.17:5:
And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith. Jesus calls the attention of his listeners. It is a way of saying: do not miss what this man has just admitted. Although he did not fear God or respect anyone, he ended up giving justice to the widow, only so that she would stop bothering him.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples with a parable about praying always and not losing heart (Luke 18:1). He uses a contrast: if a wicked judge gives in because of a widow's persistence, how much more will God, who is good, attend to his children! Jesus does not say that God is like that judge, but quite the opposite.

When prayer goes on for a long time and it seems that God is slow, do not give up. Keep crying out with confidence, because God is just and good, and he hears his own.
exp.10:8:
Jesus tells his disciples to ask, seek, and knock. These are three ways of approaching God with confidence and persistence. The promises that it will be given to you and that it will be opened to you assure us that God answers. The words "persistent begging" and "bothersome" speak of insisting without growing weary.

Jesus has just taught the Lord's Prayer. Then he tells the story of a man who asks a friend for bread at midnight, and the friend in the end gets up because of his insistence. Afterward Jesus compares God to a good father who gives good things to his children. If a tired friend responds, how much more will the Father. Many understand that these verbs point to persevering prayer.

For today: bring your needs to God honestly and do not give up quickly. Pray with confidence, knowing that He is a good Father, even though his answer does not always come the way or the time we expect.
exp.21:55:
This verse tells that a servant girl saw Peter sitting near the fire. She looked at him closely and said that he was with Jesus. A servant girl is a young woman who works serving in a household. To look at someone closely means she observed him carefully.

The one speaking is this servant girl, who recognizes Peter by the light of the fire. Jesus had just been arrested and taken to the house of the high priest. Peter was following at a distance, out of fear, and mixed in among the crowd so that he would go unnoticed. Jesus had already warned him that he would deny Him, and here that warning begins to come true.

For today: pressure does not always come as a great persecution; sometimes it is only a simple question in an uncomfortable setting. If we follow Christ "at a distance," it will be easier to keep silent. Let us draw near to Him with prayer and sincerity, and remember that Jesus forgives and restores those who return to Him.
exp.4:22:
Jesus asks a question: which is easier, to say to someone "your sins are forgiven," or to say "rise up and walk"? The point of the question is that both statements are impossible for an ordinary man. Jesus invites his hearers to think about this before he answers.

Jesus speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, who were accusing him in their hearts of blasphemy. A paralyzed man had just been lowered through the roof to where Jesus was. No one could check with their own eyes whether sins had been forgiven, but they could see whether the man was healed. In this way Jesus shows, through a visible act, that he has the authority to forgive sins, something they believed only God could do.

Today we can remember that Jesus cares about our bodies as well as our hearts, but above all about forgiveness. If there is guilt in your life, bring it to him with confidence.
exp.20:10:
This verse says there will be strong earthquakes in various places, and famines and diseases that spread from one place to another (plagues). There will also be fearful sights, that is, things that cause great fear, and great signs seen in the sky.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in the temple, shortly before his arrest. They asked him when the things he had announced about the temple would happen. He prepares them for hard times and warns them that these events do not mean the end will come right away. Some believe he is speaking of the destruction of Jerusalem, others of the end of the age, and others of both.

For today: when the news frightens us, we can remember that Jesus already warned us. Instead of living in panic, let us trust in him, pray, and remain faithful in what we are called to do.
exp.16:4:
The apostles ask Jesus, "Increase our faith." That is, they want to trust God more. The word "increase" here means to make it grow, and "faith" means trust in God and in his power.

Jesus had just taught them to forgive a brother who sins against them, even seven times a day if he repents. That is very hard. So the apostles, who speak to the Lord, feel they need more faith to carry it out. Jesus answers that even a small faith, like a grain of mustard seed, can accomplish great things. Some think he is showing them that the issue is not the amount of faith, but truly trusting.

If forgiving costs you, ask God for help sincerely, as the apostles did. Then take a concrete step of trust: pray for the one who wronged you and offer them forgiveness.
exp.22:16:
This verse says that Pilate was under an obligation, or a custom, to release one prisoner each time the feast came. The word that matters here is "necessity," which means he had to do it. To release means to set free.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke, who explains a detail for the reader. Pilate had just declared that neither he nor Herod found any fault in Jesus, and he proposed to punish him and then let him go. This custom of the Passover feast sets up what follows: the crowd would ask for Barabbas instead of Jesus. Some older versions leave out this verse, and scholars debate why.

For today: Jesus was declared innocent and yet took the place of another. Today we can give thanks for that self-giving and, in response, show mercy to those who do not deserve it, just as we received it.
exp.16:19:
It says that the Pharisees asked Jesus when the kingdom of God would come. He answered that it does not come "with observation." This old expression means that it will not arrive in a visible way, with signs that can be watched and observed, like someone waiting for a parade.

Jesus speaks while he is on the way to Jerusalem. He has just healed ten lepers, and only one foreigner, a Samaritan, returned to give thanks. The Pharisees were expecting a kingdom with spectacular signs. Jesus corrects that idea and then says that the kingdom is "among you," that is, in the midst of them, since the King was present. Some also translate it as "within you," and there is debate about this.

Today, instead of looking for striking signs or setting dates, we can recognize Jesus and live under his reign right now. This shows up in simple faith, gratitude, and practical love in each day.
exp.3:27:
What they say: When those in the synagogue heard what Jesus had just said, they were all filled with anger. Nobody was indifferent; their reaction was rage.

Context: Jesus was speaking in Nazareth, the town where he had grown up. He reminded them that God, in the days of Elijah and Elisha, helped a widow and a leper who were not Israelites. With this he showed them that God's grace does not belong to only one group, and this offended their pride.

For today: Sometimes God's truth makes us uncomfortable because it touches our pride or our prejudices. Instead of getting angry, we can ask God, "What do You want to correct in me?" And remember that his love is greater than our borders.
exp.2:30:
This verse is part of a list of ancestors. It says that Jesus, following the line backward, was descended from Melea, and that Melea was from Menan, Mattatha, and Nathan. The phrase "which was the son of" appears throughout the list, and in this context it can mean "a descendant of."

The writer is Luke, the author of the Gospel. He presents this genealogy after Jesus's baptism to show that He truly belongs to human history. This line reaches David through Nathan, one of David's sons. Some scholars believe Luke follows the line of Mary and others the line of Joseph; there is no single certain explanation.

For today: God works through people whom almost no one remembers. Your faithfulness each day, though it may seem small, can be part of what God is doing in your family and in others.
exp.6:30:
Jesus asks a question to get the attention of those who are listening. He asks what the people of his time can be compared to. The word "generation" in the verse means the people who were living in that time, and the phrase "to liken" in the verse means to set something beside another thing to understand it better, and "like" means similar.

Jesus speaks after praising John the Baptist. The ordinary people and the tax collectors recognized that God was right and were baptized. The Pharisees and the teachers of the law, however, rejected God's plan for them. That is why Jesus uses a comparison to show their attitude.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we make excuses so as not to obey God. It is better to listen with humility, even when his message comes in a way we did not expect.
exp.11:36:
Jesus says that happy are the servants whom their master finds awake and attentive when he returns. He makes them a surprising promise: the master himself will tie on his work clothes, seat them at the table, and go around serving them. "Watching" means being awake and alert; "blessed" means happy or fortunate.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, in the middle of a teaching about not living anxious over material things. He uses the picture of servants who wait for their lord, who is returning from a wedding feast and may arrive late at night. He teaches them to live prepared, because the Lord will come, and shortly afterward he compares that coming to a thief who arrives without warning.

For today: live each day with your heart ready for the Lord, faithfully doing what is yours to do: praying, loving, serving, and obeying. This is not about living in fear, but about waiting with joy for the One who promises to honor us.
exp.4:18:
This verse tells how some men wanted to bring a paralyzed man before Jesus, but the crowd filled the house and there was no way through. So they went up onto the roof, made an opening, and lowered the sick man, lying on his bed, right in front of Jesus. The bed was a simple mat or cot.

Luke recounts this while Jesus was teaching, with religious teachers of the law present who had come from many places. The paralyzed man's friends did not give up in the face of the obstacle. Jesus saw their faith, and this led him to forgive the man's sins and sparked the debate with the Pharisees. The exact details of the roof are understood in various ways, but the central idea is clear.

For today: when something hinders you from coming close to Jesus or from bringing someone to Him, do not just stare at the closed door. Look with faith and humility for another way, and pray for those who cannot come on their own.
exp.13:16:
He says that when the time for the supper came, the master of the house sent his servant to tell the guests who had been invited that they could now come, because everything was ready. The word "ready" means prepared. The guests are the people who had been invited.

Jesus speaks in the house of a Pharisee, during a meal. Someone remarked how blessed it would be to eat in the kingdom of God, and Jesus answered with this parable. Many interpret that the banquet represents God's invitation, and that the guests who had already been notified were the people who were expected to respond. The verses that follow show that they began to make excuses.

For today: God's invitation is kind and real, but it calls for a response. Today we can ask ourselves what occupations, even good ones, keep us from drawing near to Him. Let us accept His call without putting it off.
exp.8:11:
What it says: The day was already drawing to a close, and the twelve disciples ask Jesus to send the crowd away. They wanted the people to go into the villages and the countryside around them to find places to spend the night and get food. The disciples remind him that they are in a deserted place, that is, a remote spot with no resources.

Context: The twelve apostles are speaking, having just returned from their mission. Jesus had withdrawn with them to rest, but the crowd followed him, and he welcomed them, taught them, and healed the sick. The disciples see a practical problem and propose a sensible solution, but Jesus will answer them: "You give them something to eat."

For today: It is good to see real needs and to plan with common sense, but we must not forget that Jesus can act beyond our calculations. Before saying "there is no way," let us present what little we have and trust him.
exp.2:6:
What it says: John the Baptist speaks to the crowds who were coming to be baptized by him. He addresses them with harsh words: "O generation of vipers," meaning people like poisonous snakes. He asks who warned them that they could escape the wrath to come, that is, God's judgment.

Context: The speaker is John, the prophet who prepared the way of the Lord, as Isaiah foretold in the passage before. His baptism was a sign of repentance. John suspects that many were coming out of habit or fear, without a real change of heart. That is why he asks them for fruits of repentance and warns that being descendants of Abraham is not enough.

For today: Performing a religious practice is not enough, nor is belonging to a family or church. Ask God to show you one concrete attitude you should change this week, and take a visible step toward it.
exp.22:20:
The text says that the crowd shouted again and again that Jesus should be crucified. "They cried out again" means they shouted once more. To crucify him means to nail him to a cross, a form of Roman execution.

Pilate, the Roman governor, wanted to release Jesus because he found no fault in him. But the people, encouraged by the chief priests (the religious leaders), demanded instead that Barabbas be set free, a prisoner accused of rebellion and murder. Pilate tried to reason with them, but their shouting grew louder. The passage shows the pressure of the crowd and the weakness of Pilate.

For today: do not let yourself be swept along by group pressure. Before repeating what everyone says, stop, think, and ask what is right before God. Ask Him for the courage to do what is right even when you are in the minority.
exp.3:41:
At daybreak Jesus left the town and went off to a lonely place. The people searched for him until they found him, and they tried to hold him so that he would not leave them.

The phrase "they tried to hold him" in the verse above describes what the explanation calls people trying to keep him from leaving.

Luke tells what happened in Capernaum after a night of healings and deliverances. Jesus does not speak in this verse, but what follows shows his reason: he had to proclaim the kingdom of God in other towns as well. Luke does not say what Jesus did in the deserted place, though in other passages he is seen praying alone.

After days full of crowds and work, Jesus looked for a moment of solitude. Today we too can set aside a quiet time to be with God, and so remember why he has called us, instead of letting only what is urgent guide us.
exp.1:8:
This verse tells that, suddenly, an angel of the Lord appeared before the shepherds. The glory of the Lord, the brilliant light of God, surrounded them with a huge brightness. They were filled with great fear. The words "lo" and "came upon them" are old-fashioned ways of saying "look!" or "suddenly," as in "behold," pointing the reader's attention to what happens next.

Luke narrates what happened on the night of Jesus' birth. The shepherds were tending their flocks, a humble and little-valued job. Even so, God gave them the news first. Here it is not a person speaking; it is the narrator, Luke, describing the scene. The angel will speak in the following verse.

For today: when God draws near, we are sometimes frightened by what we do not understand. But his arrival brings good news. We can receive him with confidence, knowing that he seeks us even in the ordinary and simple moments of life.
exp.0:6:
It says that Zechariah and Elisabeth had no children. Elisabeth was barren, meaning she could not bear children, and the two of them were already well stricken in years, an old-fashioned way of saying that they were elderly.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks, wanting to tell in order what God did. He has just said that this couple was righteous and blameless. That is why this verse is surprising: they were faithful, yet they lived with a great sorrow. In that culture, having no children usually brought sadness and shame. Luke sets the stage to show that God can act where there seems to be no hope left.

For today: being faithful to God does not always remove losses or long waiting. If you are waiting for something, keep serving God with simplicity, as Zechariah did in the temple, and hand your waiting over to him. He has not forgotten you.
exp.5:7:
Luke 6:8 says that Jesus knew what the scribes and Pharisees were thinking. Without hiding or avoiding the conflict, he asked the man with the withered hand to rise and stand in the midst of everyone. The man got up and stood there, in plain view of all.

The narrator here is Luke. It was the Sabbath, in a synagogue, and the religious leaders were watching Jesus closely to see whether he would heal so they could accuse him. Jesus did not act in secret but openly, and he placed this man's need at the center.

For today: God sees what is in the heart, and people in need matter more than our rules or appearances. Ask yourself who near you needs help, and do not let the fear of criticism keep you from doing good.
exp.22:42:
Jesus answers the man who asked him to remember him. He solemnly assures him that, on that very day, he would be with Him in paradise. The word "paradise" speaks of a place of rest and of God's presence. There are differing views on how the sentence is punctuated in the original text, but most understand it this way: the promise is for "today."

Jesus speaks from the cross, while dying beside two criminals. One of them mocked him, but this other man acknowledged his own guilt, defended Jesus' innocence, and asked for a place in his kingdom. He had no works to offer, only trust.

For today: you do not need a perfect life to come to Jesus. You can come with sincerity, recognize your need, and trust in Him. His grace reaches even to the last moment.
exp.7:9:
Jesus tells his disciples that God has given them the ability to understand the secrets of the kingdom of God, that is, truths that God reveals and that cannot be discovered by human intelligence alone. To the others he speaks in parables, so that they look but do not see, and hear but do not understand.

Jesus has just told the parable of the sower, and the disciples ask him to explain it. In this answer he quotes the prophet Isaiah, who described a people with hardened hearts. Scholars debate whether the parables are meant to hide the truth or to invite people to seek it; in any case, the explanation that follows shows that Jesus does want to be understood by those who come to him with their questions.

Today we can imitate the disciples: approach Jesus with humility, ask him questions, and ask him to open our understanding when we read the Bible.
exp.20:14:
Jesus promises that he himself will give his followers words and understanding to speak when they are accused. Those who oppose them will not be able to resist or contradict what they say.

Jesus speaks to his disciples in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He warns them that they will be persecuted, brought before authorities, and even betrayed by their own family. For this reason he tells them not to worry in advance about preparing their defense: those moments will become an opportunity for testimony. Some understand the promise to refer mainly to those situations of trial, not to mean that every believer will always win every argument.

For today: when you are called to explain your faith under pressure, do not be paralyzed by fear. Pray, trust that God is with you, and speak with simplicity, truth, and gentleness.
exp.1:25:
This verse says that God, through the Holy Spirit, had made known to Simeon that he would not die before he had seen the Lord's Christ. "Christ" means "the Anointed One," that is, the promised Messiah. "Had received an answer" indicates that Simeon received a revelation from God; the Bible does not explain how he received it.

The one who tells the story is Luke. He speaks of Simeon, a righteous and devout man, who was waiting for the "consolation of Israel," that is, the coming of the Savior. This promise prepares the moment when he recognizes Jesus as a baby in the temple, when Mary and Joseph present him.

For today: Simeon trusted God's promise and waited in faith, without knowing how long it would take. We can learn to wait on God with patience, staying attentive and close to Him, sure that He keeps what He says.
exp.10:52:
After Jesus spoke those hard words, the scribes and the Pharisees became very hostile toward him. The phrase about pressing him hard means pressing him with force, harassing him. To "provoke" him here means trying to get him to speak so that he would make a mistake. They wanted him to say many things without thinking.

Jesus had just eaten at the house of a Pharisee, and there he denounced the hypocrisy of the teachers of the law. He told them that they had taken away the key to knowledge: they did not enter in themselves, and they kept others from entering. Instead of admitting their error, they grew angry. The verse that follows shows that they were looking for something he said that they could use to accuse him.

For today: when a word of God makes us uncomfortable, let us not become defensive or look for ways to silence it. Instead, let us humbly ask ourselves: "Lord, what do you want to correct in me?"
exp.22:44:
While Jesus was on the cross, the sun stopped giving its light, and the veil of the temple was torn in two. "Was darkened" means it became dark. The veil was a large, thick curtain inside the temple. "In the midst" means it was split down the center.

Luke, the narrator, tells what happened just before the death of Jesus. Darkness covered the land from noon until three in the afternoon. Many understand that the veil separated the most holy place from the rest of the temple, and that its tearing shows that the way to God is opened through the death of Jesus. Scholars do not explain the darkness in only one way.

For today: you can come near to God with confidence, without fear or complications. Today, speak to Him sincerely, sure that Jesus opened that way.
exp.15:7:
The master praised the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly, even though he had been dishonest. The word "wisely" in the verse means acting with practical intelligence and foresight. "The children of this world" are people who live for this present age, and "in their generation" refers to how they deal with those of their own kind. Jesus says that people of the world are often more skillful at handling their affairs than the children of light, that is, believers, are at handling theirs.

Jesus tells this parable to his disciples. A manager, about to be dismissed, reduced the debts owed to his master by the debtors in order to win friends for himself. Jesus does not approve of the dishonesty; he highlights the man's foresight about his future. Some scholars understand this in different ways, but the central point is the wisdom of preparing ahead.

Today: if people put so much effort into their earthly future, we can use our money and time wisely to help others and serve God, keeping eternal things in mind.
exp.23:29:
This verse tells how Jesus, already seated at the table with two of his disciples, took the bread, gave thanks to God, broke it, and handed it to them. "Blessed" here means that he gave thanks or asked God's blessing over the food. "It came to pass" means "it happened."

It is part of the account of the road to Emmaus, written by Luke. After the resurrection, Jesus walked with two sad disciples, but they did not recognize him. They invited him to stay, and he, though he was the guest, acted as the host. When he broke the bread, their eyes were opened. Some think they recognized him by that familiar gesture; the text does not explain exactly how it happened.

For today: make your meals a time of gratitude and attention to Jesus. Invite him to stay with you, and remember that he can be present in everyday life.
exp.6:19:
The two messengers came to Jesus and repeated John the Baptist's question: "Are you the one who was to come, or should we look for another?" In this verse, the word "should come" refers to the promised Messiah.

John was in prison. He had announced Jesus boldly, but now he had questions. Some think he was doubting; others think he wanted to confirm things or encourage his disciples. The Bible does not make it clear. Jesus did not rebuke him: he answered with deeds, healing many and reminding them of what the prophets had foretold.

When God does not act the way we expect, we can bring our questions to him honestly. Asking Jesus sincerely is not a lack of faith; it is drawing near to him in search of answers. He knows how to respond with patience and truth.
exp.16:5:
Jesus says that a very small faith, like a grain of mustard seed (a tiny seed), can accomplish things that seem impossible. A sycamine tree is a large tree with deep roots. "Be thou plucked up by the root" means "be uprooted," and "it should obey you" means the tree would do as they said.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He had just taught them to forgive up to seven times a day, and they, feeling that this was very hard, asked him: "Increase our faith." He answers that the point is not to have a great amount of faith, but to truly trust in God. Many understand the image as a figure of speech, not as an instruction to move trees.

For today: when forgiving or obeying is hard for you, do not wait to feel strong. Take a small step of trust in God, and He can work through that step.
exp.11:44:
This verse speaks of a servant in charge of the household who thinks, "My lord is taking his time coming back." Because of this, he begins to mistreat the other menservants and maidservants, and he devotes himself to eating, drinking, and getting drunk. "Getting drunk" means becoming intoxicated. "Beat" here means to strike or mistreat.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, and also to the crowd around him. He teaches them to be ready for his return, using the parable of a manager. Peter had asked who the parable was addressed to. The faithful servant is rewarded, but the one who abuses his position and lives without thinking about being held accountable will be judged.

For today: do not use the wait as an excuse to live carelessly. Treat with respect and justice those who are under your care, and live each day as someone who knows that one day they will give an account to God.
exp.21:56:
Peter answers a servant girl who recognizes him as a follower of Jesus. He says, "Woman, I know him not." Peter denied it, meaning he rejected or disowned something that was true. Here, "know" speaks of having a close relationship, not merely knowing who someone is.

Jesus had just been arrested and taken to the house of the high priest. Peter followed at a distance and sat down by the fire, among hostile people. He speaks out of fear, because being identified as a disciple could put him in danger. This is the first of three denials that Jesus had already foretold to him.

For today: all of us can stay silent or hide our faith when we are afraid or under pressure. If you fail, remember that Peter fell, but Jesus sought him out afterward and restored him. Ask God for courage, and return to Him with humility when you go wrong.
exp.22:15:
Pilate says he is going to let Jesus go, but only after "chastising" him. The word "chastised" here refers to having him whipped, that is, beaten with a lash. Pilate offers this as a kind of middle-ground solution.

Pilate, the Roman governor, is speaking before the chief priests and the people. He had already said that he found no fault in Jesus, and that Herod had not either. Even so, he proposes a punishment to calm the crowd. Many readers notice the contradiction: he declares Jesus innocent and yet wants to have him whipped. The leaders and the people are not satisfied and ask for Barabbas.

For today: sometimes we know what is right, but we give in out of fear of the pressure from others. Let us ask God for the courage to defend the truth firmly and not bargain away what we know to be correct.
exp.18:40:
He says that Jesus, as he drew near to Jerusalem and saw the city, wept over it. The word "wept" here indicates loud crying with deep grief, not just a few tears. "As he drew near" means "when he came close."

Luke tells this right after Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, when his disciples were praising him as king. Some of the Pharisees wanted him to silence them, but Jesus kept on his way. Now, seeing the city, he grieves that many do not recognize what brings peace. Then he announces that hard days will come upon it. Many understand this as a reference to the destruction of Jerusalem years later.

For today: God does not look coldly on those who turn away from him, but with sorrow and love. We can ask him for a tender heart, one that prays and weeps for the people around us, instead of judging them harshly.
exp.21:70:
Here the Jewish religious leaders say they no longer need any more witnesses. A "testimony" means a declaration or proof. They take Jesus' words as a confession and believe they already have enough reason to condemn him.

Jesus is standing before the Sanhedrin, the council of Jewish leaders. He had just said that the Son of Man would sit at the right hand (the place of honor) of the power of God. When they asked him whether he was the Son of God, he answered: "You say that I am." They understood that he was claiming to be the Messiah, and they charged him with blasphemy. Afterward they brought him before Pilate.

When we hear something that makes us uncomfortable, we can close our hearts and make up our minds in advance. Let us ask God for humility to listen to Jesus sincerely and to let his words examine us, rather than using them only to confirm what we already think.
exp.16:27:
Here Jesus says that in the days of Lot people lived as usual: they ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and built. None of those activities is evil in itself.

Jesus speaks to his disciples about the coming of the Son of Man, that is, himself. He compares that time with the time of Noah: life went on in its routine, without thinking about judgment, until it came suddenly. Lot left Sodom and that same day judgment fell. Christians understand the details of when and how his return will happen in different ways, but the emphasis here is on being watchful.

For today: take care of your daily tasks, but do not let them absorb you completely. Set aside time to pray, read the Bible and live with your eyes on God, ready to meet him at any moment.
exp.3:37:
He left the synagogue and went to the house of Simon, who would later be called Peter. There, Simon's mother-in-law was very sick with a high fever. Then the people of the house begged him to help her; they asked Jesus to help her.

Luke is the one who tells this. Jesus had just driven out an unclean spirit in the synagogue, and the people were amazed at his authority. Now that same authority comes into a home. Then Jesus rebukes the fever, she recovers and begins to serve them. After that, when evening comes, many more sick people are brought to Him.

For today: do not hesitate to bring to Jesus in prayer the needs of your family and your friends. He cares about the troubles of your home, not only the affairs of the church.
exp.2:31:
This verse is part of a list of Jesus' ancestors. It goes backward in time: it names David, son of Jesse; Jesse, son of Obed; Obed, son of Boaz; Boaz, son of Salmon; and Salmon, son of Naasson.

Luke, the author of the Gospel, presents this genealogy right after Jesus' baptism. It is not a speech but a historical record. It shows that Jesus belongs to the family of David and of Judah, as God's promises had announced. Luke goes all the way back to Adam, and in this way he highlights that Jesus brings salvation for all of humanity. Scholars explain the differences with Matthew's list in several ways.

God works through generations and through ordinary people. Your faith and your faithfulness today can also touch those who come after you.
exp.3:10:
What it says: The devil quotes a biblical promise (Psalm 91:11-12). He says the angels will bear Jesus up in their hands, so that he will not dash his foot against a stone. The temple's high edge is the place from which the devil wants Jesus to throw himself.

Context: The devil speaks during Jesus' temptation in the desert. He wants Jesus to test God by throwing himself down from a high place. He uses Scripture, but applies it wrongly, because the promise is for the one who trusts God, not for the one who puts God to the test. Jesus answers with another text: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God."

For today: Trusting God does not mean demanding signs or taking senseless risks. Before applying a verse, read the whole context and ask whether it honors God. We can trust his care and, at the same time, act with wisdom and obedience.
exp.18:2:
It says that Zacchaeus wanted to see who Jesus was. The word "sought" means that he made an effort, he tried. But he could not see him, because there was a large crowd around and he was short in stature.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. Jesus was passing through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem. Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector, a collector of taxes for Rome, and he was rich. Many people saw them as corrupt and as traitors. Although it does not explain why he wanted to see Jesus, the text shows his sincere interest. The story continues with Jesus calling him by name.

For today: if you truly want to draw near to Jesus, do not let obstacles stop you, whether they are crowds, shame, your past, or your own limitations. Take one concrete step, even if it seems uncomfortable. God responds to those who seek him with sincerity.
exp.7:36:
The whole crowd from the region of the Gadarenes asked Jesus to leave them, because they were overcome with great fear. Jesus did not argue. He got into the boat and went back.

Luke is the one telling the story. Jesus had just freed a man who had been tormented by demons, and the people found him sitting there, clothed and in his right mind. They had also lost a herd of pigs, according to the account. Their reaction was fear, not joy. Jesus respected their request, but he left the healed man behind among them as a witness.

For today: sometimes the power of God unsettles us because it changes what we take for granted. Let us ask him to give us the courage to receive his changes, rather than pushing him away, and to tell what he has done.
exp.11:32:
Jesus says: "Sell what you have and give to the poor." "Alms" means help given to people in need. The "bags that do not wear out" are like purses that never run out of money. A "moth" is the insect that eats away at clothing. He is speaking of a treasure in heaven that cannot be lost or stolen.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, whom he calls a "little flock." He has just told them not to worry about food or clothing, because the Father will give them the kingdom. Since they should not live anxious lives, they are free to be generous. He will go on to say that the heart follows the treasure. Some believe this is a literal command for everyone; others understand it as a call to let go of attachment to money.

Today, ask God what you can share. Perhaps it is helping someone with a specific need this week, trusting that He cares for you.
exp.18:17:
This verse tells us that the second servant came and said to his lord that the pound he had received had now gained five more pounds. A pound was a considerable amount of money, about several months' wages for a worker.

Jesus tells this parable as he is on the way to Jerusalem. A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and leaves a pound to each servant to put to work. When he returns, he calls them to account. The first servant earned ten and the second five. Both receive authority over cities according to their faithfulness. It is interesting that neither earns the same amount, and yet the lord values their effort.

For today: God does not ask us for the same results as others, but for faithfulness with what he has given us. Ask yourself what you have at hand, such as time, abilities, or resources, and take one concrete step this week to use it in love in the service of others.
exp.23:5:
He is not here; he has risen. The two men in shining clothes ask the women to remember what Jesus told them while he was still in Galilee. The verse's wording calls for remembering, not for something new.

The two speakers are the men standing beside the women who went to the tomb early on Sunday. Many understand them to be angels, although Luke simply describes them as men. The women were frightened and confused at finding the tomb empty. The men remind them that Jesus had announced his death and resurrection, and the next verse says that they remembered.

For today: when you have doubts or fear, return to the promises of Jesus. Read his Word and remember what he has already said. Faith grows when we remember that he keeps what he promises.
exp.10:19:
Jesus says that he drives out demons "by the finger of God," that is, by the power of God. "Finger" is a way of speaking about God's direct action. The words "I cast out" mean "I drive out." If that is so, then "surely" the kingdom of God "has come upon you," that is, it is already present among them.

Jesus speaks to a crowd. Some accused him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of the demons. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, and reminds them that their own followers also drove out demons. Then he speaks of a stronger man who overcomes the strong man who is armed, and many understand this as a picture of his victory over evil. Here "the finger of God" also recalls Exodus 8:19.

Today we can trust that Christ has authority over whatever oppresses us. Even so, it is fitting to acknowledge his work with humility and not to close our hearts to it.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that some people were speaking about the temple in Jerusalem and admiring how beautiful it was, adorned with fine stones and with "gifts," that is, offerings and presents that people had dedicated to God. Then Jesus began to answer them.

Jesus is in the temple, and he has just praised the poor widow who gave everything she had. Now some are focused on the beauty of the building. Jesus will use that moment to tell them that all of it will be destroyed, and so he leads them to think about what truly lasts.

For today: it is easy to admire what looks grand and beautiful. Today let us ask God to teach us to value what he values: a sincere and devoted heart, more than outward appearances.
exp.10:47:
Jesus tells them that by their own actions they show they agree with what their ancestors did. Those ancestors killed the prophets, and now these teachers of the law are building tombs for them.

Jesus speaks in the house of a Pharisee, where he has been invited to eat, and he addresses the experts in the law. He rebukes them because they honor the dead prophets with monuments, yet they reject God's message in their own time. Many understand that they were rejecting Jesus himself, the last great messenger.

For today: it is easy to admire the heroes of faith from the past and, at the same time, to resist what God tells us now through his Word. Let us ask him for a humble heart that obeys, not only one that honors.
exp.9:40:
Jesus calls Martha twice by her name, which shows affection, not anger. He tells her that she is "careful," that is, full of worries, and "troubled," restless and agitated by "many things" she has to do.

Jesus is in the house of Martha and Mary. Martha was busy preparing everything to take care of her guests, while Mary sat down to listen to Jesus.
