Martha, tired, complains and asks Jesus to tell Mary to help her. Jesus responds with tenderness: he does not correct her service, but her anxiety and her divided heart.

Serving is good, but we can lose our peace when we fill ourselves with tasks. Today, before you begin your day, find a few quiet minutes to listen to Jesus in his Word and to pray. From there, your service will be more serene.
exp.7:0:
Luke says that Jesus, after the events described before, went through cities and villages. He went from place to place preaching and announcing the good news of the kingdom of God. The twelve disciples, the apostles, went with him and stayed close to him.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking, not Jesus. He wants to show what Jesus' ministry in Galilee was like: steady, moving from town to town, not confined to one place. The verses that follow add that some women who had been healed also traveled with him and helped him with their own resources. So we see a varied group of followers.

For today: Jesus did not wait for people to come to him; he went out to find them. We can ask ourselves to whom I can bring a word of hope this week, in my home, my work, or my neighborhood, and do it with simplicity and love.
exp.13:18:
A man here says he has bought five yoke of oxen, that is, five pairs of animals for plowing. He says he is going to prove them and asks to be "have me excused," that is, to be excused from attending. "Prepared" means ready, and "I go to prove them" means he is going to see whether they work well.

Jesus is telling this parable while eating in the house of a Pharisee. A man prepares a great supper and invites many, but all of them make excuses. Jesus shows that many turn down God's invitation to his kingdom, not because they cannot come, but because they put other things first. The purchase had already been made, so the testing could wait.

For today: ask yourself which good things, such as work or business, are taking the place that belongs to God. Respond today to his invitation.
exp.1:38:
The explanation says that Joseph and Mary did everything the law of Moses required after Jesus was born, such as the presentation in the temple and the offering. Then they went back to Nazareth, in Galilee, where they lived.

The one who speaks is Luke, the narrator. He has just told of Jesus being presented in the temple, with Simeon and the prophetess Anna. This verse closes that scene and sets up what follows: Jesus grows up in Nazareth. Luke does not give the details of that time here, and Matthew tells other events, such as the journey to Egypt. Scholars explain in different ways how the two accounts fit together.

For today: God works in the simple and the everyday. Faithfully doing what we know God asks of us, even when it seems small, is a good way to live.
exp.23:38:
Jesus invites his disciples to look at his hands and his feet, and to touch him, so that they will realize it is really himself. He tells them that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, and that they can see that he does. The sentence about the old wording is removed, since the reader's verse does not contain those words.

Jesus speaks after his resurrection, when he appears to his disciples who are gathered together. They were frightened and thought they were seeing a ghost. He shows them the marks of the crucifixion to calm their fear and to confirm that his resurrection is real and bodily. Right after this, he asks for something to eat, as one more proof.

For today: the Christian faith rests not on vague ideas but on a real event. When you doubt or feel afraid, bring your questions to Jesus with sincerity; he is patient and knows how to give us reasons to trust him.
exp.18:30:
Jesus tells two disciples what to say if anyone asks why they are untying the colt, the young donkey. They are to answer, "Because the Lord hath need of him." In other words, the Lord requires it, and that is reason enough.

Jesus speaks near Bethphage and Bethany, as he draws close to Jerusalem. He is about to enter the city riding a colt that no one had ever used before. His instructions are carried out just as he gave them. Some see in this his special knowledge of what was going to happen; others think he may have arranged it beforehand. The text does not make this clear. What it does show is that Jesus acts with purpose and authority.

For today: what we have, whether time, talent, or resources, can be useful to God. If he asks for it, we can give it with confidence, knowing that he knows what he is doing.
exp.1:21:
It says that when the days of purification required by the law of Moses were over, Mary and Joseph took the child Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to God. The phrase "according to" is used here in place of the wording "conforme á," and the expression "to present him" stands in for the wording "presentarle," which means presenting him. The law required this period after childbirth (Leviticus 12).

The speaker is Luke, the narrator. He wants to show that Jesus was born into a family that obeyed God's law. The verses that follow explain that every firstborn son belonged to the Lord and that an offering had to be given. That the offering was a pair of turtledoves or young pigeons suggests a family of modest means.

For today: God draws near with humility and obedience. We can offer him our family, our children and our plans, and obey him in the simple things of each day.
exp.14:17:
This verse says that the younger son makes a decision: he will get up, go to his father, and confess his guilt. The old spellings "é" and "á" are now written "and" and "to." The phrase "sinned against heaven" means against God, since "heaven" was a respectful way of naming him. It also acknowledges that he offended his father.

The younger son is the speaker, within the parable Jesus tells. He had spent his inheritance and ended up looking after pigs, going hungry. When he came to his senses, that is, when he recognized his real situation, he remembered how good life was in his father's house and decided to go back. His plan is to ask to be treated like a hired servant.

For today: when we fail, there is no need to hide it or wait until we feel better. We can honestly acknowledge our wrong before God and take the step of returning. The rest of the parable shows that the Father receives us with compassion.
exp.4:17:
Here it says that some men arrived carrying a paralyzed friend on a mat. The word "bed" means a bed or stretcher, and "bring him in" means to get him inside the house. Their goal was to place the sick man in front of Jesus.

Here Luke speaks, recounting what happened. Jesus was teaching in a house full of people, including Pharisees and teachers of the law who had come from many places. Luke says that the power of the Lord was present there to heal. These men did not give up because of the crowd. Afterward, Jesus saw their faith and forgave the paralyzed man's sins.

For today: when someone you love cannot reach Jesus on their own, you can bring them near through your prayer, your company, and your concrete help. Do not be discouraged if there are obstacles; persistent faith full of love matters to God.
exp.5:30:
This verse tells us to treat others the way we would like to be treated ourselves. The phrase "as ye would that men should do to you" is older English for "as you would want people to do to you," and "do ye also to them likewise" means "do the same for them." It is a simple rule: think about what you hope to receive, and give it to others first.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and to a crowd in what is called the Sermon on the Plain. Just before this, he taught them to love their enemies and to give without demanding anything in return. Afterward he makes clear that loving only those who love us is nothing extraordinary, since even sinners do that. This saying ties together everything that came before.

For today: before answering someone with anger or indifference, stop and ask yourself how you would want to be treated in their place. Then act with that same kindness, even if the other person does not deserve it.
exp.23:9:
This verse names the women who went to the tomb and brought the news to the apostles: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and others who were with them. "The rest" refers to other women in the group.

Luke is narrating the morning of the resurrection. The women had heard the angels, who reminded them of Jesus' words about his death and resurrection. Then they ran to tell the eleven disciples. Luke tells us that the apostles considered their words to be nonsense. Even so, Peter went to see the tomb. Luke gives their names, and that shows they were real witnesses.

Today, God can use ordinary people, whom many overlook, to carry good news. If you have experienced the goodness of God, tell it with humility, even if some doubt it. And if someone shares their faith with you, listen to them with respect before you reject it.
exp.0:55:
Luke tells us that Mary stayed with her cousin Elizabeth for about three months and then returned to her own home. The verse's wording "abode with her" is the key point here, meaning she lived with Elizabeth during that time. This is a simple verse that closes Mary's visit.

Here the narrator is Luke. Just before this, Mary had sung her song of praise to God (the Magnificat). She had visited Elizabeth, who was pregnant with John the Baptist. Many think Mary stayed with her until near the birth, since the next verse speaks of the birth, although the text does not say whether she was present. Luke only notes the approximate time and her return home.

For today: accompanying someone during an important moment is a real way of serving. Mary, young and with an enormous promise from God, spent months supporting her cousin. Today we can do the same through a visit, a practical help, or constant prayer for someone who needs us.
exp.13:7:
Jesus says that if someone invites you to a wedding, you should not sit down in the place of highest honor at the table. The host may have also invited someone more honorable than you. A wedding here simply means a wedding feast.

Jesus is in the house of a prominent Pharisee on the Sabbath, and he watches how the guests choose the best seats. Then he tells them a parable. Many understand that he is speaking not only about good manners, but about the attitude of the heart and how God sees pride and humility.

For today: before seeking recognition, applause, or a place of prominence, practice humility. At work, at church, or in your family, serve without demanding the first place, and trust that God knows how to honor whom he chooses, in his own time.
exp.1:49:
This verse says that Mary and Joseph did not understand what Jesus said to them. It refers to his words about being in his Father's affairs, meaning the things of God his Father, or in his house (the temple). Both ways of understanding it are possible.

Jesus was twelve years old, and his parents had searched for him anxiously for three days. They found him in the temple, and his mother spoke to him with pain. Luke notes that they did not understand, even though they already knew Jesus was special. Then Jesus went back with them and obeyed them, while Mary kept all these things in her heart.

For today: we will not always understand what God does or says. We can do as Mary did: not dismiss what we do not understand, but keep it humbly, go on obeying, and trust that God will make it clear in time.

sum.11: In Luke 12, Jesus teaches his disciples to avoid hypocrisy, not to fear people because God cares for them, and to confess him boldly. He warns them against greed with the parable of the foolish rich man, invites them to trust the Father instead of worrying, and to always be ready for his coming.
sum.8: Jesus sends his twelve disciples out to preach and heal, feeds five thousand people with five loaves of bread and two fish, and Peter recognizes him as God's Christ. Then Jesus announces his coming death and resurrection, is transfigured on the mountain, and teaches that following him requires denying oneself, humility, and total surrender.
sum.20: Jesus praises a poor widow who gave everything she had, more than the rich people who gave out of their surplus. Then he announces the destruction of the temple and warns about deception, persecution, and signs, and about his coming in glory. He asks his followers to stay alert, pray, and not let themselves be weighed down by the worries of this life.
sum.10: Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray with the Lord's Prayer, and he encourages them to keep asking, searching, and knocking, because the heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. He then answers those who doubt him, warns about the inner light, and sharply rebukes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and teachers of the law, who begin to watch him closely.
sum.21: At Passover, Judas agrees to hand Jesus over. Jesus shares the Last Supper with his disciples, speaking about the new covenant in his blood and about humble service. He prays in anguish on the Mount of Olives, is arrested, Peter denies him three times and weeps, and the leaders question him.
sum.3: Jesus, filled with the Spirit, resists the devil's temptations in the desert by quoting God's Word. Then he announces in Nazareth that the promises of Isaiah are fulfilled in him, but they reject him and try to throw him off a cliff. In Capernaum he teaches with authority, frees a man from a demon, heals the sick, and keeps preaching the kingdom of God.
sum.1: Jesus is born in Bethlehem, and an angel announces to some shepherds that the Savior has been born. They go, see him, and praise God. Afterward, Simeon and Anna recognize in the child the salvation that had been promised. At age twelve, Jesus is in the temple, saying he must be about his Father's business, and then he returns to Nazareth, obedient and growing in wisdom.
sum.17: Jesus teaches people to always pray and not lose heart, using the parable of the persistent widow, and he teaches humility through the parable of the proud Pharisee and the tax collector who asks for mercy. He then blesses the little children, tells the rich young man that he still lacks giving up his wealth to follow him, announces his death and resurrection, and heals a blind man who cried out in faith.
sum.19: In the temple, the religious leaders ask Jesus what authority he has to act as he does, and he leaves them without an answer with a question about John the Baptist. Then he tells the parable of the wicked tenants, and after that he answers questions about paying taxes to Caesar and about the resurrection. At the end, he warns against proud and abusive scribes.
sum.2: John the Baptist preaches in the desert that people should repent and bear fruit of a changed life, such as sharing and being fair, and he announces that someone more powerful than him is coming. Herod imprisons him. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father says, "You are my beloved Son." Then his genealogy is presented, going back to Adam and God.
sum.18: Jesus passes through Jericho and changes the life of Zacchaeus, a wealthy tax collector, who repents and makes right what he had done wrong. Then he tells the parable of the minas about being faithful while the king is away. He enters Jerusalem as king, weeps over the city, and cleanses the temple.
sum.7: Jesus teaches with the parable of the sower that God's word bears fruit in those who receive it with a good and patient heart. Then he shows his power: he calms the storm, frees the man tormented by demons, heals a sick woman, and restores life to Jairus's daughter. All of it invites us to trust in him.
sum.5: In Luke 6, Jesus teaches that he is Lord of the Sabbath and heals a man with a withered hand, though the Pharisees become angry. Then he chooses twelve apostles and teaches about the blessings, love for enemies, mercy, and not judging others. He ends by saying that whoever hears his words and obeys them builds on the rock.
sum.13: Jesus heals a sick man on the Sabbath and teaches people to be humble and to invite the poor to their meals. He tells the parable of the great banquet, in which the people who were invited make excuses, so others are brought in to take their place. He then explains the cost of following him: putting him first, carrying the cross, and giving up everything.
sum.16: Jesus teaches his disciples not to cause others to stumble, to forgive always, and to serve with humility. He heals ten people with leprosy, but only one of them, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks. Then he explains that the kingdom of God is already among them, and he warns that his final coming will be sudden, as it was in the days of Noah and Lot.
sum.9: Jesus sends seventy disciples out in pairs to announce the kingdom of God, and they return full of joy. He then tells the parable of the Good Samaritan to teach that a neighbor is the one who shows mercy. Finally, at the home of Martha and Mary, he says that sitting down to listen to his word is what matters most.
sum.23: Some women find the tomb empty, and angels tell them that Jesus has risen, though the apostles do not believe them. Jesus walks with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, explains the Scriptures to them, and makes himself known to them when he breaks the bread. Later he appears to all of them, shows them his body, sends them out to preach, and ascends to heaven.
sum.6: In Luke 7, Jesus heals the servant of a centurion who trusted in his word, and he raises the son of a widow in Nain. Then he answers the doubt of John the Baptist and praises him. At the end, he forgives a sinful woman who loved him much, and he tells her, "Your faith has saved you."
sum.15: Jesus tells of a manager who, about to lose his position, acts shrewdly to secure his future, and he teaches people to use wealth wisely, because no one can serve both God and money. He then describes how a rich man who ignored the needs around him and a poor man named Lazarus both die, and their fortunes are reversed. He says that people should listen to Moses and the prophets.
sum.12: In Luke 13, Jesus calls people to repentance and tells the parable of the fig tree that bears no fruit, which is given another chance. He heals a bent-over woman on the Sabbath and shows how the kingdom of God grows, like a mustard seed. He teaches people to enter through the narrow door, and he laments that Jerusalem did not want to be gathered by him.
sum.22: Jesus is brought before Pilate and Herod. Although Pilate finds no guilt in him, he gives in to the crowd that demands he be crucified, and he releases Barabbas. On the cross, Jesus forgives those who are executing him, promises paradise to a repentant criminal, and gives up his spirit to the Father. Joseph of Arimathea buries him with respect.
sum.0: An angel tells Zechariah that he and his wife Elizabeth will have a son named John. Because Zechariah doubts this, he is struck mute until the child is born. Then the angel Gabriel tells Mary that she will have Jesus, the Son of the Most High, and she accepts this in faith. Mary visits Elizabeth and sings songs of praise to God. When John is born, Zechariah regains his speech and prophesies.
sum.14: The Pharisees complained that Jesus welcomed sinners, so he told three stories: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a son who left home and then came back. In each one, there is great joy when what was lost is found. In the same way, God rejoices over a sinner who repents, and the father welcomes his son with love.
sum.4: In Luke 5, Jesus calls Peter, James, and John after a miraculous catch of fish, and they leave everything behind to follow him. He heals a man with leprosy and a paralyzed man, and he forgives the sins of the paralyzed man. He calls Levi, eats with sinners, and teaches that he came to call the sick, not the healthy, using examples of new and old.
